# The Movemental Written Work Bundle

*Every article, essay, paper, guide, memo and page of written copy by Movemental, LLC and Joshua Shepherd that exists in retrievable form as of 2026-09-18.*

**60 pieces · roughly 217,789 words · assembled from 35 markdown files, 15 HTML documents, 8 PDFs and 2 artifacts.**

---

## What is and isn't here

**In:** prose written to be read — articles, essays, working papers, memos, playbooks, method documents, strategy narratives, letters, case studies, site copy and client documents.

**Out, and listed in the appendices:** technical specifications, build prompts, repo maps, component inventories and interactive tools (Appendix A); and sixteen documents that are distributed as page images rather than text, so their prose cannot be extracted without OCR (Appendix B). Appendix B is the significant gap — it holds the Field Guides, the four Playbooks, the AI Reality Paper and the signed agreements.

Conversion notes: markdown is reproduced verbatim, with headings demoted two levels so they nest under this structure. HTML is converted to markdown with navigation, scripts and styling stripped. PDFs are text-extracted and reflowed into paragraphs; page breaks appear as horizontal rules, and the letter-spaced display chrome of the original — eyebrow labels, wordmarks, running heads, page numbers — has been dropped, since it extracts as gibberish and carries nothing. Prose-set PDFs come through cleanly. The two decks (Praxis, and the *How it actually works* working deck) are the exception: slide layouts are absolutely positioned, so fragments occasionally land out of order. Check those two against the originals before reusing.

Two pairs overlap deliberately and are both kept: *The Evergreen Engine* exists as both the original Edition One PDF and the generalized markdown rebuild, and *How It Actually Works* exists as both the prose companion and the working deck.

## 1. I asked it about wisdom on the first day

`story-spine-v2.md` · 2,360 words

### I asked it about wisdom on the first day

*Draft 2, rebuilt on the real story. Canonical `/story`. ~1,850 words. First person, plain, no em dashes.*
*Two bracketed items left. The employer is unnamed throughout.*

---

I build AI systems for organizations whose work runs on trust, and I train the people who use them. Here is how that started, because it did not start where people assume.

On November 30, 2022, I was sitting at my desk at a construction chemicals company, where I was the director of marketing. I saw that something called ChatGPT had been released. I opened it that day.

I asked it about the difference between wisdom and information. I have no idea why that was my first question. I expected something like the chat toys from years earlier, a keyword match dressed up as a conversation.

[THE REAL ANSWER GOES HERE, if you can recover it. Placeholder below, marked as reconstructed until you find the original.]

> *Reconstructed, not the original: it said information is data given form and context, the kind of thing that can be transmitted and looked up, while wisdom is different in kind rather than degree. Wisdom is knowing which information matters in a situation and what to do with it. A person can hold a great deal of information and still act unwisely. It said wisdom develops through lived experience rather than study alone.*

Read that now and it is flat. Slightly textbook. The kind of draft you would send back.

In 2022 it stopped me cold. Not because it was deep. Because it was sane, in complete sentences, in answer to a question I had asked in my own words. Nothing had ever done that before.

So I kept asking.

#### Day five

Within a few days I was telling it about myself. Enneagram, personality type, how I think. I wanted to see whether it would hold any of that and answer differently because of it. I started pushing on voice and style.

Then I went and did something that turned out to matter more than any of it.

Ben is my best friend. I know his work, and I know what is hard about it. So I spent about five days doing deep dives on OSHA documentation and training, inside a context window the size of a napkin, so that when I showed him this thing it would already be standing inside his problem instead of next to it.

The intuition was this. Only if I could meet him where he actually worked would he be able to judge whether it was any good. A demo of a clever machine proves nothing. A machine that knows your world is a different claim.

Eight days after launch he came back from vacation and I pulled him into a conference room, which I had never done in all the years I have known him, and I told him the world had changed while he was gone.

He read it. He was impressed. He seemed to miss the entire point.

He did not use AI again for another two years.

#### Where that instinct came from

The going-and-learning-OSHA move is the only part of the first week I would defend as skill, and it did not come from marketing.

Before any of this I did bilingual frontline work with immigrant and Hispanic families in Kansas City, in family services and early childhood and ESL. That is where my Spanish came from. I was called to ministry in 2007. From 2011 to 2022 I founded and led Mission House Network, an intentional community here, and about a hundred young adults came through it over eleven years. I learned digital marketing during those years for a plain reason, which is that I wanted to tell that community's stories and nobody else was going to.

Eleven years of that teaches you one thing above all others. You do not learn what a person needs by studying the category they belong to. You learn it by being in the room with them for a long time, in their language.

That is why my fifth day with a general purpose machine was spent learning occupational safety documentation for a friend. And it is the reason the company I run now is built on context rather than on capability. Capability is the part everyone has. Context is the part that makes it worth trusting.

#### The stack

By early 2023 I believed this thing was going to change content marketing, and that it would land hardest in a business like ours, where the writing is technical and precise and nobody wants to do it.

So I started drafting. Articles about concrete chemicals. And for about a month I walked around that building carrying a stack of them roughly an inch thick, knowing that not one person there had any idea a computer could write now.

I was not worried about getting in trouble. I was worried about something else.

I knew there were two easy readings available. The first was that I had lifted the articles off the internet. The second was that I had gotten distracted by a tech fad. If either one landed, the idea would not just be rejected. The organization would be inoculated against it, and I would have spent the one chance anybody gets.

So I waited for a version of the reveal they could accept, which is the opposite of what I wanted to do. When I finally moved, I told a senior executive I had done some internet research and wanted to know whether the drafts might have any legitimacy as blog posts.

He said they were pretty great.

I showed the president almost as an afterthought. He called it our first breakthrough.

I want to sit on that for a second, because it is the strangest thing in my own story. To get the most advanced work in the building read at all, I had to obscure who wrote it. I now run a company whose entire argument is that authorship has to be visible and checkable. I did not arrive at that from theory.

#### The sandbox

What happened next looked like a demotion and was not one.

I went from director of marketing, running a team, to building everything digital and AI. Off the org chart, into a sandbox. My title got smaller and the work got much larger, and I preferred it. I had trust and a strategy people could see working and could not entirely follow, and I did whatever I thought was right.

I built a content operation. Hand-fed context at first, then Whisper, then the API, then retrieval. Organic traffic went from around fifty thousand visits a year to around a hundred and forty thousand.

It took me three more years to notice that I had built myself a sandbox with real trust and real stakes and no audience watching, and that this is the exact thing I now tell organizations they need before they touch any of it.

#### Three years of showing people

The rest of it I did for free.

First Ben. Then a team from Honeywell. Then a philanthropy group. Then Youthfront. Then movement leaders, including Alan Hirsch and Tim Catchim. All of it free, all of it alongside a full time job.

People ask why. The honest answer has three parts. I had a job that paid better than anything I had ever made. There was no market yet, and trying to charge in 2023 would have cost me most of the chances I got to build. And I do not really think about money. I did not start thinking about it until I decided to start a business.

But the timeline had to be this way, and I only understand that in hindsight. This is a market built on trust, and it is opening now. Three years of building in front of the people who knew me best meant that when it opened, they were the first ones to ask me to build for them.

Here is what those three years actually taught me, and it is not what I went looking for.

People were astonished. People did not adopt.

They would call me a wizard. They would move their schedules to watch me work. They would pass the thing around. And then nothing. Not Ben. Not the smartest published authors I know, after years of watching me do this constantly. Almost nobody.

I had assumed anyone would see it once and understand. I was wrong about that for three years running, in front of a sample size of everyone I know.

For a long time I read that as a failure in people. I do not anymore. It is the fastest spreading technology in history and also the hardest to actually grasp, which is a combination nobody has dealt with before. It looks like a party trick, so you try it, and then it makes a mistake, and some part of you is relieved. Or you sit in front of a blank box and cannot think of what to ask. Or you can, and you do not have the stamina for the back and forth, which is genuinely tiring and looks like nothing from outside.

It was not that people could not. It was that it was too early. It is just starting now.

That result is the reason my company sells a hundred hours of in person training and not a login.

#### What it cost me

By 2025 I was building with agents, running two builds at once, and shipping at a rate I would not have believed a year earlier. I had gone from vibe coding a front end to assuming a full stack app would work the same way.

It does not. I walked straight into it.

A week into building a custom agentic CRM, I gave a demo. It was bad. Not close to working. And I had spent the previous two years teaching that room to expect a mobile app in a week.

I diagnosed it fast, and this is the part I want to state plainly because it is usually told wrong. Within days I went back and said we needed real timelines and real expectations, and we set them. What took months was not figuring out that something was wrong. It was learning back end architecture. Data, type safety, migrations, how an application actually holds and moves information. There was no map for that in 2025. There still barely is.

I delivered the full system in about six weeks against a three month timeline, and it did not matter. The room had already decided in week one.

Two things came out of that.

The first is a rule. I do not test in public anymore. I show it when it works. I watch other capable people hit this same wall now, including my own co-founders, and from outside there is no visible difference between this is hard and this was oversold.

The second is the thing I would not trade. The same day it became clear I had to build a real data chain was the day it became clear I could build one from the prompt level. That idea is under everything I have made since, including the design work.

Sometimes you say you will be back in a week and it turns out to be a longer trip, and you come back with a map nobody had.

#### The Sunday call

Alan and I had a standing call, Sundays at seven, for years. One week I asked Brad to join.

I had built a quick site for it. A hundred potential authors laid out as a network, with the two of them at the origin. You could click any node and see the person, a rough estimate of what a platform could earn them, and what the network came to as a whole. I did not describe the idea. I let them click it.

What I said on that call is close to what the business is now. What I did not know was that it would lead to organizations. I knew it had to lead somewhere.

Alan asked me to build his platform for real, and I thought side project. Then it was Alan and Brad. Then it became clear that building for leaders and building for organizations were the same work, and that leaders come first only because leaders can decide faster. Then Youthfront had grant money and wanted their people trained.

In March 2026 I went full time on Movemental. Brad is CEO, because we sell trust and he is the one who already holds it in the rooms that matter. Alan is the voice the network gathers around. I built the engine, and I own it.

#### What I hold to

**AI does the gathering and the drafting. It never does the discernment, the care, or the human voice.**

You can take that line and use it without ever speaking to me. It settles most of the hard questions on its own.

The rest of it. Every word that goes out under someone's name is theirs. Sources get named. Nothing gets invented. If a claim is not checkable, it does not get made. Where vulnerable people are involved the bar goes up, not down. And nothing gets built for an organization before its people are ready for it, which is why the order is safety, then sandbox, then training, then tech, and never the reverse.

Those are refusals. They cost me work I would otherwise take.

#### Who this is for

If you lead an organization whose work depends on people trusting you, and you are trying to work out what to do about this without either ignoring it or handing it the parts that matter, this is written for you.

I have been at it since the first day, mostly for free, mostly in front of people who were not ready. I am not going to sell you urgency. I already know how that ends.

[Newsletter invitation, one line.]

#### For Alan

Alan Hirsch is a category author. Over twenty-five years he has published more than twenty books, and the frameworks inside them are taught in graduate programs, used by large organizations to train their people, and repeated daily by practitioners who could not tell you where the language came from. [SALES FIGURE, verified, or cut.] His work is in [number] languages.

He did not stop at writing them. He built the organizations that carry the ideas into practice: a training network that began in Australia and now operates across [number] countries, and [100 Movements] and [the Movement Leaders Collective], which convene [number] of the most senior practitioners in the field. [Verify all of this. Cut anything you cannot check.]

That combination is rarer than it sounds. Most people who originate ideas at that scale hand them to somebody else to operationalize, and most people who build institutions are working from someone else's ideas. He did both, for thirty years, and the field he did it in is Christian mission.

If you work somewhere else entirely: he is the person in his field whose vocabulary everyone uses, who also built the places where it gets taught. Some fields have one.

I read his book The Forgotten Ways in 2010, and then spent a decade running an intentional community that taught his material to young adults, about a hundred of them over eleven years. So I came to this having received the work and then taught it for ten years, which is a different kind of knowing than reading.

##### Typing it in by hand

In 2020 the pandemic cancelled the summer internship I was running, and moving it online meant the material had to exist somewhere a group of young adults could actually work through it. [DATE RANGE and ROUGH VOLUME.] Night after night I sat there and typed excerpts from Alan's books into a course platform by hand.

His work was published, edited, printed, bought, and widely read. And the only way to get it in front of twenty people in a usable form was for someone to retype it, one paragraph at a time, for weeks.

That is fragmentation. Not disorganization. The work is intact, finished, and unreachable.

##### Why it takes a system

Here is the thing most people have wrong, and there is no reason they would have it right.

When you have a PDF of a book, it feels like you have the book. So it seems obvious that a computer has it too.

It does not. A PDF is closer to a photograph of a book. The words are marks positioned on a page for a human eye, and nothing in the file says this line is a chapter title and that line is a footnote. Copy a few pages out and you will see it. Page numbers land in the middle of sentences. The running header repeats every thirty lines. Footnote markers detach from the words they belonged to. Two column layouts interleave into nonsense.

That is the best case, where the file has real text in it. A book scanned from a 1994 printing has no text at all, only an image of text.

A talk is worse. Thirty years of speaking exists as audio nobody has written down. To a computer an audio file is a waveform, not words. Until someone transcribes it, that hour does not exist as anything you can search or quote or check.

Then the articles, thirty years of them, a good portion simply gone when an organization folded or a domain lapsed. And about twenty thousand notes accumulated over more than a decade in whatever tool he was using that year.

##### What it costs him

A thirty year body of work turns out to be four or five bodies of work in incompatible forms, none of which can talk to any of the rest.

He cannot search his own work. If Alan wants everywhere he has written about a single idea across thirty years, there is no way to ask. He has to remember. The most complete index of that body of work is one man's recall, and there is no backup.

And he cannot see anyone moving through it. Someone finds an idea in a post, orders a book, sits with it for a year, takes a course, and starts teaching it in their own church. That journey is the point of the work, and it is invisible to him, because the work it runs through is in pieces that do not connect. He knows a book sold. He does not know what it started.

Meanwhile, search the questions he has spent his life answering and you will mostly find other people restating him. Some get it right. Some do not, and the ones who do not are frequently the easier read, so they travel further.

##### What happens when someone asks a machine

For twenty years, a person who wanted to understand his work went and found it. Bought the book, searched the site, asked someone who had read it.

That is not how it works now. Increasingly the first move, and often the only move, is to ask an assistant. Explain this idea. What does he mean by that. Give me the argument in a paragraph.

And it answers. Immediately, fluently, with no source.

The answer is assembled from whatever was reachable, which is the restatements. Posts by people working from a summary, conference notes, somebody's seminary paper, the tidy version that traveled because it was easy to repeat. His own words, sitting in photographs of pages and untranscribed audio and articles on dead sites, were not in the pool at all.

So the reader gets a competent, plausible, confident answer that is nobody's actual position. And nothing about it looks wrong, which is the part that matters. A misquote in print looks like a misquote. A misquote from a machine looks exactly like a correct answer, because everything it produces looks the same.

Multiply that by everyone learning about his work this year and the paraphrase quietly becomes the record.

##### And it runs the other way

The same problem blocks him from using any of this himself.

Ask a general assistant to help think through one of his own frameworks and it returns the secondhand version, because that is all it has. Ask it to draft something in his voice and it produces an imitation assembled from other people's summaries of him. The author gets a worse answer about his own work than a stranger gets about a well documented subject.

That is the trap. The people with the most to contribute are served worst by this technology, because it can only work with what it can reach, and their life's work is the part it cannot reach.

##### Which is true of you as well

Somebody is going to ask a machine about your organization. Probably today.

It will answer, it will not say it is unsure, and it will answer from whatever it could reach. Your website, a few press mentions, whatever anyone else has written about you. Not your case studies, not your evaluations, not the twenty years of thinking that would have made the answer accurate.

You do not get to opt out of that. The only decision available is whether the thing answering has your real work to draw on.

##### What I built

There is a system that answers questions from his own writing. Someone asks in their own words and gets an answer drawn from what he actually wrote, with the source attached. [SPECIFIC: what a citation looks like, and what happens when the material is not there.] If it does not have the material, it says so rather than filling the gap. That one behavior cost more than anything else in the build.

Around it there is a site: his themes, pathways, courses, articles, and library, connected so a person who arrives through one idea can move into the rest instead of hitting a dead end.

[PROOF. A link, a number with a date, a capture.]

The moment you make an archive answerable, you have built something that speaks in a person's name. If it says one thing he would not say, you have not helped him. You have added another confident, fluent, wrong voice to the pile that was the original problem, and it will be more persuasive than the pile because it sounds official.

So the system is organized around a refusal rather than a capability. It only says what he said. It shows you where. When it does not know, it says so.

I could hold that line because I taught this material for ten years. I know which ideas people misunderstand first and which ones do the actual work. That is not devotion, it is knowledge, and it is why the build is any good.

##### What publishing takes

One more loss, and it is structural rather than accidental.

When a book sells, the author sees about a dime of the dollar. That part people know. The part they do not know is that the publisher keeps the reader. The author never learns who bought it or what they did with it. Twenty years of writing, hundreds of thousands of readers, no relationship with a single one of them.

Ninety percent of the money and one hundred percent of the relationship.

Our terms are inverted. [SPECIFIC: the 90/10 split, plainly, and what it covers.] Not generosity. It is the only arrangement consistent with the argument, which is that the work belongs to the person who made it, and so does the relationship with the people it reached.

##### This is not a church problem

An agency has thirty years of strategy decks, research, and post-mortems on a server, findable only by the four people who were in the room. A nonprofit has two decades of stories, evaluations, and donor history spread across a database, a shared drive, an email archive, and the memory of a director about to retire. A seminary has faculty work nobody outside can reach and course material nobody inside can reuse.

In every case the work is done, it is good, it was expensive, and it cannot be reached from where anyone is standing. The organization pays for that twice a year: once when someone rebuilds what already existed, and once when someone leaves with the only copy of how it worked.

Alan's version is unusual only in how public it is.

---

#### What it takes

Doing that for Alan took six months, and most of it was failing at each layer until something held. Here are the layers, because if you have a body of work of your own you should know what you are looking at.

**Getting the words out.** Turning a photograph of a book back into language. The tools for this are all wrong in different ways depending on what you point them at, and the failures are not obvious. The output looks fine. You have to go hunting to find that chapter four lost its last two pages.

**Proving nothing was lost.** The step everyone skips. After a conversion you have a file that looks like a book. You do not know it is the book. Text goes missing quietly, a column drops, a section repeats, nobody notices for a year, and by then it is being quoted to readers as though it were complete. Something has to compare what came out against what went in before anything moves forward.

**Putting the structure back.** The system has to know that this paragraph is in chapter seven of this book, under this heading, and that this note belongs to that sentence. That is what lets a reader be sent to the right page instead of a vague direction.

**Cutting it into pieces, carefully.** To retrieve anything from a large body of work you have to break it up. Too large and the answer arrives buried. Too small and you get a sentence that means the opposite of what it meant in place, because the qualifier was in the previous paragraph. And a fragment on its own does not know where it came from, so it gets presented as a general claim. That is the mechanism by which these systems misquote people. It is not exotic. It is the default. Every piece has to carry its own context.

**The talks.** Transcription at volume, and then the harder half: a transcript is not writing. People speak in false starts and digressions that resolve twenty minutes later. Getting to something usable without smoothing away what was actually said is its own problem.

**Voice.** If you are going to produce language on someone's behalf, even a summary, you have to know how they write. Not their topics. Their rhythm, their moves, the words they would never use, what they refuse to say. Derived from the corpus, written down where a person can argue with it, and held to. Otherwise everything sounds like a general purpose machine wearing a name badge, and every reader can feel it.

**And then the chain.** Six layers, each depending on the one before it having gone right. I ran them by hand for a long time, which is why the first took six months. What I built runs them in order, holds its state so a failure at step four does not send you back to step one, and stops where a human being has to look at something.

What took six months now takes hours, and the parts that need a person still get a person.

That is the actual product. The site is what you can see. This is what makes it possible, and it is why the next leader did not take six months.

---

#### Before any of this

I could build that because of four years at a construction chemicals company, which is not where anyone expects this to have happened.

I went in as director of marketing. Two months after ChatGPT was released I had used it to draft a stack of technical articles about concrete, and my job changed shape. I came off the org chart and spent three years building everything digital and AI.

What I built there, for a business selling construction chemicals, was the working prototype of everything I do now. A content operation that took organic traffic from around fifty thousand visits a year to around a hundred and forty thousand. A custom CRM with voice input and agents underneath it. A product system covering more than three hundred products. Mobile apps on two platforms in a two week build.

By mid 2025 I was running two builds at once with coding agents. One was theirs. The other was what I thought Alan needed.

---

#### For Brad

Brad Brisco equips people who start churches, at [the church-planting arm of one of the largest denominational networks in North America: confirm]. Six books. He coined the term a whole field now uses for the idea that ordinary work and ministry are not competing calls, which means his language is in other people's mouths constantly, usually without his name attached.

Out of the sector, that is a familiar figure: the practitioner who trains the trainers, whose framework is on the whiteboard in rooms he has never been in.

His fragmentation has the same shape as Alan's. It took weeks instead of six months, because by then the chain existed. That is the whole argument for having built it.

[PROOF. A link, a date.]

##### The other half

But Brad's work needed something Alan's did not, and this is where the platform stopped being one thing repeated.

His ideas are not primarily about texts. They are about places. A leader in his world is trying to understand an actual neighborhood, with actual people in it, and act accordingly. The failure mode is a leader who is deeply formed and knows almost nothing verifiable about the six blocks around their building. They plan from impression.

So for Brad I built something that gathers what is actually true about a place and puts it in front of a leader in a form they can act on. [SPECIFIC: what it pulls, what a leader sees, what they do with it.]

One build reverses fragmentation in a body of work. The other reverses it in what a leader knows about their own context, which is scattered across census records and local reports and things everyone assumes somebody has already checked.

Same underlying problem. What you need is real, it exists, and it is not reachable from where you are standing.

---

#### For Youthfront

Youthfront is a nonprofit in Kansas City where I have known people for years. Their situation had nothing to do with archives.

AI was already inside the organization and nobody had decided anything about it. [SPECIFIC: what was actually happening.]

Nothing had gone wrong. That is the part people miss. Nothing had gone wrong yet, and the absence of a bad day was being read as evidence there was nothing to decide.

I could have written them a policy in a week. It would have sat in a folder.

##### Why there had to be an order

By then I had spent three years showing this technology to organizations, and I watched the same thing every time. People got excited, tried something, hit a wall, stopped. Or they got worried, wrote a rule nobody could follow, stopped. Either way, stopped.

What was missing was not enthusiasm or caution. It was a path.

**Safety.** Decide what this is allowed to touch before anyone uses it for anything that matters. Written down, agreed, in language your staff actually use.

**Sandbox.** A bounded place where people use it on real work with real stakes, where being wrong is survivable, and where someone is paying attention.

**Training.** Not a workshop. Enough hours that a practice forms, because a demonstration changes nobody.

**Tech.** Build the thing. By now you know what to build, because the people who will use it have been working with it for months and can tell you.

Everyone wants to start at the end. The tools are the exciting part and the part with a price on them. Starting there gets you a capable system in an organization with no formed judgment about it, which is worse than having nothing, because now the mistakes are fast and confident.

##### Why safety could not wait

Every day an organization goes without deciding this, staff decide it individually, in private, on their own accounts, with the best intentions. They paste in the things that are hardest to write, which are exactly the things involving real people. A donor situation. A family circumstance. A young person's story. A personnel matter.

Nobody is being unreasonable. They are trying to do their jobs and a tool showed up that helps. But information about vulnerable people is leaving the organization, nobody decided that it should, there is no record, and there is no way to walk it back.

That is not a future risk. It is the current state of most organizations I talk to.

##### The hundred hours

At Youthfront we are doing a hundred hours of in person training across ten teams and every part of the organization. Not a pilot group. Not the technically inclined. The whole thing.

[SPECIFIC: what a session is. Who is in the room, what happens, what changes between hour one and hour forty.]

It runs across every team because fragmentation in an organization is not a technology problem. It is that the person who knows why a donor gives is not the person writing the appeal, and the person who was at camp is not the person telling the story, and none of it is written down. A tool does not fix that. People deciding to work differently fixes that, and then a tool can help.

[PROOF. What exists now that did not before.]

A hundred hours is a lot to ask of a nonprofit and I am not going to dress that up. It is the most expensive thing about how I work and I have not found a way around it that I believe in.

---

#### Now

Movemental is the company those builds turned into. I built the platform and I own it. Brad is CEO, because this is a business that runs on trust and he already holds it in the rooms where it matters. Alan is Chief Movement Officer. Both of them put thirty years of their own credibility behind something one person had built and nobody had seen yet. They did not have to do that.

[CURRENT STATE. Platforms live or in build, the four stages, whatever is checkable as of this month.]

I knew all of them before I built anything, and that is the method rather than a coincidence. You do not learn what someone needs by studying the category they belong to. You learn it by being in their world long enough to see what is missing from it.

---

## 3. I started with two people, not a product

`how-i-built-it-two-people-v2.md` · 1,931 words

### I started with two people, not a product

*Draft 2, rebuilt. `/how-i-built-it/two-people`. ~1,750 words. First person, plain, no em dashes.*
*Bracketed items need a real detail from you. The build sequence and the proof are the two that matter.*

---

Alan and I had a standing call on Sunday nights at seven. We had been doing it for years. One week I asked Brad Brisco to join.

I did not want to describe the idea, so I built it instead. A quick site, made in an afternoon, showing a hundred potential authors as a network with the two of them at the origin. You could click any node and get the person, a rough estimate of what a platform might earn them, and what the whole network came to. I shared my screen and let them click on it.

What I said on that call is close to what the business is now. I offered them ten percent each.

What I did not know, and I want to be accurate about this, is that it would lead to organizations. I knew it had to lead somewhere. That took another year to see.

#### Why I started with people I knew

By then I had spent close to three years using this technology in front of people, all of it free, all of it alongside a full time job. Ben first, then a team from Honeywell, then a philanthropy group, then Youthfront, then movement leaders.

The obvious move with that experience is to pick a market and build for it. I did not, for a reason I would defend and one I would not.

The one I would defend is that I do not think you learn what somebody needs by studying the category they belong to. I ran an intentional community for eleven years before any of this. You learn what a person needs by being in the room with them, in their language, for a long time.

The one I would not defend is that I did not think about money at all until I decided to start a company. That is not discipline. It is just how I am built, and it happened to work out, because a market built on trust was not open yet and would not be for another two years.

So I built for two situations I actually knew.

#### The first. A body of work in pieces.

Search for the questions Alan Hirsch has spent his life answering and you will mostly find other people restating him. Some of them get it right. Some do not, and the ones who do not are frequently the easier read, so they travel further.

Twenty thousand notes. More than a decade of them. Books, talks, half finished thoughts, things written on planes. The work was all there. It was not anywhere you could get to.

The problem was never storage. Anyone can put twenty thousand notes in a database.

The problem is that the moment you make an archive answerable, you have built something that speaks in a person's name. If it says something he would not say, you have not helped him. You have added one more confident wrong voice to the pile that was the original problem.

So the build had two requirements that pull against each other. It had to actually answer. And it had to only ever say things he had said.

[THE BUILD. Six to ten sentences, chronological, plain. The retrieval approach and why grounding in his own notes rather than a general model wearing a persona. How citation works and what it refuses to do without sources. What had to be structured before any of it worked. Name the real choices, including ones you would make differently now. Specific enough that a builder could follow it.]

[THE PROOF. One checkable thing. A link someone can open, a number with a date on it, a capture. If the honest proof is small, use the small one. "It works well" is not proof.]

#### The second. An organization AI had already walked into.

Youthfront is a nonprofit here in Kansas City where I have known people for years.

Their problem was not an archive. It was that AI was already inside the organization and nobody had decided anything about it. [SPECIFIC. What was actually happening. Staff on personal accounts, information going into tools nobody had approved, whatever the real version was. One or two sentences, said plainly, without making anybody look foolish, because nobody did anything unreasonable.]

Nothing had gone wrong. That is the part people miss. Nothing had gone wrong yet, and the absence of a bad day was being read as evidence there was nothing to decide.

I could have written them a policy in a week. It would have sat in a folder.

What we are doing instead is a hundred hours of in person training, alongside the build. [WHAT A SESSION ACTUALLY LOOKS LIKE. Two or three sentences. Who is in the room, what happens, what is different for a staff member between hour one and hour forty.]

A hundred hours is a lot to ask of a nonprofit and I am not going to dress that up. It is the most expensive thing about how I work and I have not found a way around it that I believe in.

#### Why the hundred hours exists

This is the part I would skip if I were trying to make the work sound easier, so here it is.

For three years I showed this technology to everyone I knew, for free, as well as I know how to show anything. People were astonished and people did not adopt. They called me a wizard. They moved their schedules to watch me work. They passed it around. And then nothing.

My best friend, who I prepared personally by spending five days learning his profession so the demo would sit inside his actual work, was impressed and did not touch AI again for two years.

I read that as a failure in people for a long time. I do not anymore. It is the fastest spreading technology in history and also the hardest one to actually grasp. It looks like a party trick, so you try it, it makes a mistake, and some part of you is relieved. Or you sit in front of the empty box and cannot think what to ask. Or you can, and the back and forth is genuinely tiring and looks like nothing from outside.

It was not that people could not. It was too early. It is just starting now.

But the result stands, and it is the most expensive thing I know: **astonishment is not adoption, and a demonstration changes nobody.** Three years of the most patient demonstration I could run produced almost no adopted practice anywhere.

That is why the training is a hundred hours and why it is in person. Not generosity. Findings.

#### Where the two halves met

I did not set out to build a platform. I set out to solve two problems for people I knew, and they turned out to be the same problem in different clothes.

Alan's problem was a body of work scattered into pieces the world cannot reassemble. Youthfront's problem was AI arriving before anyone decided what it was allowed to touch. In both cases something was about to speak in their name, authoritatively, with nobody having decided what it could say.

The tool half without the training half hands an organization a capable machine and no formed judgment about it. The training half without the tool half gives you careful people and nothing to be careful with. I had watched both fail.

It also became clear that building for leaders and building for organizations is the same work. Leaders come first only because a leader can decide on a Tuesday and an organization takes a year.

Between September 2025 and April 2026 I built the platform, the agents, and the system underneath, working in context with Cursor and Claude Code, alongside a full time job for most of it. In March 2026 I went full time.

#### What I got wrong on the way

I had been building front ends fast enough that I assumed a full stack application would work the same way. It does not, and I walked straight into it.

A week into building a custom agentic CRM for the company I was working for, I gave a demo. It was bad. Not close. And I had spent two years training that room to expect a mobile app in a week.

Within days I went back and said we needed real timelines and real expectations, and we set them. What took months after that was not diagnosis. It was learning back end architecture from a standing start. Data, type safety, migrations, how an application actually holds and moves information. There was no map for that in 2025 and there still barely is.

I delivered in about six weeks against a three month timeline. It did not matter, because the room had decided in week one.

Two things came out of it. One is a rule I now keep: I do not test in public. I show it when it works. From outside there is no visible difference between this is hard and this was oversold, and I watch capable people hit that same wall constantly, including my own co-founders.

The other is the thing I would not trade. The same day it became clear I had to build a real data chain was the day it became clear I could build one from the prompt level. That idea is underneath everything I have made since, including the design work.

Sometimes you say you will be back in a week and it turns out to be a longer trip, and you come back with a map nobody had.

#### What it proved

**Building for one real person beats building for a category.** Everything good in the platform came from a specific problem Alan or Youthfront actually had. Everything I built from a guess about what leaders in general would want, I threw out.

**A grounded answer is worth more than a fluent one.** Fluency is cheap now and it is about to be free. What will still be scarce in five years is an answer you can check, in a voice the person would claim.

**The training is not the soft part.** It is what the build is for. A tool without a formed person is not progress. It is replacement, and it arrives looking like help.

#### Still open

[Required. The thing you have not solved. My candidate: whether a hundred hours can ever be delivered at scale, or whether it only works when the person delivering it already knows the organization. That is a real unresolved question and admitting it costs you nothing worth keeping.]

---

If you have a body of work scattered across fifteen years of platforms, or an organization where AI showed up before the conversation did, I would rather hear about your situation than tell you more about mine. [Contact or newsletter line.]

---

**How AI was used here.** I built this software working in context with Cursor and Claude Code across about seven months. I wrote this piece. AI helped me gather notes and find things I had written elsewhere. The thinking, the argument, and the sentences are mine. Every number in it can be checked, and if you want to check one, ask me.

## 4. Shrewd as serpents

`shrewd-as-serpents.md` · 2,533 words

### Shrewd as serpents

*For church leaders. ~2,600 words.*

---

There is a line in Luke that I have not been able to get out of my head for about two years now.

Jesus tells a story about a manager who is about to be fired. Before the books close, the man goes to everyone who owes his master money and reduces what they owe, so that when he is out of a job there will be people willing to take him in. And then the master commends him. Not for his honesty, which Luke pointedly does not grant him. For his shrewdness.

Then Jesus says the thing. The children of this age are shrewder in dealing with their own generation than the children of light.

I have been in and around ministry for most of my adult life, and I have spent the last three and a half years watching what churches and Christian organizations do when a genuinely new technology arrives. I do not think that sentence has ever been more plainly true than it is right now.

#### What I have actually watched

Since December 2022 I have shown this technology to church leaders, denominational staff, nonprofit teams, seminary people, and about every kind of ministry organization there is. Most of it for free, most of it alongside a full time job.

The pattern almost never varies. People are impressed. And then nothing happens.

Sometimes nothing happens because the leader has decided this is a threat, and that waiting is the faithful posture. Sometimes nothing happens because the leader is enthusiastic but has no idea what the next step would be. And sometimes something does happen, but it happens sideways: nobody decides anything at the top, so the youth director and the communications person and the executive assistant each quietly figure it out on their own accounts, at night, using it for the tasks that are hardest to write, which are exactly the tasks that involve real people.

Two failures, opposite in appearance. One organization is paralyzed. The other is unsupervised. Neither has deliberated.

What strikes me is that Scripture has a word for each of them, and it is not the word most of us reach for.

#### Both halves of the command

When Jesus sends the twelve out, he tells them they are sheep among wolves, and then gives them a two-part instruction that most of us can quote and few of us hold together.

Be shrewd as serpents. Be unmixed as doves.

Start with the first half, because it should be more shocking than it is. The serpent is not a neutral image in the Hebrew Scriptures. The word used of the serpent in Genesis 3 is the same word Proverbs uses over and over for the prudent person, the one who sees trouble coming and takes cover while the naive walk straight into it. One word, condemned in Eden and commended in Proverbs.

The tradition never resolved that by getting rid of the faculty. It resolved it by locating the moral weight in what the craft is aimed at. Cunning aimed at deceiving is serpentine. The identical cunning aimed at protecting the people in your care is wisdom.

So when Jesus says be shrewd as serpents, he is reaching for the most negatively charged picture of cleverness available in his own Scriptures and telling his people to match it.

The second half is where most of us have quietly changed the meaning. The Greek word behind "innocent" does not mean naive. It means unmixed, unalloyed, the way metal is described when nothing has been added to it. It is a word about purity of composition, not about being uninformed.

Which means the command is not be clever but also a little bit stupid. It is: **be maximally competent in your means and completely unadulterated in your motives.**

And notice where it is said. Sheep among wolves. This is not general life counsel. It is what you tell people walking into danger. The reason for shrewdness is that the situation is dangerous. Naivety in a dangerous situation is not innocence. It is negligence that has learned to describe itself as innocence.

Both halves are commanded. Shrewd without unmixed is the serpent in the garden. Unmixed without shrewd is a sheep in a wolf pack. We have spent a long time treating the second one as the safe error. It is not. It is just the more respectable one.

#### The buried talent

The parable that will not leave the fearful alone is the one about the talents, and specifically the third servant.

He does not steal. He does not squander. He buries what he was given and returns it intact, and he gives his reason plainly: he was afraid. He knew the master to be a hard man, so he protected what he had.

The verdict is severe, and it is worth sitting with why.

First, his fear is named as the cause, and it is not accepted as a defense. It is treated as the offense itself.

Second, and this is the part I find most convicting, the fear had produced a theology to justify itself. "I knew you to be a hard man." He had an account of the master that made his paralysis reasonable. That is almost always how this works. Inaction rarely arrives announcing itself as cowardice. It arrives as a considered position about the nature of the risk, and it is usually articulate.

Third, the master's response closes the last exit. At minimum, he says, you could have put it with the bankers. Even the most cautious available option involved handing it to somebody else and letting it work. Burial was not the low-risk choice. It was the only guaranteed loss.

I want to be careful here, because this parable has been used to bless a great deal of ordinary ambition by dressing it in Scripture, and church leaders are right to be wary of that. I am not saying God will judge your technology decisions. I am saying the parable makes a specific claim about the structure of fear, and that claim is portable: **doing nothing is not the neutral position, and sincerity about your reasons does not make them true.**

If your organization has decided to wait, the question worth asking is not whether the decision is defensible. It probably is. The question is whether it is a decision at all, or a fear that has found language.

#### The oil that could not be lent

Then there are the ten young women waiting for a wedding party that is late.

Five are called wise and five foolish, and the difference between them is one thing. The wise brought extra oil against a delay they could not predict. It is worth noticing that all ten fall asleep. The wise are not more vigilant. They are better provisioned.

The line that lands hardest comes at midnight, when the foolish ask to borrow. The answer is no, and it is not cruelty. There will not be enough for both. Go and buy your own.

That refusal is a statement about what kind of thing oil is. **Some capacities cannot be transferred at the moment of crisis, and cannot be acquired at the moment they are needed.**

This is the part of the current conversation that I think church leaders most consistently get wrong, and I say that having watched it up close for three years.

The assumption is that when this technology matters enough, the organization will learn it then. There will be a workshop. Somebody will figure it out. We will catch up when catching up becomes necessary.

Formation does not work that way. It never has, in any domain your church already understands. You cannot disciple someone at the moment they face the crisis. You cannot build a culture of discernment during the week you need discernment. The reason your church invests years in people before anything visible happens is that you already know this about every other kind of formation. It is equally true here.

The capacity to use a powerful tool wisely is built slowly, in low-stakes conditions, before the stakes arrive. When it arrives first and the capacity is missing, you do not get a slower version of the same outcome. You get a capable instrument in the hands of an organization with no formed judgment about it, which is worse than having nothing at all, because now the mistakes are fast and confident and they carry your name.

#### Reading the moment

There is a rebuke in Luke 12 that I find harder than the others because it is aimed at competent people.

Jesus tells the crowd they can look at the sky and tell you what the weather is doing, and then asks why they cannot interpret the present moment. And then, sharper: why do you not judge for yourselves what is right.

The charge is not ignorance. These are people who read their world expertly in ordinary matters. The charge is a selective competence, sharp about everything except the thing that carries the most consequence.

And the second sentence is the one I would put in front of every leader I know. Judge for yourselves. Not wait for a denominational statement. Not wait until a consensus forms among your peers. Not wait for someone with more technical credibility to tell you what moment this is. The waiting for permission is itself the failure being named.

#### Count the cost

I want to put one guardrail on all of this, because everything I have written so far pushes in one direction and the Scriptures do not leave it there.

Jesus also tells two short stories about estimation. A man begins a tower, runs out of money, and cannot finish it, and everyone who walks past mocks him. A king considers whether ten thousand can meet twenty thousand.

Notice what these are not. They are not arguments against building. Both assume the project. The failure is beginning without honest estimation, and the specific damage is public humiliation in front of everyone who watched you start.

I have been on the wrong side of that one. In 2025 I told a leadership team a build would take three months. I had spent two years training them to expect things much faster than that, and I was confident. Then I hit a part of the work I did not understand, and a week in I gave a demo that did not work. I diagnosed the problem quickly and I delivered the whole thing in about six weeks, which was well inside what I had promised. It did not matter. The room had decided in week one, and I never got it back.

The lesson was not that I moved too early. It was that I announced a tower I could not yet see the top of, in front of people who were watching. Shrewdness includes knowing the difference.

So: build. But size it to be finished, and say out loud what it will actually cost.

#### What I am not saying

Three things, plainly, because this kind of argument is easy to abuse and you should be able to see me refusing to.

I am not saying the moment Jesus tells you to read is this technology. It is not. In Luke 12 it is his own presence, and reading a market window into that is a category error. What transfers is a claim about how fear and competence and timing relate to each other in decisions people actually have to make. That structure is portable. The urgency of the kingdom is not on loan to anybody's product.

I am not saying that faithfulness requires adopting this. It requires deciding about it. Those are different, and a church that deliberates carefully and concludes it will use very little of this has done the thing I am asking for. What I am against is drift, in either direction.

And I have an obvious interest here. I build these systems for a living, and I sell exactly the kind of training I have just argued you need. You should weigh what I have written accordingly. I would rather say that plainly than have you notice it and wonder why I did not.

#### What shrewdness actually looks like this year

If I had to reduce all of it to a sequence, it would be this, and the order matters more than any single part.

**Decide what this is allowed to touch, before anyone uses it for anything that matters.** In your own words, in language your staff would actually use, written down. Not a policy nobody reads. A short set of lines about what does not go into these tools, particularly anything about the vulnerable people in your care, and what always requires a human being.

This is the innocence half, and there is real urgency in it. Every week you do not decide, your staff are deciding individually, in private, with the best intentions. Nobody is being unreasonable. They are trying to do their jobs and a tool showed up that helps. But information about real people is leaving your organization, nobody chose that, and there is no way to walk it back.

**Then make somewhere for people to actually learn.** A bounded place, real work, real stakes, where being wrong is survivable and someone is paying attention to what happens. This is the oil. Buy it before midnight.

**Then form people, at a scale that feels excessive.** Not a workshop. Enough hours that a practice forms. I have watched three years of astonishing demonstrations produce almost no change in behavior, in people I know well, who wanted it to work. Demonstration does not form anybody. It never has, in any part of your ministry.

**Then, and only then, build.** By that point you will know what to build, because the people who will use it will have been working with it for months and can tell you.

Everyone wants to start at the end. The tools are the interesting part and the part with a price attached. Starting there is the tower with no foundation.

#### The sentence I cannot get past

The children of this age are shrewder in dealing with their own generation than the children of light.

That is not a compliment to the children of this age. It is a rebuke to us, and it is observably accurate right now. The commercial world is deliberating about this with enormous seriousness. Meanwhile the institutions whose entire work runs on trust, which is the thing this technology most directly threatens, are largely doing neither. Not deciding what is permitted. Not building anything. Not shrewd, and not particularly innocent either. Just late.

We have a command with two halves. We have spent a long time treating one of them as optional and calling that faithfulness.

It is not the safe error. It is just the one that looks better while it costs you.

---

*Joshua Shepherd builds AI systems for organizations whose work depends on trust, and trains the people who use them. [Contact or newsletter line.]*

## 5. What shrewdness actually looks like

`what-shrewdness-looks-like.md` · 2,764 words

### What shrewdness actually looks like

*Companion to "Shrewd as serpents." For church leaders. ~3,100 words.*

---

In the first piece I argued that Scripture commands two things and we have been treating one of them as optional. Innocence without shrewdness is not faithfulness. It is negligence with better manners.

Fair enough as an argument. But an argument that ends there is worthless, because shrewdness is a word about means, and a claim about means that stays abstract is not a claim about anything.

So here is my attempt to say exactly what it consists of, for a church, this year. Not principles. The actual content of the competence.

I will start with what a shrewd leader knows, because most of the mistakes are knowledge failures rather than courage failures. Then what a shrewd church does. Then, at some length, what it refuses, because refusal is part of the competence and not a limit on it.

#### What a shrewd leader knows

##### That the tool is worst at the thing everyone asks about first

Every conversation I have with a pastor arrives at sermons within four minutes.

Here is the honest answer. These systems can produce a competent, structured, theologically unobjectionable sermon on almost any text in about ninety seconds. It will be usable. It will also be assembled from the average of everything ever written about that passage, which means it will contain no encounter, no risk, and nothing that came from you sitting with the text until it did something to you.

A shrewd leader understands why that matters, and it is not squeamishness. Preaching is not the transmission of content about a text. If it were, the machine would be fine at it. Preaching is a person who has been changed by a passage standing in front of people they know and telling them what they found. The congregation is not receiving information. They are watching someone who has been somewhere.

The average of the internet has not been anywhere.

So the sermon question is the wrong question, and the fact that it comes first is itself the tell. It reveals that the leader is thinking of this as a writing tool, which is the least interesting and most dangerous frame available.

##### That the actual leverage is memory, not efficiency

Here is what I think most churches have never noticed about themselves.

You are an institution whose entire theology is continuity. You baptize people and expect to bury them. You tell a story that spans generations. And you have catastrophic amnesia.

A pastor takes a call. Within eighteen months, most of what the previous pastor knew is simply gone. Not the records. The knowledge. Which family is still hurting from a split fifteen years ago. Why the trustees will not discuss the parking lot. Which of the older members quietly funds most of the benevolence. What was tried in 2011 and why it failed. Who has been asked to serve too many times and who has never been asked once.

A long-tenured member dies and takes forty years of congregational history with her, and nobody thought to ask.

You have twenty years of sermons in a folder, thirty years of newsletters in a box, session minutes going back further than that, mission trip reports, annual reports, prayer chains, funeral homilies. All of it is a record of what this congregation has believed and done and suffered, and none of it is reachable. Nobody can ask it anything.

The shrewd leader sees that as the asset. Not because it makes anything faster, but because the thing this technology is actually good at is making a large, scattered body of material answerable. That is not an efficiency play. It is an antidote to the specific way churches lose themselves.

##### That something is already answering questions about your church

Somebody in your community asked a machine about your church this month. Someone considering visiting, someone whose kid is thinking about your youth group, a reporter, a family looking for a funeral.

It answered. It did not say it was unsure. And it answered from whatever it could reach, which is your website, your Google listing, a couple of reviews, and anything anyone else has said about you. Not your actual theology. Not what you have learned in twenty years of being in that neighborhood. Not the sermon series that would have told them exactly who you are.

You do not get to opt out. The only decision available is whether the thing answering has anything real to work with.

##### That the cost curve moved and nobody told you

The kind of system that used to cost a church a quarter of a million dollars can now be built for a fraction of that. That is not marketing; it is the actual reason I have a company.

Practically, this means capabilities that were previously available only to churches with a communications department are now available to a congregation of ninety. That window will not stay open in this form. Right now the tools are cheap, the stakes are low, and being wrong is survivable. Both of those conditions are temporary in opposite directions.

##### That someone in your congregation is already fluent

There is a twenty-six-year-old in your pews using this six hours a day at work. There is a nurse in your congregation whose hospital has already run the whole governance conversation you are dreading. There is probably a schoolteacher living through the most intense version of this debate happening anywhere.

Churches consistently reach for an outside consultant while ignoring three people in the fourth row who know more than the consultant does about how this actually goes in an institution.

Shrewdness is noticing what you already have.

#### What a shrewd church does

##### Writes down its lines before anyone needs them

Not a policy document. Half a page, in your own words, that a volunteer could read and follow.

What never goes into these tools: anything a person told you in confidence, anything about a minor, anything from a pastoral conversation, anything from a counseling session, giving records tied to names, personnel matters.

What always has a human being on it: anything sent under the pastor's name, anything going to a family in grief, anything that will be read from the front, anything involving a child.

The reason to do this before rather than after is not legal. It is that your staff are currently deciding it individually, in private, at nine at night, on their own accounts, with the best intentions. They are pasting in the hardest things to write, which are exactly the things involving actual people, because those are the tasks where help is most wanted. Nobody is being unreasonable. But information about people in your care is leaving your church, nobody chose that, and it cannot be recalled.

##### Picks a real sandbox and staffs it

A bounded piece of real work, with real stakes, where being wrong is recoverable and someone is paying attention.

Concretely, the good candidates in a church are the ones with volume and low pastoral risk. The newsletter. The bulletin. Event descriptions. Grant applications. Meeting minutes. First drafts of routine correspondence. The website copy nobody has had time to rewrite since 2019. Making twenty years of sermons searchable.

The bad candidates are the ones people reach for first: anything pastoral, anything for a family in crisis, anything that involves speaking to a person about their own life.

What makes it a sandbox rather than just usage is that somebody is watching and writing down what happens. Which tasks got better. Which got worse. Where somebody caught something wrong. Where somebody nearly did not.

##### Forms people at a scale that feels excessive

This is the part I would defend hardest, because I have three years of evidence and it all points the same way.

I have shown this technology to hundreds of people, most of them free, most of them people who trusted me and wanted it to work. They were astonished almost every time. Almost none of them adopted anything.

My best friend, for whom I spent five days learning his profession so the demonstration would sit inside his actual work, was impressed and did not touch AI again for two years.

**Demonstration does not form anybody.** You already know this. It is why you do not disciple people with a really good sermon. It is why your best volunteers were formed over years by somebody who stayed with them. Nothing about this technology suspends the way human beings actually learn.

So the honest number of hours is much larger than anyone wants it to be, it has to be with people rather than a video, and it has to be on their own real work rather than on examples. At Youthfront we are doing a hundred hours across every team in the organization. Not a pilot group. Not the technically inclined. Everyone.

A church can do a smaller version. But if the plan is a two-hour workshop, the plan is to have had a workshop.

##### Puts its own house in order first

Before any tool, ask who knows what around here, and what happens when they leave.

Most of the fragmentation in a church is not technological. It is that the person who knows why the Hendersons give is not the person writing the appeal. The person who was on the mission trip is not the person telling the story. The person who remembers the 2011 attempt is retired.

A tool does not fix that. People deciding to write things down fixes that, and then a tool makes it reachable. In the wrong order you get an expensive system that indexes nothing.

##### Talks to the people who already know

The nurse. The teacher. The twenty-six-year-old. Ask them what they have watched go well and badly, and what they wish their institution had decided earlier.

You will get better counsel in ninety minutes than most churches get from a consultant, and you will have done something more important than gathering information, which is to signal that this is a congregational conversation rather than an office decision.

##### Says out loud what it is doing

If your newsletter is drafted with AI assistance and edited by a person, say so once, plainly, somewhere findable.

There is a version of this that is fear management and a version that is shrewdness. The shrewd version understands that trust is the only asset a church has that cannot be rebuilt quickly, and that the way you lose it is not by using a tool. It is by having used it quietly and being found out. Disclosure is cheap now and priceless later.

#### What a shrewd church refuses

I want to be careful not to present refusal as the safety half of this. Knowing what a tool is for includes knowing what it is not for, and getting that wrong is a failure of competence, not just of nerve.

**Anything that is constituted by presence.** A hospital visit. Sitting with someone after a diagnosis. The conversation in the parking lot after the meeting. These are not tasks with outputs. The presence is the substance, and a more efficient version of it is not a version of it.

**Anything a person said to you in confidence.** No exceptions and no clever workarounds. Not summarized, not anonymized, not "just to help me think it through." The moment a congregant's disclosure becomes input, you have changed what confession means in your church, and you will not be able to change it back.

**Discernment.** A machine can lay out considerations, and that is genuinely useful. It cannot weigh them, because weighing requires knowing what this congregation has already been through and what it can bear. If a decision requires knowing your people, the tool is not a participant.

**Prayer.** I am not going to argue this one.

**Anything where the person on the other end thinks they are getting you.** A note to a grieving family. A response to someone in crisis. If they believe a person attended to them and no person did, you have not saved time. You have taken something from them without telling them.

**And anything involving a child, until you have thought about it much harder than you want to.** Photos, stories, safety records, anything a minor said. Churches have learned expensive lessons about child safety in the last thirty years and every one of those lessons applies here in a new form.

Notice that these refusals are not arbitrary and they are not about risk tolerance. They mark the places where the work is constituted by a human being doing it. That is a knowable line, and knowing where it falls is precisely the competence I am arguing for.

#### The first ninety days, concretely

If you did nothing else this year, this would be enough, and it is genuinely achievable for a church of any size.

**Weeks one and two.** Three or four leaders, separately, answer the same three questions on paper. What should this never touch here. Where would it obviously help. What are we afraid of. Then compare. The disagreements are the whole exercise, and there will be more of them than you expect.

**Weeks three to six.** Draft half a page of lines. Read it aloud to your staff and let them argue with it. Revise. The read-aloud is not a formality; anything that cannot be read aloud without qualification is not written clearly enough to be followed.

**Weeks seven to ten.** Pick two tasks with volume and low pastoral risk. Give them to two people. Ask them to keep a running note of what actually happened, including the near misses.

**Weeks eleven and twelve.** Sit with the notes. Decide what graduates into normal practice, what stops, and what still needs watching. Then talk to your congregation about what you have decided and why, before anyone asks.

Ninety days, no budget, no vendor. And at the end you will have something almost no church has, which is a decision.

#### The part I have to disclose

I build these systems and I sell exactly the kind of training I have just described. You should weigh what I have written accordingly, and I would rather say it than have you find it.

I will add one thing that cuts against my own interest. Most of what I have listed above does not require me or anyone like me. The half page, the sandbox, the conversation with the nurse and the teacher, the ninety days — a church can do all of it alone, this quarter, for nothing. If you do only that, you will be ahead of nearly every congregation I have talked to in three years.

The place outside help earns its keep is later, when you want to make a large body of material actually reachable, which is a real technical problem that does not solve itself. Not at the start.

#### Why this is shrewdness and not caution

Read back over the list and notice what is not in it. There is nothing about protecting yourself, nothing about liability, nothing about waiting to see how it shakes out.

Every item is about competence. Knowing what the tool is good at. Knowing what you already have. Knowing who in the room already knows. Knowing where the line falls and why it falls there. Building the capacity to judge before the moment when judgment is needed, because that capacity cannot be borrowed at midnight.

That is what practical wisdom has always consisted of, in Proverbs and in Luke and in every ordinary decision your elders have ever made well. It is the intelligence of a person who has to act, in a situation that will not wait, with responsibility for people who did not choose the situation either.

The children of this age are shrewder in dealing with their own generation. They are, at the moment, and it is not because they are smarter than you. It is because they decided it was their business to be competent about this, and we decided it was somebody else's business.

It is not somebody else's business. There is a twenty-six-year-old in your pews who has already formed her habits, and nobody in your church has said one word to her about it.
