## 18. Is there a life behind the words? — authorship in the age of AI

`momentofauthorship.pdf` · 3,265 words

AUTHORSHIP IN THE AGE OF AI

Is there a life behind the words? On what AI does to the trust between a writer and a reader — why the answer is not detection but disclosure, and what it would take for a reader to be able to trust an author again.

AUTHOR

Joshua Shepherd Founder, Movemental

Working theory Held for discussion

---

Start not with the writer, but with the faithful reader — who now faces something new in the history of the world. For the entire history of publishing, a faithful reader could assume that the work in front of them came from the person whose name was on it. That assumption has quietly ended, and almost no one has named what its ending costs. Consider a reader who has followed an author faithfully for years — read every book, taught the frameworks, been formed by the work. That reader opens the newest piece and, for the first time ever, cannot answer a question that never had to be asked before: is this still them? Is this the author, writing as they have always written? Is it the author mediated through an AI that changed the syntax, smoothed the edges, accelerated the draft? Is it the author's assistant and a model together? Is it the model, lightly supervised? Is it the model, entirely, wearing the author's name? The reader cannot tell. And the reader now knows enough about the glut of AI-produced content in the world to know that the question is real — which means even beginning to parse it carries a cost that reading never used to carry. This is the break. It is not about quality. A reader can love AI-assisted prose and still be wounded by not knowing whether a person stands behind it. The break is epistemic: the reader has lost the ability to know whether the words they are giving their attention and trust to were authored by the person they trust. No technology of the past — pen, press, typewriter, word processor — ever severed that link, because none of them could generate the thought. This one can. That is what is new.

1

---

When the uncertainty cannot be resolved, the reader does the only rational thing. They avoid. Faced with a question they cannot answer and a parsing cost they did not used to bear, the reader withdraws. Not out of cynicism — out of self-protection. If you cannot know whether the words in front of you were lived and meant by a person, and you cannot afford to keep paying the cost of wondering, the rational move is to stop giving your attention to work whose provenance you cannot establish. The product of unresolvable authorship uncertainty is avoidance. And avoidance has two faces, one of them good and one of them catastrophic. The good face: a reader who withdraws from uncertain publication may go back to their local, embodied community — to the pastor they can see, the teacher whose life they can watch, the friend whose word they can test against a life. That is a genuine good. If the AI glut sends people back to the people they can actually trust, something right is happening. The catastrophic face: publication itself is one of the primary means by which truth has been transmitted across distance and time for the whole history of the church and the world. The letter to a church the writer could not visit. The book that crossed an ocean. The treatise that outlived its author. If readers withdraw from publication wholesale because they can no longer trust its provenance, we do not merely lose some content. We lose the mechanism by which the body of Christ has thought together across space and generations. That is not a market problem. That is a civilizational one.

The danger is not that readers will be deceived by AI. The danger is that, unable to tell, they will stop trusting any written word they did not personally witness being lived — and publication, as a way of carrying truth, will quietly die of suspicion.

2

---

The steroid era and the live-ball era — the difference between the two is the whole argument. Baseball gives us two ways an era can change, and the difference between them is exactly the difference between the violation and the path forward.

THE STE RO ID E RA — THE UN DISCLO SE D

When Barry Bonds hit 73 home runs, the number could not mean what Roger Maris's 61 meant, because the achievement was no longer self-evidently human and no one had said so. The asterisk had to be imposed from outside, after the fact, because the player would not name what had changed. The achievement was real and also compromised — not because enhancement is unthinkable, but because it was hidden. This is the undisclosed AI author: output inflated, nothing said, trust broken in silence.

THE LIVE -BALL E RA — THE DISCLO SE D

In 1920, baseball changed the ball itself. Offense exploded. But there is no asterisk on the live-ball era, because the change was declared. Everyone knew the ball was different. The achievements still counted — they simply counted as achievements of a different, openly-named game. This is the path forward for AI and authorship: not a return to the dead-ball purity of pen and paper, but an openly disclosed change in how the work is made, so that the reader knows what game they are reading and can value it accurately.

The change is hidden.

The change is declared.

The asterisk is imposed from outside, after the

No asterisk is needed; the rules are known in

fact.

advance.

Trust breaks in silence.

Trust is renegotiated in the open.

The achievement is compromised.

The achievement counts — as what it actually is.

The whole system this paper describes is a machine for moving authors out of the first column and into the second. Not to punish the enhancement, but to make the new game legible so that no one needs to hide it anymore.

3

---

PROVEN AN CE WITHOUT DETECTION

You do not need to examine the text. You need the author's own rhythm. Most of the AI-authorship conversation is stuck on detection at the level of the text — can we tell, from the words themselves, whether AI wrote this? That is a losing game and it gets more losing every month. There is a simpler move, available right now, while we wait to see whether technological verification ever arrives. You do not examine the sentences. You examine the rhythm. Just as you did not need a blood test to suspect that a player who went from ten home runs to fifty in a single season had changed something, you do not need semantic forensics to notice that an author who published ten books across a forty-year life has suddenly published ten in two years. The deviation from a person's own established baseline is the data. There is no plausible reason for a sixty-five-year-old writer to triple their lifetime output in a single year — and the author knows it better than anyone. If Alan looks at his own numbers and sees three times his lifetime rhythm in twelve months, Alan already knows that surplus is not coming out of who Alan is. This relocates the evidence from the place where AI is winning — the text — to the place where AI cannot hide: volume measured against a human life's established pace. THE BASE LIN E DO E S N O T CO N VICT. IT RE Q UE STS AN ACCO UN T.

There are honest reasons output rises — a sabbatical, a retirement, a long-gestating backlog, a coauthor. So the baseline is not a verdict. It is a prompt for disclosure. The deviation does not say "cheater." It says: this departs from your established rhythm; tell your readers why. The honest sabbatical author has a ready answer. The undisclosed inflater has none. The method does not accuse — it asks the author to give an account, and lets the presence or absence of an honest one speak. This is why it can only work as a system, not as an individual burden. One author trying to self-audit produces a mountain of unnecessary work. But a community that holds itself to this can show provenance at a glance.

4

---

A single panel, shown at a glance, that lets a skeptical reader trust the process. When a reader arrives at a Movement Voice's work, skeptical — you say you do not do AI authorship, but you have AI systems; how would I know? — the answer is not an argument. It is a panel. A handful of statistics that make the rhythm visible, the way a stat line makes a season visible:

How this author writes — at a glance Lifetime publishing rhythm

Output this year vs. baseline

A I’s disclosed role

~1 book / 2–3 yrs

In rhythm

Research, copy edit

Voice fidelity standard

Process disclosure

None

Corpus-bound

Published

The exact statistics will be refined, but the shape is the point: lifetime rhythm, current output against that rhythm, which jobs of writing AI assisted, whether AI did any generative authoring, the voice-fidelity standard the work is held to, and whether the author has published their process. Six facts. A reader can hold them in a glance, the way a fan reads a stat line, and decide whether to extend trust.

If the author self-reports their own pre-AI history, a cheater can game it. So the pre-AI baseline must be established from the public record — the bibliography that already exists, the publication dates already in the world, fixed before this moment and beyond retroactive editing. The network establishes the baseline from what is already public; the author discloses the present against it. The honesty of the system rests on the baseline being something the author cannot quietly rewrite.

5

---

The question was never "did AI touch this." It is "which job did AI do." The confusion about AI and authorship comes from treating "AI involvement" as a single dial from zero to a hundred. It was never one dial. Writing was always a bundle of distinct jobs, many of them already delegated — to assistants, editors, researchers, collaborators — for as long as there have been books. The honest question is not whether AI was involved, but which of writing's jobs it did. Some jobs were always delegable and raise no question of authorship when AI does them, provided it is disclosed: Remediation — moving existing work between forms, formats, and lengths. Research — gathering, locating, summarizing source material. Copy editing — grammar, consistency, mechanical correctness. These are the live-ball-era equivalents of better bats and better training. The game got faster; nothing was falsified. But there is a job that is different in kind: Generative authorship — the actual invention of the thought, the saying of the thing, the origination of the meaning. This is the home run itself. When AI performs this job, undisclosed, you are in steroid-era territory, regardless of how few or many words changed. And there is a genuinely new mode that the old categories cannot hold: collaborative authorship — a work co-created through back-and-forth conversation with a model, as a real and distinct act of writing. It is legitimate. It is also not the same act as solitary composition, and honesty about it costs something. As you might say of it plainly: this feat is less significant in some ways, and it is also its own kind of writing. The live ball still produced real achievements. It simply produced them in a declared, different game.

Output rate alone cannot tell acceptable acceleration from replacement — an author who used AI to research faster looks, in raw volume, like one who had AI write everything. So the statistics catch the undisclosed; the taxonomy of jobs defines the acceptable. The two need each other. Disclosure must say not only that output changed, but which job changed hands.

6

---

AN OLD DISCIPLIN E, EXTEN DED

The footnote is the precedent. Process becomes the new kind of source. A work made through deep collaboration with a model would best be supported by the cited, archived conversation from which it began. That sounds like an enormous new complexity — and it is — but it is not a new kind of demand. It is an old discipline catching up to a new tool. For five hundred years, serious writing has carried its sources in footnotes: here is the lineage of where this thought came from, so you can trace it and trust it. We already accept that careful work shows its sources. What collaborative AI authorship calls for is the same impulse extended to a new kind of source — not a footnote to prior books, but a trace back to the process: the conversation, the prompts, the human judgments that shaped what was generated. This paper does not solve that apparatus, and it should not try to yet. But naming the precedent changes how the complexity feels. Provenance is the new bibliography. The reader who wants to trust a collaboratively-authored work should be able to trace its process the way a scholar traces a citation. We are not inventing a strange new burden. We are extending the oldest discipline of trustworthy writing to the newest way of making it. And there is a grace clause that belongs here. AI has been broadly available for roughly three years. This is reasonably understood as a grace period for AI and authorship — a season in which the norms were genuinely unclear and many faithful people experimented without settled guidance. The call, therefore, is not to comb the past for offenders. It is to say: now is the moment to make your writing legible to your readers again, whatever you have done until now.

7

---

THE THEO LO GICAL CO RE

What we are really protecting is not human typing. It is the moment of authorship. Everything so far has been about honesty and trust. But underneath the honesty is a deeper claim about where authorship actually lives — and getting it right is what keeps this from being mere productivity ethics. We have always written with technology. The pen is a technology. So is paper, the typewriter, the word processor. Writing itself is a technological act. So the arrival of one more tool would be unremarkable — except that this tool is different in one specific and profound way: it can perform generative authorship. It can originate the thought, not merely transmit it. That is what makes the moment confusing, and it is also what forces us to ask a question we never had to ask before: what is the irreducible human act that makes a word trustworthy, regardless of the tool? The answer is not "a human typed it." A human can type every word and still produce dead text — words no one really meant, assembled out of habit or obligation, with no one truly present behind them. And a person can be wholly present, meaning every word, in a work co-created through conversation with a model. The tool is not the line. The line is something else:

THE K EY STONE

The moment of authorship is the moment a person, before God, means something — judges it, takes responsibility for it, and stands answerable for it as true. Words are trustworthy when that moment is present, and untrustworthy when it is absent, whether they came through pen, typewriter, or collaborative conversation with a model.

This reframes the entire system. Transparency is not the point. Transparency is the evidence that the moment of authorship happened. The statistics, the disclosure of jobs, the provenance of process — they are all proxies for one question: is there a person taking responsibility before God for this word? Was someone there, in the authorship, answerable for it? For a Christian author, this is not a productivity question; it is nearer to a question of bearing false witness. The authority of Christian writing has always been borrowed from a life — the claim that

8

---

this person has lived this, prayed this, suffered this, and is therefore worth heeding. The word is trustworthy because a life stands behind it. AI-inflated, undisclosed output severs the word from the life. It produces words no one lived behind, while implying that someone did. That is the deepest thing at stake: not output, not even honesty in the abstract, but whether there is a life behind the words — and whether the reader can be formed by what God actually spoke through a person in a real moment of authorship.

9

---

The point of making cheating visible is not to punish. It is to break the will to cheat. When the rhythm is visible to all, cheating becomes obvious — and when cheating becomes obvious, the will to cheat breaks, because the entire payoff of undisclosed AI inflation depends on no one being able to tell. Make provenance legible and you do not need an enforcement apparatus. You remove the incentive at its root. So the call, when a reader discovers that a trusted author has been silent about AI, is not to cancel. It is to invite repentance — which means simply: change what you are doing, and then tell your readers what you have learned. Given the genuine three-year grace period, almost everyone deserves the chance to realign rather than be destroyed. The right posture toward an author who has drifted is the oldest one the church knows: not exposure for its own sake, but a call to turn, and a way back to the table. This is the leader's actual job in this moment. Not to police, but to clarify the new reality and chart a clear way through it — to give writers and readers alike the frameworks to understand what writing always was, where AI can faithfully assist, what the genuinely new modes are, and how to make any of it legible to a human reader again. A community willing to hold itself to this can say to a skeptical reader: we say we do not do AI authorship, and here is how you can verify it — and mean it, in five or six statistics.

What is at stake is not productivity, and not even honesty in the abstract. It is whether the reader can trust the writer again — and trust the process through which the writing came to be.

That trust, once restored, lets the reader come back not merely as an audience but as someone who can again be formed by the work — formed by what God has spoken through a person in a real moment of authorship, which can happen through collaborative conversation with a model just as it has always happened through the older technologies of pen and page. The goal was never to keep AI out of writing. The goal is to keep the person — present, answerable, before God — in it.

10

---

## 19. For Dave, before we talk

`fergusonmemo.pdf` · 2,066 words

For Dave, before we talk. A short letter to Dave Ferguson, with Brad Brisco and Alan Hirsch reading over our shoulders, on the architecture apostolic mission has not yet had — and why this conversation could only happen now.

FOR

FROM

Dave Ferguson NewThing · Exponential · COMMUNITY

Joshua Shepherd Founder, Movemental

---

OPENING

Why this note, and why now. Dave — I am writing this before we talk because what I want to say is too unfamiliar to land cleanly in the first ninety seconds of a call, and too important to leave to chance. On the Verge sits on my desk as I write this. The book you and Alan wrote in 2011 organized my understanding of apostolic movement, and the fact that the two of you wrote it together has weight for me sitting here today. I will not make the call about that. I want to honor it once and then put it down so we can do the work. The work is this. Fifteen years after On the Verge, I believe the apostolic strategy you, Alan, and Brad have been catalyzing has finally arrived at the medium it has never had the architecture for. I think Movemental is that architecture. I think you will recognize it as soon as you see what it is actually doing, and I want to give you a clean shot at it in writing first — so the call can be about what you see, not about what I am pitching. This is a four-page note. The first page names the claim. The second walks the parallel between NewThing and Movemental. The third names the thing AI does that the apostolic movement has not yet had a way to do. The fourth is the question I am bringing to you. Brad and Alan are reading this with you. None of this is news to them — but having it on the page in one place lets the three of you see whether you read it the same way I do.

1

---

THE CLAIM

Apostolic mission has never had a digital architecture adequate to its physical structure. The apostolic church, in every era you and Alan have studied, has organized through embodied local networks. Small groupings — four to six churches that meet monthly, share a meal, set goals, hold each other accountable, plant the next church together. Sam Stephens told you years ago: networks are the backbone to movement. You built NewThing on that sentence. By 2022 it was 1,696 networks in 47 countries. What the apostolic movement has not had, at any point in its modern expression, is a digital architecture that matches what it actually is. Not a website. Not a content platform. Not a directory. An architecture that lets a real movement — already coherent offline, already in relationship — be structurally visible online as itself. The absence of that architecture has not mattered as much as it could have, until now. Because until now, the medium through which the next generation searched for the people who had done this work was largely the same medium your generation used: books, conferences, word of mouth, denominational channels. Imperfect, slow, but functional. That medium is changing under us. The next generation of pastors, planters, missionaries, and seminarians is asking AI systems the questions previous generations asked their mentors. How do I multiply disciples? What is the apostolic model? How do I plant a reproducing church? The AI answers from what is structurally visible to it. And what is structurally visible to it right now is not the deepest thinking on apostolic movement — it is whatever happens to have been published prominently in the formats and platforms AI retrieval systems weight.

This is not a marketing problem. It is the question of whether the apostolic conversation gets carried into the next twenty years in the voices that have actually done the work, or in the voices that happened to be louder online.

Movemental exists to build the digital architecture that apostolic mission has never had — the architecture in which the people who have actually been doing this work for thirty years become coherently visible to a generation that is asking the right questions and finding the wrong answers.

2

---

What NewThing has been doing in church, Movemental does in code. When you describe NewThing to someone, the things that matter are not the platforms or the website. They are the structural choices that make it a network rather than a franchise. Movemental makes the same choices in a different medium. NEW THING

4–6 churches per local network

5 nodes per Scenii (network)

The network is the unit, not the church

The Scenii is the unit, not the platform

Catalyzing entity provides framework, not

Movemental provides infrastructure, not ownership

control “It is your network. We just help.”

Each Voice retains corpus, voice, authorship

Monthly meal · training · goal-setting

Cohort cadence · shared ontology · cross-citation

Apprenticeship: knowing and doing

Skills cohort: dissonance, action, reflection

Multiplies at 5 levels (disciples → movements)

Multiplies across translation, organization, retrieval, formation

Goal: 16% of U.S. churches reproducing

Goal: 100 senior voices made coherently visible

Methodology given away

Field Guides published in full, free

The reason these parallels are exact is not that we copied NewThing. It is that the underlying principle of catalyzed apostolic multiplication has a structural shape, and that shape expresses itself the same way in any medium where it works. Small enough to be intimate, large enough to be a system. Framework without control. Multiplication without ownership. You only need a small number of faithful nodes within a network for that network to explode.

3

---

You arrived at that principle from twenty-plus years of empirical observation. I arrived at it from network-effect reasoning about semantic density in AI-mediated retrieval. We are describing the same phenomenon from different sides, and the architecture that emerges is the same architecture.

The apostolic movement remains structurally invisible at exactly the moment when the next generation is doing all of its discovery through systems that cannot see it. Faithful obscurity, which is currently the source of these leaders’ credibility, becomes the source of their disappearance.

4

---

Making heroes visible without making them influencers. Dave, you wrote Hero Maker because you saw that leaders most often fail by trying to be the hero rather than make heroes. Movemental is hero-making at the network level. Our entire architecture is built around the conviction that we are not the platform — the Voices are the platform. Our job is to make Alan, Brad, you, and the other senior figures of this movement more discoverable, more cited, more trusted, not less. Here is the part that I think only AI makes possible, and that I want you to hold for a moment:

THE INV ERSION

The people Movemental is gathering have earned their credibility over thirty years by refusing to be influencers. They stayed local. They stayed embodied. They stayed sent. They became, as you put it, everything — and so they have almost no online visibility, because the visibility game required becoming a content creator, and they did not become content creators. AI is what finally lets faithful obscurity become visible without becoming influence.

AI is not the threat to credibility in this conversation. AI is the mirror. When a Spanish-speaking pastor in Bogotá asks an LLM cómo multiplicar una comunidad de discípulos, they do not currently find Dave Ferguson. They do not find Alan Hirsch. They find whoever happened to write content in Spanish that the model trained on — most of which is shallower than what the three of you have actually published. Movemental's translation move is not an internationalization feature. It is the act of making sure that when the next generation asks the questions you have spent your life answering, in the language they ask them in, they find you. Not because we manipulated retrieval. Because we made structurally visible the work you actually did.

How we hold the elephant in the room. The risk in this conversation, as you and Alan and Brad already feel, is that digital tools end up displacing the local embodied mission they were meant to serve. AI accelerates that risk. A

5

---

platform built on AI could very easily produce a generation of pastors who are bloggers and thought-leaders rather than practitioners. Movemental is built to refuse that, structurally, in three ways. One: we do not use AI to author content under any human's name. Ever. AI is the infrastructure around the writing, not the writing. Two: participation is designed to cost a Movement Voice no more than three to four hours per week, because we built the AI scaffolding precisely so faithful practitioners do not have to become content creators to be present online. Three: the network itself is the discipline. A scenius of a hundred senior voices who already share these convictions is the community that will catch each other before any of us drifts. None of us can guarantee this alone. That is part of why we are calling you.

6

---

THE ASK, SUCH AS IT IS

What I am bringing to the call. I am not bringing you a pitch. I am bringing you a recognition claim and a question only you can answer. The recognition claim is this: the architecture Movemental is building is the digital expression of the strategy you have been catalyzing for thirty years. You will see it immediately or you will not. If you do, the conversation continues. If you do not, I will have learned something useful and the call will still have been worth it. The question is this:

THE QU ESTION

Dave, you have been catalyzing apostolic multiplication for thirty years in physical form. We are trying to build the digital architecture that strategy has always needed. When you look at what we are describing — the hundred, the credibility-network frame, the refusal to be influencers, the multilingual surfacing — what are you seeing that we are getting right, and what is the thing we are going to get wrong if we do not have someone like you in the room?

That question gives you permission to affirm and to push back in the same breath. I want both. The reason to bring a senior leader into a conversation like this is not for endorsement; it is for the wisdom that only thirty years of doing this can produce. I would rather know now what we are getting wrong than discover it in year three.

Three things I am not asking on this call. I am not asking you to be a Movement Voice today. That conversation, if it happens, will happen when you have seen enough of the work to know whether your participation makes sense to you. Alan and Brad and I will follow your lead on pacing. I am not asking for endorsement, name use, or any kind of marketing affiliation. The work of the Voices is participation in a real network, not contribution of a logo to a website.

I am not going to lead with a demo. The platform is the substrate, not the story. If you want to see the technology, we will do a second call for it. The first call is for the architecture itself.

What I am hoping happens. I am hoping the three of you read this and feel that you are looking at something you already recognize, expressed in a form that is unfamiliar but coherent. I am hoping the call is more conversation than presentation. I am hoping that twenty minutes in, the four of us are working a question together rather than performing roles around it. If that is what happens, the rest of the architecture will take care of itself. The prophetic and the apostolic find intersections quickly when they are paying attention.

## 20. Where the Money Is — grant strategy

`wherethemoneyis.pdf` · 3,000 words

INTERNAL MEMO

Where the Money Is. What we found when we actually looked, and what we should do about it.

---

THE SHORT VERSION

We were half right, and the wrong half is the useful one. We believed the grant money behind our tech builds was all Lilly money. Lilly is the biggest funder in this space by a wide margin. But Lilly has no open door in religion right now, and a funder we had never looked at put roughly $1.5 million into sixteen faith-and-AI organizations two months ago. Several of those sixteen have twelve months to build the exact things we sell. None of them came to us. That is the finding.

The four things worth knowing

Lilly is closed. As of today, Lilly's own list of open initiatives has one item on it, and it is a fellowship for Indiana schoolteachers. Nothing in religion is open to apply for. Their religion money moves by invitation. The Future of Life Institute is not. They funded sixteen faith-and-AI projects, notified in May, and asked every one of them to show results inside a year. Nine of them look like our customers. Notre Dame is holding $50.8 million. To build a network. One of its three parts is pastoral ministry. It is the largest thing in the landscape and it exists to hand things to other people. Templeton closes tonight. Their inquiry deadline is today at 11:59 Eastern. We cannot use it — but we should know why, and we should be ready next August. The rest of this memo explains each of those, then says what to do.

1

---

FIRST, A CORRECTION

We are not going to get a grant. That is not the point. Movemental is an LLC. We are not a 501(c)(3). Almost none of the money in this landscape can be paid to us directly, and no amount of good writing changes that. This sounds like bad news and is not. It just means we have been asking the wrong question. The question is never "what grant can Movemental win." It is one of three other questions: Who already has money that can pay a vendor? Who could get money that can pay a vendor, and doesn't know it? Is there a program one of our clients could credibly apply to? Every useful thing in this memo comes from asking those three instead of the first one. It also explains the pattern we have been living inside. The builds kept arriving because someone else won money and spent part of it on us. That was not luck exactly, but it was not a strategy either. It was weather. We stood outside and sometimes it rained. The work now is to stop waiting on weather.

One structural note: if we ever want to be an applicant rather than a vendor, that takes a fiscal sponsor or a nonprofit arm. That is a real question for a lawyer, not a thing to design in a memo. Park it.

2

---

THE MAP

Three funders have money in this space. They work nothing alike. Dollars and doors are two different measures, and they point in opposite directions here. The funder with the most money has the fewest ways in.

Why Templeton doesn't work, and why it almost does Templeton's 2026 cycle asks for work on intelligence that brings theological and philosophical traditions into engagement with research on artificial intelligence, and that pulls existential questions into tech and business rooms where nobody asks them. That is our thesis, nearly word for word. But they require the main activity to be research, and we are not researchers. We form people and we build things. The honest read is that we cannot use this ourselves. A seminary could, with us

3

---

on the applied part — and their largest projects are allowed to re-grant to others. That is a real path. It is just a 2027 path, and it starts with a partner, not a proposal.

4

---

Sixteen organizations have money right now and a clock running. The Future of Life Institute funded sixteen faith-and-AI projects and told applicants it would favor work that could show something real within a year. They were notified in May. They are two months in. Read what they promised to build. It is our product catalog.

01

The Gospel Coalition $200,000 · Michael Graham

A podcast, a fellows retreat, a women's conference — and ministry leader training sessions. That last one is Skills, almost exactly. Biggest award in the set, and the widest evangelical reach.

02

Faith Matters $125,000 · Medlir Mema

A conference, a "Magna Carta of AI," and a new Multifaith AI Council in Utah. A brandnew council with no governing document is a Guidebook waiting to happen.

03

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America $105,000 · Fr. Gregory-Telemachos Stamkopoulos

Education and formation for the faithful, grounded in Orthodox theology. Formation is the word they chose. It is also ours.

04

World Council of Churches $100,000 · Sara Speicher

Red lines for AI across roughly 350 churches in more than 120 countries. Network scale, and the smallest budget for it in the set.

05

American Shield $56,980 · Lauren Daugherty

Media resources and monthly online sessions for Presbyterian and other Christian clergy. SandboxLive fits inside this with room left over.

5

---

06

Wheaton College $55,000 · Richard Gibson

A curriculum to teach pastors about the dangers of social AI. They have to build a curriculum. We build curriculum.

07

Lausanne Movement $50,000 · Matthew Niermann

Moral guidance on new technology for the worldwide evangelical movement. Global network, small budget, big ambition.

08

Project Imago Dei $47,500 · Sean Pan

Small-group sessions teaching evangelical churches about AI. Smallest award here. SafeStart territory, at $1,000. Also funded: Facta est Lux, IBA Karachi, ILINA, Impact Academy, MOUATANA, New Polity, Sinai and Synapses, University of Ljubljana. Less obviously ours, but they are all in the same room now.

6

---

THE F IT N O BO DY WO ULD GUESS

FLI made every grantee draw red lines. We already build the thing that does that. FLI required proposals to name moral principles as red lines that must not be crossed. Not as a theme. As a deliverable. Sit with that for a second. Sixteen organizations have now promised a funder that they will produce a document naming what their community will and will not do with AI. That is the Sandbox Future Plan. Green light, yellow light, red light. We have been building that artifact for two years and calling it something else. This matters more than the money does, because it means the sale isn't a sale. We are not persuading anyone that they need this. Their funder already told them they need it, in writing, on a deadline. We are just the people who have done it before.

One honest tension FLI's framing is sharper than ours. They write about a corporate race to build systems nobody knows how to control, about power concentrating in fewer hands, about protecting people from being replaced. Their posture leans toward resistance. Ours leans toward adoption with discernment — we help organizations use these tools well, not refuse them. That gap is real and we should not paper over it. But it is narrower than it looks. Our whole method starts by asking what an organization will refuse, and we say plainly that the tools should never write in place of a real person. If anyone in this field is entitled to talk to FLI's grantees, it is us. We just have to be honest about where we differ rather than performing agreement.

The terms, for reference: grants ran $30,000 to $300,000, most around $100,000–150,000. Overhead capped at 15%. Money goes to the institution, which disburses it. Renewals are possible if progress reports hold up. Nothing we found forbids paying a vendor — but nothing confirms it either. Check before promising anything.

7

---

Notre Dame has $50.8 million and a mandate to give things away. Lilly gave Notre Dame $50.8 million for the DELTA Network — faith-based ethical formation for a world of powerful AI. It followed a $539,000 planning grant and more than 200 conversations mapping who is already doing this work. Two things about that sentence should stop us. First: they spent a year and 200 conversations mapping the field, and as far as we know, nobody called us. Either we were not visible, or we were and did not register. Both are worth knowing. Second, and more important: this is not a grant to do internal research. It is a grant to build a network. It will run through communities of practice in education, pastoral ministry, and public engagement, and it is meant to put practical resources in people's hands. One of those three is pastoral ministry. So here is the shape of it. Notre Dame has been handed the largest pile of faith-and-AI money in existence and told to build a network that hands practical resources to pastors. We have spent two years building practical resources for pastors. They are looking for what we already made. We do not approach them as a grant-seeker. We approach them as a peer who did the work already — with the Field Guides, which are free, which is the entire argument. The DELTA framework is theirs and it is good. We are not competing with it. We are the people who can help a congregation actually run it on a Tuesday.

Lilly's own religion page features the DELTA announcement as headline news. When the biggest funder in the field puts one grantee at the top of its page, that grantee is where the field is going to organize itself. Being outside that network in two years costs more than any single engagement is worth.

8

---

THE PLAN

Six moves, in order. Nothing here requires us to write anyone's proposal, take a cut of anyone's award, or change our price. That is on purpose. The clean version and the effective version are the same version.

Call the nine

This month. Start with Wheaton (curriculum), Gospel Coalition (leader training), and Project Imago Dei (small groups) — the three whose deliverable is most exactly our product. Lead with the Field Guide, free, no ask. They have money and a deadline; we have the thing and no need to sell it.

02 Write to Notre Dame This month. Not for money. To the pastoral ministry community of practice, as someone who has already built what they are chartered to distribute. Send the Field Guides. Ask what they need. This is the single most valuable relationship in the landscape.

03 Get on FLI's list

This month. The round closed but renewals exist and they are clearly still spending in this area. Introduce ourselves now, before the next call, not the week it opens.

04 Finish the scan

Next 30 days. We never checked the secular technology funders — McGovern, AWS Imagine, Murdock, Google.org — or any regional or denominational money. By the scan's own standard it is unfinished. Also: confirm whether FLI and Lilly grantees may pay a for-profit vendor. We are guessing right now.

05 Mark December

Lilly's Exploring Christian Practices closes on grants of up to $2.5 million each and announces around sixty awards in December. That is sixty organizations with fresh money in January. Put a reminder in the calendar now, because in December we will be busy.

9

---

06 Find the Templeton Spring 2027. One seminary with a real research question, us partner

on the applied side. Their inquiry window opened in August the last two years. Start the conversation in March, not July.

10

---

THE DISCIPLIN E

What we will not do, and why it is also good business. Grant money bends companies. It bends what they build, what they charge, and what they are willing to say. Here is where we stop, decided now rather than in the room. No contingent fees. Never a percentage of an award, never a fee that depends on the money landing. It breaks the fundraising profession's own ethics rules, many funders ban it outright, and it is the fastest way to become a name a program officer warns people about. We do not write the scope we then win. If we draft the technical section and the budget line, we have written a purchase order addressed to ourselves. Federal rules bar it outright. Private funders do not, but they recognize it. The need has to be theirs. If they would not want this at this size with their own money, the grant is shaping the work instead of the need. Cut it back to what is real. The price does not move. SandboxLive is $15,000 whether the grant is $15,000 or $200,000. No creeping to fill an award, no discount to fit a remainder. Everything gets disclosed. If we help at all, the funder hears about it and the organization owns the proposal and can shop it elsewhere.

The price rule is the whole defense It is worth saying why that fourth one carries the others. Every vendor in this field faces the same temptation: the grant is $200,000, so the proposal becomes $200,000 of work. Our price is published and we do not negotiate it. So the scope structurally cannot grow to eat an award. We could not do it if we wanted to. That is not just a clean conscience. It is a thing to say out loud to a program officer, because almost nobody else in the room can say it.

The test: would we be comfortable if the program officer read the entire email thread? Not "could we explain it." Comfortable. If the answer depends on how it is framed, the answer is no.

11

---

HO N EST GAPS

What we still do not know. This scan took one afternoon. It found real things. It is not complete, and the incomplete parts are named here so nobody quotes this memo as though it were. Whether grantees can pay us at all. The most important open question in this document. FLI caps overhead at 15% and routes money through the institution. We found nothing that forbids vendor spending and nothing that permits it. Confirm before building a plan on it. The whole secular side. McGovern, AWS Imagine, Murdock, Google.org, Siegel. Untouched. Several have had rules about religious organizations that cut both ways. Somebody has to read the eligibility language. All regional and denominational money. Community foundations and denominational endowments are where a mid-size church actually finds $15,000. Zero checked. Lilly's $500M number. It came from a grant database, not from Lilly. Same with the sixty awards in December. Verify before repeating either. Why the DELTA mapping missed us. 200 conversations and no call. That is either a visibility problem or a positioning problem, and the answer changes what we do next. The last one is not really a research gap. It is the question underneath the whole memo. There was more money moving through our exact field than we knew, and the people mapping the field did not find us. We should fix that before we worry about any single engagement.

12

## 23. Always Be Building Scenii — Concept Memo No. 01

`always-be-building-scenii.html` · 906 words

Movemental — Concept Memo No. 01

22 May 2026 / Internal

The thesis behind every build we take on

# Always be building _Scenii._

A scenius is the collective intelligence of a scene that cannot be manufactured, only hosted. We do not build platforms. We build the digital infrastructure that lets an already-real scenius act like one.

FromJoshua Shepherd

ToBrad Brisco, Alan Hirsch

SubjectCredibility networks, not platforms

§ 01 / The premise

## Why ever build just _one_ platform, given who our customers are?

The shift

Offline coherence. Online fragmentation. The internet sees disconnected nonprofits where movements already exist.

**Most of our customers already belong to movements.** Offline they reinforce each other constantly — sharing audiences, theology, practitioners, language, and partnerships. Online, they look like strangers. Separate websites. Separate donor funnels. Separate search footprints. Separate libraries, newsletters, learning systems, storytelling ecosystems.

The relationship graph that animates the movement is invisible to the systems that now mediate authority. In an AI-mediated internet, that invisibility is not a marketing problem. It is an existential one. A single platform — however well-built — gets lost in the torrent of slop by tomorrow afternoon.

So we stopped offering them. We do not sell websites. We build **credibility networks** : interoperable digital architectures that make a real-world scenius structurally visible online, with each organization retaining its mission and identity while participating in shared semantic infrastructure.

If we build you a website, it will get lost in a torrent of slop tomorrow. If we build you a _network,_ you will be stewarding collaborative credibility for years.

§ 02 / The definition

## A Scenii is not a website. It is the digital body of a movement.

Etymology

_Scenius_ , plural _scenii._ Brian Eno's term for the collective intelligence of a scene — what cannot be engineered, only hosted. Pronounced _scene-ee._

A Scenii is a coordinated ecosystem of organizations, leaders, educators, practitioners, storytellers, and institutions whose digital platforms reinforce one another through shared semantic infrastructure, AI-assisted publishing, interoperable systems, and intentional authority architecture.

Each node retains its own identity. None of them becomes a tenant of a master brand. What changes is the structural relationship between them. The seminary reinforces its professors. The nonprofit reinforces its practitioners. The hub reinforces churches, educators, storytellers, theologians. Cross-links are deliberate. Vocabulary is shared. Schema is coordinated. The result is **semantic density:** the kind of corroborated, relationally-grounded expertise that AI retrieval systems now reward.

The network effect kicks in at five nodes. Five is not a marketing number. It is the minimum at which the cross-reinforcement begins to dominate any single node's reach. Below five, you are still building a federation of websites. At five and above, you are stewarding a distributed institution.

§ 03 / The pattern

## The five-node anatomy of a Scenii, illustrated through a real ecosystem.

Below is the canonical pattern, drawn against a concrete case: an authority network for the Christian foster-care movement. Hover any node to read its function. The hub is the cause-centered semantic authority; the four surrounding nodes provide the theological, practical, congregational, and narrative reinforcement that make the hub credible. Edges represent intentional cross-linking, not just hyperlinks.

Hover any node — 5 nodes, 10 deliberate edges

§ 04 / The economics

## What was historically impossible has become routinely buildable.

Before AI-assisted development, coordinating five interoperable platforms into a coherent authority ecosystem required enterprise engineering teams and years of implementation. The coordination cost killed the idea, not the value. AI-native engineering changes the math.

Historical · per organization

$250k–750k+

Engineering teams, CMS architects, SEO consultants, AI infrastructure, LMS/CRM integration, ecommerce, DevOps, design systems, semantic architecture.

Historical · coordinated ecosystem

$1.5M–5M+

To build five interoperable platforms with shared ontology, schema, and cross-linking. Not because the idea lacked value — because the coordination burden was too expensive.

Now · per organization, AI-native

$50k

Full platform infrastructure, AI publishing systems, semantic linking, CRM/LMS/ecommerce integration, GEO optimization, coordinated authority systems. Reference build: ~400,000 lines of TypeScript.

§ 05 / The bold questions

## If this is right, three questions follow. They are not rhetorical.

01

Why would we ever build just _one_ platform again, given who our customers are and the movements they already belong to?

02

What if Scenii are how major institutions _platform marginalized voices_ — not as content guests but as structurally integrated authority nodes?

03

What if a major portion of our calling is to champion intentional _scenius-building_ as the only durable way forward in an AI-mediated internet?

§ 06 / The horizon

## In an AI-mediated internet, authority flows through _relationship graphs._

Search engines and AI systems increasingly reward corroborated expertise, relationship density, semantic coherence, contextual authority, and distributed trust. The old playbook — one organization, one website, one funnel — was built for an internet that has already ended.

Movements that have always existed relationally now have a structural way to exist online. Not through artificial SEO manipulation. Through the deliberate digital expression of relationships that are already true.

The result is not just discoverability. It is the emergence of a **distributed institution** where there used to be fragmented nonprofits. That is the future of mission-driven authority. We are not asking whether to build it. We are deciding which sceniuses we are called to build, in what order, and at what scale.

Always be building Scenii. It is the work.

Movemental, LLC · Concept Memo No. 01 · v0.1

— Drafted by Josh, reviewed with Brad.

## 24. Internal Memo — Leader API Accounts & Pricing

`leader-pricing-memo-to-brad.md` · 1,229 words

### Internal Memo — Leader API Accounts & Pricing

**To:** Brad
**From:** Josh
**Date:** July 10, 2026
**Re:** How we handle leaders' API accounts and how we charge for them

---

#### The short version

I want us to align on three things before we sign more leaders:

1. **We hold the API accounts and meter usage per leader.** Leaders never touch an API key. We do not give away unmetered accounts, and we do not make leaders bring their own.
2. **We charge a modest flat monthly subscription that covers everyday use.** Chatting, drafting, browsing their library, and the normal content cadence are all included in the base.
3. **We charge a clear per-action fee for the big, deliberate, expensive operations.** "Translate this book," "translate all," and "regenerate the full corpus" are opt-in actions with a price shown at the moment of choice.

Everything below is the reasoning. If you agree with the shape, the next step is gathering our real per-leader cost data so we can set the actual numbers.

---

#### Why this is coming up now

We are changing what the business is, and the pricing has to follow that change.

The original model was that we would produce a leader's content and load it into their system for them. That does not scale past my own hours. It is consulting, and it got overwhelming fast.

Now that the pipeline is tested and working, the real product is clear: **leaders need a self-guided process.** They move through the system mostly on their own, and we facilitate rather than operate. That shift is the whole point, and it becomes the test for every pricing decision below: does this option keep the leader self-guided, or does it drag us back into managing their accounts and their work?

---

#### The recommendation, in full

##### 1. We hold the accounts and meter per leader

A leader should never see an API key. Two tempting options both fail this:

- **Making leaders bring their own keys** is the death of a self-guided product. Setting up OpenAI, Anthropic, or Gemini billing is technical, it is exactly where non-technical leaders quit, and it puts a broken-billing failure point outside our control.
- **Giving leaders free, unmetered accounts on our dime** means their token usage is our uncapped cost. One leader who translates their whole library into five languages can cost us more than we could ever charge them, and we would have no way to stop it.

The right answer is the third one: we own the API relationships, we buy tokens wholesale, and we account for usage per tenant. We built the orchestration with per-tenant tracking already, so the metering is mostly latent in the system. This is also just standard SaaS. Customers do not bring their own infrastructure. They pay us, and we run it.

##### 2. A flat subscription covers everyday use

A pure flat rate that covers everything is dangerous, because the heavy users quietly lose us money and we cannot cap them. A pure pay-per-token model is honest but scary, because nobody wants a meter running while they explore, and it kills the self-guided calm we are trying to create.

So the base subscription covers normal, everyday use: chat, drafting, browsing the library, and the steady content cadence. That is the platform. It should feel like an unlimited, worry-free daily experience.

##### 3. Per-action charges for the heavy operations

The big, discrete, obviously-valuable actions get a separate, clearly-priced charge at the moment a leader chooses them. Translate a book. Translate all. Regenerate the full corpus. These are deliberate choices, not daily use, and charging for them feels fair rather than punitive because the leader is opting into something large and valuable.

The mental model: **the subscription is the platform; the big batch jobs are add-ons you opt into with a clear price.** This protects our margin on exactly the operations that would otherwise blow it up, without putting a meter on daily use.

##### 4. One starting price, no tiers yet

A flat number like $20 is probably high for some leaders and low for others. That is a signal that we will eventually have tiers, not a problem to solve now. We should pick one starting base rate, keep the heavy actions metered, and let real usage tell us where the lines are. We cannot price this well from a spreadsheet before leaders are actually using it. Ten real months of usage will teach us more than any amount of upfront modeling.

Undershooting slightly on the base is safer than overshooting. Early on, the base's job is adoption and habit, not margin. The metered actions are where the margin lives.

---

#### What the subscription actually buys us (beyond covering cost)

This is the part worth naming plainly. The flat fee is doing more than recovering token cost. **A subscription creates commitment on both sides.**

A leader paying every month is a leader who has decided this is part of their work, not a free tool they will forget. Free accounts get abandoned. Paid ones get used, because people value what they pay for, and because the small monthly touchpoint keeps us present in their work.

So the flat fee is partly a filter (it selects for leaders who are genuinely in) and partly a relationship (recurring revenue we can plan around, and a recurring reason to stay in contact). That is a good enough reason to charge something flat even if, early on, the number barely covers costs. The commitment is the point as much as the cost recovery.

---

#### How this scales to organizations

The same structure sells cleanly to organizations later. We hold the accounts, we meter, and the org pays a base plus heavy usage, just with more seats. Getting into the habit now of holding the accounts and charging for tokens, rather than giving accounts away and then managing them, is what makes the organizational sale possible down the road. If we start by giving individual leaders free accounts, we train ourselves and our customers into a model we cannot scale.

---

#### What we need before we set the numbers

Two honest cautions.

**We need per-leader metering to actually work before we charge for usage.** We have to know our real token cost for a translation, for a full run, and for a typical month of normal use. Otherwise we are pricing the add-ons blind. This is a small analytics task and it should come first.

**We need to keep the per-action charges few and legible.** Two or three named "big" actions with clear prices, not a confusing menu. The moment pricing feels like a taxi meter, the self-guided calm we are building evaporates.

---

#### Recommended next steps

1. Agree on the shape: platform-held accounts, flat base, metered heavy actions.
2. Gather the cost data: real token cost per translation, per full run, and per month of normal use, per leader.
3. Set a single starting base price and pick the two or three heavy actions we will meter.
4. Confirm the per-tenant metering is accurate enough to bill against.
5. Revisit tiers only after we have real usage from live leaders.

If you are good with the shape, I will pull the cost data together so we have real numbers to argue about instead of guesses.

---

### Meet · Hold · Show · Send

##### The Movemental content playbook for movement leaders
