## 26. Content Strategy for Movement Leaders

`movemental-content-strategy-for-movement-leaders.md` · 3,428 words

### Content Strategy for Movement Leaders
##### The Movemental single source of truth for how to think about your public work

*For the movement leaders of the hundred — and for the team who serves them. This is the canonical account of why we make content the way we do, what to make, and how. It is written to you, the leader, in the voice we mean to keep: partners who have been on this road, not experts standing over you.*

---

#### A word before the strategy

You did not say yes to becoming a content creator. You said yes to letting your life-work — the books, the talks, the frameworks, the fragments scattered across fifteen years of platforms that may or may not still exist — be gathered into a coherent home that the age can recognize. Hold onto that. Everything in this document serves that yes. The moment any of it starts to feel like feeding a machine, we have lost the plot, and you should tell us.

So read this less as a marketing playbook and more as an account of stewardship. The credibility was already yours. We are making sure it survives.

---

#### Part I — Why this exists

Strategy that doesn't start with the real problem becomes technique for its own sake. So start with the problem, which has a name: **fragmentation.**

Take one real person. You have spent decades planting, teaching, writing, shaping how people understand the church on mission. The work is real and it is vast. But ask the simple question — *where is it?* The honest answer is a list of scattered containers. Books locked in formats that don't speak to each other. Articles on old sites. Talks surviving as unindexed video, or not at all. Frameworks you originated that now live more in other people's paraphrases than in any home of your own. **The work was whole in you. It has been scattered into the world, and most people will never do the dig.**

Fragmentation has two faces, and you feel both:

- **Informational fragmentation — what you know, scattered.** Your ideas exist, but in pieces, across containers that can't see each other. No center of gravity. When someone searches the very question you have spent your life answering, they don't find you; they find noise, or someone else's version of your idea.
- **Relational fragmentation — who you know, scattered, and invisible.** Because your work is in pieces, you cannot see the people moving through it. You don't know that a reader found one idea in a post, bought a book, took a course, and started teaching it in her own church. **That journey — which is the entire point — is invisible to you, because the work the journey runs through is itself shattered.** One scattering, two faces: what is known and who it is for, both broken in the same event.

Now bring AI into that room. People assume it will pull the pieces together. By default it does the opposite. AI is a mirror; it reflects back what it is given, and what it is given is fragmentation. Ask a model to represent a scattered author and it assembles an answer from whatever shards it can find and hands back something that wears the name without carrying the person. That is what everyone has learned to call slop. **Slop is not simply low quality. Slop is fragmentation, reflected and multiplied** — and it flows back into the world, gets indexed, gets trained on, and becomes the next layer of the scattering.

Underneath even that sits the **authorship break**: for the first time in five hundred years, a faithful reader opening your newest piece has to ask a question that never had to be asked — *is this still you, or a model wearing your name?* When people can't answer and can't keep paying the cost of wondering, they withdraw. And publication — the word that crosses distance and outlives the one who wrote it — is one of the oldest ways truth has traveled. This is not a marketing problem. It is closer to a civilizational one.

**That is why content strategy exists here.** Not to grow a following. To heal fragmentation — to gather what is scattered into a coherent home, to make the invisible journey visible, and to keep your authorship legible in an age that would otherwise dissolve it.

---

#### Part II — The one conviction underneath everything

Before any tactic, one conviction: **the word is yours, and it comes first.**

You have something to say that is genuinely yours — a body of thinking, hard-won and lived. That authored word is generative and prior. It is the substrate from which everything else is made. Strategy *serves* it; strategy never originates it. We will use AI as the infrastructure around the writing — to gather, to shape into findable form, to surface the journey. We will not use AI to author it. Every word that goes out under your name is yours. That distinction is not negotiable, for us or for you.

Two disciplines follow directly, and they are load-bearing for everything below:

- **Corpus-grounding.** Your published work is not merely source material to cite; it is the ground from which new pieces are drawn. Claims, frameworks, and examples come from your actual corpus, paraphrased for the web, never invented. If the corpus doesn't support it, it stays out.
- **No invented quotes.** Every quotation attributed to you is a real quote from a real source, with the citation visible. AI may summarize your positions; it may never put words in your mouth.

Keep these in view. They are what make it *your* platform rather than a machine wearing your name.

---

#### Part III — The frame: SAY → FIND → MOVE

Here is the whole strategy in three moves, in order. This is not a new vocabulary bolted onto your work; it *names and sequences* what your corpus already teaches.

**SAY — the authored word.** What is actually yours to say. This is the moment of authorship (Part II). It is first and non-negotiable. Nothing downstream is worth anything if the word underneath it isn't real and yours.

**FIND — can people meet you where they are searching for what you say, even if they don't know your name?** This is the work of translating your sealed corpus into forms discovery systems can read — and it is exactly the job of the Evergreen Engine (Part VII). Findability does not invent authority; it *renders* authority you already have into a shape machines can see.

**MOVE — can it move them *through* your work?** In two senses at once: as **compelling form** in the medium you're working in, and as **participation in their own transformation** — the way a piece leads someone to grow, not just to know. This is the work of the four necessities and the formation pathways (Part VI).

##### Why the order is the whole game

The order is not cosmetic. "Meet them where they're searching" is a knife that cuts both ways. Run it **first** and it quietly inverts: you start writing toward search demand, chasing what's ranking, until the voice is gone and you are a content farm with good theology — you become the slop. Run it **second**, as a *check on a word you already had to say*, and it becomes faithful distribution instead of pandering.

So: **you say your thing first. Then you ask whether people can find it. Then you ask whether it moves them.** Findability serves authorship. It never precedes it.

##### The two questions

Everything above resolves into two questions you ask *after* you've said what you have to say — and you ask them *with* us, not because we've answered them over your head:

1. **Can people meet you where they are searching for what you say — even if they don't know your name?** (Including your past work, repurposed.)
2. **Can it move them through your work** — both as compelling form, and as their own transformation, the way your work leads them to grow or participates in that growth?

Hold these two questions. They are the diagnostic you run on any single piece and on your body of work as a whole.

---

#### Part IV — Who it's for and where they are

Relational fragmentation is the invisible journey. The cure is to make that journey visible — which means knowing that your audience is not a single undifferentiated "following" but people at different points on a path. Roughly:

- **Stranger.** Doesn't know your name. Has a question you happen to answer. Finds you by searching — or increasingly, by asking a machine. (Heavily a **FIND** stage.)
- **Knows you.** Has met your work once and is deciding whether to come back. Wants a reason to stay in relationship. (The threshold stage — where an owned channel earns trust.)
- **Being formed.** Has committed to being changed, not just informed. Willing to do the work over time. (Heavily a **MOVE** stage.)
- **Participant / multiplier.** No longer just receiving — practicing, teaching it to others, reproducing the movement. The whole point.

The strategic question that used to feel impossible — *when do I make each kind of thing?* — mostly resolves here. You are not choosing between parallel options. You are choosing **which move you are making, for whom, on this path.** That is answerable in a sentence, and Part V gives you the map.

---

#### Part V — What to make: the content types as stations on the journey

The seven content types in your studio are not a flat menu. They are **stations along the path from stranger to participant,** each tuned differently across FIND and MOVE. This is the "when and why" — best practices live with the doing (Part VI), not here.

| Type | Leans | Reach for it when… | On the journey |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Article** | FIND | you have a discrete answer to a real question people ask | a stranger finds you |
| **Article (academic)** | FIND + authority | a claim needs evidence, or you want to be *citable* by scholars and by AI engines | a stranger, and the machines, find you credibly |
| **Book** | SAY (deep) | you have a whole framework, not a point — the canonical statement and the wellspring everything else is drawn from | authority + source |
| **Lesson → Course** | MOVE | you want to take someone A→B over time — developmental, not informational | being formed |
| **Newsletter** | MOVE (cadence) | you want to keep a warm, algorithm-proof relationship and a regular presence | knows-you |
| **Podcast** | FIND + MOVE | you think aloud well, or want to leverage guests' networks | discovery + intimacy |
| **Video** | FIND + MOVE | the message needs face, demonstration, or emotion | discovery + compellingness |
| **Event** | MOVE (embodied) | transformation needs bodies and real time — you're catalyzing a moment | audience becomes participant |

A note on the **book**: it sits across the whole thing. It is both the deep authority a stranger might discover *and* the wellspring every other piece repurposes from. In the studio it is quite literally the corpus your platform and your agent draw on. Treat it as the center, not one station among equals.

---

#### Part VI — How to make it *move*: the four necessities

Here is what separates a **formation engine** from a publishing site, and it is non-negotiable: **transformation over information.** A piece that merely informs — however true, however well-written — has not yet earned the attention it asks for. Across every artifact type, aim to carry the four necessities. A single piece need not fully deliver all four, but it should gesture toward all four, and never be missing all of them.

1. **Dissonance.** The reader meets something that disturbs their existing categories — not for shock, but for the theological and cognitive tension that opens the possibility of seeing differently. A piece that only confirms what the reader already thinks has failed, even if it's true.
2. **Action.** The reader is given something specific and time-bounded to *do* — not "ten things to consider," an actual embodied practice. Action is not optional; it is constitutive of formation.
3. **Reflection.** The reader has a structured way to think about what happened when they acted — the discipline that converts experience into wisdom.
4. **Community.** The reader is pointed toward, or placed in, others doing the same work. Solitary formation is incomplete formation. The platform gathers practitioners, not just individuals.

This is the editorial spine of everything — article, newsletter, course week, event. Its fullest expression is the guided lesson scaffold (Dissonance → Reflection → Practice → Community → Integration → Going Deeper), but the four necessities live in a good article too. When you ask the second question — *does this move them through my work?* — this is what you're checking for.

MOVE's other sense, **compelling form**, is craft: does the piece hold attention and carry feeling in its medium? A dull true thing doesn't move anyone. Both senses matter, and the studio's media surfaces (podcast, video) exist partly so the form can carry what prose alone can't.

---

#### Part VII — How to make it *found*: the Evergreen Engine

The Engine does one thing: **it takes a finished body of work and makes it findable.** You have already done the hard part — the ideas, the frameworks, the research. What's missing is *form*. A book is a sealed container; search engines can't read it and answer engines can't quote it. The Engine translates that sealed work into the shapes discovery systems are built to read — a definition, a glossary entry, an FAQ answer, a numbered framework. **It does not invent authority. It renders authority you already have into a form the machines can see.**

Three ideas make this real:

- **E-E-A-T** — Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trustworthiness — is the standard search and answer engines use to judge quality. Most sites strain to fake it. You already have it; it's just trapped in books. Grounding every sentence in your corpus, naming the sources, and holding your vocabulary steady is how real expertise becomes visible to a system that otherwise can't see it.
- **Hub-and-spoke (pillar / cluster).** Your major themes become **pathways** — pillar hubs — and the articles beneath each become the spokes that link inward and outward. Coherence, not just volume, is what makes a body of work legible to both readers and machines. (For Alan, the pathways are mDNA, Metanoia, Reframation, Discipleship, and Movement Intelligence; yours are the major streams of your own work.)
- **Repurposing as multiplication.** This is the same word, stewarded into many shapes: a **book chapter → an article → a lesson → a podcast talking-point → clips → a newsletter issue.** A podcast's **transcript → an article.** An event's **recording → a video, its recap → a newsletter.** Repurposing is not repackaging for its own sake; it is refusing to let a word you already paid for stay sealed in one container.

Findability, done this way, is the answer to Question 1 — and it is how your coherent signal eventually makes its way back into the AI systems themselves, so that when the next generation asks the machine *what is the missional church, what is discipleship, what is movement,* the answer is informed by you, in your own words, rather than by the noise.

---

#### Part VIII — The Studio as instrument

The frame is not abstract; it is wired into the tool you use. Learning to see the studio through SAY → FIND → MOVE turns a set of fields into a strategy you can feel.

**The DETAILS drawer splits cleanly along your two questions.**

- **The FIND apparatus** — definition anchor, citable statistic, FAQ, citation, and the academic fields — is what makes you answerable to search and to AI engines, even when the reader doesn't know your name. These render your E-E-A-T machine-legible. Filling them well is how a stranger finds you.
- **The MOVE apparatus** — the body's compellingness, plus the pathway / series / *isPartOf* wiring — is what carries someone deeper. The pathway and series fields are not metadata housekeeping; they are how you connect a single piece into the *body* of your work, so a reader can move through it rather than land on an island. This is where you heal relational fragmentation: you make the journey visible.

**The academic modifier** is your citability setting — turn it on when a claim needs evidence scaffolding or when you want to be quoted by scholars and by answer engines. It is FIND in its most authoritative form.

**The publication themes** (mDNA, Metanoia, Reframation) let a piece wear the identity of the stream it belongs to.

So the two questions become a habit at the station: after you've said your thing, glance at the FIND fields (*can they find this?*) and the MOVE wiring (*does this connect into my body of work and carry them somewhere?*). The studio is built to let you answer both.

---

#### Part IX — Where to begin

Strategy that can't be started is just a poster. So, concretely:

- **Publish first.** The floor is always: get one true thing out, cleanly, to completion. Never let strategy talk block a leader from finishing a piece. Confidence comes from having crossed the line, once.
- **Prove one cluster before scaling.** Take your richest, most foundational theme first and build it out fully — the pillar and its articles, interlinked. That one complete cluster is both the proving ground and the cleanest demonstration of the whole. Then fill the matrix theme by theme; it becomes a fill-the-slots exercise rather than a blank page.
- **Start where fear is lowest and volume is highest.** For most leaders that's **articles and the newsletter** — the FIND floor and the owned relationship. Build toward **course and event**, where the deepest transformation lives but the craft demand is highest.
- **Cadence over heroics.** A regular, owned rhythm (the newsletter) beats sporadic brilliance. Presence is a form of faithfulness.

---

#### Part X — The non-negotiables

These are the guardrails. When a decision is unclear, these decide it.

- **Every word that goes out under your name is yours.** AI is the infrastructure around the writing, never the writing.
- **Corpus-grounded, sources named, no invented quotes.** If your work doesn't support it, it stays out.
- **Transformation over information.** Every piece gestures toward the four necessities. Informing is not the goal; formation is.
- **Say first — never open a piece from search demand.** Findability is a check on an authored word, not its origin. The day we reverse that, we've started making slop.
- **Partner posture.** We teach and decide *with* you, framing choices and their tradeoffs, not prescribing over you. The strategic calls that are yours to make stay yours.
- **You are not alone in the frame.** Your pieces link to your peers' — the hundred is a *scenius*, a scene whose collective intelligence no one can manufacture, only host. Your coherence deepens theirs, and theirs yours.

---

#### Coda — what this is finally about

We do not call this a strategy. We call it a **stewardship.**

The wound was fragmentation — your whole word scattered into pieces the world can't reassemble, and the people moving through your work invisible to you. The cure is not more content. It is coherence: your authored word, gathered into a home, made findable in forms the age can read, and wired so that the journey through it becomes visible at last. SAY, then FIND, then MOVE. The credibility was always yours. We are only making sure it survives — and that when someone finds it, it can still move them.

---

*This is the single source of truth for content strategy on the platform. It sits above any one feature or tutorial; the per-type "how to cook this" guidance in the studio, and the four-layer station tutorials, are downstream of the convictions here. Update it when the convictions change — rarely — not when the tactics do.*

*Grounded in the Movemental corpus: the fragmentation thesis, the moment of authorship, the transformation-over-information necessities, the Evergreen Engine, and the letter to the hundred.*

---

## 27. The context method

`the-context-method.md` · 2,775 words

### The context method

##### How an organization's working reality is gathered, made reachable, and turned into a decision

*Method document. Six phases, twenty-two steps.*

---

#### What this is

A structured process for establishing how work actually moves through an organization, converting that into a reachable context layer, and producing a determination about what should happen next.

It runs about fifty hours of gathering and fifteen of synthesis, plus one meeting.

**Its output is not a recommendation. It is an artifact, and a decision that follows from the artifact.** What that decision turns out to be is not known at the start and is not supposed to be.

#### The principle it rests on

Every improvement an AI system can make to an organization happens at a moment of interface between a person and the system. There is nowhere else for value to enter.

Those moments occur only inside the discrete acts that make up somebody's work.

**Therefore the set of possible improvements is bounded by the set of acts in the organization's workflows**, and that set is finite and enumerable.

Which means an organization that has not mapped its workflows cannot know its own opportunity space. Not has not got around to it. Cannot, because the space is defined by acts nobody has articulated.

#### Two properties of the artifact

**It is tool-independent.** Models change, vendors change, plans change. A map of how work moves through a building is stable for years and every subsequent decision runs on it.

**It is complete on its own.** If nothing is built afterward, the organization owns a working description of itself that it did not previously have.

---

### Phase 0 · Frame

*Roughly 3 hours. Before anything is gathered.*

##### 0.1 · Scope and access

Establish which parts of the organization are in scope, who authorizes access, and whether the sponsor decides or recommends.

**Output.** A one-page scope note, agreed in writing.
**Gate.** Do not proceed without knowing who decides. Discovering it in week five is the single most common cause of a stalled engagement.

##### 0.2 · Role census

List every distinct role, not every person. Two people doing the same job is one role. One person doing two jobs is two.

**Output.** A role list with a name against each, marked for interview order.
**Failure mode.** Accepting the org chart. It describes reporting, not work. Ask the person who books the meetings who actually gets pulled into things.

##### 0.3 · Artifact request

Request what exists, in whatever state it exists. Ten categories. Do not ask anyone to prepare, summarize, or clean anything.

**Output.** Whatever arrives, plus a record of what was requested and did not.
**The absence is data.** A category that produces nothing has told you more than one that produces forty files.

---

### Phase 1 · Intake

*Roughly 8 hours. Before the first interview.*

##### 1.1 · Inventory what came in

Every document, its form, its date, where it lives, whether it is current, and whether a machine could reach it as it stands.

**Output.** The artifact inventory, first pass, with a reachability state against each row.

##### 1.2 · System inventory

What holds the work. Project system, file storage, communication, finance, and whatever else. Note what is authoritative and what is a copy.

**Output.** A systems list marked for whether each is reachable, and by whom.

##### 1.3 · Build the provisional map from documents alone

Before speaking to anyone, construct the workflow as the documents describe it.

**This is the official version and it is going to be wrong.** Build it anyway, because the gap between it and what people say is one of the two most valuable findings in the whole process.

**Output.** A provisional flow diagram, explicitly labelled as the documented version.

##### 1.4 · Hypothesis set

Name the three to six flows you expect to find, and write down what you expect each interview to confirm.

**Why.** So that a surprise registers as a surprise. Without a stated expectation, everything sounds equally interesting and nothing stands out.

**Output.** A written hypothesis sheet, dated. Do not revise it during the interviews. Revise it once, in Phase 3, on the record.

---

### Phase 2 · Interview

*Roughly 30 to 35 hours. One hour per role.*

##### 2.1 · The instrument

**Twelve questions. Same twelve, every role, every time.** Consistency is what makes triangulation possible. Where a role requires a follow-up, ask it after the twelve, not instead of one.

**1. Walk me through the last piece of work you finished. Start from the moment you first heard about it.**
*A specific recent job, never a general description. General descriptions produce the official version. A specific job produces what happened.*

**2. Where did it wait?**
*Queue detection. People will name waiting readily because it is not their fault.*

**3. What did you have to go and find out that somebody else here already knew?**
*Context reconstruction, measured directly.*

**4. Who did you have to ask?**
*Produces the real network, which is never the org chart.*

**5. What did you have to explain to someone that you had already explained to someone else?**
*Seam detection. Every repetition is information failing to travel with the artifact.*

**6. Where in this is there an actual rule, and where is it just how we do it?**
*Separates decided from habitual. This question produces the undecided register and nothing else does.*

**7. What would you have to tell a new person that is not written down anywhere?**
*The tacit extractor. Ask it slowly and wait through the silence.*

**8. What part of your job is not a sequence? Where are you just thinking?**
*The craft exclusion. Marks what must not be decomposed.*

**9. What do you put into an AI tool now, if anything, and on what account?**
*Asked without judgment, in a flat voice, as an inventory question. It is one.*

**10. What would you never put into one?**
*People name their own line, and the lines they name are usually better than the policy would have been.*

**11. If you got two hours a week back, what would you do with them?**
*The value anchor. Also the only question in the set that is about them rather than about the work.*

**12. Who else should I be talking to?**
*Census correction. Run until the names stop being new.*

##### 2.2 · Recording protocol

Every interview recorded, with consent, stated at the top: this is recorded, it is not shown to anyone as an individual response, and nothing attributed to you appears anywhere.

**The reason recording matters is not capture. It is that it frees the interviewer to listen.**

Extraction happens downstream. In the room, do not take structured notes and do not attempt to build the map. One job only: listen.

##### 2.3 · What to listen for

Not content. The transcript holds the content. Listen for the things that will not survive transcription.

**Hesitation before an answer about who decides.** Almost always an undecided rather than an unknown.

**"Technically we're supposed to."** The gap between the documented process and the real one, offered voluntarily.

**"It depends."** Followed by a pause. Either genuine judgment, which is a craft marker, or an unresolved rule, which is not. Ask which.

**A handoff described differently than the person on the other side described it an hour ago.** The highest-value finding available and it only appears across interviews.

**A workaround, described casually.** People do not flag these because they have stopped noticing.

**A person named where a role should be.** Single points of failure announce themselves this way.

**Anything said with a laugh.** Almost always a known broken thing that everyone has agreed not to fix.

##### 2.4 · Order

Operations or traffic first, because they see the whole flow and their account is the frame everything else adjusts against.

Then the disciplines, in the order work moves.

Leadership last, not first. A leadership account taken early becomes the frame and distorts everything after it.

**And at least one person who has been using AI on their own initiative, whoever that turns out to be.** Frequently the most useful hour in the whole phase.

**Gate.** Stop interviewing when question twelve stops producing new names. Continuing past that point costs money and adds nothing.

---

### Phase 3 · Integration

*Roughly 12 hours. Where the map is actually made.*

##### 3.1 · Transcribe and structure

Every recording to text, then to a structured document with the twelve questions as the spine. Machine-assisted, checked by a person.

**Output.** One structured document per interview, plus a combined corpus organized by question rather than by person.

##### 3.2 · Extract against the known targets

The targets are known in advance, which is what makes this tractable. For each interview, extract:

Acts and their sequence · queues and their causes · handoffs · context reconstruction moments · rules, marked as decided or habitual · tacit knowledge, marked as articulable or not · craft, marked as not-a-sequence · tools in use, sanctioned and not · data categories touched · stated refusals.

**Output.** Ten extraction sets, each traceable to the interview it came from.
**Rule.** Nothing enters an extraction set without a pointer to the source. An extraction with no provenance is an opinion.

##### 3.3 · Triangulate

Compare every account of the same flow against every other.

**Agreement is not the finding. Contradiction is.** Where account and traffic describe the same handoff differently, the truth is in neither and the seam is real.

**Output.** A contradiction register, ranked by how much work passes through each contested point.

##### 3.4 · Second pass on contested seams

Go back to the two or three seams where the accounts conflict most, with both parties, separately, and ask about that specific handoff.

**This is not optional and it is where most of the value in the whole method concentrates.** It is also the step most likely to be cut for time.

**Output.** A resolved account of each contested seam, or an explicit statement that it remains contested, which is itself a finding.

##### 3.5 · Mark the craft

Go through the map and mark every act that is not a sequence.

**A map that decomposes judgment into steps is wrong, and a practitioner will see it in ninety seconds.** Marking these honestly is what earns the right to decompose everything else.

**Output.** The map, with craft regions bounded and labelled.

##### 3.6 · Revise the hypothesis, on the record

Return to the Phase 1 sheet. Write down what was expected, what was found, and where they differ.

**Output.** A one-page revision note. It goes in the final artifact.

---

### Phase 4 · Ingestion

*Roughly 8 hours. Making it reachable.*

##### 4.1 · Assemble the corpus

Everything gathered, converted, structured, and organized by retrieval intent rather than by origin.

**Output.** A reachable corpus with structure preserved.

##### 4.2 · Attach provenance

Every passage carries what it is, when it is from, and where it came from, inside the text rather than in metadata a system may drop.

**Gate.** Nothing enters the corpus without provenance. No exceptions, including for convenience.

##### 4.3 · Build the exclusion set

From the answers to questions nine and ten, plus the governance layer, plus judgment.

Three categories: **reachable**, **reachable behind a wall**, and **never**. The third is removed from every denominator, because the correct coverage on some rows is zero.

**Output.** The exclusion list, named, with a reason against each row, ratified by the sponsor.
**Gate.** No corpus goes live before this is signed. A context project without an exclusion list is a breach with a roadmap.

##### 4.4 · State every artifact

Against the ten layers, each artifact marked reachable, stranded, tacit or unmade, with unmade split into unwritten and undecided.

**Output.** The coverage picture, computed rather than estimated, with the gap shape per layer: how many stranded, how many tacit, how many undecided, and what each would take.

---

### Phase 5 · Iteration

*Roughly 8 hours. Working the context before anyone else has to.*

##### 5.1 · Query the corpus against the real questions

Take the questions people actually asked during the interviews and run them.

**Output.** Per question: grounded, thin, or not covered.

##### 5.2 · Locate the danger cells

Identify questions that are unsettled, internal, and unreachable. These are the ones where a general system will produce a fluent answer about nobody.

**Output.** A named list. This is the finding that makes the case, and it is made of their own questions rather than examples.

##### 5.3 · Build two or three small things

Not a system. Small, real, from their context, at points the map identified.

**Purpose is demonstration, not delivery.** Show, do not describe.

**Rule.** Nothing shown that does not work. No mockups, no staged data, no happy path only.

---

### Phase 6 · Determination

*One meeting. What, so what, what now.*

##### 6.1 · Deliver the artifact first, separately

The full pack goes to the sponsor at least three working days before the meeting.

**Reason.** The meeting is a decision, not a reveal. A room seeing findings for the first time reacts rather than decides.

**The pack contains.** The workflow map, all flows, with craft marked. The contradiction register. The artifact inventory with states. The coverage picture with gap shapes. The exclusion set. The danger-cell list. The hypothesis revision. And what was built, working.

##### 6.2 · The meeting

Three movements, in order, and the order is the whole structure.

**What.** The map, read back. No interpretation. The room corrects it. Corrections are recorded and change the artifact.

**So what.** Where work stalls, what it costs, and which questions currently land where the system cannot help. Still no recommendation.

**What now.** The room determines the next step from what is now in front of it.

##### 6.3 · The bounded outcome set

The determination is not open-ended. Given an artifact of this shape and a meeting of this structure, the outcome falls within a known set, and the set is stated in advance so nobody suspects the conclusion was pre-written.

**Fix the workflow first.** The constraint is organizational and no tool touches it. **In this case the honest answer is that the next work is not ours.**

**Do it with what you already own.** The gap closes with configuration, templates, a database, and the tooling already licensed. Recommended with the specifics, and no further engagement follows.

**Close the gathering gap.** The map shows the cost is stranded and tacit material. The work is conversion and extraction, not building.

**Build something specific and bounded.** A named intervention at a named seam, with success and failure criteria.

**Or not yet.** Something needs deciding first, usually in the undecided register, and no build survives an unresolved decision underneath it.

**And one refusal, stated in advance and held.** Partial implementation on partial context produces confident output about nobody. **That outcome is not offered and will not be assisted with, regardless of who asks or what they are prepared to pay.**

---

#### What is not in this method

No training before the system exists. Formation of judgment about a system attaches to a system, and there is nothing to form judgment about beforehand.

No open-ended sandbox. A bounded place to experiment, with nothing of the organization's own in it, is a blank page, and nobody explores a blank page.

No policy written ahead of the intake. The exclusion set and the governance layer fall out of questions nine and ten, and a policy written before the intake describes an organization nobody has met yet.

No recommendation formed before Phase 6. A recommendation carried in from the start is a conclusion looking for evidence, and the people worth working with can identify one at a distance.

---

#### Failure conditions

**Access slips and the interview phase compresses.** Raise it at the midpoint and choose explicitly between narrowing scope and extending, rather than doing thirty rushed hours.

**Leadership is interviewed first.** Their account becomes the frame and every subsequent interview adjusts toward it.

**The contested seams are not revisited.** The most valuable step is skipped, and the map records the official version.

**Craft is decomposed.** The map is accurate about the routine and blind about the work, and a practitioner dismisses it in ninety seconds.

**The exclusion list is deferred.** Everything downstream is now a liability.

**Or the determination can only conclude one thing.** If the meeting cannot end in an outcome that does not involve us, it is not a determination. It is a sales close with a whiteboard, and the room will know.

---

## 28. The Evergreen Engine — Generalized

`evergreen-engine-generalized.md` · 17,988 words

### The Evergreen Engine — Generalized

*A markdown reprisal of the Content Production Guide, rebuilt so it runs for any author, not just one. Every content type is described in full, and every article prompt is reproduced complete and ready to run.*

---

#### What this is, and how it runs

The Engine does one thing: it takes a finished body of work and makes it findable. The author has already done the hard part — the ideas, the frameworks, the research. What is missing is form. A book is a sealed container; search engines can't read it and answer engines can't quote it. The Engine translates that sealed work into the shapes discovery systems are built to read: a definition, a glossary entry, an FAQ answer, a numbered framework. It doesn't invent authority. It renders authority the author already has into a form the machines can see.

The original guide built this for one author (Alan Hirsch) and one set of themes (his five pathways — mDNA, Metanoia, Reframation, Discipleship, Movement Intelligence). This version generalizes that instantiation. It runs off **three inputs**, and only these change from author to author:

- **The corpus** — the author's actual books, loaded in the notebook. Everything written is drawn from here and nowhere else.
- **`voice.md`** — the author's voice: their register, posture, and signature rhetorical devices. Every prompt writes *in* this voice.
- **`themes.md`** — the author's themes (what the original called "pathways"). For each theme, `themes.md` names its signature framework, its signature concepts, its native binaries, and the historical witnesses the corpus ties to it.

Everywhere the original said "Alan Hirsch," read "the author, per `voice.md`." Everywhere it named a specific pathway, read "the chosen theme, from `themes.md`."

**How one prompt runs.** The agent loads the corpus, `voice.md`, and `themes.md`. It picks one theme. It applies one archetype prompt. It goes to the books, retrieves what that theme and that archetype need, and writes the piece in the author's voice — grounded entirely in the corpus, never invented. A human reads the draft for fidelity and voice before it publishes. That loop — *take `voice.md` and `themes.md`, go to the books for the identified theme, apply the article prompt, write in the author's voice* — is the whole engine. The ten article prompts below are that loop, written out ten ways.

---

#### The strategy, in short

**Three rules decide whether the translation works.**

*E-E-A-T* is the standard search engines use to judge quality — Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trustworthiness. Most sites strain to show it. A real author already has it; it's just trapped in books. Grounding every sentence in the corpus, naming the sources, and holding the vocabulary steady is how you make real expertise visible to a system that otherwise can't see it.

*SEO* here means the hub-and-spoke model. A theme's pillar page ranks for the broad term; the cluster of articles beneath it ranks for the hundred narrower questions around it; internal links bind them so authority earned by one page lifts the others. Fifty interlinked, corpus-grounded pieces read to a search engine not as fifty pages but as one deep treatment of a whole field.

*GEO* — Generative Engine Optimization — is the newer and more important half. People increasingly ask an AI a question and read the synthesized answer without clicking. Those systems favor sources that are clearly structured, self-contained, definitional, attributable, and internally consistent — which is an exact description of what the Engine produces. **SEO decides whether you're ranked. GEO decides whether you're quoted.** Being the source the machine quotes is becoming the new first page.

**The load-bearing condition.** None of this survives thin content. A network of shallow, duplicative, machine-generated filler is not an authority graph; it's a liability, and both search and answer engines are built to catch it. The discipline running through every prompt — every sentence grounded in a real corpus, every claim checkable, every article genuinely different from its neighbors — is not a style preference. It is the whole strategy. The faithfulness *is* the strategy.

**The production method — five disciplines.**

1. **Templates, not one-offs.** Every prompt is a reusable template with a fixed scaffold and one or two variable slots. Fill the slots, run it, get a draft. Ten article templates produce all the articles; nine pathway templates produce every pillar.
2. **Corpus grounding.** The model retrieves; it does not recall. Every draft comes from the author's actual books, paraphrased for the web — never from the model's own training data.
3. **A voice layer.** The author's register is defined once, in `voice.md`, and carried in every prompt.
4. **A standardized skeleton.** Each archetype has a fixed structure. Standardization is what makes fifty articles read as one library and makes the human review fast.
5. **A human editorial gate.** AI-first is not AI-only. Every draft passes a human review for fidelity, voice, and accuracy against the corpus before publishing. The fidelity check is the one step that cannot be automated — and the one that protects the author's name.

---

### Part II — The Article System

Fifty articles is not fifty decisions. It is ten archetypes run across five themes — a clean grid where, by design, no two articles compete for the same query. Each archetype is a distinct search intent, so articles within a theme's cluster reinforce each other instead of cannibalizing. Run every archetype once per theme and the grid is complete; a few archetypes — Concept Spotlight, Comparison, Case Study — can run more than once where a theme offers more than one term, binary, or witness, which is how a fifty-article target is comfortably met or passed.

##### The archetype grid

| # | Archetype | Target search intent | Funnel stage |
|---|-----------|----------------------|--------------|
| 01 | The Definition | "what is {theme}" | Top — awareness |
| 02 | The Problem | a "why" / cause query | Top — problem-aware |
| 03 | The Framework Explainer | "{model} explained" | Middle — consideration |
| 04 | The Concept Spotlight | "what is {concept}" | Top / middle |
| 05 | The How-To | a "how to" query | Bottom — application |
| 06 | The Comparison | "{X} vs {Y}" | Middle — consideration |
| 07 | The Misconceptions | "{theme} myths / misconceptions" | Middle — objection |
| 08 | The Case Study | named-movement / story query | Middle — trust |
| 09 | The Biblical Foundation | "biblical basis for {theme}" | Middle — validation |
| 10 | The Diagnostic | a self-assessment query | Bottom — decision |

##### The universal article skeleton

Whatever the archetype, every finished article shares the same bones: an SEO title and H1; a sharp two-to-three-sentence direct answer placed immediately after the H1, written to win the featured snippet and to be quotable by AI answer engines; the archetype's specific body; a key-takeaways block; standardized internal links up to the pillar and laterally to siblings; and clean metadata. Standardization is not a limit on quality — it is what makes the library coherent and the review fast.

**The non-cannibalization rule.** Before publishing any article, confirm it targets a query the theme's pillar does not. If the article and the pillar would compete, the article is wrong — narrow it.

##### A note on the prompts below

Each prompt is complete and self-contained: everything between **PROMPT BEGINS** and **END OF PROMPT** is copied into a fresh notebook window (loaded with the corpus, `voice.md`, and `themes.md`) and run as written. The shared blocks — Role, The Variable, Source Discipline, Audience, Voice — repeat on every prompt by design, so any single prompt works on its own. Fill the one or two variable slots at the top, and rerun once per theme.

---

#### Archetype 01 — The Definition

**"What is {theme}?" — the cornerstone explainer.**

This is the highest-volume, top-of-funnel article in every cluster, and the one most people meet first. Its whole job is to be the definitive answer on the web to a first-time searcher: what the theme is, where it comes from, and what it is commonly mistaken for. It has to stand entirely on its own — someone who lands here from a cold search and reads nothing else should leave understanding the idea. It names the theme's framework only at a high level; walking the framework element by element is a different article (Archetype 03), and this piece must not stray into that depth or it will collide with the pillar and the Framework Explainer. Run it once per theme.


#### Archetype 02 — The Problem

**"Why {the pain}?" — the diagnostic piece.**

This one catches the problem-aware reader at the exact moment the obvious fixes have failed. The reader senses something is wrong but hasn't yet found the framework that explains it. The article's only job is to name the ache honestly and expose the root cause beneath it — *not* to solve it. The solution lives in the other articles; this piece diagnoses and then hands the reader onward, oriented and hopeful. The discipline that makes it work is restraint: it must resist the urge to fix, and it must diagnose without turning cynical or alarmist. Run it once per theme.

#### Archetype 05 — The How-To

**"How to {practice the theme}" — practical, application stage.**

This is the closest article to action. It converts the theme's practices into a clear, doable sequence for a reader ready to begin, and routes naturally toward a next step. Its steps must come from the theme's own practices material in the corpus — never invented — and it has to be honest about what the work actually costs, including time. The temptation it must refuse is the marketing temptation to promise speed and ease the corpus does not promise. It ends with a single smallest action the reader can take this week. #### Archetype 06 — The Comparison

**"{X} vs. {Y}" — high-volume comparison intent.**

Most authors' corpora run on binaries — organism versus machine, addition versus multiplication, and so on. Comparison queries carry real search volume, and these articles come almost free from the source material because the contrast is already there. The article sets two terms side by side as that binary is understood within the theme, defines each cleanly, shows what is genuinely at stake in the difference, and guides the reader — directionally, not polemically. The discipline is fairness: state the weaker side as its own advocates would, and don't turn a directional difference into a moral hierarchy the corpus doesn't claim. ### Part III — The Pathway System

The articles hang on the pillars. A pillar that is shallow or inconsistent weakens every article beneath it, so the pillars get the same standardized, prompt-driven treatment as the articles. A complete pillar is built from nine components, each with its own prompt. The relationship to the cluster is constant: **each pillar component summarizes and links down; the matching article archetype is the standalone depth.** Every pathway prompt names this relationship so the two never compete.

##### The nine components

| # | Component | What it is | Feeds |
|---|-----------|------------|-------|
| 01 | Overview & Reframe | the opening essay and the reframe turn | Definition & Problem articles |
| 02 | Framework Exposition | the named model as the spine of the hub | Framework Explainer article |
| 03 | The Biblical Mandate | the curated source-text set that grounds the theme | Biblical Foundation article |
| 04 | Historical Witness | one featured case study, told in depth | Case Study articles |
| 05 | Common Confusions | the pillar FAQ | Misconceptions article |
| 06 | Reflection Questions | formation questions for the reader and their team | Diagnostic article |
| 07 | Movemental Vocabulary | the glossary of the theme's signature language | Concept Spotlight articles |
| 08 | The Practices | how to begin, and the single first step | How-To article |
| 09 | Cross-Pathway Connections | how this theme opens into the others | all other pillars |

##### The deep dives

**01 — Overview & Reframe.** The first thing a visitor reads on the hub. It frames the whole theme, carries the broad category keyword, and makes the reader feel the stakes — then hands them down into the cluster rather than exhausting the subject. It teases; it does not walk the framework (that is component 02) or fully define every term (link down instead). It runs 500–800 words and delivers the author's signature reframe once.

**02 — Framework Exposition.** The pillar's structural center. It names every element of the theme's framework with a paragraph each — enough to give the reader the whole shape — while the standalone Framework Explainer article carries the depth. The agent must retrieve the real framework and element count from the corpus and never renumber. It runs 700–1,100 words.

**03 — The Biblical Mandate.** The source-text section that grounds the theme on the hub, establishing that it is grounded in the tradition, not merely strategic. A curated set of four to six passages, each with a short interpretive note on what it establishes, drawn into one throughline. Don't reproduce long passages; give the reference and summarize. It runs 400–700 words.

**04 — Historical Witness.** One historical movement, told in depth, showing the framework operating in the real world. Its job is credibility and dwell time rather than a head keyword. The pillar carries one witness; further movements become standalone Case Study articles. It runs 500–900 words and must not invent dates or romanticize hardship.

**05 — Common Confusions.** The pillar FAQ — six to nine question-and-answer pairs answering the predictable questions and objections a newcomer brings, each question phrased the way a real person would type it, ordered from most basic to most searching. It seeds the Misconceptions article. Answer the actual question; don't be evasive or straw-man. It runs 500–800 words.

**06 — Reflection Questions.** The pillar is not only an SEO hub; it is a formation page. This component gives eight to ten questions that move the reader from information toward honest self-examination, progressing from questions of perception to questions of action and cost, with at least one addressed to the community rather than the individual. It feeds the Diagnostic article. Make the questions genuinely searching, never rhetorical. It runs 350–600 words.

**07 — Movemental Vocabulary.** The glossary of the theme's signature terms in one place — six to eight entries, each a clean, quotable definition noting the term's origin where the corpus says so. It serves the newcomer and supplies the raw material for the Concept Spotlight articles. Every definition must be plain, never jargon-for-insiders. It runs 400–700 words.

**08 — The Practices.** Moves the pillar from understanding to action. Five to seven concrete, reproducible practices drawn from the corpus, ending in one small, unmistakable first step to take this week. It gives the practices in compact form; the How-To article expands them with readiness conditions, timeline, and failure points. Don't invent practices or promise ease the corpus doesn't promise. It runs 500–800 words.

**09 — Cross-Pathway Connections.** No theme stands alone. This closing component shows how the chosen theme relates to each of the others — one short entry per other theme, each with a link to that theme's pillar — so the hubs read as one integrated whole rather than isolated pages. Its primary job is internal link equity across the network. It runs 300–500 words.

##### The nine component prompts

Each is self-contained, run once per theme. The shared blocks match the article prompts, with one difference in the closing instruction (components end with the "Sources drawn from:" line but do not lead with a target-query line).


---

### Part IV — Running the Engine

#### Sequencing and cadence

Don't generate the whole library at once. Prove the system on one cluster, then scale by filling slots.

**0 — Resolve and align.** Settle the theme list in `themes.md` and confirm the corpus and `voice.md` are loaded. Nothing downstream is stable until the themes are fixed.

**1 — Build the proving cluster.** Take the richest, most foundational theme first. Run all nine pathway components, then all ten article archetypes, fully interlinked. This is the proving ground for prompts, voice, SEO, and linking — and the cleanest possible demo: one complete cluster, end to end.

**2 — Standardize the pillars.** With the prompts validated, run the nine components for the remaining themes. The pillars become a fill-the-slots exercise.

**3 — Fill the matrix.** Run the ten article archetypes across the remaining themes. Repeat Concept Spotlight, Comparison, and Case Study where a theme offers more than one term, binary, or witness.

**4 — Edit, publish, interlink.** Every draft passes the editorial gate before publishing. Resolve all `[LINK: ...]` placeholders to live URLs as the cluster fills, so each article ships inside a connected web rather than alone.

A workable cadence, once the proving cluster is done: one theme cluster — nine components plus ten articles — per production cycle. The work compounds, because each theme reuses the same nineteen templates and the same voice and source discipline. The second cluster is faster than the first, and the fifth is faster still.

#### The editorial gate

No draft is published without passing this checklist. It is the one part of the system that is deliberately not automated.

- **Corpus fidelity.** Every claim, framework element, and historical detail is traceable to the corpus. The "Sources drawn from" line is present and accurate. Nothing is imported from outside knowledge.
- **Substantive soundness.** A qualified human has read the draft for accuracy and integrity against the author's actual positions. This check is mandatory and cannot be delegated to the model.
- **Voice match.** The piece reads as the author, per `voice.md`, and uses the signature reframe device once, where the archetype calls for it.
- **No cannibalization.** The article targets a query the theme's pillar does not. Hub and spoke do not compete.
- **Snippet readiness.** The direct answer sits immediately after the H1 and stands alone as a two-to-three-sentence response.
- **Internal links.** Every `[LINK: ...]` placeholder is resolved to a live URL, including the link up to the pillar and laterally to siblings.
- **Structure and metadata.** The archetype's structure is followed in full; SEO title, meta description, and key takeaways are present and within length.
- **No invented specifics.** No fabricated statistics, quotations, dates, or attributions. No generic marketing filler.

**Why the gate is human.** The model can match structure and voice reliably. It cannot be trusted to be the final judge of whether a sentence is true to the author's work. That judgment is the author's name, and it stays with a person.

---

### Part V — Pillars, Pathways, and Cohorts

Parts II–IV cover the public, free layer: the SEO/GEO content that makes the ideas findable. This part covers the rest of the content taxonomy — the theme hubs that anchor it, and the paid formation products beneath it.

#### A note on names

The word "pathway" is used two different ways across this system, and it's worth fixing here.

- **Pillar Page (Theme).** What Parts II–III call a "pathway" is, more precisely, a **Pillar Page** for one **Theme**. It is the public hub for that theme — the page that ranks for the broad term and links down into its article cluster. It is free, top-of-funnel, and built from the nine components in Part III. From here on, "pathway" does not mean this page; the page is the *Pillar Page*.
- **Personal Pathway (Course).** A self-paced, solo formation course on a theme — the same eight-week structure as a cohort, but taken alone, with an AI companion in place of a live facilitator. This is a paid product.
- **Cohort.** The same eight-week course, run live with a facilitator and a group. Also a paid product.

The relationship in one line: the **Pillar Page** is the free public doorway; the **Personal Pathway** and the **Cohort** are the paid formation products beneath it. And one **eight-week spine** underlies *both* the Personal Pathway and the Cohort — the Cohort simply adds a facilitation layer on top of the same content.

#### Pillar Pages (Themes)

A Pillar Page is the hub for one theme: the first place a visitor lands, the page that carries the broad category keyword, and the anchor that every article in the cluster links up to. Its job is three things at once — rank for the broad term, orient a newcomer to the whole theme, and pass authority down into the cluster. It is a summary surface, not a deep one: wherever it touches a definition, a framework, a problem, or a practice, it says just enough and links down to the article that goes deep, so hub and spoke never compete.

**Its prompt set is already written.** The nine prompts that generate a Pillar Page are the nine components in **Part III** — Overview & Reframe, Framework Exposition, Biblical Mandate, Historical Witness, Common Confusions, Reflection Questions, Movemental Vocabulary, The Practices, and Cross-Pathway Connections. Read "Pathway Component" there as "Pillar Page component." They are indexed in Part VI and not reproduced again here.

#### The eight-week formation spine

Both paid products are built on the same eight-week course. Write this spine once per theme; the Personal Pathway and the Cohort then wrap it differently. This is what the original guide left as a "coming soon" placeholder; it is defined here.

##### The anatomy of a course week

Every week of the course, whatever the theme, shares the same bones:

1. **Week title and aim** — the one thing this week is for.
2. **The opening reframe** — a framing question, or the author's signature reframe device, that turns the reader toward the week's work.
3. **The core teaching** — the heart of the week: the main content, drawn from the corpus and written in the author's voice.
4. **The grounding** — the key passage or source the week rests on.
5. **The practice** — one concrete experiment to run before the next week.
6. **Reflection** — prompts for honest self-examination.
7. **The bridge** — a short lead into next week.

The eight weeks move as an arc: orientation and the reframe at the start, the theme's framework walked and practiced through the middle, integration near the end, and a sending in the final week. The specific scaffold that shapes the arc (for example, a four-necessities scaffold) is defined in the author's course spec and retrieved from the corpus — never invented.

##### Prompt — The Course Arc

Run once per theme. It designs the eight-week progression that every Weekly Session prompt then fills.


#### Personal Pathways (self-paced Courses)

A Personal Pathway is the eight-week course taken alone, at the learner's own pace, with no live facilitator. It is a real product, not a lighter one: the content is the full spine above. What changes is that the human facilitator is replaced by two supports — an **AI companion** configured to walk each week with the learner, and a **self-check** the learner uses to gauge their own progress. The companion's job is not to answer for the learner but to hold the week's tension open, press the reflection, and keep the practice honest — the discipline that keeps self-paced formation from collapsing into a video library someone merely finishes. Where the corpus and voice permit, the companion should move the learner toward the deeper, facilitated forms (a Cohort) rather than treating the solo path as the end.

#### Cohorts (facilitated Courses)

A Cohort is the same eight-week course, run live with a facilitator and a group, on a set rhythm. The content is identical to the Personal Pathway's — the shared spine above — but the Cohort adds what a solo path cannot give: a human who holds the tension, presses the questions, and notices who has gone quiet, plus the accountability and formation that only happen in community. Two layers deliver this, both sitting on top of each Weekly Session: a **facilitator guide** (how to lead the week) and a **group session plan** (the run of show for the live gathering).

M_SOWHAT

The So What. What an evergreen content engine actually returns — to the writer, to the movement, and to a hundred leaders linked together. Every strategy document eventually has to answer one question: so what? You can build the prompt system, fill the five pathway pillars, produce the fifty articles, and interlink the whole thing — and a reasonable person can still ask what, exactly, that effort buys. This section answers that. It is the case for the Engine, told plainly, with the mechanics shown rather than asserted. Begin with the shift underneath everything else. Alan Hirsch’s authority is real. Three decades of work, fourteen books, frameworks that have shaped a generation of leaders — this is not authority that has to be manufactured. It already exists. The problem is purely one of form. A book is a sealed container. Search engines cannot read it. AI answer engines cannot cite it. A leader at eleven at night searching “how do I actually disciple people” will never be handed a paragraph from a book she has not bought. The ideas are sound; the ideas are simply not findable. The Engine does one thing, and it is worth being precise about it: it does not invent authority, it translates it. It takes a body of work that already carries weight and renders it into the formats discovery systems are built to read. Everything that follows — every effect on the platform, the movement, and the network — is a downstream consequence of that single act of translation.

The translation, and the three rules that govern it. Three frameworks decide whether the translation succeeds.

E-E-A-T is the standard Google uses to judge content quality: Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trustworthiness. Most websites have to strain to demonstrate it. The unusual fact of Alan’s situation is that the E-E-A-T is genuine and abundant — it is simply trapped in books. The Engine’s discipline of grounding every sentence in the corpus, attributing its sources, and holding terminology consistent is not bureaucratic caution. It is the act of making real expertise visible to a system that would otherwise have no way to see it.

Organic SEO, in the form this strategy uses it, is the hub-and-spoke model. A pathway pillar page ranks for the broad term; the cluster of articles beneath it ranks for the hundred narrower questions that surround it; internal links bind them so authority earned by any one page lifts the others. Search engines reward topical authority — comprehensive, coherent coverage of a

3

---

subject — so a cluster of fifty interlinked, corpus-grounded pieces is read not as fifty pages but as one deep, authoritative treatment of a whole field. GE O

GEO — Generative Engine Optimization — is the newer and more consequential half. Search is becoming answer. People increasingly ask ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, or Google’s AI overview a question and read the synthesized reply without ever clicking through. Those systems assemble answers from sources, and they favor a specific kind of source: clearly structured, semantically self-contained, definitional, attributable, internally consistent. This is — not by accident — an exact description of what the Engine produces. A definition block, a glossary entry, an FAQ pair, a numbered framework: each is a clean, retrievable unit an answer engine can lift with confidence.

The distinction to hold onto. SEO decides whether you are ranked. GEO decides whether you are quoted. And being the source the machine quotes is quickly becoming the new first page.

For the writer — Alan Hirsch and the platform. For Alan, the first effect is a change in the nature of the asset. A book, once written, is finished; it does not grow. An evergreen article behaves in the opposite way. It earns its position slowly, accumulates links and ranking signals over months, and then holds that position for years, working continuously without further input. The corpus stops being a shelf of finished objects and becomes a living, queryable surface of the same ideas. The second effect is authority consolidation. Search the broad territory Alan has worked in — missional church, discipleship, movements — and you find a fragmented field: many partial voices, no obvious center. A fully built cluster makes alanhirsch.com the canonical hub of that field, the place both readers and machines treat as the origin of the frameworks. The third effect is the one that matters most for a person whose time is finite: the Engine decouples reach from his hours. He is not being asked to write fifty articles. The fifty articles already exist, dissolved across fourteen books. He is being asked to supervise their faithful translation. Reach scales; his calendar does not have to. Quantitatively — and here it is worth teaching the shape rather than inventing the numbers — picture two curves. A social post or a piece of news content spikes hard within hours and decays to nothing within days: a tall, thin shape. An evergreen page does the reverse — almost nothing on day one, a slow climb over six to eighteen months, then a long plateau. The decaying piece usually wins the first day by a wide margin. The evergreen piece wins the area under the curve — total cumulative reach — and it is not close. A single evergreen article can, over three years, out-deliver a social post that beat it a hundred-to-one on its opening afternoon. Two more mechanics. First, entry-point multiplication: a lone pillar page is a few doorways into the platform; a pillar plus its ten articles and nine components is roughly twenty distinct doorways, each matched to a different real question. Long-tail queries are individually small and collectively

4

---

enormous — most of all search is long-tail — so breadth of coverage, not just rank on one head term, is what drives total capture. Second, cost asymmetry: the cost of producing the content is paid once and is roughly fixed, while the return arrives every month thereafter. The effective cost per reader reached therefore falls for as long as the page stays live, trending toward zero. ROI here is not a fixed figure; it is a function of time held.

For the movement. A book reaches the people who buy it. A page that ranks reaches the people who are searching — a far larger audience, and a better-qualified one, because they are looking at the precise moment they have the need. This is the movemental payoff, and it is not a traffic metric. It is discipleship meeting people at the point of need. The leader searching at eleven at night finds Alan’s framework instead of generic, decontextualized advice. The seeker who would never buy a theology book encounters the ideas anyway — free, in digestible form — and can follow them as far as they want to go. The barrier to first contact with the movement’s thinking drops to a single search. There is also a quieter, structural effect: language. When the glossary terms and concept pages rank and get cited, the movement’s vocabulary becomes the default vocabulary — the words search engines and answer engines reach for when the subject comes up. A movement that shares language coheres; a movement whose language is also the search-default language has a gravitational center. The Engine is, among other things, an instrument for setting that shared language.

For a hundred leaders, linked. Here the arithmetic changes, and this is the part most worth understanding. Suppose the same system is run not by one platform but by a hundred movement leaders — each on their own site, each translating their own corpus and their own practice into the same architecture, and each interlinking with the others wherever the content genuinely connects. What that produces is not a hundred websites. It is a single distributed authority network: a web of mutually reinforcing, corpus-grounded content covering adjacent territory around a shared center. No one site could ever rank for the whole field. A hundred interlinked sites, between them, can — and search and answer engines read the result not as a hundred competitors but as a field with a recognized middle. The math is the reason this is more than additive. A hundred leaders each producing some number of pages grows the content linearly. But the relationships among that content — the crossreferences, the corroborating mentions, the editorial links — grow with the number of possible connections, which scales far faster than the count of sites. Authority signals, and especially GEO confidence, ride on those relationships. So the signal of the network grows faster than its size. This is not literally Metcalfe’s law, and real-world friction caps it well below the theoretical curve — but the direction is sound: the network is worth disproportionately more than the sum of its nodes.

5

---

For GEO this matters more than for classic SEO. An answer engine’s confidence in a claim rises sharply when multiple independent sources corroborate it. One site defining a framework is a source. A hundred independent, well-attributed sites defining it consistently and citing one another is, to a retrieval system, consensus. The network does not merely earn more citations — it changes what the machine treats as the settled definition of the movement’s core terms. The movement’s framing becomes the answer. And it becomes resilient: a single domain is exposed to one algorithm change, one technical failure, one person’s available time; a hundred-node network is not.

None of this survives thin content. A network of shallow, duplicative, machine-generated filler is not an authority graph — it is a liability, and both search and answer engines are increasingly built to detect and discount exactly that. The discipline running through this entire guide — every sentence grounded in a real corpus, every claim attributable, every article genuinely distinct from its neighbors — is not stylistic preference. It is the loadbearing wall. The faithfulness is the strategy.

So what. The Engine is, in the end, a way of answering a simple question: what happens to a body of work after the books are written? The unmanaged answer is that it grows quietly less findable each year, as the discovery systems move on and the books stay sealed. The managed answer is that the work keeps doing missionary work — translated into the forms search engines rank and answer engines quote, consolidated into a canonical hub, extended into a movement-wide vocabulary, and finally woven into a network no single algorithm change can unmake. That is the so what. Not traffic. Reach for the ideas — compounding, durable, and increasingly the substrate from which the world’s machines explain what this movement believes.

6

---

M_LOGIC

The logic of the system. Before the prompts, the reasoning that makes them work. An AI-first content system is only as strong as the architecture it is pointed at. Alan Hirsch’s corpus is fixed and finished. The hard intellectual work — the frameworks, the theology, the historical research — is already done. That changes what the content task actually is. It is not authorship. It is the translation and repackaging of a bounded source into a standardized format, at volume, in a consistent voice. That is close to the ideal use case for a language model, which is why an AI-first approach is the right tool here and not a shortcut.

Build demand-shaped slots, then fill them from the corpus. The instinct with a great corpus is to work supply-first — find a strong passage, turn it into an article. That produces good writing and weak search performance, because nothing about it is anchored to what a person actually types into a search box. The AI-first move is the opposite: define the standardized set of search intents every evergreen theme predictably generates, turn each intent into a content slot, and only then retrieve the pieces of the corpus that answer it. The intents are the constant. The corpus is the variable poured into them. That single inversion is what makes the system both SEO-sound and genuinely scalable.

Pathways are pillars; articles are the cluster. The five pathway pages function as pillar, or hub, pages. The articles are the topic cluster beneath them. The pillar ranks for the broad category term; each article ranks for one long-tail query the pillar cannot. There is one trap, and the whole system is built to avoid it: the pillar pages are already content-rich, so if the articles simply repeat them, hub and spoke compete for the same keyword and the cluster cannibalizes itself. The rule throughout this guide is therefore strict — every article targets a query the pillar deliberately does not, and goes narrower and deeper. The pillar summarizes a topic and links out; the article is the definitive standalone treatment.

7

---

M_METHOD

The production method. AI-first means a pipeline, not a chat window. Five disciplines turn a fixed corpus into a standardized library.

01

Templates, not one-offs

Every prompt in this guide is a reusable template with a fixed scaffold and one or two variable slots. Fill the slots, run it, get a draft. Ten article templates produce all fifty articles; nine pathway templates produce every pillar component.

02 Corpus grounding

The model retrieves; it does not recall. Every draft is generated from Alan’s actual books, paraphrased for the web — never written from the model’s own training data. The AI Lab is already a corpus-grounded retrieval system over the books and topic guides; it is the front half of this pipeline.

03 A voice layer

Alan’s register is defined once and carried in every prompt: theologically serious, movement-urgent, hopeful, recoveryoriented, concrete. The existing pathway pages are the style exemplar — including the signature “usual question / better question” device.

04 A standardized skeleton

Each archetype has a fixed structure. Standardization is what makes fifty articles read as one library and makes review fast: a reviewer always knows where the snippet answer, the takeaways, and the links should be.

05 A human editorial gate

AI-first is not AI-only. Every draft passes a human review for theological fidelity, voice, and accuracy against the corpus before publishing. The theology check is the one step that cannot be automated — and the one protecting the brand.

The universal article skeleton. Whatever the archetype, every finished article shares the same bones: an SEO title and H1; a sharp two-to-three-sentence direct answer placed immediately after the H1, written to win the featured snippet and to be quotable by AI answer engines; the archetype's specific body; a key-takeaways block; standardized internal links up to the pillar and laterally to siblings; and clean metadata. The non-cannibalization rule: before publishing any article, confirm it targets a query the pathway pillar does not. If the article and the pillar would compete, the article is wrong — narrow it.

M_PATHSYS

The anatomy of a pathway pillar. The articles hang on the pathways. A pillar that is shallow or inconsistent weakens every spoke beneath it — so the pillars get the same standardized, prompt-driven treatment as the articles. The five live pathway pages are the strongest content on the site today: each already carries an overview, a named framework, Scripture, a case study, an FAQ, and practices. This system does not replace that work — it standardizes it, deepens it where it is thin, and makes each component reproducible. A complete pillar is built from nine components, each with its own prompt in this part of the guide.

Overview & Reframe

The opening essay and the usual/better-question turn.

02 Framework Exposition

The named model presented as the spine of the hub.

03 Biblical Mandate

The curated Scripture set that grounds the pathway.

04 Historical Witness

One featured case study, told in depth.

05 Common Confusions

The pillar FAQ.

06 Reflection Questions

Formation questions for the reader and their team.

07 Movemental Vocabulary

The glossary of the pathway's signature language.

08 The Practices

How to begin — and the single first step.

09 Cross-Pathway

How this pathway opens into the other four.

Connections

---

Building on what exists — four things to resolve. The current pillars are strong, but not finished. This system assumes four corrections as it standardizes them. First, the five-pathway model is told two different ways: the pathways index lists mDNA, Metanoia, Reframation, Discipleship, and Movement Intelligence, while the pathway map lists a different five — with a sixth “Forgotten Ways” integration node and two entries pointing at the same page. This guide standardizes on the five with live pages; resolving the map is a Phase 0 decision. Second, the Courses sections read “coming soon” on every pillar — a placeholder, not a component. Third, the Resources sections are generic: every pathway currently points to the same mDNA links and the same featured book, so per-pathway wiring is needed. Fourth, the pathways index lists each pathway twice, which should be reconciled to one treatment.

The relationship to the cluster: each pillar component has a matching article archetype that goes deeper. The pillar component summarizes and links down; the article is the standalone depth. Every pathway prompt names this relationship so the two never compete.

The editorial gate. No draft is published without passing this checklist. It is the one part of the system that is deliberately not automated. E VE RY DRAF T MUST CLE AR:

Corpus fidelity. Every claim, framework element, and historical detail is traceable to Alan’s corpus. The “Sources drawn from” line is present and accurate. Nothing is imported from outside knowledge. Theological soundness. A qualified human has read the draft for theological accuracy and integrity. This check is mandatory and cannot be delegated to the model. Voice match.
