One place for the whole of your work. When your studio launches, here is what's waiting for you: a single place to write, publish, teach, sell, and stay close to the people your work reaches. Your studio is built around two kinds of work. One is your own making — writing, recording, teaching, publishing. The other is everything that connects you to the people who read, watch, learn, and give: your inbox, your subscribers, your contacts, your numbers, and the wider movement you belong to. Your home screen keeps both within reach. Open it and you can jump straight to writing something new, pick up the piece you had open last, answer the people who have written to you, or look at how your work is doing. It also shows the current Kairos cycle — the movement's shared rhythm — and when it closes, with a way straight in. Nothing here asks you to save. Every word you type and every field you change is kept as you go. This guide walks through both halves in plain terms. Take it as a map of what you can do the moment you sign in.

A calm place to write. The heart of the studio is a clean editor that gets out of your way and keeps everything you have ever written within reach. The editor is quiet by design. When you stop typing, the menus and buttons around the edges fade back, so it is just you and the page. You can rename a piece right where its title sits, move between your drafts, and trust that all of it is being saved. From this one editor you can start seven kinds of work: Articles — long-form writing with images, quotes, citations, and embedded media. Books — many chapters, each its own section you can write and reorder. Lessons — teaching content that can carry quizzes and its own section-by-section navigation. Newsletters — email editions with a subject line, preview text, and delivery settings. Podcasts — audio episodes gathered into a series. Videos — projects built from separate recorded or designed pieces. Events — gatherings with scheduling, registration, and tickets. When you are writing a book, a chapter strip along the top lets you move between chapters, add new ones, reorder them, and switch between the writing, an outline of the whole thing, and the numbers for that book. The outline is its own view — a map of your piece as a set of parts you can rearrange before or while you draft. There is a scholarly mode for academic work. Turn it on and you get structured abstracts, a bibliography, peer-review notes, and proper handling of math and code. Academic pieces can be registered with a DOI when you publish. Alongside the page, a details drawer holds everything else about a piece: its title and description for search, its web address, tags, featured image, who is listed as author, and — for events — the when, where, speakers, agenda, and registration questions. Every saved version is kept, too, so you can look at an earlier draft and bring it back with a single click.

AI help, when you want it. Four assistants sit inside the editor: a writing partner for drafting, refining, and thinking out loud; a voice coach for tone, rhythm, and readability; an SEO guide for titles and keywords; and a guardrails check that keeps you true to your own style guide. As you type, the studio can suggest the next few words — accept them with the Tab key. You can also hand it a passage to rewrite, or open a longer back-and-forth in a side panel.

## 31. Twenty Rules — linking, credibility and launch

`claude_network-rules-linking-credibility.md` · 2,023 words

### Twenty Rules

**For every leader building a platform in this network.**

*Linking, credibility, and launch — what to do and what not to do.*

---

#### Why any of this matters

Two things are happening to your work at once.

The first is that people find things differently now. A pastor with a question is as likely to ask an AI system as to search for it, and that system decides which sources to draw from and which to leave out. It makes that decision partly on what's on your site and largely on whether the rest of the internet corroborates you.

The second is that being alone online is now a real disadvantage. A single site — however good — is one more voice among millions. A group of leaders whose work genuinely connects, and whose connections are visible, reads as something different: a body of thought that more than one serious person stands behind.

You already have that offline. You cite each other, you speak at each other's events, you've written together, you send people to each other. The whole point of what follows is to make what is already true online too.

Every rule below serves one of two ends: **being believed**, or **being found**. Most serve both.

---

### The ten things to do

#### 1. Own your address

Buy your own domain, registered in your name, and keep it. Every link anyone ever makes to your work, every mention in a book or a podcast description, every time someone types your name into a phone — all of it accumulates against that one address, and it accumulates for years.

This is the one thing on this list that cannot be undone later. If your work lives at an address someone else controls, or at a temporary one, you are building on ground you can't keep.

#### 2. Make every profile of you point at the same place

Right now there are probably a dozen pages on the internet with your bio on them. Publishers, conference sites, networks you belong to, organizations you've founded, denominational directories. Most of them link somewhere stale or nowhere at all.

Go through them and get each one pointing at your site. It's about ten emails, each one two lines long: *could you update my link to this address?*

This does more than send traffic. It is how a machine confirms that the person on your site is the same person on your publisher's page and the same person in that conference program — that you are one real, verifiable human rather than a name on a website. If your name is shared with anyone else notable, this is the only thing that resolves the confusion.

#### 3. Link to another leader only where you actually build on their work

If your thinking genuinely extends someone else's — you use their framework, you're arguing with them, you learned it from them — link to it and say what the connection is. Those links are true, they help the reader, and they hold up under any scrutiny.

The test is simple: **would you make this link if search engines didn't exist?** If yes, make it. If the only reason is that you're both in the network, don't.

#### 4. Link with the actual name of the thing

Never "click here." Never a bare web address dropped in the middle of a sentence. Write the name of what you're pointing at: *Alan's work on the fivefold*, *Brad's covocational readiness questionnaire*, *the essay on theology of place*.

A reader learns what's on the other side before they click. So does a machine. This costs nothing and it's the difference between a link that carries meaning and one that carries none.

#### 5. Say out loud who you're connected to

Put the affiliations on the site. The network you're part of, the platform you build on, the organizations you work with, the people you've written with.

Hiding a relationship is what makes it look like something to hide. Every publisher group, every university system, every professional association states its connections plainly and nobody thinks worse of them for it. Stating yours converts a connection that looks arranged into one that looks ordinary — because it is.

#### 6. Put your own experience on the page

Not just what you think — what you've done. You planted the church. You lived in that neighborhood for eleven years. You trained those two hundred leaders. You made the mistake and here's what it cost.

This is the thing no one else can copy and no machine can generate. It's also, specifically, what search and AI systems are now built to look for: evidence that the person writing has actually been where they're writing about. Cite it plainly, in the first person, with details.

#### 7. Name your sources

When you make a claim, say where it came from. When you quote, give the book, the edition, and the page. When you use a statistic, link the study.

Two reasons. A reader trusts a writer who shows their work. And a machine deciding whether to draw on your page is looking for exactly this — claims that are anchored to something rather than floating.

#### 8. Publish under your own name, with your real bio and your real face

Every article carries your name, links to a full biography, and shows a photograph of you. The bio names your books, your roles, your training, your track record.

An anonymous page is a page nobody vouches for. A page with a named, verifiable author behind it is a page with a person's reputation attached. That's the whole distinction, and it's the cheapest one to get right.

#### 9. Keep your dates visible and refresh what goes stale

Show when a piece was published and when it was last updated. Then actually update the important ones once a year.

This matters more than most people realize. In controlled testing of how AI systems choose sources, a stale date was one of the few things that got a page ruled out almost entirely, regardless of how good it was. An undated page is treated as an old one.

#### 10. Get talked about somewhere other than your own site

Podcasts. Filmed conversations. Guest pieces on other people's sites. Interviews. Conference sessions that get posted publicly. Your name in someone else's article.

This is the single strongest predictor anyone has found of whether AI systems will draw on your work — stronger than anything you can do on your own pages, and much stronger than links. A new site with nothing said about it anywhere else is invisible no matter how well it's built. Being discussed in places that are already established is what gets you admitted.

Video especially. It's the highest correlation in the available research and almost nobody in our world is doing it on purpose.

---

### The ten things not to do

#### 1. Don't link to another leader just because they're in the network

A link between two people who genuinely build on each other is evidence. A link between two people who've never engaged each other's work is decoration, and at scale it stops looking like decoration and starts looking like a scheme.

The network's whole advantage is that our connections are real. Manufacture a few and you've traded the one thing that can't be copied for something anyone can fake.

#### 2. Don't run two sites for yourself

If you have an older site — a blog, a ministry site, an assessment tool — don't leave it running alongside the new one. Two sites in your name compete with each other, split every link you've ever earned, and leave every system that encounters you unsure which one is actually you.

Pick one address. Point the other one at it permanently. A decade of accumulated credibility moves in a single afternoon, and if you skip it, that decade goes on working against you instead of for you.

#### 3. Don't buy links, trade links, or put keyword phrases in press release links

Paying for a link, swapping links as a favor, or sending out an announcement stuffed with links that use your target search phrase as the clickable text — all three are explicitly named as manipulation by Google, and press releases are called out by name.

If a link is paid or placed, it gets marked as such. This is a solved problem with a technical answer, and your web person knows it. Just don't let anyone talk you into the shortcut.

#### 4. Don't hide who you're connected to

The mirror of rule five. An undisclosed relationship discovered later costs you more than a disclosed one ever could. Say it plainly and it's context. Let someone find it and it's a story.

#### 5. Don't send email to a list that isn't yours

If an organization has an audience you'd like to reach, ask them to send your note to it. Do not ask them to export it. Those people subscribed to that organization, not to you, and mailing them from an address they don't recognize damages your ability to reach anyone's inbox for months — and costs you the relationship on top.

The organization sends, or nobody sends.

#### 6. Don't ask your people for three things at once

Read this, subscribe to that, share this, buy the book, join the cohort. Every one of those is reasonable and all of them together are noise.

One clear invitation. You get a limited number of moments when the people who trust you will act on your word, and the way to waste them is to spend several at once on a crowded ask.

#### 7. Don't block the AI systems from reading your site

There's a file on every website that tells automated readers what they may and may not look at. It's easy to set it defensively, and some platforms do it by default. If yours blocks the AI crawlers, you have removed yourself from the systems that decide what gets recommended — and you won't notice, because nothing breaks. You just quietly aren't there.

Ask whoever built your site to confirm the AI readers are allowed. It takes them two minutes.

#### 8. Don't claim the network is bigger than it is

Describe what's actually true. Two colleagues whose work connects is interesting and verifiable. "A movement of leaders" said over two websites is a claim your audience will check.

Our readers are unusually good at spotting the gap between what's promised and what's on the shelf. Under-claim and let the thing grow into its description.

#### 9. Don't publish volume for its own sake

Twenty thin pages written quickly to cover more search terms will do less than four pieces that genuinely say something. Search and AI systems are now explicitly built to detect and discard exactly that pattern, and your actual readers detect it faster.

Publish when you have something. The one exception is that dormancy has a cost too — see the next one.

#### 10. Don't let launch be the loudest week you ever have

The most common failure is not a bad launch. It's a good launch followed by silence.

Everything about how this works rewards accumulation. Sites that matter are years old. Audiences are built by showing up repeatedly. A single burst tells everyone watching that this was a project. A steady rhythm — even a modest one — tells them it's a place.

Before you announce anything, decide what you're publishing in week four, week eight, and week twelve, and write the dates down. Month two should be bigger than month one.

---

#### The one-sentence version

**Make the true things visible, say the connections out loud, get talked about somewhere other than your own site, and keep showing up.**

Everything above is a footnote to that.

---

*Written for the Movemental leader network, July 2026. Grounded in current published research on how search and AI systems evaluate sources. Revise as the evidence changes — and it will.*

---

## 32. The Launch Guide — for Josh, Brad and Alan

`claude_launch-guide-brisco-hirsch.md` · 12,252 words

### The Launch Guide

**For Josh, Brad, and Alan — going public together, August 2026**

*Linking, launching, sharing, and what the numbers are actually for.*

---

#### How to read this

There are three of you and you need different things from this document.

**Alan**, read Part One and Part Seven. Part One is what's true about your site right now, including one thing about your own name in Google that you'll want to know. Part Seven is the short list of what only you can do. It's genuinely short.

**Brad**, read Part One, Part Two, and Part Seven. Part Two is the argument for why your launch is different from a book launch, and it's the part that determines whether the next year compounds or evaporates. Your list in Part Seven is longer than Alan's, on purpose, because your network is the distribution and you're the one standing in it.

**Josh**, read all of it. Parts Three through Six are yours: the blockers, the linking order, the analytics build, and the questions the analytics exist to answer. Part Eight is the calendar.

One note on tone. I've written the uncomfortable parts plainly rather than softening them, because a launch guide that flatters you is worthless. Where I'm confident, I say so. Where the evidence is thin, I mark it. Where something is a judgment call rather than a fact, I've said which.

---

### PART ONE — What is actually true right now

Before any strategy, here is the state of things as of July 31, 2026. Some of this will be a surprise.

#### Alan's site is already public

alanhirsch.com is live, serving, and reachable by anyone. It has a homepage with the line "The church was made for movement," five thematic pathways, a Library, a Formation section, an AI Lab, and a newsletter signup offering the mDNA Field Guide. Nothing is behind a login.

Google has already indexed it. A `site:alanhirsch.com` search returns the homepage, /about, /content, /terms, /privacy, and /accessibility.

One detail in those results worth catching now: **every indexed URL is on `www.alanhirsch.com`, not the apex.** If both hostnames serve a 200, that's a duplicate-host split on the exact domain that's already in an identity fight. Pick one — www or apex, it genuinely doesn't matter which — 301 the other to it, and put an absolute self-referencing canonical tag on every page pointing at the winner. Ten minutes, and skipping it halves whatever authority the site accumulates.

So "going public next week" is not a technical event for Alan. The site went public whenever the domain was pointed at it. What happens next week is an *announcement*. That distinction matters enormously for the plan, because it means the risky part — the cutover — has already happened without a launch checklist, and we should go back and do the checklist now.

#### Alan's site has no robots.txt and no sitemap

Both `alanhirsch.com/robots.txt` and `alanhirsch.com/sitemap.xml` return 404. I checked directly.

No robots.txt is not fatal — the default is "crawl everything," which is roughly what you want — but it means you have no ability to steer crawlers, no reference to your sitemap, and no explicit permission for the AI crawlers that matter. No sitemap means Google is discovering your pages by following links only, which for a site with deep pathway and library structure is a real handicap.

This is a two-hour fix and it should happen before the announcement.

There's a specific trap here worth naming, because it's a common Next.js bug rather than an oversight. In the App Router, `app/sitemap.ts` is cached by default unless it uses a request-time API or explicit dynamic config ([Next.js docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/sitemap)). A sitemap that silently stops updating as you publish is worse than no sitemap, because you'll believe you have one.

#### Alan's biggest search problem is Alan

Search for "Alan Hirsch" and here's what comes back: the Wikipedia article for **Alan Hirsch the law professor** at Williams College, Amazon's author page, IVP's author page, and **alanhirsch.org** — twice, homepage and /about — a Squarespace site whose most recent blog post is from December 2015.

alanhirsch.com does not appear at all.

So there are two problems stacked on each other. The name itself is ambiguous to machines, and a different Alan Hirsch is currently winning it. And the older of *his* two sites is the one Google has decided represents him.

Both are identity problems rather than ranking problems, which is good news — they're solvable much faster than a ranking fight would be.

The Ahrefs study on ranking timelines is the relevant hard number here: only **1.74%** of newly published pages reach Google's top ten within a year, and **72.9%** of pages currently in the top ten are three or more years old ([Ahrefs, 1.3M keywords](https://ahrefs.com/blog/how-long-does-it-take-to-rank-in-google-and-how-old-are-top-ranking-pages/)). Age is not a tiebreaker; it's most of the game.

But identity fights are winnable quickly, because they're won by consolidation rather than by volume. Four moves, in order of value:

**Person schema with a complete `sameAs` list.** This is now the top item, given that a different Alan Hirsch is holding the first result. `sameAs` is the mechanism by which you tell a machine "the Alan Hirsch on this page is the same one as on the IVP page, the Baker page, the Amazon author page, the 100 Movements page, and the missiologist Wikipedia article — and not the law professor." Without it, every system resolving the name has to guess.

**Redirect alanhirsch.org to alanhirsch.com,** if Alan still controls it. This is the highest-value *technical* action available and it moves a decade of accumulated links.

But do it properly rather than pointing the whole domain at the new homepage. The .org has blog posts, an APEST assessment, and organization pages, and most of those deep URLs have no equivalent on the .com yet. Google treats an irrelevant redirect target as a soft 404, which means blanket-redirecting to the homepage loses the equity rather than transferring it ([Google, site moves](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/site-move-with-url-changes)). So: crawl the .org first, map what has a real equivalent, redirect those one-to-one, and send the genuine orphans to the closest topical page rather than the front door. Same discipline as Brad's migration below — the caution applies equally.

If the .org can't be redirected, at minimum a prominent link from it to the .com.

**Get the author pages pointing at the right place.** IVP, Baker/Brazos, 100 Movements, Forge, 5Q Central, Movement Leaders Collective, Missio Alliance. Most currently point somewhere else or nowhere. Each is a mention on an already-indexed, already-trusted site, which is the mechanism that matters most for a new domain.

**Get the Wikipedia external links section corrected.** Wikipedia is the second-most-cited domain on ChatGPT, though notably *not* top-three on Google AI Mode or Perplexity ([Semrush, most-cited domains](https://www.semrush.com/blog/most-cited-domains-ai/)) — so it's valuable but not the universal key it's often described as. It also feeds Google's entity understanding directly, which is what matters for the professor problem.

On the how: [conflict-of-interest guidance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Conflict_of_interest) is a guideline, not a prohibition, and neither of you should edit the article body directly. But a disclosed edit request on the talk page — the `{{edit COI}}` mechanism — is explicitly permitted and takes about fifteen minutes. That's the route.

#### Brad's site is public too, and that's a problem

brad-brisco.vercel.app is live and publicly reachable. Title "Brad Brisco," full navigation, hero image, courses, books, a Neighborhood Intelligence tool.

**There is no custom domain attached.** Not bradbrisco.com, not anything.

A production `*.vercel.app` alias does not get a `noindex` header — only preview deployments do, and even then not if a custom domain is assigned to a non-production branch ([Vercel](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/are-vercel-preview-deployment-indexed-by-search-engines)). So Brad's site has been sitting publicly crawlable on a URL you're going to throw away.

The good news: a search for the vercel.app URL returns nothing, so it's probably not indexed yet. Do the migration this week and you get away clean.

Wait a month and it's genuinely awkward, because you can't clean it up the normal way. You don't control DNS for `*.vercel.app`, so you can't add the TXT record a Search Console Domain property needs, and Google's [Change of Address tool](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/9370220) requires verified owner access to both the source and the destination. You'd be reduced to canonical tags and hoping.

**Get Brad a domain this week. Before anything else on this list.**

Two more things on Brad's live site that the plan has to account for. It already has a **Pricing page and a Donate page**, and it has a **Neighborhood Intelligence tool** that collects user-submitted data. The pricing page needs a decision before launch — see the note on gating in Part Eight — and the neighborhood data needs the security fix below before anyone is invited to use it.

#### Brad already has a site, and it's been quiet for over a year

missionalchurchnetwork.com. Squarespace, seventeen blog categories, an RSS feed. It is Brad's, it is indexed, and it is where the internet currently thinks Brad's writing lives.

It is also mostly dormant — the most recent post I can find is from **April 2025**, sixteen months ago. I'm naming that because I criticized alanhirsch.org for exactly the same thing, and it changes how much the domain is worth. I could not measure its actual link profile or registration date from outside, so treat "it has accumulated authority" as a reasonable assumption to *verify*, not a fact to plan on. Ten minutes in Ahrefs or Semrush settles it, and that check should happen before the decision below rather than after.

Either way, Brad's launch is not a greenfield launch. It's the same consolidation problem Alan has. Whatever domain the new site lands on, missionalchurchnetwork.com needs a decision:

**Option A — redirect it to a new personal domain.** Every URL 301s to its closest equivalent. The link equity transfers.

**Option B — make missionalchurchnetwork.com the new site's domain.** Point the new platform at the existing domain and 301 the old Squarespace URLs to the new equivalents. You inherit the domain's age and links outright rather than transferring them, which is strictly better if the domain has real authority. And "Missional Church Network" may be the better search asset regardless, because people search the category more than they search the person.

**Option C — leave it running.** Two sites competing for the same queries, splitting the same links, confusing both Google and every AI system trying to decide what Brad's canonical home is. This is what happens by default if nobody decides. Don't let it.

I lean toward B *if the link check supports it*, with A as the fallback. If the domain turns out to have thin links after all, the decision collapses to whichever name Brad wants to be known by, which is a much easier question.

Either way, before anything is redirected: crawl the old site completely, export sixteen months of Search Console data, and pull the "best by links" report. Those three lists unioned are your redirect map. Blanket-redirecting everything to a new homepage is the classic way to lose it all — Google treats an irrelevant redirect target as a soft 404 and the equity evaporates rather than transferring ([Google, site moves](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/site-move-with-url-changes)).

#### There is no email list

Platform-wide, across every tenant, there are **40 newsletter subscribers**. Thirty-seven of those are on the Movemental house account. Alan has three. Brad has zero.

I want to be direct about what this means, because it reshapes the whole launch. Every launch plan I've read in the project docs assumes a newsletter as a distribution channel. There isn't one. The newsletter is not a channel at launch — it is *the thing launch week exists to build*.

The upside: everything I was going to warn you about regarding cold-list blasts and sender reputation is moot. You cannot damage a list you don't have. Resend's domain warm-up schedule still applies when you start sending (150–400/day for the first three days, 700–2,000/day through day seven, then roughly 1.4× per day — [Resend](https://resend.com/docs/knowledge-base/warming-up)), but at your volumes you'll be nowhere near a limit for months.

The downside is bigger, and it's the single most important strategic fact in this document. **Launch week's entire distribution is Brad's and Alan's existing audiences — and those audiences live inside organizations neither of them owns.** Alan's reach runs through 100 Movements, Forge, Movement Leaders Collective, his publishers, and his speaking calendar. Brad's runs through Send Network, Forge, Sentralized, and his LinkedIn.

Those are partner lists, not personal ones. Which means every one of them is a *conversation with a partner*, on the partner's schedule, in the partner's template — not a send either of them can execute alone. Plan the lead time accordingly; a newsletter mention from Send Network is a two-week ask, not a two-day one.

**And do not export a partner list and import it into Resend.** I said above that you can't damage a list you don't have, and that's true right up until someone imports one. Those subscribers opted in to Forge, not to Brad. Mailing them from a new domain is a cold blast with all the reputation consequences intact, and it would burn a partner relationship on top. The partner sends, or nobody sends.

There may also be a list on missionalchurchnetwork.com — ten years of Squarespace usually collects something — but I couldn't find a signup form on it, so treat that as a question to ask Brad rather than an asset to count on.

#### The content is thinner than the counts suggest

Raw numbers look healthy. Alan's tenant has 503 content items, Brad's has 400. But most of it is in draft.

**Alan:** 392 drafts, 11 archived, 86 published. Of the published items, only **16 are articles**. The rest are quote bank entries, events, topic guides, endorsements. Pathways: **5 of 31 published**. Courses: **5 of 13**.

**Brad:** 306 drafts, 54 archived, 39 published. Only **4 published articles**, plus 17 podcast guest entries, some events and endorsements. Pathways: 5 of 5 published. Courses: 1 of 4.

Sixteen articles and four articles. That's the actual public surface.

I don't think this is a reason to delay. Nobody has established a minimum article count for launch — that number is folklore, and I looked for a study establishing it and didn't find one. But it does determine what launch week *is*. With sixteen articles you are not launching a body of work. You are launching a home, credibly, with a promise of what fills it. Say that plainly rather than implying more, because the gap between the promise and the shelf is the thing a skeptical network leader will notice first.

The good news is that Alan's pathways and courses are the real differentiator and 5 of each are live. Lead with those, not with the article count.

#### Vercel Web Analytics is not enabled anywhere

I checked alan-hirsch, brad-brisco, and zenwrite. All three return "Web Analytics not found," which is what Vercel says when the feature was never turned on.

#### Search Console has never delivered data

The `zw_search_metrics` table is empty. A sync record exists in `zw_search_metrics_sync` — one row, dated July 23 — but no metrics ever landed. Either Search Console isn't connected, isn't verified, or the sync is failing silently.

This matters more than it sounds. **Search Console does not backfill.** Whatever it hasn't collected is gone permanently, and the same is true of Google Postmaster Tools. (Product analytics tools are more forgiving — Plausible and PostHog both support historical imports, and server logs are retroactive by nature. It's the Google properties that are one-way doors.) Every week Search Console isn't verified is a week of baseline you can never recover, and you're about to run the week where the baseline matters most.

#### Something is capturing events, and it works

`zw_page_views` has 825 rows and `zw_analytics_events` has 756, both current as of the day I looked. Twenty days of history starting July 11. Sessions, referrers, UTM fields, time on page, country, resource type.

Almost certainly all internal traffic — Alan 617 views, Brad 176, and single digits elsewhere. But the pipe exists and functions. That's the foundation for Part Five and it means the analytics build is an extension rather than a start.

#### Three things that should block the launch

> **Josh — handle this section carefully.** It describes a live, unfixed vulnerability specifically enough to reproduce. Fix and rotate first, then share the guide. If you need to send it before then, cut this section and describe the finding to Brad and Alan verbally as "a database permissions issue we're fixing this week." Don't put the reproduction path in a document that circulates.

I'd hold the announcement for these. Not the site — it's already up — but the announcement, and any invitation for a network leader to look closely.

**One: stored OAuth credentials are readable through the public API.** One table in the `public` schema holds access and refresh tokens with row-level security switched off, which means the anon key that ships in every site's client bundle can read it.

This is the most serious thing in the audit. It's not a launch risk in the marketing sense — it's a live incident waiting to be found. Fix the policy, then rotate every credential in that table on the assumption it has already been read.

**Two: sixteen more public tables have RLS disabled.** Including the one holding user-submitted reports from Brad's Neighborhood Intelligence tool — which is exactly the kind of data a church leader would reasonably assume was private. There's also an application table with an anonymous INSERT policy whose check always passes, meaning anyone can write rows into it.

**Three: the security posture is the product.** You are selling an AI governance and trust layer to churches and nonprofits. The Youthfront AI Safety Charter, the Safety Field Guide, the whole Governance category in the market segmentation doc. A leaked-tokens finding on the flagship platform doesn't just cost you a customer — it costs you the argument. Brad and Alan are lending their names to this. They are entitled to have it be secure before they do.

Two smaller items while you're in there: `deb-hirsch` and `david-docusen` both have failing production builds, and the production `organizations` table contains about twenty test fixtures with names like `assess-e2e-*` and `playwright-e2e-*`. Neither blocks launch. Both are the kind of thing that shows up in a screenshot at the worst moment.

---

### PART TWO — The situation you actually have

This is the strategic core, and it's the part I'd want Brad to read carefully.

#### What's unusual here

Most people launching a website have one credibility problem: nobody has heard of them. You have the opposite problem, which is rarer and much better, and it has a specific shape.

Brad and Alan have written eleven books between them. They have co-authored together. They share a network — Forge, Sentralized, Send Network, 100 Movements, Movement Leaders Collective — and that network contains a dozen more people with their own books and their own audiences. They cite each other. They endorse each other. They speak at each other's events. Offline, they are visibly one movement.

Online, they look like strangers with separate websites.

The linking build order document in the project says this well, and it's right: in an internet where AI systems increasingly decide which sources are credible, being a lone site is not a marketing problem but an existential one. A single voice is one more voice in the slop. A corroborated network of voices is a different kind of object entirely.

So the thing you have that almost nobody else has is **the ability to link honestly**. Not link building. Not outreach. The links are already true — Brad and Alan genuinely build on each other's work — and they simply haven't been made machine-readable yet.

#### Why this matters more than it did two years ago

The evidence on what gets a source cited by AI systems has gotten much better in the last year, and it points somewhere useful.

The strongest study available is a controlled experiment across six models and 252,000 trials, testing eighteen content factors one at a time ([arXiv 2605.25517](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.25517)). Four factors behaved as gatekeepers, with odds ratios above 10,000 across most models: being exactly on-topic, containing the specific attribute the question asked about, being fresh rather than stale, and being retrieved in the first position. Secondary factors — confident rather than hedged language, claims backed by evidence, no internal contradictions — separate the sources that clear the gates.

Two honest caveats, because this is the study I lean on hardest. Its documents are competing *product* listings, and the "specific attribute" gatekeeper is literally "price not mentioned." That it generalizes from product pages to theology essays is a reasonable inference, not a demonstrated result. And odds ratios that large in a forced-choice design usually indicate near-total separation — the model essentially never picks the stale document when offered a fresh one — which is real but is not a number you can carry into the wild unchanged.

Formatting was weak, though weaker in one direction than the other: structured versus dense scored 0.79 to 1.68, organized versus scattered 1.13 to 3.87. So layout is not nothing at the top of that range. It is one to two orders of magnitude below the gatekeepers, which makes it a tiebreaker, and makes the GEO content mill's obsession with markdown structure badly misallocated attention.

Separately, Ahrefs correlated AI visibility against site metrics across 75,000 brands ([study](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-brand-visibility-correlations)). YouTube mentions correlated at 0.737. Branded web mentions at 0.664. Domain Rating at 0.266. Backlink counts Ahrefs describes as "very weak" without publishing a figure.

Read those together and a picture emerges — though I want to be careful how firmly to hold it. **Being talked about on properties that are already indexed appears to matter more than being linked from them, and video appears to matter most of all.** That is one correlational study with an obvious confound: large brands accumulate mentions, links, domain authority, and AI visibility simultaneously, and nothing in the data establishes the direction. The one timeline observation pointing the same way — a new domain picked up by ChatGPT one day after external PR went live ([FogTrail](https://fogtrail.ai/blog/how-fast-new-website-indexed-and-cited)) — is a single site, once.

Strong enough to plan against. Not strong enough to bet everything on. What it argues for is that launch week's highest-value activity is **getting written about, interviewed, and filmed on properties that are already indexed** — and that the YouTube number, being the highest in the entire evidence base, has earned a line item rather than a mention. It gets one in Part Seven.

#### The thing to build toward, and the thing not to overreach on

The linking build order describes a five-node network with cross-node citation strips, a shared glossary, federated search, and a network map. It's a good target. It is also, correctly, described as a Phase 3 capability that needs at least two leaders with stable addresses and internally sound sites first.

You have two leaders. You are at the start of Phase 3, not the middle of it. The temptation at launch is to describe the network as though it exists — "a movement of leaders," "the Scenius" — and that's the overreach to avoid. Two sites and a footer is not a movement, and the audience for this is exactly the audience that will notice the gap between the claim and the thing.

So at launch: build the footer, build the cross-links, make the co-authorship visible, and describe it as what it is. Two colleagues who have worked together for twenty years, whose work now visibly connects. That's true, it's interesting, and it's more credible than the bigger claim. The bigger claim gets made at five nodes, when it's true.

Worth flagging that alanhirsch.com's live homepage already presents the site as part of "the Movemental Network." That copy is making the bigger claim today. Either soften it before the announcement, or make the network page it points at honest about being two leaders with more coming — the second option is fine and arguably better, because a visible "here's who's next" reads as momentum rather than as overreach.

#### What "credible linking" actually means in practice

Four things, in rough order of value.

**Real co-authorship, made visible.** Brad and Alan have actually written together. Every page on either site that touches a shared framework should link to the other's treatment of it, with descriptive anchor text — not "click here," not the bare URL, but the actual title of the thing you're pointing at. This is the cheapest credible signal available and it costs nothing but attention.

**Mutual, typed citation.** When Brad's covocational work builds on Alan's APEST material, that's a real intellectual relationship and it should be marked as one on both ends. The reason this is a moat rather than a tactic is that it's mutual by construction — no single party can fake it, which is precisely why a machine can trust it, and precisely why someone building five separate sites can't reproduce it.

**A shared vocabulary with one canonical source.** APEST, mDNA, communitas, covocational, missional. If both sites define these terms the same way and point at the same definition, they read as one knowledge surface. If they define them differently, they read as two people who happen to use similar words.

**Consolidated identity.** Person schema on both, with a complete `sameAs` list pointing at every verified profile — Wikipedia, publisher author pages, Amazon author pages, ORCID if it exists, the network organizations. This is what tells a machine that the Alan Hirsch on this site is the same Alan Hirsch on the IVP page and the Wikipedia article and not the law professor.

#### The risk nobody names

The way this fails is not technical. It's that Brad and Alan each ask their network for something once, get a modest response, and never ask again — and the network concludes that the platforms were a project rather than a place.

I looked for a rigorous study establishing that a day-one ask burns network goodwill and I didn't find one. So I'll say it as what it is: practitioner judgment, not evidence. Everything downstream of it in this document — including the "one clear ask" rule in Part Eight — inherits that status.

What *is* documented is the adjacent problem. Nielsen Norman's participation-inequality work found that roughly 90% of users lurk, 9% contribute occasionally, and 1% produce most of the content, and that this holds across communities rather than being a startup phase you grow out of ([NN/g](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/participation-inequality/), 2006, updated 2009). It doesn't give a threshold, and I shouldn't invent one. What it means practically is that a community opened cold shows its first visitor an empty room, and empty rooms stay empty. These are multi-year assets. Nothing about them is won in a launch week.

The practical version: **launch week is a beginning, not a spike.** Design it so that the second month is bigger than the first. If launch week is the peak, you've built a press release.

---

### PART THREE — What to do before you announce

Ordered. Things above the line block things below it.

#### This week, before the announcement

**Fix the security findings.** RLS on `google_oauth_accounts`, rotate the tokens, RLS on the other sixteen tables, remove the always-true anon insert policy on `movement_leader_applications`. Non-negotiable, for the reasons in Part One.

**Get Brad a domain and point the site at it.** Whether that's missionalchurchnetwork.com or a new personal domain is Brad's call, but it has to be made this week. Then:
- Redirect the vercel.app production alias to the custom domain, path-preserving, and keep it for at least a year ([Google](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/site-move-with-url-changes)). This is fiddlier than a normal 301 because you don't control DNS or edge config for `*.vercel.app`. Vercel's own guidance is a **WAF custom rule** issuing the redirect, plus absolute canonical tags, plus `X-Robots-Tag: noindex` scoped to the vercel.app host for anything the rule doesn't catch ([Vercel](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/avoiding-duplicate-content-with-vercel-app-urls)). Budget an hour, not ten minutes.
- Self-referencing absolute canonical tags on every page pointing at the custom domain.
- Turn on Vercel Deployment Protection for the *preview* environment specifically, so preview URLs are genuinely non-public. A `noindex` header works when it's actually set — the failure mode isn't Google ignoring it, it's the header silently not being present on production aliases and on custom domains attached to non-production branches. Protection removes the guesswork.
  - One consequence to plan for: once preview protection is on, Brad and Alan can't open a preview link without authenticating. Generate shareable bypass links for them rather than discovering this mid-review.

**Verify Search Console properties.** Domain properties (DNS TXT) for alanhirsch.com and Brad's new domain. URL-prefix properties for alanhirsch.org and missionalchurchnetwork.com — you need to own the old properties to file a Change of Address, and you need their sixteen-month history exported before you redirect anything. Import both into Bing Webmaster Tools; it's one click from Search Console and it's the cheap entry into Copilot and several AI surfaces.

**Ship robots.txt and a working sitemap on both sites.** Explicitly allow the AI crawlers. This matters and it's easy to get wrong in the defensive direction:

- `OAI-SearchBot`, `PerplexityBot`, `ClaudeBot`, and `Claude-SearchBot` all respect robots.txt. Blocking them removes you from the pools that decide whether you're retrievable at all.
- `ChatGPT-User` and `Perplexity-User` are user-triggered and may not apply robots.txt rules. **`Claude-User` is the exception — Anthropic states all three of its agents honor robots.txt,** and disallowing `Claude-User` blocks retrieval in response to a live user question. Don't lump it in with the others; blocking it is a silent way to disappear from Claude. All of these user-triggered agents are your best live signal, because they fire when a real person is getting a real answer.
- `Google-Extended` has no user-agent string. It's a robots.txt token only, and it controls Gemini training and grounding — **not** AI Overviews, which are served from the regular Googlebot index ([Google](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/google-common-crawlers)). You cannot appear in Google Search and opt out of AI Overviews this way.
- **Check that Vercel's AI Bot managed ruleset is off.** It blocks GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and others. It's opt-in rather than default, but verify rather than assume — this is a silent way to be invisible.
- Skip llms.txt. John Mueller has said plainly that no AI system uses it, and 97% of llms.txt files received zero requests in May 2026 ([PPC Land](https://ppc.land/llms-txt-adoption-rises-8-8x-but-97-of-files-get-zero-ai-requests/)). Five minutes if you want it for completeness. Not a strategy.

**Verify the sitemap actually regenerates.** Publish something, check that it appears. The Next.js caching default will bite you otherwise.

**Turn on analytics.** Part Five has the full build, but at minimum: Search Console verified, Plausible installed, and the existing `zw_page_views` pipeline confirmed working on production domains. Whatever isn't collecting on announcement day is history you never get.

**Decide the alanhirsch.org question.** Redirect, or at minimum link. This is worth more than anything else on the list for Alan's search position.

#### The week of

**File Change of Address for the old properties**, once redirects are live. Signals forward for 180 days and then Google stops recognizing any relationship, so the 301s are the load-bearing part; the Change of Address just accelerates it.

**Submit sitemaps** in Search Console and Bing. Use URL Inspection to request indexing on the ten most important pages — homepage, about, the pathways, the flagship pillar articles. There's a quota and re-requesting doesn't speed anything up.

**Wire IndexNow.** Bing, Yandex, Naver, Seznam, Yep and Amazon participate; Google does not and hasn't in the four and a half years since they said they'd test it ([IndexNow](https://www.indexnow.org/faq)). It's about thirty lines in a route handler called from your publish hook, and it's free. Do it, and don't expect Google effects.

**Do not use the Google Indexing API.** It's restricted to pages with `JobPosting` or `BroadcastEvent` schema, confirmed in Google's docs as recently as this month. Every plugin that pipes blog posts through it is operating outside policy.

---

### PART FOUR — The linking sequence

The build order document has the full dependency chain and I'm not going to restate it. This is the launch-week subset: what to actually build, in order, and why each one earns its place.

#### Before launch — the substrate

**Canonical URLs that will never move.** Everything below points at these. A link is only durable if its target is stable.

**Person schema on both about pages, with complete `sameAs` arrays.** This is the entity resolution layer. For Alan it's the thing that separates him from the other Alan Hirsch. For Brad it's what connects the new domain to ten years of missionalchurchnetwork.com reputation. Include Wikipedia, publisher pages, Amazon author pages, Goodreads, the network organizations, LinkedIn, and any academic profile that exists.

**Article schema on every published piece,** with `author`, `datePublished`, `dateModified`, and `citation`. The freshness gate in the citation study is severe — a 2019 timestamp versus a 2026 one produced an odds ratio above 10,000. Make publication and update dates visible to humans and machine-readable to crawlers. This is cheap and it's load-bearing.

**Book schema on every book page,** with ISBN, publisher, edition. Eleven books between them is a real asset and it's currently invisible to machines.

#### Launch week — the internal graph

The internal linking discipline from the build order, applied to what's actually published:

- Home links to every pillar.
- Every pillar links down to all its clusters.
- Every cluster links up to its pillar and sideways to at least two siblings.
- Every pathway links to at least three articles and out to one clear next step.
- Anchor text is drawn from the target's title. Never "click here," never a bare URL.

With sixteen and four published articles this takes an afternoon. Do it anyway — it's the discipline that has to be in place before the corpus grows, because retrofitting it across two hundred articles is a different job entirely.

#### Launch week — the network layer, minimum viable version

**The movement footer.** Both sites carry a strip naming the other, with one line on how they connect and a link to a short "about this network" page. The build order calls this the cheapest, highest-signal item available and I agree. It reframes each site from one person's website to a node in something larger, and it costs a component.

**Cross-node bylines on co-authored work.** Where Brad and Alan have written together, both bios appear, pulled live, each linking home.

**Cross-citation on the frameworks they actually share.** Not everywhere. Only where it's intellectually real. Brad building on APEST, Alan pointing at Brad's covocational work as the practitioner treatment. Mutual on both ends. Five or six of these, done honestly, are worth more than fifty done mechanically — and the fifty would read as a link scheme to both Google and a discerning reader.

**A shared glossary with one canonical source.** Even if it's a single page on one site that the other links to. The point is one definition, not two.

#### What to defer

Federated search, the network map, the authority convergence view, the shared ontology editor, the translation dashboard. All of it is in the build order and all of it is correct — at five nodes. At two, it's building infrastructure for a network that doesn't exist yet, and the time is better spent on the mentions in Part Seven.

#### On link building, and what Google actually penalizes

Two things worth settling because they generate a lot of bad advice.

**Velocity itself is not what's judged.** John Mueller, in 2019, on the question of two hundred backlinks in two days — and it's worth quoting the setup as well as the answer, because the setup is a warning: "if you're jumping in with a question like this and you're saying I'm going to get 200 backlinks in two days... then that sounds a lot like you're not getting natural backlinks." Then: "It's not so much a matter of how many links you get in which time period... if these are links that are unnatural or from our point of view problematic then they would be problematic. It's like it doesn't really matter how many or in which time" ([SEJ](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/google-link-velocity/331637/)).

So a launch-week burst of genuine coverage is fine. A launch-week burst of manufactured coverage is the thing the first half of that quote is describing.

**What *is* named as spam:** "links with optimized anchor text in articles, guest posts, or press releases distributed on other sites" ([Google spam policies](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies)). So a wire distribution with keyword-anchored dofollow links is explicitly a violation. Brand-name anchors and bare URLs are fine. Anything paid or placed gets `rel="sponsored"`.

**The actual launch-week link risk** is coverage that links to the old vercel.app URL or an old-site URL your redirect map missed. That's the one that costs you something real, and it's why the redirects go in before the announcement rather than after.

---

### PART FIVE — Analytics

#### The principle to build on

The Alan Hirsch Platform Manual says the primary success metric is formation, not traffic. That's not a slogan; it's a technical constraint, and it determines the whole stack.

If your primary metric is formation, it cannot live in a vendor's database with a twelve-month retention window. Pathway completions, course attendance, and practice logs are *product state* — they're facts about what happened to a person, they belong in your own Postgres, transactionally, forever. Traffic and referrers are different: high volume, low value per row, and genuinely hard to do well. Buy that.

So: **roll your own for formation, buy for web telemetry.** The mistake in both directions is real — self-rolling pageview analytics means maintaining bot lists and session logic you'll never keep current, and vendoring formation events means your company's core measurement is a rented number that doesn't match your database.

#### The stack

**Supabase Postgres — the system of record.** You already have `zw_page_views` and `zw_analytics_events` and they work. Extend rather than replace. What to add:

- **An envelope on every event, enforced as a TypeScript type rather than a convention:** `event_id` (client UUID, unique-indexed, for deduplication — `sendBeacon` retries and double-mounted React effects produce duplicates), `event_name`, `occurred_at`, `received_at`, `user_id` or `anonymous_id`, `tenant_id`, `session_id`, `source`, `schema_version`, and properties.
- **`tenant_id` on every event, no exceptions.** In a multi-tenant codebase this is the field that, if it's missing on five percent of rows, makes per-leader reporting permanently untrustworthy.
- **Monthly range partitioning** on the timestamp, a BRIN index on it, and a btree on `(tenant_id, user_id, occurred_at)`.
- **Nightly rollup tables** via `pg_cron`. Dashboards read rollups, never raw events.
- **Watch row-level security on analytical queries.** RLS policies that re-evaluate `auth.*()` per row will kill these queries — and the advisor report already flags 698 instances of exactly that pattern. Run rollups from the service role and apply RLS on the rollup table instead.
- **Emit formation events server-side,** from route handlers, in the same code path as the database write. Client beacons get stripped by ad blockers at rates commonly reported in the fifteen-to-thirty percent range — I couldn't find a source I'd stand behind for that figure, so treat the number as folklore and the direction as certain. Whatever the rate, if "course enrolled" fires client-side then your funnel is wrong by an unknown amount and you can't tell which part.

**Plausible Business — web telemetry, per leader.** $19/month at the entry tier covers ten sites, which means a dashboard per leader plus a consolidated view, funnels, custom properties, and an API. Note the meter: that price is for 10,000 pageviews a month across everything, and it steps up with volume — fine for a while, but don't model it as a flat cost forever. It's cookieless, which is the main reason to prefer it here, and it excludes about 32,000 datacenter IP ranges by default.

On consent: cookieless means you're not storing anything on the device, which is what triggers the ePrivacy consent requirement, and it's why Plausible markets itself as banner-free. That's their position, not a legal opinion — IP-based processing still gets argued about in several EU jurisdictions. It's a much better starting posture than GA4, not a guarantee.

That bot filtering matters more than it sounds at your scale. Cloudflare Radar put automated traffic at 57.5% of HTML requests in June 2026; Imperva had already put it past 50% the year before. And Plausible ran a controlled test where three bot scenarios produced **95 sessions counted as unique visitors in GA4 and zero in Plausible** ([writeup](https://plausible.io/blog/testing-bot-traffic-filtering-google-analytics)). On a site with three thousand real visits a month, one monitoring bot and two AI crawlers can double your apparent traffic and destroy every ratio you compute.

**PostHog free tier — product analytics.** One project, `tenant_id` as a group property. A million events a month free, which you will not approach. It's the only option here that does cohort retention, funnels, and paths properly. Set `person_profiles: 'identified_only'` so anonymous marketing traffic stays cheap and only authenticated formation events become identified.

**Skip GA4.** It adds a consent banner, it counts bots as humans, and it can't answer a formation question. There's no version of this where it earns its place. (Where I mention GA4's "AI Assistant" channel grouping further down, that's context for why the number you'd see elsewhere is wrong — not an instruction to install it.)

**Skip Vercel Web Analytics** except as a free sanity check. Pageviews only, and UTM parameters require a paid add-on.

**Never put a third-party advertising pixel on a content page.** The reasoning here is specific to your audience, and I want to be precise about how much of it is settled.

What's settled: Australia's privacy regulator issued determinations in June 2026 (Medmate and Monash IVF) finding that tracking-pixel data was personal information, because individuals could be singled out even without being named. Those cases concerned health data. And religious belief is separately listed as sensitive information under the Privacy Act, which carries a higher bar — express opt-in rather than notice.

What's inference, mine and not a regulator's: that a pixel firing on a page about a specific denominational practice would be treated the same way health data was. Nobody has determined that. It's also not certain the Act binds you at all — it applies to entities with an "Australian link," which a US-incorporated company may or may not have.

So this isn't a legal bright line and I'm not qualified to draw one. It is a good enough reason to simply not do it. Alan is Australian, a meaningful share of the audience will be, and the upside of an ad pixel on a formation site is close to zero. If real money ever rides on the question, ask an Australian privacy lawyer rather than this document.

#### The one thing to build yourself

**An engaged-time beacon.** This is the highest-value custom instrument on the site and it's about fifty lines.

Scroll depth is close to useless. It measures pixels traversed, not attention. Fast scrollers who read nothing hit 100%; short viewports trigger 90% on load; a reader who studies the top third carefully scores worse than a bot that scrolls to the bottom.

Engaged time is defensible. Chartbeat's method is the reference: interaction events — scroll, mouse move, click, keypress — each mark the user engaged for a rolling five-second window; ping every fifteen seconds while engaged; stop the clock entirely on tab blur ([Chartbeat](https://help.chartbeat.com/hc/en-us/articles/360045890913-User-Engagement-Tracking-Methodology)).

Then derive a read ratio: engaged seconds divided by estimated read seconds (word count over 238 words per minute). Above 0.6, emit an **`Article Read`** event.

That last move is the important one. It converts a noisy continuous number into a discrete countable event that composes with everything else in the schema. You can funnel on it, cohort on it, and join it to formation outcomes. "Pageviews" cannot do any of that, and for a platform whose whole claim is depth over reach, the difference between a view and a read is the difference between the metric that flatters you and the metric that tells you something.

**And require an engagement signal before counting a read at all.** A pageview with zero engaged seconds and no scroll is a crawler or a bounce. This single rule does more for data quality on a three-thousand-visitor site than any bot list.

#### Event schema — the twenty events, and the rules

Instrument about twenty events, not two hundred. A large taxonomy nobody maintains is worse than a small one that's enforced.

The naming convention that's converged across Segment and Amplitude: object-action, past tense. `Pathway Step Completed`. `Article Read`. `Newsletter Subscribed`.

Four rules that prevent the data from becoming useless in six months:

**Never put a variable in an event name.** Not `Pathway 3 Completed`. That's `Pathway Completed` with a `pathway_id` property. If you emit an event per pathway, every new pathway silently breaks every existing chart.

**Properties over event proliferation.** One `Lesson Completed` with `course_id`, `week_index`, and `lesson_type` — not one event per course.

**Same properties for the same object regardless of action.** `Lesson Started`, `Lesson Completed`, and `Lesson Abandoned` all carry the identical lesson property block.

**Distinguish event properties from user properties.** Event properties describe the instance. User properties are persistent traits that apply to future events — `first_utm_source`, `cohort_id`, `is_practitioner`. Getting this backwards is the single most common reason people can't segment historical data later.

And **`user_id` must be the Supabase UUID, never the email.** Emails change and emails are personal data you don't want in a vendor's event stream. Same rule for properties generally: no names, no free-text reflections, no prayer requests. Enforce a denylist server-side rather than trusting discipline.

#### Attribution — and the honest limits

Technical attribution is more broken than most people assume, and pretending otherwise will send you chasing ghosts.

Chrome's default referrer policy has sent origin-only since Chrome 85 — you get `https://example.com/`, not the path, so you cannot tell which article referred someone. Safari caps cross-site referrers similarly, and iOS 26 extended link tracking protection to all Safari browsing, stripping `gclid` and `fbclid` (though **`utm_*` parameters are not stripped** — they aren't treated as cross-site identifiers). Native apps, email clients, Slack, Discord, and every messaging app send no referrer at all.

Which means "Direct" is a bin containing your entire word-of-mouth channel. For an audience that finds things through conference talks, podcast mentions, and one leader telling another over coffee, **that bin is your dominant channel and it is unmeasurable by technical means.**

Three responses:

**Enforce UTM discipline where you control the link.** Lowercase everything — `utm_source=Twitter` and `twitter` are two rows forever. A closed vocabulary for `utm_medium`. Structured campaign names that sort chronologically: `2026-08_launch`. Generate links from a helper, never by hand.

**Capture first-touch UTMs server-side and store them on the user row,** not only in the analytics vendor. `first_utm_source`, `first_landing_path`, `first_referrer`, plus a `last_*` set. Without this on your own user table, joining acquisition to formation is impossible.

**Add a "how did you hear about us?" field at signup.** Free text plus a few options. At your scale this is the single most accurate attribution instrument you have. Technical attribution describes the last twenty seconds; self-report describes the six months of speaking and podcasts that actually did the work. Use the technical data to rank channels you control. Use self-report to decide where to invest.

#### Measuring AI visibility — and what's honestly measurable

This deserves care, because it's where the most money gets wasted on the least reliable numbers.

**What to instrument, free:**

Segment your server logs by user agent, and split them into two groups that mean completely different things. Training crawlers — `GPTBot`, `ClaudeBot`, `Bytespider` — tell you nothing about visibility. The user-triggered agents — `ChatGPT-User`, `Claude-User`, `Perplexity-User` — fire when a real person is getting a real answer right now. A rise in those is the closest thing to a live citation signal available.

If either site sits behind Cloudflare, AI Crawl Control is free on all plans and gives per-crawler logs plus robots-compliance tracking. Cheapest reliable instrument in the category.

Track referrals from `chatgpt.com`, `claude.ai`, `perplexity.ai`, `gemini.google.com`. Build a custom channel group rather than relying on GA4's default "AI Assistant" grouping — Google hasn't published which referrers it includes, and critically, **it excludes AI Overviews and AI Mode**, which continue to be classified as organic search. So the default number omits the largest source of AI-mediated traffic.

Report every AI traffic figure as a floor, never a count.

**What Search Console gives you, and what it doesn't.** Google shipped a generative AI performance report in June 2026 ([announcement](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/06/gen-ai-performance-reports)). It reports **impressions only**. No clicks, no queries, no position. AI Overviews and AI Mode are merged into one bucket. Rollout began with a subset of UK properties, earliest data around mid-May 2026, so there's no historical baseline for anyone. Clicks from AI surfaces remain silently mixed into your regular organic clicks and cannot be separated.

For calibration on what those impressions are worth: Pew studied 68,879 real searches and found users clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits where an AI summary appeared, versus 15% without, and clicked a link *inside* the summary on 1% of visits ([Pew](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/22/google-users-are-less-likely-to-click-on-links-when-an-ai-summary-appears-in-the-results/)).

**On buying a monitoring tool: not yet, and here's the number.** A study repeatedly sampling identical prompts found that Gemini reproduces less than a third of its own citation set run to run — domain-level overlap of 0.29 to 0.31. Perplexity managed 0.50. SearchGPT managed 0.33 to 0.40. Getting a usable confidence interval on citation share requires roughly 40 to 50 queries on Gemini, around 100 on Perplexity, and **150 or more on ChatGPT-class surfaces** ([arXiv 2603.08924](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.08924v2)).

Which means the $99 tiers — Profound Starter is 50 prompts on ChatGPT only, Otterly Lite is 15 — sit *below the noise floor*. They'll show you movement that is entirely random and give you no interval to know it. The honest floor for defensible multi-engine monitoring is $400 to $500 a month, and possibly more: the paper describes achieving a confidence-interval *span* of 0.05, which is ±2.5 points rather than ±5, so if anything I'm understating the sample sizes needed.

Don't spend it in month one. Spend it in month four, if there's a decision it would change. In the meantime, run twenty fixed questions by hand once a month across ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and Google AI Mode, and log the answers in a spreadsheet. Questions like "what is covocational church planting," "what is APEST," "who developed the mDNA framework," "how does a church become missional." That's a crude instrument, but it's honest about being crude, and it will tell you the one thing that matters early: whether you appear at all.

One more thing to track separately: **mentions and citations are different metrics.** Semrush found that on Gemini, the overlap between brands mentioned in an answer and domains cited as sources can be as low as 30%. Alan can be recommended by name without alanhirsch.com being linked. Counting only citations will systematically understate you.

#### What is honestly not measurable

Say this out loud so nobody wastes time hunting for it:

- Which specific article referred someone (browser referrer policy).
- Whether a reader came back next week, if they're anonymous — cookieless tools rotate their visitor hash every 24 hours. Longitudinal measurement requires authentication.
- Whether an AI system recommended you without linking you.
- Whether a conference talk drove a signup, except by asking.
- Email open rates. Apple Mail Privacy Protection preloads the tracking pixel, manufacturing opens that never happened; documented cases show lists jumping from 28% to 55% apparent opens ([beehiiv](https://www.beehiiv.com/blog/apple-mpp-open-rate)). Open rate survives only as a deliverability canary — a sudden *drop* still means something.

For email, use click-to-delivered rather than click-to-open, discard clicks under three seconds after send as bot prefetch, and — the highest-leverage thing you can build — make email links carry a signed token that resolves to a `user_id`. That turns an email click into a first-party event that joins to formation data, and converts email from a black box into an actual node in the funnel.

---

### PART SIX — What the numbers are for

Analytics that don't change a decision are decoration. Here are the questions the first ninety days should answer, roughly in the order the data arrives.

#### Weeks 1–2: is anything working at all

**Are we indexed?** Search Console coverage. Are pages landing in "Discovered — currently not indexed"? That's Google declining to spend a crawl, which is a quality-and-links signal, not a technical one.

**Do we own our own names?** Rank for "Alan Hirsch," "Brad Brisco," "covocational church planting," "APEST," "mDNA." For Alan the specific question is whether alanhirsch.com has passed alanhirsch.org yet.

**Did the redirects hold?** Any 404s in the logs from old missionalchurchnetwork.com URLs or vercel.app URLs. This is the one that quietly costs you ten years of links.

**Where did people actually come from?** Both the technical attribution and the self-report field. Expect them to disagree and believe the self-report.

#### Weeks 3–6: is anyone staying

**What's the read ratio on the published articles?** Not pageviews — the proportion of visitors whose engaged time suggests they read it. This is the first honest quality signal you'll get, and with sixteen articles you can look at every one individually.

**Article to pathway conversion.** The platform manual sets the bar: below 2% means the invitation is too weak, above 8% means it's working. This is testable with the traffic you'll have.

**Does anyone come back?** Second visit within seven days, for authenticated users. The classic activation signal, and one of the few things that predicts everything downstream.

**Time to first value.** Hours from signup to first completed pathway step. In my experience this is the most predictive single number in any formation product, and it's measurable from day one.

**Is the AI Lab used, and does using it correlate with anything?** This is the platform's most distinctive surface and nobody knows yet whether it's a novelty or a doorway. Worth finding out early because it changes what you build next.

#### Weeks 6–12: the strategic questions

These are the ones that actually shape the next year, and they're the reason the schema has to be right in week one.

**Which of the five pillars is the real front door?** Both strategy documents flag this as open. Traffic and pathway entry data answers it. For Brad specifically: does covocational lead, or does missional church? That determines the publishing queue for a year.

**Are the personas real?** The Brisco strategy plan describes six personas and honestly marks most as hypotheses. Which ones show up? The signup self-report field and the pathway data will tell you inside two months whether the planter, the pastor, or the network leader is the actual audience.

**Do the network links do anything measurable?** Cross-site traffic between alanhirsch.com and Brad's site. If the footer and the cross-citations move nobody, that's important — it means the Scenius argument works on machines but not humans, and the pitch should be built accordingly. If they do move people, that's a number worth putting in front of the next three leaders you recruit.

**Does the corpus depth actually convert?** Alan has 186 books and 21,201 blocks ingested. Do the deep library and citation surfaces get used, or do people only read the top-level essays? This is a large investment and it deserves an honest verdict rather than an assumption.

**What are people asking that you haven't written?** Search Console queries and the site's own search logs. This is where the next twelve articles come from, and it's better than any keyword tool because it's your actual audience.

**Is the free-to-paid path real?** Zero data on this today. The best available benchmark for a comparable publication is a median around 3% free-to-paid, with only one in five publications above 5% ([analysis](https://www.yana-g-y.com/p/substack-free-to-paid-conversion-rate)) — though that dataset's methodology isn't published, so hold it loosely. What's firmer: cohort courses complete far better than self-paced ones, 64% versus 48% in platform data across 32,000 courses, and courses with discussion enabled complete at 66% versus 43% without ([Ruzuku](https://www.ruzuku.com/learn/articles/cohort-vs-self-paced)). That's an argument for cohorts over self-paced, and it's stronger evidence than anything about pricing.

#### The statistics conversation, had once and settled

With a few thousand visitors, here's what you can and cannot conclude.

The rough sample size needed for a two-arm test at conventional thresholds is `16 × p(1−p) / δ²` per arm. At a 3% baseline conversion, detecting a 50% relative improvement needs about 2,070 per arm. Detecting a 20% improvement needs about 12,900 per arm.

Note what that *n* counts: people exposed per arm, not conversions. At a 3% baseline, 2,070 exposures produce about 62 conversions per arm — which is why the requirement looks so brutal. To detect a modest improvement on a downstream formation metric you'd need tens of thousands of people entering the funnel.

So: **A/B testing is pointless for you.** Not "difficult" — pointless. Pathway completions arrive in the dozens per quarter, not the thousands per arm.

Worse, underpowered tests that do reach significance systematically overestimate the effect, often by two to four times. A small site that "wins" a test has usually measured noise and attached a plausible story to it, and will then generalize the wrong lesson. That is worse than not testing.

And watching twenty metrics on a weekly dashboard at 5% each gives you a 64% chance of at least one spurious "significant" move every single week. A weekly dashboard review is an unregistered multiple-comparisons machine.

What to do instead:

- **Designate three decision metrics.** Everything else on the dashboard is descriptive only, and you agree in advance not to act on it.
- **Ship big obvious changes without testing them.** Testing distinguishes 3% from 5%. If you've rebuilt pathway onboarding, the effect is either visible in a before-and-after or not worth detecting.
- **Write a prediction before you ship.** "I expect time-to-first-step to drop below 24 hours; I'll look at six weeks; if it doesn't, I'll revert." Not statistically rigorous, but it defeats the actual failure mode at your scale, which is telling yourself a story after the fact.
- **Interview people.** Five to eight structured conversations with cohort participants will surface more usable causal information than any test you could run this year. At small numbers, qualitative research gets *better*, not worse.
- **Report counts with intervals, not rates.** "17 of 42 completed — 40%, 95% confidence interval 26–56%" is the honest way to report a cohort. Showing the interval stops everyone in the room from over-reading the point estimate.
- **Compare cohort to cohort, not A to B.** You have naturally sequential cohorts. Change one thing per cohort and accept the confounding openly. With thirty people that's anecdote with numbers — but it's honest anecdote, and it's the right unit for formation work.

And read retention curves for **shape, not level**. A curve that flattens at 20% is a real product. A curve decaying toward zero isn't, whatever its week-one number looks like.

---

### PART SEVEN — Who does what

#### Josh

**Before the announcement:** the security fixes, Brad's domain and redirects, robots.txt and sitemaps on both, Search Console and Bing verified on all four properties (both new, both old), Plausible installed, the event schema envelope shipped, the engaged-time beacon built.

**Launch week:** submit sitemaps, request indexing on the top ten pages, wire IndexNow, monitor 404s obsessively, watch Search Console daily.

**Ongoing:** the weekly number, sent to both of them, every Monday. Five lines, not a dashboard. What happened, what's up, what's down, one thing you learned, one thing you need from them. The discipline of writing it is what keeps the analytics honest, and it's what keeps two busy people feeling like participants rather than subjects.

**The thing to guard against:** you're the only one who can see the whole picture, which means you're the only one who'll notice if launch week is a spike rather than a beginning. Watch for it.

#### Alan — the light list

Five things. That's the whole ask.

**One: settle alanhirsch.org.** Redirect it to alanhirsch.com, or if that's not possible, put a prominent link on it. This is worth more to your search presence than everything else on this page combined, and it's a single decision.

**Two: ask three partner organizations to send.** You have three subscribers of your own, so the reach has to come through 100 Movements, Forge, Movement Leaders Collective, your publishers. Those are their lists, not yours — so this is three conversations, not three sends, and each needs a couple of weeks' notice.
