Write one short note in your own voice (here's where my work lives now, here's what's there, one link) and ask them to send it. **Don't let anyone export those lists and load them into our system** — those people subscribed to Forge, not to you, and mailing them from a new domain would be a cold blast with a burned partnership on top.

**Three: three introductions.** Not asks — introductions. Three people in your network who might write about, link to, or mention the site. Publishers, podcast hosts, organizational partners. Hand them to Josh and let him do the follow-up. Mentions on already-indexed sites are the single strongest predictor of AI visibility in the available evidence, and you can generate three of them in twenty minutes.

**Four: name your frameworks consistently.** When you talk about APEST or mDNA anywhere — a podcast, a talk, an article — use the same words and point at the same page. This is what makes you the resolvable origin of your own concepts rather than one voice among several discussing them.

**Five: one video or podcast in the first month, where the site gets named.** Video specifically, if there's a choice — YouTube presence is the strongest single correlate of AI visibility in the best data available (0.737, against 0.266 for domain authority), and it's the cheapest thing on this list for you because you do interviews anyway. Anything already recorded but unaired counts. The only change is naming the destination.

**What you don't have to do:** post on social media, write new articles for the launch, learn any of the analytics, or attend a launch meeting. If you do one thing from this list, do the first one.

#### Brad — the heavier list

Your network is the distribution. Nobody else can work it, and this is the part of the launch that determines whether it compounds.

**One, and this week: decide the domain question.** Missionalchurchnetwork.com becomes the new site's home, or it redirects to a new personal domain, or — the option that happens if you don't decide — two sites compete with each other forever. Ten years of links are on the table. My recommendation is that missionalchurchnetwork.com becomes the domain: it's older, it's more linked, and the category name is a better search asset than a personal name. But it's your call and it needs making now, not after launch.

**Two: write down your network, honestly.** Send Network, Forge, Sentralized, NAMB, the denominational relationships, the planters you've trained, the podcast hosts you've been on. Names, not categories. Who would genuinely want to know about this, versus who you'd be imposing on. The second list matters as much as the first — the point is to spend the goodwill precisely rather than broadly.

**Three: personal notes, not a broadcast.** Ten to fifteen of them, written by you, to specific people. "Here's what I built, here's the thing in it I think you'd actually use, no ask." The readiness questionnaire is the obvious thing to point at — it's concrete, it's yours, and it's useful on its own. Ten personal notes will out-produce a blast to two hundred, and they don't spend anything.

**Four: three to five network placements over the first month.** Not launch week — spread them. A guest post on a network site. A newsletter mention from Send Network or Forge. **At least one on video** — a YouTube interview, a recorded training, a conference session that gets posted. Video carries the strongest correlation with AI visibility in the available data by a wide margin, and almost nobody in this space is deliberately using it that way. Each placement is a mention on an already-indexed site, which is the mechanism that admits a new domain into the pool AI systems retrieve from. This is the highest-value thing anyone can do for either platform, and you're the one positioned to do it.

**Five: sustain a rhythm.** One framework post a week on LinkedIn, in your native form — the inherited assumption, the reframe, one image, a line to sit with. Six weeks of that is worth more than a launch-week burst, and it's how the second month ends up bigger than the first.

**Six: decide which pillar leads.** Covocational or missional church. The strategy plan flags this as open and it sets the publishing queue for a year. Your instinct plus the first month of data should settle it.

**What you don't have to do:** touch the analytics, understand the linking architecture, or make any technical decision beyond the domain.

---

### PART EIGHT — What not to do, and what to definitely do

#### Don't

**Don't announce before the security fixes are in.** You're selling AI trust and governance to churches. A leaked-credentials finding on the flagship platform doesn't cost you a customer, it costs you the argument.

**Don't launch Brad on a vercel.app URL.** Every link, every mention, every screenshot points at a URL you're throwing away, and you cannot properly file a migration for it afterward.

**Don't let launch week be the peak.** The evidence on how content platforms grow is unambiguous — 73% of pages ranking in Google's top ten are three or more years old. This is a multi-year asset. Design for month two being bigger than month one, and treat any plan whose shape is a spike as a plan that failed.

**Don't blast a purchased, scraped, or borrowed list.** You don't have one of the first two, so mostly this is about not importing a partner's. Addresses abandoned for twelve months or more are the raw material mailbox providers recycle into spam traps ([Spamhaus](https://www.spamhaus.org/resource-hub/deliverability/spamtraps-fix-the-problem-not-the-symptom/)) — not a guarantee that a dormant list contains them, but a good reason not to find out. And Microsoft began enforcing SPF/DKIM/DMARC on bulk senders in May 2025, initially by routing non-compliant mail to Junk with `550 5.7.515` rejection as the later phase.

**Don't put keyword-anchored links in a press release.** Explicitly named as link spam in Google's policies. Brand anchors and bare URLs, `rel="sponsored"` on anything placed.

**Don't build llms.txt, buy a GEO monitoring tool in month one, or run an A/B test.** All three are money and attention spent on instruments that cannot produce a signal at your scale, and all three feel productive.

**Don't over-claim the network.** Two sites and a footer isn't a movement. Your audience is precisely the audience that notices. Describe what's true; the bigger claim gets made when it's true.

**Don't gate anything new at launch, and look hard at what's already gated.** Brad's site ships a Pricing page and a Donate page today. Decide deliberately whether those stay up on announcement day. Paywalling early caps the monetizable audience at a small share of a list you haven't built yet, while shrinking the indexable surface search needs to work at all — and a price tag on a platform with four published articles invites a comparison you don't want. My read: keep the pages, make sure nothing substantive sits behind them for now, and gate later and narrower once there's a body of work to gate.

**Don't launch with analytics uninstrumented.** Search Console doesn't backfill. Neither does anything else. The baseline you don't collect this week is gone permanently, and this is the week it matters most.

**Don't ask Brad's network for more than one thing.** One clear invitation. A network leader who feels marketed to is expensive to get back. Flagging honestly: this one is practitioner judgment, not evidence — I looked for a study and there isn't one. I'd still follow it.

#### Do

**Do fix the identity problem first.** For Alan: `sameAs` schema, the www/apex split, and the alanhirsch.org redirect. For Brad: the missionalchurchnetwork.com decision. These are decisions rather than work, and they move things that publishing can't move at all — no volume of new articles resolves an entity collision or recovers a decade of links.

**Do get the mentions, and get some of them on video.** The best available data has branded web mentions correlating with AI visibility at 0.664 and YouTube mentions at 0.737, against 0.266 for domain authority — one correlational study, causally unproven, and still the clearest signal anyone has. Brad's network is the mechanism. Nothing else on this list produces it.

**Do build the engaged-time beacon.** Fifty lines, and it converts your whole content operation from counting views to counting reads. Everything else in the measurement plan gets better once this exists.

**Do instrument formation from day one, in your own database.** Pathway steps, course sessions, practice logs. It's your primary metric and it cannot live in a rented system with a retention window.

**Do add the self-report field at signup.** "How did you hear about this?" It will be your most accurate attribution instrument, and it takes an afternoon.

**Do ship the footer and the honest cross-citations.** Cheapest credibility signal available, mutual by construction, and impossible for a competitor building five separate sites to reproduce.

**Do send the weekly number.** Five lines to Brad and Alan every Monday. It keeps them participating, and writing it keeps you honest.

**Do write down what you expect before you ship.** Not for rigor — to defeat post-hoc storytelling, which is the actual failure mode when the numbers are small.

**Do plan the second wave now.** What goes out in week four, week eight, week twelve. If it isn't planned before launch, it won't happen after, and the shape of the year is decided by whether it does.

---

### PART NINE — The calendar

**This week (before announcing)**
Security fixes and token rotation · Brad's domain decision and DNS · 301s from vercel.app and old site · robots.txt and sitemaps on both · Search Console and Bing on all four properties · Plausible installed · event envelope and `tenant_id` shipped · Person and Article schema · alanhirsch.org decision · export sixteen months of Search Console history from both old properties before redirecting

**Launch week**
Alan's email to his own list · Brad's ten to fifteen personal notes · movement footer live on both · cross-citations on the shared frameworks · sitemaps submitted, top ten pages indexed manually, IndexNow wired · Change of Address filed · daily 404 monitoring · first weekly number sent Monday

**Weeks 2–4**
Engaged-time beacon shipped · self-report field at signup · rollup tables and the three decision metrics · Brad's first two network placements · first manual AI-visibility spot check (twenty questions, four engines) · first read of read-ratios across every published article on both sites — sixteen of Alan's, four of Brad's

**Weeks 5–12**
Brad's remaining network placements and weekly LinkedIn rhythm · publish against actual Search Console queries rather than guesses · five to eight participant interviews · answer the front-door question for both leaders · verdict on the AI Lab · decide whether a GEO monitoring subscription would change a decision, and only then buy one

---

#### What I'd still want to know

Six open questions, honestly marked, because a plan that hides its unknowns is worse than one that names them.

1. **Does Alan control alanhirsch.org?** Everything about his search position turns on this and I can't determine ownership from outside.
2. **What list does missionalchurchnetwork.com have?** Ten years of Squarespace probably collected subscribers. If so, that's the real launch list and it changes Brad's plan considerably.
3. **Was anything else ever live at alanhirsch.com?** If a previous site occupied that domain, there's a redirect map that should exist and doesn't.
4. **Which Supabase project do the live sites actually read from?** There are two — `movemental` with 340 tables and a legacy `alan-hirsch` one — and the connection isn't visible through the tools I have. Worth confirming before you trust any number.
5. **Is the Search Console sync broken, or was it never connected?** The empty metrics table with a sync record suggests the former, which is a bug rather than a task.
6. **Do Brad and Alan agree on the shared vocabulary?** The glossary needs one canonical definition per term. Two definitions is worse than none.

---

Claims about the state of the platforms were verified the same day. Most research claims carry a link; a handful of widely-reported figures don't, and I've flagged the ones where that bothered me. This draft was fact-checked adversarially and about thirty things in it were wrong the first time — assume a few survived. Revise after the first month, when you'll know which half was right.*

## 33. The house guide — how to write for joshshepherd.ai

`joshshepherd-house-guide.md` · 4,357 words

### The house guide

##### How to write for joshshepherd.ai

*Written by Joshua Shepherd. Version 1, 5 August 2026.*
*This is written to an agent, in my voice, so that what comes back sounds like me and not like the average of everyone who has written about this.*

---

#### Before anything else

You are writing for my personal platform. Not for Movemental, which is the company, is fronted by Brad Brisco, speaks as we, and has different rules. This site speaks as I.

The whole site rests on one argument, and every rule below follows from it. **A claim should be checkable, and where it cannot be checked, that should be visible.** If you ever find yourself weighing a rule against that argument, the argument wins and the rule was probably my mistake.

So the failure I care most about is not a clumsy sentence. It is a sentence that is fluent and unverifiable, sitting on a site that argues fluency without verification is the problem. My audience is equipped to notice that, and one instance costs more than ten flat paragraphs.

Read the whole of this before you write anything. It is long because the mistakes are specific.

---

#### Part one · The three tests

Every sentence I publish has to pass three things. Most of the rest of this document is a longer way of saying them.

**Is the authority inside the sentence, or borrowed?** I do not have standing yet. I have not published a book, I do not have a following, and my credentials are in three fields I have left. So a sentence that works because an expert said it, or because it sounds like the kind of thing an expert says, does not work for me. A sentence that works because I watched something happen does.

**Am I the witness, or the subject?** Witness, almost always. I am the person who happened to be standing near something. Pieces where I am the subject exist, and there are two of them, and they are pages rather than articles.

**Does the sentence open something, or close it?** Open. A sentence that settles a question invites the reader to stop. A sentence that names a problem invites them to keep going.

---

#### Part two · The portrait

Underneath every piece there is one picture of me, and it is narrow on purpose.

**Something is wrong, and I happen to be standing near it.**

Not that I fixed it. Not that I saw it first. Not that I have a method for it. Just that I was there, and I paid attention, and here is what I noticed.

If a draft starts to read as though I solved something, the draft has drifted. The version where I found out something the hard way is both truer and more persuasive, and it is nearly always available, because that is how it actually went.

---

#### Part three · The voice

##### Sentences

Plain prose. Short sentences. Vary them, but the default is short.

Say the thing. Do not build to it. If the paragraph has a point, put it in the first or second sentence and then earn it, rather than withholding it for effect.

Concede before claiming. Almost every argument I make is stronger if the objection to it goes first, in its strongest form, in my own words. This is not politeness. It is that I would rather state the objection well than have a reader think of it before I do.

State refusals plainly. When I will not do something, the sentence is short and it does not apologize.

##### Words I do not use

**No em dashes. Anywhere.** Not in the body, not in the apparatus, not in a source list. Use a comma, a full stop, a colon, or rewrite the sentence. The only exception is a quoted title that contains one, because changing it would misquote the source, and when that happens say so in the file.

**No marketing vocabulary.** Not solutions, empower, transform, unlock, journey, passionate, cutting-edge, revolutionary, seamless, game-changing.

**No register-jargon.** Not substrate, load-bearing, leverage, scaffold, surface as a verb, primitive, robust, unpack. These are the words that make writing sound like a consulting deck. They are also the ones I reach for when I am not sure what I mean, which is the real reason to ban them.

**Not genuinely, honestly, or straightforward.** I am honest by default. Saying so makes it sound like a claim.

**Bold is not a sentence.** If a line needs bold to land, it usually needs rewriting. Use bold rarely, for the one claim a section exists to make, and never more than once or twice a page. A page of bold reads as a slide deck.

**Lists are not arguments.** Use prose unless the content really is enumerable, which mostly means steps, criteria, or refusals.

##### Rhythm

I like a short paragraph that lands, followed by white space. I do not like a page of symmetric medium-length paragraphs, which is the most reliable tell of machine writing and the thing I catch most often in my own drafts.

---

#### Part four · How a piece opens

This is the rule I break most and it matters most, so it is the longest section.

##### The five moves available to me

**The correction.** Tell the reader something they reasonably believe is not so. *A PDF of a book is closer to a photograph of a book than to the book.* This is my strongest all-purpose move and the one I underuse.

**The reported question.** Open with something somebody actually asked me. *A nonprofit director told me she had been pitched by four consultants in a month and could not tell them apart.* This is my biggest available asset and it was completely unused until recently.

**The one-person problem.** State somebody's predicament as a plain fact. *Alan Hirsch cannot search his own writing.*

**The durative.** A repeated condition rather than a moment. *I spent three years teaching AI to organizations before a single one of them made a move.* Duration is the one form of standing I actually have.

**The plain report.** An unadorned statement, with the surprise in the next sentence. *On November 30, 2022, I was sitting at my desk at a construction chemicals company.*

##### The moves that are not available to me

**The pronouncement.** Any sentence that declares what the world is like. I have not earned it.

**The count or inventory.** Three shifts, four forces, five reasons. It signals a framework arriving and it closes rather than opens.

**The credential.** Any opener that establishes who I am before establishing why the reader should care. The name is in the navigation. The fold owes them a problem, not a biography.

**The trend opener.** In the last eighteen months, the landscape has. No.

**The rhetorical question.** What if I told you. Never.

**The thesis-first opener.** Stating the argument and then supporting it. It works for people with standing.

**The presumptuous second person.** You are reading this and you feel uneasy. I do not know what the reader feels and claiming to is the fastest way to lose them.

**The lyrical.** Weather, light, a room going quiet. Not this site.

##### One exception, and it is budgeted

**The situational second person** works when it describes something that is happening rather than asserting what the reader feels. *Someone is going to ask their computer about you this week.*

**There are two of these on the entire site and one is already spent** on the fold. Before using the second, name what it is for and confirm nothing better is coming. This is a real budget and it is not negotiable.

---

#### Part five · Facts, brackets, and sources

##### Never invent a fact

Not a number, not a date, not a name, not a scene, not a link. If one is needed and unavailable, insert a visible bracket saying exactly what is required and who can supply it.

A bracket is not a failure. A bracket is the system working. An invented placeholder statistic on this site is a contradiction the audience is equipped to notice, and it costs more than the piece is worth.

##### Two kinds of bracket

**Blocking.** The piece cannot publish with it in. Any claim the argument rests on, any number, any statement about another person.

**Optional.** The piece is better with it and works without it. Colour, texture, one more concrete beat.

Mark which is which, and pull the optional ones out of the body into a note, so that what is left in the text is only what actually stops publication.

##### Verify at the source, not through the coverage

If a claim rests on a paper, read the paper. Not the blog post summarizing it. I have been caught by this once already and the difference was substantive, not cosmetic.

##### The source marker

Factual claims carry an inline marker that reveals the source on hover or tap.

**One marker per page attaches to an opinion instead, and reads: no source. This is a judgment, not a fact.** That refusal marker is the single most persuasive element on the site, so choose it carefully. It should attach to the judgment I have the largest interest in, not the safest one.

---

#### Part six · The taste and permission gate

This is separate from voice and separate from facts, and a piece can pass both and still fail here. Run it on everything.

**One. Does any sentence make a claim about my ability that only I can vouch for?** Hover over "I am regarded as excellent at this" and nothing appears. In a piece arguing that claims should be checkable, the unverifiable claim that flatters me is the one a hostile reader finds first. Cut it, or attach it to something observable.

**Two. Count the compliments.** One is a detail. Two is a pattern. Three is an inventory, and the reader stops following the argument and starts keeping score. If a piece structurally needs praise to exist, keep the single strangest and most specific one and cut the rest. Prefer one I confess to enjoying over one I simply report.

**Three. Is a named living person quoted praising me, and have they seen it?** Publishing real people saying flattering things about me, on my own site, uses them in a way they cannot easily object to. Either they have agreed, or the name comes out and the scene survives unnamed. Default to unnamed.

**Four. Does the piece disclose something about another person that they have not been told is going public?** This includes anything charming and self-incriminating. Charm is not consent. Flag it as a conversation, not an edit.

**Five. Would this embarrass me in five years, or embarrass the person it names now?** And is anything here about somebody else's failure, money, or family?

Report every gate item found, and say for each whether it was cut, unnamed, or flagged. **Never resolve a permission item by quietly editing around it.**

---

#### Part seven · The hard rules

**The construction chemicals employer is never named.** Permitted framings: a construction chemicals company, the company I was working for, in March 2026 I went full time. Nothing about how it ended.

**Anything touching young people involves minors.** No identifying detail about a young person, ever, in any draft, including one that is only sitting on a disk.

**No AI-generated imagery, ever.** On this site it is disqualifying rather than off-brand.

**Clients are anonymous until the work is finished and they have agreed to be named.** A progress report is not a case study. Ask for permission early, while the work is going well, because it is easier to say no to a hypothetical than to a finished draft.

**Disclose the conflict, high and plainly.** I build these systems and I sell the training. Any piece that argues for something I sell says so in the first quarter, not in a footer. And it should include at least one thing that cuts against me, because a disclosure with no cost attached is a formality.

---

#### Part eight · What a piece has inside it

Four things, by design. These are what I check for. They are not laws about writing.

**One idea the piece exists to earn.** One sentence, usually near the top, that everything else justifies. If I cannot name it after finishing the draft, the piece does not have one and polishing will not introduce one.

**A clear from-to.** The reader arrives in one state and leaves in another. I should be able to say which.

**A visible debt to prior work.** It references, it cites, it builds. A piece that pretends to stand alone is usually thinner than it thinks.

**A hook that survives a second reading.** The first-reading test is easy and every surface-engineered piece passes it. The second is the honest one.

---

#### Part nine · Which job the piece is doing

I have four jobs and one of them is my bottleneck.

**Found.** Someone who does not know my name encounters me. Cluster articles, guest podcasts, co-bylines.

**Kept.** That attention becomes a channel I own. The letter, a diagnostic tool, a welcome flow.

**Proven.** Evidence I am worth the time. **This is my empty column and it gates the others.** How-I-built-it with the wrinkle, screen capture, case study, a properly cited paper.

**Moved.** They do the thing. One ask per piece, always the same ask, always small.

**Every piece should know which column it serves.** A piece serving a column I have already filled feels productive and changes nothing. When in doubt, serve Proven.

Three things fill the Proven column, and they are the ones I keep skipping. A how-I-built-it proves nothing without the part where something broke and I say what it cost. One checkable result, a link or a number with a date. And a screen capture, which is sixty to ninety seconds of the thing running, cannot be faked, costs almost nothing, and is still the cheapest credibility available to me.

---

#### Part ten · Clusters and links

**The unit of discovery is the cluster, not the piece.** A single excellent article on a topic is close to invisible. Six to eight interlinked pieces around one hub, each answering a distinct real question, is what search and retrieval systems resolve to.

**A finished cluster compounds. Two half-clusters do not.** So finish one before starting another, even when the second one is more interesting.

The linking rules. A hub links to all its spokes. A spoke links back to its hub plus two lateral spokes. Every letter links to at least one substantive piece. **Links go in the prose where they belong, not in a related-reading block at the foot,** which reads as an afterthought because it is one.

An article has to answer a question in the form people actually ask it. *What is an AI sandbox and how does a church run one* is findable. *Reflections on discernment in a technological age* is not, however good it is.

And it needs a self-contained answer near the top that could be lifted whole, because being quoted by a machine is the new front door.

---

#### Part eleven · Who owns which beat

This is the rule nobody thinks of and it caused me the most trouble.

**Every story belongs to exactly one piece.** When the same scene appears in four articles, I do not have a body of work. I have one piece with four front doors, and a reader who finds two of them stops trusting both.

Current ownership, and it is binding until I change it:

| Beat | Owner |
|---|---|
| Typing Alan's books in by hand, 2020 | Three years of magic shows |
| The PDF as a photograph of a book | Three years of magic shows |
| Three years of demonstrations producing no adoption | Three years of magic shows |
| The MIT ninety-five percent finding | Three years of magic shows, and its hedge is canonical |
| The first Zoom call, recorded | Three years of magic shows |
| The Sunday call and the ten percent offer | I started with two people |
| The CRM demo failure and the three-month promise | I started with two people |
| The five days of OSHA preparation | The story page |
| The first question about wisdom | The story page |
| The information audit acknowledgment | The context method |
| The four states of unreachability | The question nobody asks first |
| The danger cells | The question nobody asks first |

Anywhere else, those beats appear in one or two sentences and link. If one starts to grow back, cut it again.

---

#### Part twelve · Claims I have already fixed, and their canonical form

Use these versions. Do not re-derive them, and do not soften them.

**The MIT figure.** In 2025, MIT's Project NANDA published a report called *The GenAI Divide*, which found that ninety-five percent of enterprise pilots produced no measurable impact on profit and loss. The figure has been contested and the methodology is reported inconsistently, so hold the number loosely. Hold the finding. And note what the finding is: not that those organizations failed, but that they ran pilots and the pilots produced nothing anyone could measure.

**The board liability standard.** This is Delaware corporation law, from Caremark, and most churches and nonprofits are not Delaware corporations. Matera's 2026 paper establishes that AI does not alter the standard, it alters the evidentiary terrain, and that the doctrine stays loyalty-based rather than becoming negligence. Never imply Caremark applies directly to a nonprofit board without saying it is analogous rather than identical.

**The information audit.** Organizations have been inventorying their information resources since Burk and Horton in 1988, with Orna, Buchanan and Gibb, and Henczel building out from it. What changed is not the idea. It is that the catalogue became answerable and the gathering became cheap enough to repeat. Never claim the context inventory as new.

**Tacit knowledge.** Separate articulable-but-unwritten, which comes out in an interview, from the strictly tacit, which does not come out at all. The knowledge management literature is consistent that the more tacit the knowledge, the less a high-technology solution helps. Never claim tacit knowledge extracts cleanly through a pipeline.

**Measured refusal.** Corrective retrieval already evaluates whether material is correct, incorrect or ambiguous and acts on insufficiency. What is mine is the internal-versus-external axis and the argument that an ungrounded internal answer is undetectable in a way an ungrounded external one is not. Claim only those.

**Displacement.** Never measured, including by me. It is the contribution and it is unproven, and absence of a literature is not evidence.

---

#### Part thirteen · What I will not write

I would rather have these on the record than argue them each time.

Anything with an invented person in it. No composites, no illustrative executive directors, no representative pastors. If I need a person, it is a real one with permission or it is nobody.

Anything that predicts what will happen to a sector in the next decade. I do not know.

Anything that ends in "reach out if you would like to chat."

Anything whose numbers I cannot check on request. The site says every number is checkable. That has to be true.

Anything using a young person's story, ever, in any form.

Anything that makes a build sound smooth.

---

#### Part fourteen · How to run a revision

The order matters, because editing in the wrong order wastes work.

**One. Read the whole file before changing a word.** Twice, I have had an instruction that turned out to be wrong about the file, and the file was right. If the instruction and the file disagree, say so rather than obeying.

**Two. Facts first.** Verify at source. Resolve or mark every bracket. This can remove a section, which is why it goes before line editing.

**Three. The gate.** Names, compliments, disclosures, permissions.

**Four. Structure.** Opener, one idea, from-to, ownership of beats, length.

**Five. Line editing last.** Em dashes, banned words, bold, rhythm.

**Six. Then tell me what you did that was a judgment call**, separately from what you did because I asked, so I can reject the judgment calls without rejecting the work.

Do not line-edit a section that should be cut. Do not verify a claim in a paragraph that is about to go.

---

#### Part fifteen · Definition of done

A piece is finished when all of this is true.

No em dashes. No banned words. No bold doing a sentence's work.

The opener is one of the five, or the budgeted second person with a reason stated.

Every fact is verified at source or bracketed. No blocking bracket remains.

The source markers are placed, and one refusal marker attaches to the judgment I have the largest interest in.

The gate has been run and every item is cut, unnamed, or flagged for a conversation.

The conflict is disclosed in the first quarter, with one thing that costs me.

The piece knows which of the four jobs it serves, and it has one ask.

It links to its hub and to two laterals, in prose.

It does not contain a beat another piece owns.

I can say, in one sentence, what it is for.

---

#### Part sixteen · Prompt templates

##### To write a new article

```
Write a new article for joshshepherd.ai. Read the house guide first and
follow it exactly.

Topic: [what]
Job it serves: [Found / Kept / Proven / Moved]
Cluster and hub: [which]
Length: [target]

What I actually watched that lets me make this claim from inside a sentence
rather than from above it: [tell it here, in whatever state]

What I do not know and should say so: [here]

Before drafting, tell me three candidate openers, one from three different
moves in the five, and say which you would use and why. Wait for my answer.

Then draft. Then list separately: every bracket, marked blocking or optional;
every gate item; every claim needing verification and where you would verify
it; and every judgment call you made that I did not ask for.
```

##### To revise an existing piece

```
Revise the attached piece for joshshepherd.ai. Read the house guide first.

Work in this order: read the whole file, facts, gate, structure, line edits.
Do not line-edit anything you might recommend cutting.

If the file contradicts my instruction, tell me. The file is often right.

Return the full revised file, then separately: what still blocks publication,
what is optional, every permission item, and every judgment call you made.
```

##### To assess whether a piece should survive

```
Do not revise this yet. Read it and answer three questions.

One. What arguments does it actually make, deduplicated, and for each, is the
argument mine, borrowed and attributed, or borrowed and unattributed?

Two. For each surviving argument, what did I actually watch that would let me
make it from inside a sentence? If there is nothing, say the argument is not
mine to make yet.

Three. Does anything remain after the corrections in part twelve of the house
guide are applied? If the honest answer is no, say so plainly. I would rather
cut a piece than publish one that has been hollowed out to survive.

Return an assessment and wait.
```

##### To mine a long document for site pieces

```
This is not a site piece and will not become one. Extract from it.

Find the passages where something broke, where I was wrong, or where a real
cost is named. For each candidate piece, give me: the opening sentence using
one of the five moves, the failure it is built around, what the checkable
result would have to be, and where a screen capture would go.

Then list every claim that would need verifying if it moved to the site,
since this was written to a lower standard.

Say which to write first and why. Do not draft.
```

---

#### Part seventeen · Things I have got wrong, so you do not repeat them

I would rather hand you the list than have you rediscover it.

**I put four compliments in one paragraph** and one of them was the only claim on the page nobody could check. Count them.

**I named a client in one piece while another piece was blocked on that client's permission.** Check names across pieces, not within one.

**I cited a legal argument through a blog post summarizing the paper.** Read the paper. When I finally did, it changed the argument and turned up a jurisdiction problem nobody had noticed.

**I told the same story in four pieces.** Assign ownership before writing, not after.

**I wrote a discernment guide for choosing an AI consultant without saying I am one.** The disclosure was there, at eighty percent, phrased as context. It needed to be at the top and phrased as a warning.

**I proposed a criterion my own company was designed to pass** and presented it as neutral. When that happens, mark it and argue against it in the text. The concession is more persuasive than the criterion.

**I labelled something part one of three** when parts two and three did not exist.

**I described a build as prep work for six months** when it was the actual work. That one is in an article now, so at least it earned its keep.

---

#### Last thing

If a rule in here produces a worse piece, break it and tell me which one and why. I wrote these from about a dozen drafts and one long argument with myself, and some of them are certainly wrong.

But do not break them quietly. The whole argument of this site is that the work should be checkable, and that has to include the work of writing it.

---

## 34. Where These Numbers Come From — the ReNeighbor sources

`where-these-numbers-come-from.md` · 6,294 words

### Where These Numbers Come From

A guide to every source behind your ReNeighbor report.

---

#### Start here

ReNeighbor doesn't know anything about your neighborhood on its own. Everything in your report comes from somewhere — a government survey, a set of old maps, a health model, a search of the open web. This page tells you where each piece came from, what it actually measures, and how much weight to put on it.

You don't have to read all of it. Skim to whatever number you're looking at.

Three habits will keep you honest with any of it:

**Check how big an area the number covers.** Some sources describe your specific neighborhood — a census tract, usually a few thousand people. Others describe your whole county or metro. A county unemployment rate tells you nothing about your street. Every entry below says which one you're getting.

**Most of these are estimates, not headcounts.** The Census figures are a five-year average with a margin of error. The CDC health numbers come from a model. The historical sources are years or decades old. Read them as strong signals, not exact truth.

**Blank almost never means zero.** Several of these feeds come back empty because of a coverage gap or a plumbing problem on our end — not because the thing they measure isn't there. An empty eviction number doesn't mean nobody gets evicted. Where a source is prone to this, we say so.

---

#### Who lives here

##### American Community Survey (Census Bureau)

The Census counts everyone once every ten years. In between, it runs a smaller rolling survey and pools five years of answers together so the numbers hold up for a small area. That's why your report says 2023 but really means "the average picture from 2019 through 2023."

**Covers:** your census tract — a few thousand people.
**Tells you:** how many people live there and their median age; what households earn and how many are below the poverty line; who owns and who rents; home values, rents, and how much of income goes to housing; education, commutes, and how long people have stayed.

This is the ground floor. Before you can love a place you need to know who's actually there. A young renting neighborhood asks different questions of you than an aging one full of paid-off homes.

Two things to hold. It's a survey, so every number carries a margin of error — a small tract's poverty rate might really sit anywhere in a wide band, which is why we show the band instead of a single confident figure. And because it averages five years, it lags. A neighborhood that just gentrified will still look like its older self here. If you want the direction of change, compare an older survey to a newer one; the trend is more honest than any single year.

*Source: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2023.*

##### CDC PLACES

The CDC can't survey the health of every small neighborhood — too expensive. So PLACES takes big national health surveys and models what health probably looks like down at the neighborhood level.

**Covers:** your census tract.
**Tells you:** about forty measures. Health outcomes like diabetes, high blood pressure, depression, and obesity. Behaviors like smoking and inactivity. And life conditions — no insurance, no regular doctor, food insecurity, housing trouble, trouble paying utilities, and **loneliness** and lack of emotional support.

This is where a neighborhood's hidden aches show up. A place can look fine on income and home values and still carry high loneliness or depression — and those are exactly the wounds a rooted community is built to meet. "Loneliness 30%" means the model estimates roughly three in ten adults there usually feel lonely. That's not a headcount. It's a door.

These are modeled estimates, not counts of diagnosed people. And a bare percentage means nothing on its own — is 30% loneliness high or normal? We always show each figure against a national and state benchmark so "compared to what?" has an answer.

*Source: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, PLACES, 2023.*

##### CDC Social Vulnerability Index

Built for disaster planners to answer one question: if a flood or a pandemic hit this neighborhood, how hard would it be for people here to cope and recover? The CDC bundles a stack of Census facts into one score.

**Covers:** your census tract, ranked against every other tract in the country.
**Tells you:** a score from 0 to 1. A tract in the 90th percentile is more strained than 90% of the country. It's built from four things: money and work (poverty, unemployment, income, education); household makeup (the very old and very young, disability, single parents, language); race and ethnicity; and housing and transportation (crowding, mobile homes, no car, group living).

Think of it as one "how much strain, how little cushion" number. A high score means people have less to fall back on when something goes wrong — and it's where practical care lands hardest: rides, meals, showing up in a crisis.

The catch is that it ranks rather than explains. "0.14" tells you where the place stands next to others; it doesn't tell you why. We translate the source's raw column names into the four plain themes above and phrase the score as a percentile so you can read it as "less strained than most of the country" instead of a bare decimal.

*Source: CDC / ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index, 2022.*

##### BLS Local Unemployment

The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes an unemployment rate for counties and metros, updated every month.

**Covers:** your whole county.
**Tells you:** the share of people who want work, are looking, and don't have it.

Because it updates monthly it catches turns the Census is too slow to see — a plant closing, a local boom. But it's county-wide, so treat it as weather over the whole region, not a report on your streets. A struggling county can hold a comfortable neighborhood, and the reverse.

Honest note: this feed often fails mid-run and comes back empty. That's our plumbing, not a statement that everyone's employed. When it's blank, use the Census employment numbers instead.

*Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics.*

---

#### What's on the ground

##### Google Places

The same database behind the pins on Google Maps. We ask it what's actually near your address.

**Covers:** a radius around your address.
**Tells you:** real places, sorted — everyday businesses and third places (coffee shops, restaurants, shops); grocery stores and supermarkets; churches and places of worship; schools and civic anchors. For each one, a name, a rating, and how many people reviewed it.

This is the built world you'd see if you drove the streets. Where do people here get food — a real grocery store, or gas stations and dollar stores? Is there a coffee shop where the neighborhood gathers? How many churches already sit on these blocks?

Two things we handle for you. Google's categories are messy — searching "grocery" drags in liquor stores and pharmacies — so we filter that out and keep the actual food stores. And it's a living database, so a place that closed last month may still show a pin. Read the list as a strong current sketch, not a certified registry. The neighborhood name Google returns is Google's label, and it sometimes isn't what locals call the place.

*Source: Google Places API.*

##### Urban Institute Education Data (schools)

Every public school reports basic facts to the Department of Education each year. The Urban Institute cleans that up and makes it easy to pull.

**Covers:** public schools near your address.
**Tells you:** name, district, and distance; enrollment; grade range and type (regular, charter, magnet); and a read on economic need.

Schools are anchors. They tell you where the families are, which blocks feed which building, and where a neighborhood's kids spend their days. The district name matters more than a map suggests — one neighborhood can straddle several.

One thing worth understanding, because it trips up almost everyone. The old shorthand for school poverty was the free-and-reduced-lunch rate. But many districts now feed *every* child free regardless of income, so a school shows 99% even in a mixed-income neighborhood. That's a lunch policy, not a poverty measure. We drop that number and show **direct certification** instead — the share of kids automatically enrolled because their family already qualifies for food or cash assistance. That's a truer read of real household need, and it's often wildly different: one school in our worked example shows about 13% direct certification against a misleading 99% lunch rate.

*Source: Urban Institute Education Data Portal, drawing on the federal Common Core of Data, 2022.*

##### IRS Nonprofits

Every tax-exempt organization in the country — every charity, church, food bank, and civic group — has an IRS record. The IRS publishes the master list.

**Covers:** your ZIP code, widening to city or state when needed.
**Tells you:** names and addresses of registered nonprofits, and what kind each one is (the IRS classification code "X" means religion; others cover human services, health, education, arts).

This is the map of a neighborhood's existing ability to care. You are rarely the first person to love this place, and this shows you who your partners and elders might be. The religion-coded rows pull out the congregations and faith ministries specifically.

Two cleanups we do. A single ZIP can hold a thousand registered organizations, many of them duplicate chapters of the same group, so we collapse duplicates and put religion and human-service organizations first. And "registered with the IRS" is a legal fact, not proof anyone's still working — some entries are dormant. Treat this as a good lead list, then go find out who's really operating.

*Source: IRS Exempt Organizations Business Master File, 2025.*

##### U.S. Religion Census

Roughly every ten years, a coalition of religious bodies tries to count religious membership across the country, denomination by denomination.

**Covers:** your county.
**Tells you:** which religious groups are present and roughly how many adherents each claims; the share of the population that adheres to some religion, and by implication the share that doesn't; and the mix — heavily Catholic, heavily evangelical, mainline, unaffiliated.

This is the religious weather. Are you entering a churched region where most people already have a tradition, or a secular one where faith is thin? That shapes how a new expression of church lands — who your neighbors already are spiritually, what language will resonate, where the gaps are.

Two cautions. It counts adherents *as denominations report them*, which is self-reported and uneven — some groups count generously, some barely count at all, and unaffiliated people are inferred rather than asked. And it's county-level. Pair it with the actual congregations found nearby to get from region to neighborhood.

*Source: U.S. Religion Census 2020 (ASARB), via the Association of Religion Data Archives (ARDA).*

##### Census County Business Patterns

Once a year the Census tallies the businesses operating in each county.

**Covers:** your county.
**Tells you:** how many business locations there are, how they break down by industry, and how many people they employ.

Where Google Places shows you the shops on the corner, this shows you the shape of the whole local economy. Is this a place built on health care, on warehouses and logistics, on retail? That tells you what kind of work the people around you do, which shapes their schedules, their stresses, and when they can be reached.

County-level, so it describes the region your address sits inside, not your specific streets. Use it for the big picture and lean on Google Places and the Census commute numbers for what's happening outside your door.

*Source: U.S. Census Bureau, County Business Patterns, 2022.*

##### Walk Score

A private company (owned by Redfin) that scores how easy it is to get around without a car.

**Covers:** your address.
**Tells you:** three numbers from 0 to 100. **Walk Score** — could you run daily errands on foot, given how close groceries, restaurants, schools, parks, and shops are and how the streets are laid out? Over 90 and you barely need a car; under 50 and most trips mean driving. **Transit Score** — how good the bus and train service is. **Bike Score** — how safe and connected riding is.

This is a quick read on the rhythm of a place — whether life happens on sidewalks or through windshields. That shapes how a neighborhood gathers. A high walk score often means people bump into each other at the corner store, and a church can meet them in those third places. A low score usually means a private, car-dependent neighborhood where connection has to be planned rather than stumbled into.

Read it next to the Census commute numbers. If almost everyone drives to work but the walk score is high, you're looking at a place with the bones to be walkable that nobody uses that way — worth noticing. And take it as texture, not gospel: it's one company's model, tuned for real-estate listings.

*Source: Walk Score.*

---

#### How the place got this way

##### HOLC Redlining Maps

In the 1930s a federal agency drew color-coded maps of American cities to tell banks where it was safe to lend. Green and blue meant best. Yellow meant declining. **Red meant hazardous** — and those red areas, almost always Black and immigrant neighborhoods, were cut off from mortgage money for generations. That's where the word *redlining* comes from. Historians at the University of Richmond scanned and digitized every one of those maps, including the surveyors' handwritten notes.

**Covers:** your address, if it falls inside a mapped city.
**Tells you:** the grade — A (green), B (blue), C (yellow), or D (red) — and the original surveyor's written description of the area and its residents.

This is a neighborhood's inherited wound. Redlining didn't stay in the 1930s. The red areas were starved of investment for decades, and the resulting gaps in wealth, home values, tree cover, and health are still measurable. Knowing an address sits in a formerly redlined zone lets you read its present honestly: what looks like "just how this neighborhood is" often traces back to a line someone drew ninety years ago.

Read it next to the mortgage lending data to see whether the old pattern still runs. The surveyors' notes are often bluntly prejudiced. They're preserved as a primary document, to inform lament and understanding — not to be repeated as description.

*Source: Mapping Inequality: Redlining in New Deal America (University of Richmond Digital Scholarship Lab).*

##### Renewing Inequality (urban renewal)

After World War II the federal government funded "urban renewal" — clearing neighborhoods it labeled blighted to build highways, civic centers, and public housing. In practice it bulldozed hundreds of thousands of homes, and the displaced families were overwhelmingly Black and poor. The same Richmond team that mapped redlining reconstructed where these projects happened and how many people they uprooted.

**Covers:** your address, if it falls inside a documented project area.
**Tells you:** what the project was and when it ran, how many families were displaced, and their racial makeup where it was recorded.

This is the second half of an inherited history. Where redlining *starved* neighborhoods, urban renewal often *erased* them — tearing out the homes, churches, and businesses that held a community together. If your address sits in one of these zones, the people there now may be living on ground where an earlier community was displaced, and that memory can run deep.

Knowing it helps you enter with humility instead of assuming the neighborhood's current state is natural or neutral. It's what turns a table of demographics into a story with grief and resilience in it.

*Source: Renewing Inequality, University of Richmond Digital Scholarship Lab (American Panorama), covering roughly the 1950s–1970s.*

##### The Negro Motorist Green Book

Under Jim Crow, a Black postal worker named Victor Hugo Green published an annual guide to the hotels, restaurants, gas stations, and shops where Black travelers would be safe and welcome — because most of the country was neither. It was a survival tool. The New York Public Library digitized the guides and pinned the listings to real locations.

**Covers:** about a kilometer around your address.
**Tells you:** the name and type of each historical listing — hotel, restaurant, service station, tavern, salon — its address at the time, and how far it sits from you.

This is Black history made tangible on ground you can stand on. A cluster of Green Book listings marks a place that was once a haven, often the heart of a thriving Black community that white travelers drove past without a thought. Knowing what a corner held changes how you see it.

For a leader entering a neighborhood, this is an invitation to honor a history that's easy to overlook — the elders who remember it, the institutions that survived, the losses that came with integration and urban renewal. It turns "just an address" into somewhere with a story worth learning before you presume to add to it.

Thousands of listings are loaded. Whether any show up for you depends on whether Black travel life once concentrated near your address.

*Source: The Negro Motorist Green Book listings, mapped by The New York Public Library. 1930s–1960s.*

##### Chronicling America (historic newspapers)

The Library of Congress has scanned millions of pages of old American newspapers and made them searchable.

**Covers:** your state and area, over a date range you can set.
**Tells you:** no number. Actual articles that mention the place, in the language of the time — how a neighborhood, an event, or a community was described while it was happening.

This is a neighborhood's memory in its own voice. Numbers tell you what a place *is*; old newspapers tell you what it *lived through* — the founding, the boom, the fire, the closure, the fight, the celebration. That texture helps you arrive as someone willing to learn a place's story instead of a stranger acting like history started the day you showed up.

We search the real archive rather than asking an AI to recall history from memory, so anything quoted is anchored to a genuine document.

Two honest notes. The archive is uneven — some towns and eras are covered richly, others barely — so an empty result means thin coverage, not that nothing happened. And these papers carry the prejudices of their day. The language can be ugly. It's kept as a primary source to be read with discernment and lament, not repeated.

*Source: Chronicling America: Historic American Newspapers — Library of Congress (loc.gov). Credit the individual newspaper and the Library of Congress.*

##### Longitudinal Tract Database

There's a hidden problem in comparing a neighborhood to its own past: the Census redraws its tract boundaries every ten years, so the "same" tract in 1990 and 2020 may not cover the same ground. Researchers at Brown University rebuilt old Census data onto today's boundaries so you can line up decades of history for the same patch of land.

**Covers:** your census tract, back through past Census decades.
**Tells you:** population, race and ethnicity, income, education, and housing from earlier decades, all placed on today's map.

This is the long memory of a neighborhood's numbers, where the American Community Survey only reaches back a few years. Has this place been getting whiter or more diverse over decades? Was it always this affluent, or did that arrive recently? Is today's makeup a long pattern or a sharp break? That trend line keeps you from mistaking a recent change for the way things have always been.

One technical caution we handle behind the scenes: matching old boundaries to new ones takes a translation table, and where the redraw was messy we deliberately hide a shaky match rather than report a misleading number. A gap here can mean "the boundaries didn't line up well enough to trust," not "no history exists."

*Source: Longitudinal Tract Database — Brown University (Logan, Xu, Stults).*

##### Opportunity Atlas

Economists at Harvard followed millions of anonymized tax records to see what actually happened to the children who grew up in each neighborhood — not the adults living there now, but the kids raised there decades ago who are grown today. It answers a haunting question: **does this neighborhood tend to launch its children upward, or hold them where they started?**

**Covers:** your census tract.
**Tells you:** the average adult outcomes of people who grew up there — what they earn as adults, often split by what their parents earned; rates of incarceration, teen birth, and staying in the area; and results broken out by race and gender. We focus on the most telling figure: the adult income rank of children whose parents were in the bottom quarter of earners.

This is the closest thing there is to a measure of a place's effect on a life. Two neighborhoods can look identical on income today while one quietly hands its children a ladder and the other a ceiling. That difference sits at the heart of loving a place: are the kids growing up here going to be okay?

Two cautions, one of them serious. The data is historical — it describes a track record, not a promise about today's kids. And when a group's number is missing (say, no figure for Black children in a small tract), that means **"not reported," not "zero."** Small counts get suppressed to protect privacy. Reading a blank as "none of them made it" would be a bad mistake, so we label these as not reported on purpose.

*Source: Opportunity Insights / Opportunity Atlas (Chetty et al.), Harvard Dataverse, 2018 release.*

---

#### What's pressing on people

##### Eviction Lab

Until recently nobody had gathered the country's eviction records in one place. Sociologists at Princeton, led by Matthew Desmond, collected millions of court records to build the first national map of eviction.

**Covers:** your census tract, for the years 2000 through 2018.
**Tells you:** eviction filings (how often landlords took tenants to court), actual evictions (how often people were put out), and rates measured against the number of renter households so you can compare places of different sizes.

Eviction is one of the sharpest, most personal forms of instability a family can face. It uproots kids from schools, breaks apart support networks, and is often a cause of poverty rather than just a symptom. A high rate marks a neighborhood where housing is precarious and people are quietly being churned out of their homes — a place where presence, stability, and practical help matter enormously, and where the community you're joining may be more transient than it first looks.

The big caveat is age. This runs through 2018, so it can be years behind. We flag it as stale. Read it as history and pattern — *was* this a high-eviction place? — and check it against the newer Census rent and cost-burden trend for where things stand now.

*Source: The Eviction Lab at Princeton University.*

##### HUD Location Affordability Index

The usual way to judge affordability is rent or a mortgage. HUD argues that misses half the story: a cheap house in a far suburb costs a fortune once you add the two or three cars a family needs to live there. So this index adds **housing plus transportation** together.

**Covers:** your census tract, modeled for several household types.
**Tells you:** the share of income that goes to housing, the share that goes to transportation given how car-dependent the place is, and the two combined — the true cost of living *here*.

This reframes affordability honestly. A neighborhood can look cheap on rent and still crush a family's budget because everything requires a car and a long drive. The combined burden tells you how much breathing room people actually have, which shapes their stress, their time, and whether they can afford to put down roots.

One distinction we're careful to keep: HUD uses its *own* income assumptions for those model households, which won't match the actual median income the Census reports for your real neighborhood. In our worked example HUD models about $59k while the Census tract shows about $76k. Those are two different lenses and they must not be collapsed into one, so we label the HUD figure as coming from a model, not a count of the people who live there.

*Source: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Location Affordability Index.*

##### USDA Food Access Research Atlas

The USDA studies where Americans can and can't easily buy healthy, affordable food, and flags the neighborhoods commonly called food deserts.

**Covers:** your census tract.
**Tells you:** yes/no flags. Is it low-income? Is it low-access — meaning a meaningful share of people live more than a set distance from the nearest supermarket (often a mile in cities, ten miles in rural areas)? Plus combinations of the two at different distances, and flags for households without a vehicle.

Food access is a quiet daily hardship that shapes health, budgets, and dignity. In a flagged neighborhood the nearest real groceries might be a bus transfer away, so people make do with convenience stores and fast food — which shows up years later in the health data as diabetes and obesity. Knowing a place is a food desert points to something concrete and doable: rides, gardens, a co-op, a pantry, a market. It's often exactly the kind of need a rooted community can meet.

The raw data speaks in codes like `lila_1and10` — "LILA" means low-income and low-access. We translate those into plain yes/no English. Cross-check the flag against the grocery stores Google Places found nearby; sometimes a new store has opened since the atlas was last updated.

*Source: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Economic Research Service, Food Access Research Atlas.*

##### HMDA (home mortgage lending)

Federal law requires most mortgage lenders to report every home loan they make and every one they turn down. That public record is HMDA (say it "HUM-duh"). It exists so watchdogs can check whether banks lend fairly across neighborhoods and races.

**Covers:** your county reliably; your tract when the lookup works.
**Tells you:** how many home loans were applied for and how many were approved or denied; loan amounts and applicant incomes; who's borrowing, including race and ethnicity, which is the whole point of the law; and whether loans came from ordinary banks or higher-cost lenders.

Money flowing in — or being withheld — is one of the clearest signs of where a neighborhood is headed and how it's been treated. If loans are approved and homes are changing hands, capital is moving in, often the leading edge of gentrification. If applications from a neighborhood or a group are denied at unusual rates, that's the fingerprint of the redlining that shaped so many American cities. Read it next to the HOLC maps to see whether the old pattern is still running.

Honest limitation: the tract-level lookup frequently comes back empty right now — the county call works, the neighborhood call often doesn't. That's a gap we're working on, not a finding that no lending happened. When it's blank, read nothing into it.

*Source: FFIEC / CFPB, Home Mortgage Disclosure Act data, 2022.*

##### FEMA National Risk Index

FEMA rates how exposed each community is to natural hazards — floods, wildfires, tornadoes, hurricanes, earthquakes, heat — and how well it could bounce back.

**Covers:** county or tract.
**Tells you:** a risk score built from three things: how likely and severe the natural threats are, how much the local population would be harmed, and how well the place could recover.

This is the "what could go wrong from nature" question. It matters for the long view of caring for a place: a neighborhood in a flood zone or a fire-prone area carries a recurring threat that will, sooner or later, test whoever is present to help. Churches are often the ones who show up when disaster hits, so knowing the standing risk is part of loving a place wisely.

Be honest about it, though: **this dataset currently has nothing loaded in ReNeighbor.** It returns empty everywhere, so for now it adds nothing to your report. A blank here means we haven't loaded it yet — not that your neighborhood is hazard-free.

*Source: Federal Emergency Management Agency, National Risk Index.*

---

#### What's changing

##### Census Building Permits Survey

Before anyone builds a house or an apartment building, a local government issues a permit. The Census collects those counts from thousands of local permit offices.

**Covers:** whole jurisdictions — a city or county.
**Tells you:** how many new housing units got the green light over a period, split by type, like single-family homes versus larger apartment buildings.

Permits run ahead of everything else. People pull them before construction, which happens before new residents arrive. So a rise is an early signal that a neighborhood is about to grow or shift — new families, new density, new pressure on schools and streets. Flat or zero permits suggests a settled, built-out place that will look much the same in five years.

Two limits. It's reported for a whole jurisdiction, so read it as regional momentum, not block by block. And this endpoint frequently fails or returns nothing right now — a gap on our end, not evidence that nobody's building. When it's blank, set it aside.

*Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Building Permits Survey, 2023.*

##### GDELT (news coverage)

GDELT is a giant, always-running monitor of the world's news. It reads articles in near real time and turns them into searchable data — who, what, where, and the tone of the coverage.

**Covers:** your location, over a rolling 90 days.
**Tells you:** recent stories that name the place or the area around it, roughly what they're about, and whether the coverage skews positive or negative.

This is the current-events question — the living conversation around a neighborhood that no census catches. A run of stories about a new development, a closure, a crime wave, or a community win tells you what's on people's minds right now, and what a neighbor might bring up if you asked how things are going.

Two limits. GDELT keys off published news, so it's strong on places that make headlines and nearly silent on ordinary neighborhoods that don't. An empty result usually means "nothing newsworthy lately," not "nothing happening." And this feed often returns nothing at all in our runs. Treat a blank as no signal rather than a finding.

*Source: The GDELT Project.*

##### Census LODES (commute and jobs)

By linking employer records to where workers live, the Census can trace the daily tide of commuting — where the people who *live* in a neighborhood go to work, and where the people who *work* there come from.

**Covers:** your census tract — **but only in a handful of states so far.**
**Tells you:** how many workers live there and where their jobs are (near or far, which direction, what industry); how many jobs are located there and where the people filling them commute from; and the overall pull between home and work.

This shows a neighborhood's relationship to the wider city. Is it a place people leave every morning — a bedroom community that empties out by day? Or a place others pour into for work? That rhythm tells you when neighbors are actually home and reachable, whether the place has its own economic life or borrows it from downtown, and how far people's daily worlds stretch past their front doors.

Coverage limit worth knowing: we've only loaded LODES for Colorado, Utah, New Mexico, Wyoming, and Arizona. Everywhere else — including our Missouri worked example — we label commute data as *not loaded* rather than guess. A blank means it isn't in the warehouse for your state yet, not that nobody commutes.

*Source: U.S. Census Bureau, LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics.*

---

#### What people say

##### Luna — web research

Everything above comes from an official dataset. Luna is different. It's a set of AI researchers that go read the open web about your specific neighborhood — local news, forums, reviews, blog posts, church websites — and summarize what people are saying. It's how we catch the human feel of a place that no government spreadsheet records.

There are three of them:

- **Community sentiment** — how do people who live here talk about the place? What do they love, complain about, worry about?
- **Cultural texture** — what's the identity and personality of the neighborhood? Where do people gather? What's the vibe, the local pride, the reputation?
- **Congregation enrichment** — takes the bare list of churches found nearby and fills each one out from its website: denomination, programs, ministries, who they serve.

**Covers:** your neighborhood when the web says enough about it; the wider metro when it doesn't.
**Tells you:** nothing numeric. Impressions — themes, top concerns, cultural identity, gathering spots, and fuller profiles of local churches.

This is what makes a neighborhood feel like a place instead of a table. The Census tells you the median income; only this can tell you that locals are proud of the old diner, anxious about a new development, and gather at a particular park on Sundays. For someone learning to love a neighborhood, that's gold.

But hold it loosely, and this is the part that matters most: it is **unverified web texture**, and we label it that way everywhere it shows up. The web is opinionated, uneven, and sometimes wrong — a few loud reviews aren't the neighborhood. When your neighborhood is thinly covered online, Luna sometimes broadens out to the wider metro, so we tag whether a finding is really about your neighborhood or is a metro fallback.

Treat Luna as informed rumor to check in person. It's a list of things to go ask real neighbors about. Never read it as established fact on the level of the Census or the CDC.

---

#### One more name you'll see

**Terra** isn't a source. Terra is the AI that writes your report. It takes everything above — the Census, the CDC, the old maps, Luna's web texture — and composes it into plain language. It measures nothing and adds no facts of its own. It only puts the sources together, following a strict rule about which ones are authoritative and which, like Luna, are only suggestive.

---
