The true story

### 

Reach estimator

### Roughly how far will it travel?

A teaching model, not a forecast. It sketches the reach you build from the parts you control — search and AI capture of the in-market audience, compounding over four years — on top of the owned audience you can already reach directly. Real numbers depend on your actual query volume and competition, so treat the outputs as orders of magnitude, not promises.

Total addressable market (TAM)  Searches for this question per year (from a keyword tool) ≈ 5,000 people go looking each year No keyword tool? Pick a rough size  Use my number → Niche — a few hundred a year Moderate — a few thousand a year Popular — tens of thousands a year Very popular — hundreds of thousands How many credible peers are also optimizing  Few — you can hold a top spot / get cited Some — you land mid-pack Many — a crowded field all optimizing Leaders in your cross-linking network (1 = going it alone) Owned reach (people you can push to directly)  Execution score for this piece: 100

GEO in the real world

### What GEO does — and what happens when everyone does it.

Classic SEO earns a **click** : your link appears and a person chooses it. GEO earns something different — a place **inside the answer**. When someone asks ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini about your topic, the model writes the reply and may lean on you, name you, and point to you. The first reader is the model; the human reads what the model made of you.

#### For your work, on its own

Optimizing for GEO means the model can **reach** your work (its crawlers get in), **lift** it cleanly (clear claims, statistics, definitions it can quote), **trust** it (a recognized author, corroborated across the web), and find it **current**. The prediction is concrete: answers about your topic start to carry your framing and your name, instead of a competitor's or none at all.

#### Now assume a hundred credible leaders run the same playbook

This is the real world, and it changes the story. Everyone in your field reads the same guidance and optimizes the same way. Five things follow.

  1. **It becomes the admission ticket, not an edge.** When every credible voice is extractable and crawlable, doing it no longer sets you apart — it only qualifies you to be considered. What changes most is the **penalty for absence** : the leader who skips it isn't merely behind, they're structurally excluded from the answer, invisible no matter how good the ideas.
  2. **The answer still names only a few.** A model builds each reply from a handful of sources, not a hundred. Among a field of optimized peers it has to **choose** , and the tie-breakers are no longer the mechanics everyone shares — they're authority, distinctiveness, corroboration, and freshness.
  3. **It resolves into a power law.** A small number of voices become the ones the models name again and again; the rest sit in the training data, present but rarely surfaced. Optimization gets you into the pool; it does not spread attention evenly across it.
  4. **Sameness dissolves into the average.** When a hundred people optimize identically, their content converges — same structures, same phrasings, same points — and the model blends it into a generic consensus with no one attached. What survives that blending is a **proprietary framework, original data, or a nameable position**. Distinctiveness is the only thing that comes out the other side with your name on it.
  5. **Being the origin others build on is the strongest place to stand.** If the other ninety-nine use your language — if the field argues in terms you coined — the model treats you as the source even while paraphrasing them. Owning the vocabulary of the conversation beats out-optimizing it.

Illustrative: across an optimized field, share of AI mentions concentrates on a few named voices while the rest stay in the data, rarely surfaced.

#### What to predict from ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini

Two doors lead into an AI answer, and GEO feeds both. **Training data** favors volume and long-standing, widely-referenced authority — who the web has treated as important for years. **Live retrieval** favors what is fresh, crawlable, well-structured, and currently trusted. The models differ in how much they lean on each — a retrieval-heavy assistant leans on the live web, a training-heavy one on what it already absorbed — but the levers are identical, so the same body of work that ranks also gets cited. As a whole field optimizes, each model's answer on the topic settles into a **stable consensus** dominated by the few most-authoritative and most-distinctive voices, refreshed by whoever published most recently.

#### The honest takeaway

GEO is necessary but not sufficient. Doing it moves you from **excluded to eligible** ; it does not, by itself, move you from eligible to named. In a crowded field the durable advantage isn't the optimization mechanics everyone shares — it's owning the ideas the field uses and being the most-corroborated origin of them. Optimize to qualify; differentiate and earn authority to win. For a body of work built on named frameworks, that origin position is the whole game.

The scenius effect

### What happens when the whole network cross-links, over time.

The competition story above assumes rivals. The more important story is **cooperation** : a field of credible leaders who deliberately link to and cite each other's work, meaningfully, over years. That isn't a hundred sites splitting a pie — it's a **scenius** , a scene whose collective genius compounds a shared position. It changes the prediction, because authority and citation are properties of a **network** , not of a page. One optimized site is a node shouting into the void; a hundred interlinked ones are a graph, and both Google and the AI models read that graph as the definition of who matters in the field.

Illustrative: a densely cross-linked network reads to search and AI as one authority hub — with an origin node (green) others build on.

#### In search

A backlink is worth more when it comes from a high-authority site. When every leader is individually well-optimized **and** they link to each other's pillars, every inbound link arrives from a strong domain — so the same number of links carries far more weight. Authority recirculates: each site lifts the others, which raises the value of the links they send, which lifts the others again. It's a feedback loop, not a sum. The cluster starts out-ranking outsiders on the field's terms, and a rising tide lifts the smaller nodes — a newer leader inside the network inherits credibility they could never earn alone.

#### In AI answers

Models infer who is authoritative in a domain largely from how often sources **co-occur and reference each other**. When the leaders cite each other's frameworks and name each other, they manufacture exactly that corroboration signal: these names keep appearing together as the authorities here. The models learn the **cluster** as the answer to the topic — so instead of one winner taking most, several are named together as a recognized school of thought. And because each leader owns a distinct sub-territory and points to the others for theirs, the network covers the whole subject with no internal cannibalization: every question in the field hands off to someone in the cluster, and every hand-off is another corroborating link. Comprehensive and non-redundant is precisely what a model wants to cite.

#### Over time

This compounds on a curve, not a line. In year one the cross-links exist but carry little weight. As each node earns its own outside authority and the internal links mature, the graph's total authority rises — and because it recirculates, growth accelerates before it saturates. An outsider arriving three years later doesn't face a hundred separate competitors; they face one established, interlinked, model-recognized institution. The network becomes the incumbent, and the barrier it builds is far higher than the sum of its members.

#### The one rule that makes it real

The links have to be **meaningful and editorial** — genuine intellectual references between people who actually build on each other's work — not a reciprocal link scheme on a schedule. Google has spent twenty years killing link farms, and a mechanical exchange gets flagged; real cross-citation is the strongest authority signal there is, because it is indistinguishable from the organic thing it actually is. The strategy is to make the real relationships legible to the crawlers, not to fabricate relationships that aren't there.

Corrected prediction: if the network cooperates instead of competes, you don't get a power law where a few win and the rest vanish. You get a **compounding authority commons** — a rising floor that lifts every genuine member, a shared position as _the_ recognized school on the topic in both search results and AI answers, and a moat that widens over time. Modeling a lone platform systematically undersells what's possible, because credibility is a graph — and a graph can be grown on purpose.

After creation

### The publication layer — agent drafts, human approves.

Everything after "create" runs as a pipeline that produces drafts a human signs off. Eight components make it real:

  1. **The templating engine (the invisible layer).** Emits every derived and copied field automatically on render — canonical, robots/snippet directives, Open Graph + Twitter, the type-aware JSON-LD skeleton, sitemap, breadcrumbs, image sizing, plus per-type emitters (Scholar citation_*, podcast RSS itunes:*, video VTT + SeekToAction). Built once, runs on every publish — the lift that collapses per-post work to a handful of fields.
  2. **The publish pipeline.** On publish the agent recipes run in order, each a reviewable card — title/meta, schema fill, FAQ, alt + share image, internal + network links, post-publish QA, distribution, plus transcript and DOI/RSS prep — with approve / edit / regenerate.
  3. **Human-in-the-loop review.** The pipeline is a stack of cards; voice-bearing outputs carry an Alan-ratification gate; refreshes show as a diff.
  4. **Gates as hard blocks.** Publish is blocked when a gate fails: not indexable, no transcript, no DOI, archive not public, Core Web Vitals failing.
  5. **Credential vault + integrations.** Search Console, Crossref/DataCite, ORCID, the podcast host/RSS, YouTube, a social scheduler, the newsletter platform — the agent acts through them; the human supplies credentials and approves every send, submit, and deposit.
  6. **The link-graph service.** Maintains the internal corpus graph and the peer-network graph so link proposals (internal + network) can be computed.
  7. **The monitoring / refresh loop.** Watches rankings, snippet and AI-citation capture, backlinks and decay, drafting refreshes for approval.
  8. **The provenance registry.** Every claim resolves to a source; integrity enforced at creation, surfaced at publish.

Derived and copied work is invisible and automatic; agent-authored work is a review card; earned work is tracked and drafted but human-executed. The human reviews and ratifies — they don't hand-build tags.

The whole system

### What the dashboard needs beyond a single piece.

The editor and pipeline handle a piece; the dashboard manages the system — a compounding graph. Ten layers:

  1. **Corpus / content-graph view** — every piece by tier, its internal links, orphans flagged, and a coverage map of the field's queries.
  2. **Scores view** — each piece's SEO and GEO score, its banked / authored / earned split, gate status, and reach-at-publish vs earned-over-time, rolled up to a platform authority trend.
  3. **Network / scenius view** — the peer-leader graph, where genuine overlaps exist, a framework-attribution map, outreach status, and the cluster's compounding-authority trend.
  4. **Query-coverage & gap map** — the field's query space with volume, competition, and where to publish next; feeds the brief agent.
  5. **AI-citation tracking** — the GEO analog of rank tracking: scheduled prompts across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity, logging when and how you get cited.
  6. **Framework / entity registry** — Alan's frameworks as first-class entities linked across corpus, schema and the attribution map: the origin-node strategy, operationalized.
  7. **Content health / decay** — freshness cadence, ranking and citation tracking, the refresh queue.
  8. **Production kanban** — everything in flight by state: drafting, in review, awaiting ratification, awaiting credentials, published, needs refresh.
  9. **Provenance registry** — the central claim-to-source store, shared by every editor.
  10. **Roles & ratification** — editor, producer, Alan (ratifier), the network-relationship owner, and the states that route work between them.

The value was never in one optimized page; it was in a system that grows its own authority on purpose. Build-readiness note: the templating engine and AI-citation tracking are the heaviest, least off-the-shelf pieces — the templating engine makes everything else cheap (build it first); AI-citation tracking is an immature category (treat it as a rough signal, not a precise dial).

How to read this +

**The points are an attribution, not a promise.** Each number answers: in a fully, well-executed playbook for this content type, what share of the realized credibility does this task account for? It is not "do this and get X% more traffic."

**Gates, levers, and differentiators behave differently.** Gates (foundation, performance) are pass/fail — once met they add little, but if failed they cap everything above them (toggle them to see). Levers (content, authority) hold most of the 100 points. Differentiators (schema, snippet formatting, Core Web Vitals) are small alone but decide close races.

**SEO and GEO reward the same work on different curves.** SEO rewards _rankings_ , so authority and content depth dominate. GEO rewards _citation frequency_ — being one of the few sources an answer weaves in across many prompts — so it reweights toward extractable structure, statistics, quotations, entity trust, presence on AI-trusted sources, and freshness.

**How the layers compound:** foundation makes a page _eligible_ ; content makes it _worth surfacing_ ; authority makes it _trusted enough to rank or be cited_ ; structure and schema make it _extractable_ ; distribution creates the engagement and link velocity that feed back into authority and citation. Remove one layer and the ones above it lose their footing.

**Value per edit — build-once, per-post, earned.** The 100 points don't cost the same effort. Some are **build-once** : the invisible tag, schema and performance layer you template a single time and every post inherits for free. Some are **per-post authored** : the content itself and the few fields that need human judgment. Some are **earned** off-platform over weeks — links, reviews, citations, trusted-source presence. The strip on each panel shows the split, and why a flawless post is only about two-thirds of the way to 100 on publish day.

Read this last

## What a score of 100 actually means.

The number is a model, not a dial an engine reads. No search engine or answer engine assigns your post a 100. The scale asks one honest question about a single piece of content: have you done everything on your side of the line, and has the world done its part yet?

### What 100 is not

It isn't a ranking, and it isn't traffic. You can execute a post perfectly and still sit below a stronger domain, or lose a citation to a source a model already trusts more. Ranking and citation are competitive outcomes that depend on everyone else and on the exact query. The score measures the one thing you control: how complete, legible and credible the post is. It's a readiness ceiling, not a scoreboard.

### What 100 is

A post at 100 is the best possible version of itself on every axis you can influence — crawlable and indexed, saying something worth surfacing, structured so a human, a search engine and an answer engine can all lift the point, carrying the right invisible tags and schema, loading well, showing who wrote it and why they can be trusted, and having earned the links, reviews and citations that tell the world it's real. When all of that is true it stops being a page you hope someone finds and becomes an asset that keeps paying.

### Why you can't reach 100 on publish day

The points come from three places. Some are **banked** — the invisible tag-and-schema layer and the performance work you build once as templates, inherited free by every post. Some are **authored** — the actual content, written fresh each time. And some are **earned** — the backlinks, reviews, citations and trusted-source presence that aren't yours to type and accrue over weeks as the world vouches for the post.

So a flawlessly executed post is only about two-thirds of the way to 100 the day you publish. You own the banked points — automation delivered them the moment the page rendered — and the authored points, which you wrote. The last third is a promissory note the post cashes over time. Reaching 100 is a later event, if it happens at all: the moment the post is both perfectly made and fully validated by the world. A post living steadily in the eighties is doing its job.

### What this means for your time

This is the whole reason to separate the buckets. The banked layer — the part that used to eat hours per post in tools like Yoast — is deterministic. Build it once and it costs nothing again; a publisher should never touch a canonical tag or a schema skeleton by hand. That frees every remaining hour for the only two things that move the points automation can't: writing content worth citing, and doing the slow relational work that earns authority. Automation doesn't raise your ceiling — it stops the ceiling from stealing the time you need to reach it.

Evidence-based · sourced

  * **Moz** — _Beginner's Guide to SEO_ (Mozlow's Hierarchy of SEO Needs) & the 25-step "How to Rank" checklistSEO as a cause-and-effect hierarchy, foundation first.
  * **Aggarwal et al.** — _GEO: Generative Engine Optimization_ , arXiv 2311.09735 (KDD 2024)Statistics and quotations were the strongest citation levers; keyword stuffing scored worse than baseline.
  * **Google Search Central** — Core Web VitalsLCP <2.5s, INP <200ms, CLS <0.1 at the 75th percentile; a tiebreaker, not a content override.
  * **Google Search Quality Rater Guidelines** — E-E-A-TExperience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trust: an indirect framework with Trust at the center; not a direct ranking factor.
  * **Structured data guidance** JSON-LD earns rich-result eligibility, not a guarantee; featured snippets are extracted from visible on-page content.
  * **State of AI Search (Indig, 2026)** Content under ~3 months old is roughly 3× more likely to be cited; answer engines lean on a small set of trusted sources.

The weights are an evidence-based attribution model synthesized from public guidance — a teaching model of where credibility accrues, not a reproduction of any engine's ranking algorithm. Google has repeatedly stated E-E-A-T and Core Web Vitals are not simple, direct, weighted ranking inputs. Worked examples are demonstration drafts in Alan Hirsch's voice, pending his ratification; no book text or quotations are reproduced.

## 36. Agent Build Guides — how each one would actually get built

`movemental-agent-build-guides.html` · 3,030 words

Movemental.

Agent Build Guides · How Each One Would Actually Get Built

# From map to method

Each agent with its role — and an expandable build vision: the pipeline, where a human stays in the loop, and the key pieces to build. Click **How it would be done** on any card.

These are implementation **visions** , not final specs — a starting architecture for each, written to hand a builder. They assume your existing stack: a multi-tenant hosted platform, corpus-grounded agents, voice profiles, and human-in-the-loop gates. Every one keeps a person on the irreversible or credibility-bearing steps.

Tier 1 · Scales the money

Org Build & Onboarding Agent

DoesTakes an org's intake and stands up their custom platform and tuned agents mostly automatically — the one-week build, compressed and de-personed.

WhyYour delivery cadence is the ceiling on the whole engine. The difference between 40 and 200 builds a year.

How it would be done

Turn the build from bespoke code into template selection plus parameter-filling. The agent doesn't invent a platform each time — it composes one from a library of archetypes (church, seminary, nonprofit, camp) and an agent catalog.

Pipeline

  1. A conversational intake interviews the org: type, needs, brand, existing tools, top use-cases — and produces a structured build spec.
  2. The agent maps the spec to the closest platform template and selects which catalog agents to wire in.
  3. It provisions a new tenant, pulls brand (logo, colors, voice), generates the site scaffolding, and configures the chosen agents.
  4. It runs a config checklist and flags the ambiguous 10% for a human.

**Human in the loop:** a builder reviews the generated config and finishes the flagged custom 10%; nothing goes live unreviewed.

**Key pieces:** an archetype/template library, an agent catalog, a tenant-provisioning API, a config generator — and a feedback loop that folds recurring customizations back into templates so each build gets more automatic.

Data-Migration & Records Agent

DoesIngests, cleans, and migrates an org's messy existing data into the new platform.

WhyMigration is the unglamorous thing that stalls or blows up custom builds. This clears onboarding's hardest, most human-intensive step.

How it would be done

Meet the mess where it is — spreadsheets, exports, legacy church/donor systems — and turn it into clean, mapped records in a staged, reversible way.

Pipeline

  1. Connectors and importers pull from common sources (Planning Center, church databases, Salesforce NPSP, spreadsheets, mailboxes, drives).
  2. The agent profiles the data: detects schema, flags PII, scores quality, finds duplicates.
  3. It proposes a mapping to the platform's canonical schema and normalizes (names, addresses, dedupe members/donors).
  4. It stages the migration with a preview and a rollback path.

**Human in the loop:** the org reviews the mapping and a data sample before commit; PII handling is surfaced for consent.

**Key pieces:** a connector library, a schema-mapping model plus deterministic validation, a staging/preview environment. Data never leaves the tenant it belongs to.

Agent QA / Eval & Guardrail Agent

DoesTests, evaluates, red-teams, and guardrails every client agent before and after deploy.

WhyReliability is retention. This is what lets you scale deployments without scaling risk.

How it would be done

An automated eval harness that gates every agent pre-deploy and watches it after — the reliability layer that makes agent-ops safe to scale.

Pipeline

  1. Per org, assemble a golden test set of expected questions and correct answers.
  2. Run automated red-team prompts (jailbreaks, unsafe or out-of-scope requests) against the agent.
  3. Check voice/brand consistency against the org's style guide, and verify claims are grounded in the org's source docs (citation check for hallucinations).
  4. Score, gate at deploy, then re-run continuously — especially after any model upgrade — and alert on regressions.

**Human in the loop:** failures above threshold route to a person before deploy; a health dashboard shows every agent's status.

**Key pieces:** an eval framework, a red-team prompt library, a per-org scoring rubric, grounded-citation verification. This is the safety net under the recurring line.

Tier 2 · Compounds growth & discovery

Linking / Link-Graph Agent

DoesBuilds and maintains the internal link graph across the whole network.

WhyThe gap you named. It becomes a living graph that lifts every leader at once and powers cross-recommendation.

How it would be done

Treat the whole network as one graph. Every piece of content is a node; the agent proposes and maintains the edges — contextual links and related-content modules — under a linking policy.

Pipeline

  1. Embed every asset (articles, pathways, books, leader pages) into one index; compute semantic relatedness.
  2. Propose paragraph-level internal links (anchor text + target), related-content modules, and cross-leader recommendations.
  3. Apply a policy: topical relevance, authority flow toward canonical hubs, no over-linking.
  4. Run continuously — when new content publishes, link it in and surface where existing content should point to it.

**Human in the loop:** editors accept/reject in bulk; high-confidence links can auto-apply, low-confidence ones queue for review.

**Key pieces:** an embedding index, a graph store, a linking-policy ruleset, a bulk review UI. Output is a pillar/cluster structure that compounds SEO and GEO.

GEO / AI-Answer Optimization & Monitoring Agent

DoesStructures content to be citable by AI answer engines, then monitors who cites the network and feeds gaps back.

WhyYour discovery bet is being found by AI. This measures it, so GEO becomes a dashboard instead of faith.

How it would be done

Two loops running together — one that makes content answer-ready, one that measures whether the engines actually cite it.

Pipeline

  1. **Optimize:** restructure each piece for citability — claim-evidence structure, question-based headings, explicit citations, answer-ready summaries, and schema markup (FAQ, HowTo, Article).
  2. **Probe:** regularly query the major AI answer engines with the network's target questions.
  3. **Measure:** detect whether and where the network is cited; track share-of-voice by topic and by leader.
  4. **Feed back:** route gaps to the content-gap and editorial agents.

**Human in the loop:** editors approve structural rewrites; monitoring runs automatically with alerts.

**Key pieces:** a schema/structure generator, an answer-engine probing harness, a citation-tracking dashboard.

Content-Gap / Topic-Intelligence Agent

DoesScans search demand and AI-answer gaps to tell each leader what to write next.

WhyTurns content from guesswork into targeting — aims editorial and GEO at the highest-leverage topics.

How it would be done

Match demand against coverage. Find the high-demand questions inside each leader's domain that the network doesn't yet answer well.

Pipeline

  1. Pull demand signals: search keyword data, "people also ask," mined answer-engine questions, competitor coverage, the network's own analytics.
  2. Map them against existing coverage using the same embedding index the linking agent uses.
  3. Score each gap by demand × winnability × fit-to-leader-and-voice.
  4. Output a ranked brief queue per leader.

**Human in the loop:** leaders/editors approve the briefs before they enter the editorial pipeline.

**Key pieces:** demand-data connectors, the coverage index, a prioritization model.

Distribution / Repurposing Agent

DoesTurns one piece into every downstream asset — newsletter, social, clips, audio script, discussion guide.

WhyMultiplies every leader's output without more of their time.

How it would be done

A pipeline triggered whenever a source asset lands, that fans it out into a voice-tuned family of channel-ready pieces.

Pipeline

  1. On a new asset (article, talk, sermon, podcast), transcribe if it's audio/video and clean the transcript.
  2. Extract key ideas, quotes, and structure.
  3. Generate derivatives tuned to each channel and the leader's voice: newsletter edition, social thread, short-form clips with captions, audio-narration script, discussion guide, GEO-structured article.
  4. Route each to the newsletter, social, and publishing agents.

**Human in the loop:** a review queue where the leader or editor approves or lightly edits before publish.

**Key pieces:** transcription, voice-tuned generation (via the voice-credibility agent), channel templates, a scheduling/routing layer.

Localization & Voice-Preserving Translation Agent

DoesTranslates and culturally adapts content into your five languages while holding each leader's voice.

WhyMakes launching language N cheap and faithful — the multilingual lever depends on it.

How it would be done

Not raw translation — a voice-and-culture-aware pipeline that keeps a per-leader voice and a per-language style guide, with a memory so terms stay consistent.

Pipeline

  1. Load the leader's voice profile and the target language's cultural/style guide.
  2. Translate, then adapt idioms, examples, references, and framing to the market — preserving the leader's distinctive voice markers.
  3. Enforce a per-leader, per-language glossary and translation memory so key terms stay consistent across everything.
  4. Pass the output to the Translation-QA agent before publish.

**Human in the loop:** the native-network leader or a native reviewer approves; their edits feed back into the memory.

**Key pieces:** voice profiles, per-language style guides, a translation memory + glossary store.

Translation-QA / Back-Translation Agent

DoesChecks the localization agent's output via back-translation and native-voice review.

WhyA bad translation poisons a leader's credibility in a new market. This is the gate that makes localization trustworthy at scale.

How it would be done

Catch drift before publish so a native reviewer handles only the flagged items, not every line.

Pipeline

  1. Back-translate the localized asset to the source language and diff it against the original to catch meaning drift.
  2. Run cultural-appropriateness and (where relevant) theological-accuracy checks against the per-language guide.
  3. Verify glossary/term consistency and score fluency with a native-quality model.
  4. Flag issues by severity; only clean assets pass to publish.

**Human in the loop:** a native reviewer resolves flagged items only — the agent does the triage.

**Key pieces:** back-translation diff, rubric checks, severity scoring.

Tier 3 · New products to sell

Safety-Charter Agent

DoesFrom a short intake, generates a tailored AI charter / guidebook — the $1k Safety product — in minutes.

WhyAutomating the wedge means unlimited top-of-funnel at near-zero cost.

How it would be done

Productize the guidebook you already know how to write — its layers (Statement, Policy, Context, Rules, Response Plans) become a template the agent fills from a short intake.

Pipeline

  1. A conversational/form intake captures org type, values, risk posture, current AI use, and constraints.
  2. Optionally, a research step pulls public info on the org to ground it.
  3. The agent drafts each guidebook layer from the template library, tailored to the org's specifics.
  4. Outputs a branded, editable document plus a lightweight dashboard.

**Human in the loop:** the org reviews and edits; for higher tiers, a Movemental person approves.

**Key pieces:** the guidebook template system, an org-research step, doc + dashboard generation.

Fundraising & Grant Agent

DoesFinds relevant grants an org qualifies for, and drafts and assists applications and donor communications.

WhyA product orgs pay for — and it surfaces the grant money that buys your tech. A flywheel.

How it would be done

Two functions on one org profile: find the money, then help win it — never submitting on its own.

Pipeline

  1. Build an org profile (mission, programs, geography, budget, 501c3 status).
  2. Match against grant databases and funder signals; rank opportunities by fit and winnability.
  3. For a chosen grant, draft the application from the org's materials against the funder's rubric.
  4. Draft tailored donor communications and appeals in the org's voice.

**Human in the loop:** the org reviews and edits before any submission; the agent never submits autonomously.

**Key pieces:** grant-data connectors, the org profile, rubric-aware drafting.

Formation Companion / Cohort Agent

DoesA per-learner companion through a pathway or cohort — prompts, reflection, discussion, check-ins — plus facilitator support.

WhyThe retention engine for cohorts, pathways, and the app.

How it would be done

A companion grounded in the specific course content and the leader's voice — designed to support human community, never replace it, with clear escalation on anything sensitive.

Pipeline

  1. Ground the agent in the course/pathway content (RAG) and the leader's voice profile.
  2. Deliver prompts and micro-lessons on a cadence; invite reflection and respond pastorally within scope.
  3. Track each learner's progress; nudge the stalled; surface discussion threads for cohorts.
  4. Give facilitators a dashboard of where every participant is.

**Human in the loop:** facilitator oversight, with hard escalation paths for pastoral or mental-health sensitivity — the agent hands off, it doesn't counsel.

**Key pieces:** course RAG, voice, progress tracking, a facilitator dashboard, strict guardrails and escalation.

Course / Pathway-Authoring Agent

DoesTurns a leader's corpus into a structured, sequenced course or pathway.

WhyProductizes your pathway builder — sellable courses from what a leader already made.

How it would be done

Use the corpus as the raw material and instructional-design templates as the mold — with the leader signing off, preserving the moment of authorship.

Pipeline

  1. Ingest the leader's corpus (books, talks, articles) into a grounded index.
  2. Propose a structure: learning outcomes, module sequence, lesson breakdown.
  3. Draft each lesson — readings, summaries, reflection questions, exercises — in the leader's voice, cited to the corpus.
  4. Assemble into the platform's course format.

**Human in the loop:** the leader reshapes the outline and approves lessons — their sign-off is the authorship.

**Key pieces:** corpus RAG, instructional-design templates, voice generation, the course builder.

Leader "Lab" Factory Agent

DoesSpins up a corpus-grounded conversational agent — like the Alan Hirsch Lab — for any leader.

WhyMakes the proven Lab repeatable across 100 leaders at near-zero marginal cost.

How it would be done

Generalize the Alan Hirsch Lab into a templated factory: same architecture, new corpus and voice each time, with guardrails that keep it to the leader's actual positions.

Pipeline

  1. Ingest and index the leader's full body of work (books, talks, articles, transcripts).
  2. Build a voice profile and a grounded knowledge base.
  3. Configure a conversational agent with guardrails — stays in the leader's real positions, cites sources, refuses to fabricate views.
  4. Deploy it as a branded Lab on the leader's platform.

**Human in the loop:** the leader reviews sample conversations and approves positions and guardrails before launch.

**Key pieces:** corpus ingestion, voice, grounding, guardrails, one-click deploy — the Lab as a repeatable template.

Donor / CRM Relationship Agent (org)

DoesManages an org's donor and member relationships — segmentation, personalized comms, stewardship, follow-up.

WhyDeepens the platform's role in daily operations — a stickier recurring fee.

How it would be done

Sit on the migrated donor/member data and turn it into timely, personal, on-voice relationship work — drafted by the agent, sent by a human.

Pipeline

  1. Build on the org's migrated CRM data; segment by giving, engagement, and lifecycle.
  2. Draft personalized, timely comms — thank-yous, updates, re-engagement, appeals — in the org's voice.
  3. Schedule stewardship touchpoints; flag at-risk relationships.
  4. Surface suggested campaigns for approval.

**Human in the loop:** the org approves comms and campaigns; anything financial is human-sent.

**Key pieces:** the CRM data model, segmentation, voice-tuned comms, scheduling. Pairs with the fundraising agent.

Research / Study Agent (seminary & scholar)

DoesA research assistant — sourcing, citation, literature review — grounded in trusted materials.

WhyThe premium product that fits seminaries, a core grant-funded buyer.

How it would be done

Rigor first: grounded retrieval with verified citations and no fabrication, tuned to the org's tradition — the scholar stays accountable for the work.

Pipeline

  1. Connect to academic sources and the org's own licensed/provided materials.
  2. Do literature search and source retrieval; manage citations.
  3. Draft literature reviews and answer questions with rigorous, verified citation (grounded RAG).
  4. Verify every claim traces to a real source before it surfaces.

**Human in the loop:** scholars verify and own the output — the agent assists, it doesn't author unaccountably.

**Key pieces:** academic-source connectors, grounded RAG, citation verification, a research workspace UI.

Newsletter / Subscription-Ops Agent

DoesRuns the list — segmentation, cadence, drafting, A/B, churn-watch, upgrade nudges.

WhyLifts conversion and retention across every leader's subscription business.

How it would be done

Run the whole list lifecycle on top of the repurposing agent's output, tuned per leader, with the leader approving what goes out.

Pipeline

  1. Segment subscribers by engagement, tenure, and free-vs-paid.
  2. Draft editions from the leader's new content (via the repurposing agent) and schedule on the best cadence.
  3. A/B test subjects and send times; watch churn signals and trigger win-back.
  4. Nudge free-to-paid upgrades at the right moments.

**Human in the loop:** the leader approves editions and campaigns before send.

**Key pieces:** list data, segmentation, voice-tuned drafting, send/AB infrastructure, a churn model.

Tier 4 · Runs the business

Org-Prospecting / Lead-Gen Agent

DoesIdentifies and warms org prospects — and surfaces which have grant money or active AI intent.

WhyFills the top of the tech-engine funnel with warm, grant-funded prospects.

How it would be done

Find and score the right orgs, enrich them with intent and funding signals, then hand humans a warm, prioritized, respectful first touch — not a scrape-and-blast.

Pipeline

  1. Build a prospect list of orgs (churches, seminaries, nonprofits) from public data.
  2. Enrich with AI-intent signals (job posts, RFPs, recent AI mentions) and funding signals (recent grants, 990 data, foundation awards).
  3. Prioritize by fit × ability-to-pay × warmth, using the network graph of who knows whom.
  4. Draft personalized first-touch outreach for human approval.

**Human in the loop:** humans approve outreach and own the relationship; the agent finds and warms, it doesn't spam.

**Key pieces:** org-data and funding-signal connectors, a scoring model, the network graph, outreach drafting. Permission-aware by design.

Pricing / Proposal / Sales-Motion Agent

DoesScopes an org's needs into a tailored proposal and price, and manages the follow-through.

WhyTurns each Safety-charter lead into a scoped build proposal automatically.

How it would be done

Standardize scoping and pricing so a small team runs many deals consistently, starting from the intake the Safety-charter agent already captured.

Pipeline

  1. Take a qualified org's needs (often straight from the Safety-charter intake).
  2. Scope the build: which template, which agents, migration complexity, integrations.
  3. Generate a priced proposal from a standard rate card plus scoping rules.
  4. Produce the proposal doc and run the follow-up cadence.

**Human in the loop:** a person approves scope and price before it goes out; complex deals escalate.

**Key pieces:** a scoping ruleset, a rate card, proposal generation, follow-up automation.

Movemental — Agent Build Guides · Implementation visions to hand a builder, not final engineering specs. Each keeps a human on the irreversible and credibility-bearing steps, and each assumes your shared stack: multi-tenant platform, corpus grounding, voice profiles, and human-in-the-loop gates. Illustrative, for internal planning.

# Part IV — Strategy, Frames & Standards

## 37. The Plan, Told Straight

`movemental-the-plan-told-straight.md` · 3,031 words

### The Plan, Told Straight

*An outside read on how Movemental gets from one English network to six linked ones — the story before we put numbers to it. Written the way a YC partner or an HBR case writer would work through it: honestly, step by step, and stopping at every point where a number has to be a judgment call rather than a fact.*

---

#### First, what kind of company this actually is

Start where an outside investor would, because it's the thing that's easy to miss from inside the building. Movemental looks like a Christian formation network. It isn't, or not mainly. It's a high-margin AI platform company that has quietly solved the single hardest problem those companies have: getting trusted access to buyers.

Most AI shops spend their lives buying attention. They run ads, they cold-email, they discount, and they still fight to be believed, because nobody trusts a vendor they've never heard of to touch the work that matters. Movemental doesn't have that problem. A hundred respected people vouch for it. Their names are the reason a seminary or a church network picks up the phone. That's the whole game, and it should be said plainly before we walk the plan: **the network isn't the product, it's the distribution — and it's the kind of distribution money usually can't buy.**

There are two engines here, and they do completely different jobs. Confusing them is the fastest way to misread the business.

The first is the **leaders' engine** — the movement leaders and everything they sell to their own audiences: courses, books, subscriptions, events. Movemental keeps only a thin slice of this (10%), and that's on purpose. This engine's job isn't to make Movemental money. Its job is to earn trust and reach, and to give each leader a reason to bring their audience and their organizational relationships into one place. It's the credibility. It's the front door.

The second is the **tech engine** — custom platform builds and the recurring agent management behind them, sold to organizations. This is where the money is actually made. A build takes about a week, costs almost nothing to produce, and runs at roughly 90% margin. The leaders' engine fills the room with warm, credible buyers; the tech engine sells them the thing that pays.

Hold those two apart and the rest of the plan reads clearly. The leaders are the reach and the moat. The tech is the margin. Everything that follows is about multiplying both.

---

#### Where we actually are — the proven core

It's month three, and the core is already real, not theoretical. There's a first organization in the work (Youthfront). There are founding leaders (Alan, Brad, and the early cohort). The cheap, urgent wedge is live: the Safety charter that says *you're exposed without an AI policy, and we'll give you one for a thousand dollars*. And there's a genuine pipeline behind it — a seminary, a forty-church network, several nonprofits, an agency, a path into library networks through a fundraising partner.

So the first claim in the story is modest and well-supported: **the proven core is an English leader network plus a near-pure-profit tech engine, and it works.** Even if nothing else in this plan ever happened, that's a real, valuable company. Everything past this point is about how far it can be pushed — and the honest analyst's job is to separate the part that's close to certain from the part that's a bet.

---

#### The first move: fill English to 100, then lock the door

The plan says: get to 100 English-speaking movement leaders, then close the network to new individual English leaders. On the surface that looks like leaving money on the table. It's the opposite, for three reasons that build on each other.

**A closed network is worth more than an open one.** The entire value of the thing is trust. An open door means the hundred-and-first leader, and the two-hundredth, and eventually the network stops meaning anything because anyone can be in it. Curation *is* the product. Locking the door at a round, defensible number turns membership into a status good — something leaders want to be inside, and stay inside, precisely because not everyone can be. *Therefore* the network's credibility holds instead of eroding as it grows.

**A full network is a complete distribution machine.** A hundred leaders, each with an audience and each with organizational relationships — seminaries they teach at, denominations they advise, church networks they've planted — is a warm-referral engine pointed straight at the tech engine. *Therefore* the platform business gets its pipeline handed to it, which is exactly what we see already: Tampa Underground comes in warm and discounted precisely because it's leader-affiliated.

**Locking English frees the team to do the next thing.** You can't run the same recruiting play forever. Declaring English "done" at 100 is what lets the team stop selling to individual English leaders and start building the next network. *Therefore* the door-lock isn't a limit; it's the trigger for the growth move that follows.

One honest note here, because it matters for the numbers later: locking the door also lets you *curate for reach*. A closed network of a hundred can be assembled to skew toward leaders with real audiences, rather than filling the last slots with whoever's available. That's why, when we get to the projection, I'd argue for a blended revenue-per-leader closer to the top of the range than the middle. (More on that number below — it's a judgment call, and I'll defend it as one.)

---

#### The real growth move: run the whole play again, in five more languages

Here's the part the earlier work hadn't accounted for, and it's the part that turns a good company into a large one.

Once English is full and the playbook is proven, replicate the entire model — the scenius, the formation stack, the books, the subscriptions, the tech engine — in each of the other languages: Latin American Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese, Korean, German, and Mandarin. Recruit native-speaker movement leaders in each. Link every language network to the English one and to each other. Run the same playbook. And use a mix of the existing network's pull, referrals, and paid ads to get each new one off the ground.

Walk the logic, because it's a clean chain and each link lowers the cost or raises the payoff of the next.

**The content already exists.** The translation work in the earlier plan means the courses, books, and audiobooks are already in these languages before a single leader is recruited. *Therefore* a language network launches with a full catalog on day one — which is nothing like the cold start English had, where the content was built as the network grew. The hardest, slowest part is already done.

**The playbook is proven.** By the time you launch Spanish, you've run the English network end to end — you know the pricing, the conversion, the wedge, the build motion, the recurring line. *Therefore* you're not experimenting in the new language; you're repeating a known routine. The risk in each language is execution, not invention.

**Native leaders self-seed the network.** The whole reason the English network grows without a sales budget is cross-recommendation — leaders vouching for leaders. The moment you have a few trusted anchor leaders in Spanish, that same free engine starts turning in Spanish. *Therefore* paid ads are only needed to jump-start each network — to buy the first audience and help land the first anchors — not to sustain it. That's a crucial distinction for the cost side: ads are a match, not a fuel line.

**Each native leader brings their region's organizations.** This is the link people forget. A Korean movement leader doesn't just bring a Korean audience; they bring Korean seminaries, churches, and nonprofits — which means the tech engine, the part that actually makes money, now has a warm pipeline in Korea. *Therefore* replicating the network in a language isn't only replicating content revenue. It's replicating the near-pure-profit platform business in a whole new region.

**And the tech engine doesn't care what language it's in.** A platform build is a build; agent management is agent management. The economics are the same in São Paulo as in Kansas City. *Therefore* the multiplier isn't on the small, leader-favorable content lines — it's on the biggest, highest-margin engine in the company. That's the point of the whole move.

Put the chain together and the five-year picture stops being "the English network, plus some translation revenue." It becomes **six linked trust-networks, each running the full stack, all feeding one shared, language-agnostic, high-margin platform business.**

---

#### Every revenue stream, and where it shows up in this bigger picture

To make sure nothing goes missing, here is the full stack — and the plan runs it, in time, in each language-region, not just in English:

- **Formation** — cohort courses, self-paced paths, curriculum bundles, the app, and the turnkey church *curriculum* license. The reach layer. Mostly the leaders' money (they keep 90%); Movemental's slice is thin but the credibility it buys is the whole point.
- **Books** — direct digital sales with agent tutors, the search-and-AI discovery that sells them as a byproduct, Amazon editions (no Movemental take, pure goodwill and reach), AI audiobooks, book-and-agent pairings, curriculum bundles, and print through a publisher partner (100 Movements in English; other languages would need their own print partners, which is a real to-do, not a given).
- **Subscriptions and monthly support** — direct, per-leader, sovereign. The list is the asset; the network's cross-recommendation is the cheapest subscriber acquisition in the model. No pooled all-access product — shared discovery, sovereign monetization.
- **Events** — leader workshops, brokered speaking, and a regional gathering per network.
- **The tech engine** — the Safety wedge, the Sandbox/Training/Solutions methodology, the custom platform builds, the network conversions (a Tampa in every region), and the recurring agent-management license. This is the money, and it's the stream the multilingual move multiplies most.
- **Shared-value leader comp** — the 10% referral and the paid consultation seat — flowing to leaders on the tech business they bring in, in every language.

And two effects that only exist *because* the networks are linked: **cross-recommendation across languages** (a reader of a Spanish leader discovering the English catalog, and the reverse), and **one shared platform and brand**, so the cost of running network number six is far below the cost of running number one.

---

#### Now the honest part: what's certain, what's a bet, and what could kill it

A good outside read doesn't just narrate the upside. Here's where I'd push.

**The English core is close to a sure thing.** Proven pipeline, proven wedge, a product that costs a week to build at 90% margin, and a referral network that lowers customer acquisition to near zero. If the multilingual play never happened, this is still a company worth building. That's the floor, and it's a high one.

**The multilingual replication is a real bet, and it's where the execution risk concentrates.** Three risks matter, in order:

*First, native operators and trust.* The entire moat is credibility, and credibility is local. You cannot run a Korean or a Brazilian network convincingly from Kansas City. Each language needs trusted native anchor leaders — and probably local staff — and a weak or wrong anchor doesn't just underperform, it poisons the trust the whole network runs on. This is the risk I'd watch hardest. It's a people problem, not a translation problem, and it's the one that can't be solved with a good build.

*Second, ability to pay.* English, German, and Korean audiences and organizations can pay real money. Spanish and Portuguese markets are enormous but monetize well below that. Mandarin is the extreme case — huge reach, and by your own redemptive stance, largely given away. So the revenue-per-leader is not uniform across languages, and the grant-funded dynamic that makes the U.S. tech sale so easy may not exist the same way abroad. The multilingual play multiplies reach cleanly; it multiplies *revenue* unevenly, and the model has to say so honestly.

*Third, bandwidth.* A small team running six networks, a book operation, a subscription operation, and a build shop will hit a wall unless the whole thing is genuinely productized and locally staffed. Growth that outruns the team's ability to hold quality is how trust-based businesses die.

**What makes the bet fundable rather than reckless is the asymmetry.** You are not launching cold. The content is already translated, the playbook is proven, the product is built, and the English network gives each new language a warm start. So the marginal cost of language number two is a fraction of what English cost — and that gap is the actual argument for doing it. This is a bet where the downside is bounded and the upside is a whole new region's worth of the highest-margin business you have.

**And the discipline that makes it sane is sequencing.** Don't light all five at once. Prove Spanish first — it's the largest market and the closest culturally to the U.S. work. If Spanish works, the thesis is validated and the rest is repetition. If Spanish struggles, you've learned it cheaply, before betting the team on five. That single sequencing rule is the difference between a confident expansion and an overreach, and I'd hold the team to it.

---

#### The judgment calls, named — so we can argue about them before we chart them

You asked me to be clear about every number I'd have to invent. Here they are, each with the reasoning, so when we build the projection we're stress-testing stated beliefs and not hidden ones. (The conservative/base/aggressive scale comes later; this is just me showing my work.)

**Blended revenue per English leader: I'd argue ~$90k, not $85k.** The worked example of a mid-sized leader lands near $92k. My earlier models pulled the blend down to $85k to account for a long tail of smaller leaders. But *locking the door lets you curate for reach* — a closed hundred can be assembled to skew larger than an open one would. So I'd nudge the blend up to about $90k and defend it on the curation logic. The tail still exists; it's just shorter in a network you get to choose.

**Leaders per language network: not a flat 100.** Market size and the size of the *monetizable* audience differ. I'd carry roughly: English 100 (locked), Spanish ~100 (huge market), Portuguese ~75, Korean ~50, German ~40, Mandarin ~60 (large audience, constrained monetization). These are sized to real audience and real ability to pay, not to symmetry.

**Revenue per leader by language, as a share of English.** English is the baseline. German I'd actually put slightly *above* (~105%) — small network, but high willingness to pay. Korean ~90%. Spanish and Portuguese ~55% — big audiences, lower ability to pay. Mandarin ~30% — mostly redemptive by design. The reasoning is ability-to-pay and market maturity, and it's the honest counterweight to the "just multiply by six" temptation.

**Tech-engine strength by region.** Highest in the U.S./English, where the grant ecosystem, the agency market, and your home-field build advantage all sit. I'd run the other regions at roughly 40–70% of the English tech rate, ramping, because grant funding and the agency-services market look different abroad and your delivery starts U.S.-based. This is a guess, clearly labeled — it's the variable I'd most want real data on early.

**Paid acquisition cost.** A real, new line item that English never needed. English grew on founding leaders and network gravity; a new language starts cold, so you buy the first audience and help land the first anchors, then let native cross-recommendation take over. I'd model it as a jump-start cost per language, not an ongoing one — and flag that the true number is unknown until you run the first Spanish campaigns.

**Timing.** English fills Years 1–2. Spanish launches Year 2 (largest, closest, content ready). Portuguese and Korean in Year 3. German and Mandarin in Year 4. Staggered on purpose, per the sequencing discipline above — prove the replication once before betting on five.

**Native operators as a cost and a risk, not a rounding error.** Each language needs trusted local anchors and likely local staff. I'll carry that as real cost and real risk in the model, because pretending it's free is exactly how this kind of plan flatters itself.

---

#### So what — why the plan holds together

Step back and the shape is clean. This is not a bigger content network. It's a **federation of trust-networks feeding one high-margin platform business.** The leaders are the distribution and the moat. The tech is the money. The languages are the multiplier. And the reason the plan makes sense is that each piece pays for the next: the English network proves the model and funds the ads; the ads and the cross-recommendation seed the language networks; the language networks bring native leaders whose organizations feed the tech engine in six regions; and the tech engine — near-pure-profit and indifferent to language — turns all of that reach into margin.

The bottom line an outside partner would give you: **the English core is the sure thing, and the multilingual replication is a genuine, ordered, fundable bet with a clear kill-switch in Spanish.** That combination — already good on the proven part, with a disciplined path to being large — is rare. Most companies have one or the other. The main thing that turns this story into the projection we're about to build is honest numbers on the parts that are still guesses: the per-leader revenue by language, the tech-engine strength abroad, the cost to acquire the first audience in each new tongue, and the team's true capacity to hold quality across six networks at once.

Get those four honest, and the rest of the story does what it says it will.

## 38. The Four-Stage Path — Underlying Logic

`four-stage-path-underlying-logic.md` · 2,057 words

### The Four-Stage Path — Underlying Logic

*Internal reference. Captures the load-bearing claims that justify why Safety, Sandbox, Skills, and Solutions exist in this specific order — and why the order is not arbitrary. Companion to the three-minute narratives, which are the spoken-aloud expression of the logic captured here. This document is the substrate; the narratives are the surface.*

---

#### The asymmetry that justifies everything

For the organizations Movemental serves — churches, faith-based nonprofits, theological institutions — **credibility is not a competitive advantage. It is the product.** Erode the credibility and the work itself collapses. There is no second product to fall back on.

A marketing agency with an AI mishap loses a client. A church with an AI mishap loses the authority of its pulpit. A nonprofit with an AI mishap loses donor trust, which is the lifeline. A seminary with an AI mishap loses its claim to form people, which is its entire reason to exist.

This asymmetry is the reason the four-stage path exists in this order. It is the reason "move fast and break things" is malpractice for this customer base specifically. It is the reason Safety cannot be optional. **Skipping a stage compounds in a currency these organizations cannot afford to pay.**

#### What we predict happens to organizations that don't start with Safety

Three concrete failure modes, ordered by how often they occur in the field:

**One — an AI-authorship incident.** A parishioner discovers the memorial homily was AI-written. A donor discovers the personalized thank-you was generated. A board member discovers the minutes were AI-summarized with material inaccuracies. The first crisis is almost never the AI use itself — it is the *non-disclosure* of the AI use. The org that disclosed early gets to define the terms; the org that gets caught loses the framing forever.

**Two — a confidential-data exposure.** Pastoral counseling notes pasted into a consumer AI tool for "help drafting follow-up." Donor records pasted in for "personalized appeal generation." Student records pasted in for "letter of recommendation drafting." Each violates pastoral confidentiality norms, donor data agreements, FERPA — and the staff member who did it thought they were being efficient. Without a Guidebook, they do not know it is a violation.

**Three — insurance and regulatory exposure that surfaces only when you need to make a claim.** D&O policies are increasingly carving out AI exclusions. Cyber liability policies are starting to require documented AI governance as a precondition of coverage. State legislation on AI in employment decisions (Colorado SB 205, NYC Local Law 144, Illinois HB 3773) increasingly applies to nonprofits making hiring or eligibility decisions. The org without a Guidebook is uninsured for AI-related incidents and increasingly out of compliance — and does not find out until they need to file a claim or face an audit.

The Guidebook is the document that prevents the unrecoverable version of each of these. **It does not make staff infallible. It does not guarantee safety. But not having one is a guarantee that AI use in the organization is *ungovernable*.**

#### The conveyor belt — why these four stages in this order

The four-stage path is not a taxonomy. It is a chain of consequences. Each stage states the failure mode of the one before it.

**Safety alone is laughable.** You have built barriers against AI without finding out whether it had value in the first place. If that was the goal, you should have just banned the tools. A Guidebook with no Sandbox to test against is theater.

**Sandbox without Safety is reckless.** Testing AI against real work without ratified Rules means every staff member becomes a unilateral decision-maker by default; every vendor pitch lands against a leadership team with no shared frame; every edge case produces a fresh argument. Exploration without guardrails is malpractice given what these tools can touch.

**Skills without Sandbox is abstraction.** You are forming people who have not touched the work in their context against their actual Guidebook. Formation requires friction with the real. Without Sandbox findings, Skills becomes a curriculum delivered into a vacuum.

**Solutions without Skills is replacement.** You have deployed AI into the hands of people who cannot steward it, inside infrastructure you did not rebuild for the new conditions. This is the MIT report's 95% failure mode — but for organizations whose failures cost them their reason to exist.

The conveyor belt is the thesis. We do not push anyone along it; the logic does the moving. The work is ordered because the consequences of skipping a stage compound, and for the organizations we serve, the compound interest is paid in credibility.

#### What each stage produces — concretely

##### Safety
- The **AI Organizational Guidebook**, five layers (Statement, Policy, Context, Rules, Response Plans), seven artifacts
- A board-ratified document defensible to journalists, donors, regulators
- A searchable internal platform where any staff member can find the relevant clause
- The Named Refusals: public covenants the org commits to refuse on principle
- The vendor/tool inventory, data classification, and procurement gate
- The Incident Response Plan with named owners, escalation paths, verification protocols

##### Sandbox
- A **Use Case Portfolio** adjudicated against the Guidebook's Rules — every tested use case marked green, yellow, or red
- A **Discernment Memo** capturing patterns of value, patterns of concern, what the team learned, what the team now believes is true
- A **Readiness Assessment** recommending the team's next stage (Skills, Solutions, both, or neither)
- A team that has *actually used AI against their actual work* — no longer theorizing

##### Skills
- Cohort members with developed **discernment, authorship, and stewardship** capacities
- Curriculum anchored to the org's ratified Statement and Policy from Safety
- A formed group inside the organization that can carry AI decisions across the org without external dependency
- Cohort-only by design: no self-paced version exists, because formation requires community

##### Solutions
- Scoped AI deployment across six configurations (tool optimization, custom recipes, infrastructure builds, domain-specific applications, multi-org coordination, network-scale deployments)
- Built and operated by formed people, governed by the working Guidebook, against use cases the Sandbox already adjudicated
- The technological rebuild AI necessitates, done in the right order

#### The Safety stage in operational detail

Because Safety is the front door, it deserves additional specification.

##### The Guidebook's five layers

**Statement** — *what we believe about AI in relation to our mission.* Two pages. Mission alignment clause, posture toward both fear and uncritical enthusiasm, theological or ethical grounding paragraph, scope clause, annual review cadence. Signed by senior leadership, ratified by the board.

**Policy** — *what we do and what we refuse, operationally.* Sanctioned-use clause, constrained-use clause, prohibited-use clause, consequences clause, scope clause, delegation clause. Includes the **Named Refusals** section — covenants citable when a vendor pitches the prohibited use anyway. Standard refusals: AI in eligibility determinations, AI-driven surveillance of constituents, AI-generated personal voice without disclosure, AI substitution in pastoral or counseling care, deepfakes and voice cloning.

**Context** — *what is actually true in our environment right now.* The Vendor and Tool Inventory: every AI tool in use, by whom, for what, under what vendor terms (training rights on inputs, data residency, retention, enterprise vs. consumer tier). The Data Classification: defined tiers of sensitivity (public, internal, sensitive, confidential) with examples specific to the organization. A procurement gate for new tools. Reviewed quarterly.

**Rules** — *what governs AI use in specific domains.* The Data Handling Rules map data tiers to permitted tools, answering "can I put this in this tool?" for the most common categories of work. The Disclosure & Attribution Rules specify when AI involvement must be disclosed and what language to use. The Care Boundaries specify where AI cannot substitute for human presence regardless of efficiency. Pre-approved workflows give staff a default path that does not require case-by-case judgment.

**Response Plans** — *what we do when something goes wrong.* The Incident Response Plan is required from day one: clear definition of what counts as an incident; named owners with after-hours backup coverage; escalation path (staff → senior leadership → board); pre-arranged verification protocols (code words, callback procedures, dual-authorization for fund transfers above a threshold); constituent-communication template ready to deploy; law-enforcement coordination workflow including IC3 reporting at ic3.gov for AI-enabled fraud; post-incident review process to update Rules, Inventory, and the Plan itself.

##### Two paths through Safety

**SafeGuide** — the free, self-directed path. 33-page Field Guide, all five layers, with checklists. Genuinely sufficient on its own; the trust dividend arrives the moment the board ratifies, regardless of who drafted it. Best fit: leadership teams with time, alignment, internal capacity, and the discipline to finish what they start.

**SafeStart** — the facilitated path. $1,000. Two weeks. Six steps.

1. *Engagement* (Day 0) — org signs; private dashboard provisioned within 24 hours; contributor and decider roles confirmed.
2. *One-hour kickoff Zoom* (within 3 business days) — contributor team (4–7 people across functions) and lead decider meet with Movemental; organizational context, existing AI usage, leadership concerns, organizational artifacts to inform drafting.
3. *Drafting and asynchronous review* (Week One) — Movemental drafts all five layers customized to the organization; published to the private dashboard within 7 days; contributors review asynchronously, leaving comments and proposed edits.
4. *One-hour revision Zoom* (Week Two) — contributor team walks through significant comments, resolves open questions, locks in revisions; revised Guidebook published within 48 hours.
5. *Internal ratification* (end of Week Two) — deciding team meets *internally, without Movemental in the room*, to ratify through whatever governance process the organization requires. The ratification is theirs.
6. *Publication and rollout* (Week Three) — board ratification packet exports from the dashboard; constituent-facing communication template ready; staff onboarding materials available.

**Contributor time commitment:** approximately 3–4 hours per contributor across the two weeks. The total leadership-team time is higher; the per-person commitment is modest by design.

##### What every SafeStart organization gets

- A complete five-layer Guidebook customized to their organization, board-ratified
- A **publishable internal documentation platform** — private dashboard where staff search by question and get the relevant clause; new hires see the org's full AI posture on day one; the board sees role-appropriate views
- **Format flexibility — delivered in whatever format the organization actually uses**: print-quality PDF for board packets and denominational/accreditor filings; HTML and CSS for embedding on the org's website; dashboard for living, searchable internal use
- **Pre-built rollout supports**: board ratification packet, staff announcement templates, constituent-facing communication draft, FAQ for the people the org serves, incident-readiness briefing for senior leadership
- **A pre-engagement communication framework** for talking to staff before the work begins — because quiet engagements produce suspicion, openly named engagements produce buy-in
- **Integration with the rest of the Path** — when the org moves to Sandbox, the Use Case Portfolio is adjudicated against their Guidebook's Rules automatically; when they enter Skills, the formation curriculum anchors to their Statement and Policy. The Guidebook is not a one-time artifact; it is the foundation everything else builds on

##### Free as part of the methodology — the Integrity Diagnostic

Every organization, whether or not they engage Movemental, gets a free **ten-minute, fifty-question Integrity Diagnostic** that maps their existing AI use and shows where the gaps are before they decide which path to take. Real even if they never engage further. This is consistent with the redemptive-pricing posture: the methodology is free, the execution is paid, and the diagnostic is the bridge between them.

#### What the Safety stage is and is not

Safety is **the foundation, not the whole journey.** A ratified Guidebook does not solve the AI problem in the organization. What it does is make governance *possible* — turning informal staff judgment into something the organization has actually decided.

The trust dividend arrives the moment the board ratifies. From that moment, the organization has:

- A public answer when a journalist asks
- A defensible posture when a major donor asks
- A shared frame when staff surface an edge case
- A document that can be cited when a vendor pitches a prohibited use anyway
- Integration into D&O and cyber liability conversations

AI use in the organization is no longer ad hoc. It is governed.

That is why we start here.

---

*v0.1 — May 2026. Captures the underlying logic of the four-stage path as articulated in working conversations and refined into the SSSS and Safety three-minute narratives.*
