## 41. How we choose movemental leaders

`movemental-voice-selection-standard.md` · 2,534 words

### How we choose movemental leaders

*A working document for Josh, Brad, and Alan: the definition, the standard, and the process for who joins the network. Written to be adopted, amended, or argued with. It exists so the discernment that has carried us this far can be shared, taught to a third selector, and defended when someone asks why a person is in or out.*

---

#### A note on language

We call them **movemental leaders**, not "Voices." "Voice" works as a gesture toward the collective, but it sounds strange applied to a person, and the language we use about people becomes the posture we hold toward them. "Movement Voices" can stay as the public name of the network. No individual is called a Voice.

---

#### Why this exists

The network has grown through one path: the personal, curated invitation of Brad and Alan. That has worked, and for a reason. It rests on their discernment, their relational knowledge, their taste, and their willingness to stake their own names on each person they bring in. That is the asset. It is not a gap to be fixed.

The gap is that the standard has lived only in their heads. It cannot be taught to a third selector. It cannot be explained to someone who is told no. And it cannot be defended if we are ever asked why a particular person is in and another is out.

This document makes the discernment legible without replacing it. The judgment stays human. What changes is that it now has words, a process, and a memory.

A warning at the top, because it governs everything below. The goal is not to turn discernment into a score. A network curated by trusted people is valuable precisely because a trusted person said yes, one at a time. The day we replace that with a rubric anyone can run, we have built the thing we exist to stand against: legitimacy by metric instead of by trust. The criteria here filter. They never decide. A person decides.

---

#### What a movemental leader is

A movemental leader is someone with a real body of work who actually moves others. Not a commentator on movements, but someone who starts, carries, sends, or multiplies them. Their influence is genuine rather than merely large. A big platform is not the qualification, and a modest one is not a disqualification. What matters is that real people and real work move because of them.

They carry **movemental DNA, whether they name it or not.** This is the heart of the definition, so it needs care.

mDNA is the orientation toward sending and multiplying rather than maintaining, toward forming people rather than running programs, toward decentralized and organic growth, toward incarnational presence, toward the kind of shared risk that turns a group into a movement. Some leaders name all of this in so many words, because they come from the movement-thinking world and use the language fluently. Others will never say "mDNA," may never have read a page of the literature, and will still embody it plainly in what they have built. We are looking for the conviction in the work, not the vocabulary on the page. A youth minister who multiplies young leaders, a social entrepreneur who builds something that sends people out, a justice leader who forms a movement instead of managing a cause, a lawyer who has changed how a whole field works, all can carry mDNA without the word for it. The gate is the reality, not the citation.

And their conduct is such that any of the three of us would personally vouch for them. Not "tolerate." Vouch.

That last part is the spine of the whole thing. Membership is a trust loan. Every existing leader's credibility is quietly lent to every new one. When a reader trusts the network, they are trusting that everyone in it was worth the others standing behind them. So the real question under every decision is never "is this person impressive." It is "would we stake the network's name on them." If the honest answer is no, the rest of the case does not matter.

---

#### A movement, not a guild

This deserves its own section, because it is the easiest thing to get wrong and the hardest to notice while it happens.

The danger, given who we are, is that the network quietly becomes a club of movement thinkers and authors, because that is the world we swim in and the people we most easily see. That would be a failure, not a success. A movement is not a guild of intellectuals.

Movemental leaders are everywhere. In social entrepreneurship. Youth ministry. Justice work. Law. Education. Business. The arts. The unifying thread is mDNA and trust, not a shared profession and not a shared bookshelf. So we actively seek leaders across fields, and treat drift toward a single type, all authors, all one tradition, all one kind of work, as a problem to correct, not a neutral outcome.

This reshapes the third seat, too. The independence we are looking for is not only a different demographic vantage. It is a different field. A selector who lives in the world of practitioners, or justice, or enterprise, will see movemental leaders that two movement-thinkers structurally cannot. We choose the third seat partly for the rooms it opens that the current two do not sit in.

Every nomination can be measured partly by this: does it widen the network into a field the movement-thinking world does not occupy, or does it deepen a corner that is already crowded.

---

#### The standard

A small set of gates that must all be true, and then one judgment no list can make. The gates filter out who clearly does not belong. The judgment decides who does.

##### The gates (all must be true)

1. **A real body of work.** Something they have made, taught, led, or built that exists and can be examined. Not promise, not potential, not a following alone. Work.

2. **Leadership that multiplies.** People have actually followed, multiplied, or been formed under them. They lead leaders, or catalyze movements, or have sent people who now lead. Commentary, however good, is not leadership.

3. **Movemental DNA, explicit or implicit.** The conviction is real in the work, named or not, as described above.

4. **Trustworthy in conduct and character.** No known pattern of conduct, public or private, that the network could not stand behind. This is the one gate where a single credible problem is enough, and where "we are not sure" means we wait, not proceed.

##### The judgment (after the gates, the only thing that decides)

Would we stake the network's name on this person.

That is the whole judgment. A person can clear every gate and still be a no, because the gates detect the floor and the judgment reads the fit. We make it together, as people who know the landscape and will carry the consequence. It is deliberately not a checklist, and it must stay that way.

---

#### What we do and do not gatekeep

The network's collateral is trust and movemental DNA. It is not doctrinal agreement and it is not a political coalition. This matters enough to say flatly.

**We do not gatekeep on the liberal/conservative spectrum.** The network spans it on purpose. A network that admits only one side becomes a tribe, and a tribe is not a movement. Members will disagree, sometimes sharply, on contested political and theological questions, and that breadth is a feature, not a tolerance. It is part of what would make this a movement across the church and the wider world rather than a faction within it.

**We do not gatekeep on contested doctrine or denominational distinctives.** People who land differently on debated questions can both belong. The network is not a statement of faith and should never become one.

**We gatekeep on conduct and character, not belief.** We do not admit people whose conduct the network cannot stand behind: abuse, exploitation, dishonesty, or a posture toward people that dehumanizes or targets them. The line is never "they believe something we disagree with." The line is "their conduct, or their core posture toward people, is something we cannot underwrite with our own names." We admit people we disagree with. We do not admit people we cannot trust.

**One boundary we have not yet set: the faith floor.** In the mDNA frame, the center is Jesus. If that center is essential to what we mean by a movemental leader, then the network is, at root, oriented to Christian movement, even as it spans every tradition and politics within that. If we mean something broader, that the sending, multiplying, incarnational, forming pattern can be recognized and honored even in leaders outside the faith, then the net is wider and includes the social entrepreneur and the justice leader who never name Jesus but whose work carries the pattern. This is the deepest scope decision in front of us. The "explicit or implicit" mDNA gate and the "movement, not a guild" principle both push toward the wider net. The mDNA frame itself pulls toward the Christological center. We have to decide where that line sits. Everything else here works either way.

---

#### The process

Short on purpose, and its load-bearing rule is not the nomination. It is the dissent.

1. **Nomination.** Any of us may nominate. We write a short case: who the person is, how they meet the definition, and the plain answer to "would we stake the network's name on them, and why." Where relevant, we note which field the nominee widens the network into.

2. **The written-reasons rule.** Anyone who believes a nominee does not belong must say so in writing, and must say why. A no is never a shrug or a veto by mood. It is a reason, on the record. This single rule does most of the work in this document. It turns taste into reasons. It builds a memory of precedent, so the standard sharpens over time. It makes a no as accountable as a yes.

3. **Consent, not vote.** A nominee is accepted unless one of us raises a substantive, written objection. An unresolved serious objection blocks. We do not admit by majority. One credible "I would not stake my name on this person" should be able to stop an admission, because the entire value of the network is that every member would.

4. **The record.** Every nomination, case, and objection is kept. Over time the record becomes the truest definition, because it is made of real decisions. We revisit this written definition against the record once a year and correct the words to match the discernment.

##### When an objection is personal

The written-reasons rule has a failure mode and a strength in the same place: objections rooted in personal history. One of us may have history with a nominee. An old disagreement. A falling-out. A friction that never healed. Two things have to be kept apart.

A personal disagreement or preference is **not** a reason to block. We are not building a network of people we would each choose as friends, and a difference of opinion, even a sharp one, is not a trust problem. A theological or strategic disagreement is not a trust problem either.

But sometimes a personal disagreement is exactly where a real trust issue first showed itself, because we saw, up close, something about how this person handles power, conflict, money, truth, or vulnerable people. That is not preference. That is evidence, and often the truest evidence there is.

So when an objection comes from personal history, the rule is: name it as personal, then say which kind it is. Is this "I would not choose to work with them," or is it "the network cannot stake its name on them, and here is the conduct that tells me so." Only the second blocks. The test is whether the disagreement bears on character and the network's collateral, or on taste, style, and old wounds. The one objecting discloses the history, so the other two can weigh the objection knowing where it comes from. Where the history is heavy enough that we cannot tell which kind it is, we say that too, and lean on each other to test it.

The point is not to disqualify personal knowledge. Personal knowledge is often the truest knowledge. The point is to keep a grudge from wearing the costume of a principle.

---

#### The selectors

There are three of us. For now there are two, Brad and Alan, who share a vantage and, more to the point, share a field. The third seat exists to break both kinds of sameness: a different vantage, and a different world. We choose the third selector for the independence of their judgment and the reach of their relational knowledge into rooms, and fields, the current two do not occupy. If the right person is a woman of color, that is most likely not incidental. She sees a part of the landscape the current two structurally cannot. We choose for the vantage, name the reason openly, and it stops being a checkbox.

All three hold the same power: to nominate, and to block with a written reason. The seat is a position of trust, not seniority.

---

#### Two things to settle before there is a person they apply to

**Guard against incentive drift.** The day membership has clear value, citation, credibility transfer, reach, there will be pressure to admit people who help the network's numbers rather than people who meet the definition. This is the specific way a trust network dies: slowly lowering the bar for growth. The written-reasons rule is the defense, but we name the risk out loud here so it is never a surprise. Our own thesis, claim only what is earned, has to apply hardest to who we let in.

**Decide the exit before we need it.** A network that can only add cannot protect its standard, because the cost of a wrong yes is unbounded if there is no way out. We agree, now, on what would cause someone to no longer belong: an integrity failure, a drift from the DNA, public conduct the network cannot underwrite. And on who decides, which is the same three of us, by the same written-reasons standard. The terms need not be published. They need to exist. It is far easier to write the exit rule before there is a specific person it applies to.

---

#### Open decisions for the three of us

1. **The faith floor.** The biggest one, named in the boundaries section. Is the network Christian at its root, or wider than that.

2. **The third seat.** Who holds it, chosen for a different vantage and a different field.

3. **The exit terms.** What would actually cause someone to no longer belong.

4. **Test it against ourselves.** Read this definition against the leaders already in the network. If anyone already in would not pass it, the definition is wrong, not the person, and we fix the words until they describe the people we already trust.

---

## 42. The Movemental Studio — Optimized Plan & Activation Playbook

`movemental-studio-plan.md` · 2,189 words

### The Movemental Studio — Optimized Plan & Activation Playbook

*The fully worked version of the vertical-replication idea: what it becomes when it's built right, when to turn it on relative to the core company, and the complete recommendation for how to run it. Plain prose, written to be acted on.*

---

#### The reframe: you're not licensing a platform, you're building a studio

The raw idea — help a domain expert build a Movemental-shaped company, take 25% — is good. But stated that way it's a one-off deal you do again and again. The optimized version is a category shift: **Movemental becomes a studio that mints credible-voice content-network companies, holds equity in each, and rents them the machine they run on.**

That one change — from "we did a deal" to "we run a factory" — is where nearly all the extra value lives, because a factory is worth the platform, plus the portfolio, plus the option value of every company it hasn't launched yet.

And here's the unification worth seeing clearly: **your language networks and your domain verticals are the same product.** A Spanish network is a language vertical. A sports network is a domain vertical. Both are a new tenant on one platform, anchored by a trusted voice, run on the same playbook, with Movemental holding equity and charging rent. So the studio isn't a second strategy competing with the multilingual plan. It's the general form of it. Build the machine once; it runs in any language and any field.

---

#### The single most important optimization: host the platform, don't hand over the code

Your draft said the founder gets "our full platform code and a dashboard environment." Change this before you take it to anyone. **Do not transfer the code. License it and host it.** Each vertical company runs its business *on* Movemental's multi-tenant platform — the same architecture already behind the leader sites, with a new tenant added for the new vertical. The founder gets a running business; they never get a copy of the code.

This one decision fixes four things at once:

- **It protects the IP.** Your code is the crown jewel and the thing a soured partner could walk off with. If it never leaves your servers, there's nothing to steal.
- **It creates recurring revenue.** Hosting and operating their platform is a monthly fee — the same near-pure-profit agentic-management line that makes the core valuable, now multiplied across every vertical.
- **It cleans up the equity.** The 25% is for the model, the build, and the playbook. The monthly fee is for running their tech. Two clean things instead of one muddy one.
- **It lets you support many verticals without drowning.** One platform, many tenants, one roadmap — improvements ship to everyone at once. Ten separate codebases would bury a small team; ten tenants on one platform don't.

So the optimized deal is: **25% equity for the model and the initial build, plus an ongoing platform-and-management fee for running it, plus the playbook and a set consultation cadence — all on a platform you host and never hand over.**

---

#### The optimized deal structure

- **Equity:** Movemental takes 25%; the founder side keeps 75%. Standard protective terms — pro-rata rights, information rights, a board seat or observer seat, tag-along, and a right of first offer if they sell.
- **Recurring fee:** a platform-and-management fee, ideally a blend of a floor (covers your cost to run it) and a small revenue share (rises as they grow) — think in the range of a real SaaS line, not a token. This is your cash while the equity sits illiquid.
- **The 75% is often two people, not one.** The trusted voice (the vertical's "Alan Hirsch") frequently won't want to *run* a company. Expect to pair an **anchor voice** with an **operating founder**, and let them split the 75% between them. Screen for both roles from the start; a great voice with no operator is a stalled deal.
- **Consultation, productized:** not open-ended access to Josh. A defined cadence (say a set number of hours a quarter), plus the written playbook, plus the cross-network learnings that only you have because you run all of them. Scarcity here is a feature.
- **Non-compete, narrow and enforceable:** tied to the specific vertical and to a short, *named* list of lanes Movemental has declared. Vague "areas we might go" won't hold. The real protection isn't the clause anyway — it's that they run on your hosted platform and can't easily leave it.
- **Mission and ethos clause:** a values fit requirement and an exit path if a vertical drifts from the ethos that is your whole moat. You want the right to protect the brand of the studio even across companies that don't carry your name.

---

#### When to activate it — benchmarks tied to the core

This is the part that keeps the idea from hurting you. The studio competes with the core for the one thing you can't clone: a tiny team's attention. So it's gated, hard, on the core proving itself first. Do not open the studio until all of these are true:

**Gate 1 — the core's recurring revenue is proven.** The valuation report said this is the most valuable thing you can do, and it's also the studio's prerequisite, because the recurring fee *is* the studio's business model. Benchmark: **≥15–20 organizations paying the management line, held ≥6 months, with annual churn under ~10%.** Until the monthly line is proven on your own customers, you have nothing real to rent to a vertical.

**Gate 2 — the platform is genuinely a product.** Multi-tenant, documented, and able to stand up a new tenant in about a week without Josh hand-building it. Benchmark: **you onboard a new network in ≤1 week with minimal founder involvement.** If adding a tenant still takes Josh personally, the studio can't scale and every vertical becomes a custom project you own a quarter of.

**Gate 3 — the core network isn't starved.** The English network is substantially filled (roughly **60+ leaders**) and running under its own momentum, so pointing attention at a vertical doesn't stall the thing that actually works.

**Gate 4 — capital and runway.** The studio is funded from a raise, not from starving the core. You should have closed a round with room to spare before you turn it on.

When all four are green — realistically **month 12–18** — you run **one** pilot. Not an open door. One hand-picked vertical, as the reference deal.

**Pilot success gate (before scaling):** the pilot vertical reaches its first real revenue and first cohorts or subscribers within **6–9 months**, running on the productized platform with little custom work. That proves the model *transfers* — the whole question the studio rests on.

**Then scale**, deliberately: **2–3 verticals a year** to start, rising as the studio team and your founder-selection judgment mature. Month 24 and beyond.

Note the elegant overlap: your **first Spanish network** and your **first domain vertical (see below)** are both tenant-replication pilots on the same productized platform. Run them close together and each one validates the machine the other depends on.

---

#### The full playbook — how to actually run it

**1. Productize first.** Before any of this, the platform has to become a product a stranger's company can run on: multi-tenant, self-serve onboarding, a written operating playbook turned into software where possible, and clean documentation. This is the unfunded work that unlocks *both* the studio and the languages. Fund it explicitly.

**2. Write the vertical thesis.** Decide which fields you'll enter and which you won't. Good verticals share four traits: a large, engaged audience; a credible trusted voice available to anchor it; organizations in that field that will pay for AI help; and a clean separation from anything that could contaminate the Movemental core. Sports has the first, third, and fourth in abundance. Adjacent Christian fields have all four. Write the rules down so you're choosing on a thesis, not on whoever emails you.

**3. Build the anchor-selection muscle — this is the real competency.** Studios live or die on picking the right founders, and most do it badly. Source anchors through your existing network (warm, aligned, pre-trusted is worth everything). Screen hard for three things: real credibility and audience in the field, character and values fit (trust is the moat — one bad anchor poisons a network), and either operating ability or willingness to be paired with an operator. Say no often. The best signal you're doing this right is how many good-looking deals you pass on.

**4. Standardize the deal.** One repeatable term sheet, one standard equity-plus-fee structure, one non-compete template. Studios win by repeatability; a bespoke negotiation every time doesn't scale and leaks your time. Bespoke terms are a red flag that you're doing venture deals, not running a studio.

**5. Run the pilot as a reference deal.** Pick the lowest-risk, highest-trust vertical for the first one — warm relationship, aligned values, a field close enough to your competency that you can tell good from bad. Instrument it. Its job is to prove the model transfers and to become the story you tell the next ten founders.

**6. Structure it as its own entity.** Stand up a studio or holding company separate from the core operating company, so the equity stakes and the core are cleanly divided. This makes the portfolio legible, protects the core, and lets you eventually raise for the studio on its own terms — a different and often larger story than the operating company.

**7. Build a support model that scales.** Templated onboarding, a shared platform roadmap that ships to all tenants at once, a small studio team (not Josh) handling day-to-day, and the consultation delivered on a cadence. The failure mode is a founder drowning in support for companies they own a quarter of. The hosted-platform model is what prevents it.

**8. Manage the portfolio like an investor.** Keep reserves for follow-on support to the winners, expect a spread of outcomes (a few big, several fine, some fail), and don't pour scarce time into the ones that aren't working. The winners carry the portfolio; your job is to find them and feed them.

**9. Protect the brand across companies.** Each vertical has its own name and brand — Movemental is the platform and equity holder behind it, not the face. That separation is not a limitation; it's a shield. It's what lets you capture value from voices and fields you could never put under the Movemental name.

**10. Scale on proof, not hope.** One pilot, then a trickle, then a flow — each step earned by the last one working. The urgency created by your eroding head start is real, but the answer to it is one fast, clean pilot, not an open door.

---

#### The recruitment thesis this unlocks: new core authors, not members

Here's the reframe that changes who you can land. The biggest, most independent voices in and around your world will never "join a network." But that's not the offer. The offer is: **be the founding voice of your own network — your own company — that we build, run, and co-own.** You don't recruit them as members. You recruit them as anchors of new verticals.

And because each vertical is a separate company with its own brand, the studio lets you capture value from voices you could never host inside Movemental itself — voices too big, too independent, or too controversial for the core brand to absorb. The studio structure is precisely what makes those relationships possible without risking the ethos that makes the core valuable.

That's the door this opens. It's covered in more detail in the accompanying discussion of what ten verticals would be worth — including the specific people worth building around.

---

#### Risks and guardrails, named plainly

- **Focus is the enemy.** The single biggest way this fails is turning it on before the core is proven. The gates above exist to prevent exactly that. Hold them.
- **Founder selection is unproven for you.** It's a real skill you don't yet have a track record in. The pilot is where you build it — cheaply, once.
- **IP and defection.** Solved mostly by hosting rather than transferring, and backed by narrow, enforceable terms.
- **Brand contamination.** Solved by separate entities and brands, plus an ethos clause and an exit path.
- **Adverse selection.** The best anchors may not need your deal. Counter it with warmth (pre-trusted relationships), the genuine value of the hosted platform and playbook, and a reputation built on the pilot.

---

#### The one-line version

Prove the recurring core, turn the platform into a product, run one warm pilot, and only then open a studio that mints co-owned, separately-branded content-network companies on a platform you host and never hand over — taking a quarter of each and rent on all of them. Turned on in that order, it's the move that changes what kind of company Movemental is. Turned on early, it's the move most likely to scatter you.

---

## 43. End-User Pricing Across the Movement Voice Network

`end-user-pricing-strategy.md` · 3,210 words

### End-User Pricing Across the Movement Voice Network — A Strategy Report

*A working report addressing how prices should be set for products sold to end users (readers, practitioners, churches, institutions) across the network of Movement Voice platforms. Distinct from Movemental's own engagement pricing (Safety, Sandbox, Skills, Solutions), which is treated separately. Written to be grounded, opinionated, and falsifiable — naming what I recommend, what I don't, and what I believe happens if we go a different direction.*

---

#### The question we're answering

Movement Voices on the network are selling — and will increasingly sell — products directly to end users. Books, eight-week cohort courses, subscriptions, translated editions, licensed institutional content. The question is: who decides what these things cost?

Three obvious answers, none of them sufficient on their own:

- **Full sovereignty** — each Voice sets their own prices, completely. Movemental stays out of it.
- **Full standardization** — Movemental sets prices across the network so everything looks coherent.
- **Senior council** — a council of senior Voices sets pricing norms collectively, and individual Voices follow.

What this report argues is that the right answer is **none of those in pure form**. It is a structured hybrid in which sovereignty is the default, Movemental publishes recommended bands and provides market intelligence, the network governs a small set of cross-Voice products together, and outliers are visible to peers without being vetoed by them.

The reasoning matters more than the conclusion. Let me lay it out.

#### The principles I am reasoning from

Four principles, in tension with each other. Any pricing model will have to balance all four; it cannot maximize any one without sacrificing the others.

**One — Sovereignty.** Each Movement Voice owns their corpus (Annex A.1.1 of the Participation Agreement is explicit on this). They retain the right to use, reproduce, publish, and distribute their content for any purpose, including their own books, articles, lectures, courses (A.3.1). Movemental's license is non-exclusive (A.2.1). The Voices were senior leaders with established economic relationships with their audiences *before* Movemental existed. Any pricing model that treats them as tenants of a master price-setter violates the architecture that made them want to participate.

**Two — Network coherence.** A scenius is, by definition, a reinforcing ecosystem. When a reader sees three Voices' eight-week cohorts priced at $99, $750, and $4,500, the network reads as incoherent — *what are these people actually selling, and why don't they agree?* Coherence is not uniformity, but it is also not chaos. The visible variance across the network has to remain legible to a sophisticated reader as *appropriate differences for appropriate reasons*, not *random scatter*.

**Three — Redemptive bias toward access.** The dominant Christian publishing and conferencing economy is structurally extractive — hardcover books priced at $35 with a $2 print cost, leadership cohorts priced at $5,000 to filter for executive pastors with discretionary budgets, certification programs priced like graduate seminars without graduate accountability. Movemental's whole posture, codified in the SSSS pricing architecture, refuses this. The Voices' end-user pricing should refuse it too. *The default bias is toward more readers / practitioners served, not toward higher revenue per reader.*

**Four — The pricing decision is itself part of the formation.** This one is easy to miss. *How a Voice prices their work is a statement about what kind of formation they think they are doing, who they think they are doing it with, and what they think the work is worth.* A reader who sees a $99 eight-week cohort and a $900 eight-week cohort is not just comparing prices; they are reading two different theological claims about formation. Movemental's job is not to tell Voices what claim to make, but to make sure the claim they make is conscious rather than accidental.

These four principles will pull against each other throughout. The pricing model has to hold all four in tension.

#### What is actually being priced — the products taxonomy

To make any of this concrete, here is the full landscape of what can be sold on or through the network, sorted by who properly controls the price:

**Controlled by the individual Voice:**
1. Their own books (digital, print, audio)
2. Their own eight-week formation cohorts
3. Their own subscriptions or memberships (substack/patreon-equivalent)
4. Their own teaching essays, talks, and long-form articles
5. Their own field letters and newsletters

**Controlled jointly by the Voice and a partner:**
6. Translated editions of their work (Voice + translator)
7. Co-authored content (Voice + Voice or Voice + external partner)
8. Curated pathways that combine the Voice's content with the Hub's canonical resources

**Controlled by Movemental as the network operator:**
9. Skills cohort fees (cross-Voice curriculum, governed by the existing Participation Agreement royalty pool)
10. Cross-Voice content bundles (e.g., "the missional church starter pack")
11. Licensed institutional content (a seminary licensing curriculum across multiple Voices)
12. Network-level subscriptions (access across the whole ecosystem at one price)
13. Hub-published resources where multiple Voices contribute (foster-care field guide, etc.)

This taxonomy is the foundation. Most of the pricing debate becomes much clearer once you separate these categories rather than treating "pricing" as one undifferentiated problem.

#### The recommendation, in plain language

**Voices set prices for their own products within recommended bands published by Movemental, with full sovereignty to choose, exceed, or undercut the bands as they see fit. Movemental sets prices for cross-Voice and network-level products with transparent royalty splits to participating Voices. A small annual review with elected peer-Voice representatives ratifies the bands and revises them based on what the network is learning.**

That is the spine. Everything else is detail. Let me walk through each part.

##### What Movemental recommends, but does not enforce, for Voice-controlled products

For each Voice-controlled product, Movemental publishes a recommended pricing band, with the reasoning behind it visible to Voices and (in summary form) to end users. These are not enforced. A Voice who chooses to price outside the band makes that choice with eyes open about what it signals.

**Books — digital, single Voice.** Recommended band: $9.99 – $19.99 for new releases; $4.99 – $9.99 for backlist titles older than three years. Free or pay-what-you-can for opening chapters and excerpts. Rationale: this aligns with established serious-nonfiction norms in the Christian and missional-leadership space, without falling into the $2.99 self-published bargain bin or the $35 hardcover extraction pattern.

**Books — print, single Voice.** Recommended band: $18 – $28 for hardcover; $14 – $22 for paperback. Free shipping above a threshold the Voice sets. Rationale: this prices the print artifact at fair production-plus-modest-margin levels, refusing the Christian publishing industry's extractive norms.

**Eight-week formation cohorts.** Recommended band: $300 – $900 per participant. The band is wide because the underlying work varies: a solo-led cohort of forty participants with light facilitation is appropriately priced at the lower end; a senior-Voice-led cohort of twelve with heavy facilitation and one-on-one office hours is appropriately priced at the higher end. Above $900 should be reserved for cohorts that include significant additional structure (residential intensives, multi-cohort year-long programs). Below $300 is generally a warning sign that the Voice has underpriced formation work — and that has consequences for the network, which I will name below.

Comparable prices in the field, for honest reference: a Coursera-style six-week course at $49 (insufficient depth, no formation), a graduate seminary credit at $1,500–$3,500 (different category, accredited), an executive leadership coaching cohort at $3,500–$8,000 (different audience, different work). The eight-week formation cohort is its own category and should be priced as such.

**Subscriptions / memberships.** Recommended band: $5 – $15/month, or $50 – $150/year. The Newsletter is always free; the Field Letter (the insider quarterly correspondence to active practitioners) is one of the natural paid components. The author platform's AI conversation agents, the searchable corpus, the pathway-progress dashboard, and behind-the-scenes content are other appropriate paid components. Rationale: this aligns with Substack and Patreon norms for serious independent publishers, and it doesn't price the platform out of reach for working pastors and missionaries.

**Teaching essays, talks, articles.** Recommended: free at the article level, paid as part of the subscription bundle. Single-article paywalls fracture the formation engine and degrade the EEAT/GEO signal that makes the network discoverable in the first place. *This is a recommendation I would push hard against any Voice violating, because the network-level consequences of paywalled articles are significant.*

##### What Movemental controls, with transparent royalty splits

For the cross-Voice and network-level products, Movemental sets the price, and the existing Participation Agreement royalty framework (Annex C) governs how revenue flows to participating Voices.

**Skills cohort fees.** Already set by Movemental ($15,000 + $5,000/year). The pooled royalty structure in C.3.3 governs distribution to Voices whose content forms part of the active curriculum. This is a flat, network-wide price because the product is Movemental's, not any individual Voice's.

**Cross-Voice content bundles.** Movemental sets the bundle price; each participating Voice gets a royalty on their portion of the bundle revenue. A "missional church starter pack" of three books from three Voices might be priced at $40 (vs. ~$60 if bought separately), with revenue split per Voice contribution.

**Licensed institutional content.** When a seminary, denomination, or large nonprofit wants to license content from multiple Voices for internal staff training, Movemental negotiates the institutional license. Recommended band: $500 – $5,000 per institution per year, sliding by institutional size. Revenue split per Annex C royalty rates plus institutional licensing premium.

**Network-level subscriptions.** As the scenius matures, an "all-access" network subscription becomes a real product. Recommended price: $30 – $60/month or $300 – $600/year for unlimited access to subscription-tier content across all Voices. Revenue split proportional to actual usage as measured by the network analytics, with a baseline guarantee to each Voice.

**Translation rights.** Movemental coordinates translation projects; the translator and the Voice share revenue per a translation-specific Annex. Translations into under-resourced language markets (Mandarin into mainland China, for example) may be priced at heavy discount or initially free, with the cost absorbed as a redemptive investment in the network.

#### Governance — who decides what changes, and when

The pricing model lives. It is not set once and forgotten. The governance:

**Initial bands** are proposed by Movemental and ratified by the senior Voices at the network's first formal convening. This locks in the starting position with broad legitimacy.

**Annual review** is conducted by a Pricing Council of three to five Voices elected by peers, with Movemental staffing the data and analysis. The Council reviews actual pricing decisions across the network in the past year, end-user feedback, scholarship-pool utilization, royalty-pool distribution, and proposes adjustments to the bands.

**Outlier visibility** is a transparency mechanism, not a veto. When a Voice prices significantly outside the recommended band (above the upper bound or below the lower bound by more than 20%), the network dashboard surfaces this to peers. The Voice is not asked to change. They are simply not allowed to do it invisibly. Peers can engage them in conversation if they choose. Sovereignty is preserved; the network's right to see what its members are doing is also preserved.

**The Pricing Council also governs the scholarship pool.** A defined percentage of all paid revenue across the network — recommended starting point: 5% — flows into a shared scholarship pool that funds access for under-resourced individuals and organizations. Voices contribute to the pool from their own revenue (as a cost of participating in the network), and the Council allocates from it.

#### What I specifically do not recommend, and why

This is where the report does its real work. Each of these is a path I considered and rejected; if Movemental went down any of them, I believe specific bad things would happen.

**I do not recommend full sovereignty with no published bands.** I considered it. It is the most respectful of the Voices' independence and the cleanest principle to articulate. But if Movemental publishes nothing, two things happen. *First, the variance across the network becomes chaotic within twelve months.* Some Voices, especially those with strong existing platforms and good business sense, price intelligently. Others, especially those new to direct-to-reader economics, either underprice catastrophically (because they assume formation work is "ministry" and shouldn't cost much) or overprice catastrophically (because they extrapolate from their speaking-engagement fees). *Second, end users start cross-shopping the network and concluding that Movemental does not actually mean anything by "credibility network."* The coherence claim collapses under the weight of incoherent pricing. The cost of no recommended bands is that the network's strategic position erodes — quietly at first, then unrecoverably.

**I do not recommend full Movemental-set pricing across all Voices.** I considered it. It would produce maximum coherence and would solve the cross-shopping problem in one move. But it violates the foundational principle that the Voices were senior leaders with established economic relationships *before* Movemental existed. A Voice who joined the network in part because the architecture respected their sovereignty would, six months later, be told what to charge for their own book. They would leave. And they would be right to. The Voices Movemental most wants — the most independent, the most theologically serious, the most resistant to platform capture — would be the first to walk. The cost of full standardization is that the network becomes filled with second-tier Voices who don't mind being told what to charge.

**I do not recommend giving the senior council unilateral price-setting authority.** I considered this too — it has the virtue of being distributed and apostolic, and it solves the "who decides" problem with peer wisdom. But unilateral senior-council authority creates a second-class tier of Voices whose pricing is governed by people they may not have chosen. It also makes the council's meetings into political theater, with Voices lobbying for outcomes that affect their economics. The council should *advise and ratify*, not *impose*. The cost of full senior-council authority is that the network develops factions, and the work of governance crowds out the work of formation.

**I do not recommend allowing Voices to paywall individual articles.** This is the one place I would push hard against Voice sovereignty, and the reason matters. Article-level paywalls fracture the formation engine — readers stop following pathways because they hit pay-gates mid-pathway. They fracture the EEAT/GEO signal — search engines and AI retrieval systems weight free-to-read content much more heavily than paywalled content, so paywalled articles disappear from the substrate that makes the network discoverable. They fracture the scenius — the whole point of the network is that articles cross-cite, cross-link, and reinforce each other, and paywalls break that mechanic. *A Voice who paywalls articles is not just making a pricing decision about their own work; they are degrading the network's structural integrity.* If a Voice insists on this, the appropriate response is honest conversation about whether the network model is right for them.

**I do not recommend a "pay what you can" default across all products.** I considered it as a radical access move. But pay-what-you-can pricing is psychologically extractive in a way that's not obvious — it externalizes the pricing decision onto the buyer, requires the buyer to do moral self-assessment at checkout, and tends to produce either *lower* revenue and *higher* guilt than a clear price with a transparent scholarship option. The honest move is *clear prices plus visible scholarship access*, not pay-what-you-can.

**I do not recommend tying Voice pricing to their existing speaking fees.** Several Voices command $5,000–$15,000 speaking honorariums. A reasonable-looking extrapolation would price their eight-week cohorts at $3,000+ per participant. This would be a mistake. Speaking fees price *the speaker's time and travel for one event*. Cohort fees price *the participant's formation across eight weeks*. These are different economic transactions with different price-sensitivities. Pricing cohorts as if they were extended speaking engagements would price the network out of reach of working practitioners — exactly the audience formation work is most for.

#### What happens if we do nothing

If Movemental publishes no recommended bands, sets no cross-Voice product prices, and does not establish governance for pricing decisions, here is what I believe happens within the first eighteen months of the network operating:

- Three to five Voices price aggressively (cohort fees of $1,500+, books at $25+) and start cross-selling each other's products at those prices, anchoring the network's perception toward "premium leadership formation."
- Three to five Voices price defensively (cohort fees of $99–$199) out of theological discomfort with charging for formation work, anchoring the network's perception toward "this stuff isn't worth much."
- The remaining Voices wander in between, often changing prices multiple times per year without clear rationale, creating a sense of instability.
- End users begin to perceive the network as incoherent. Some assume it is a premium product they cannot afford; others assume it is a hobbyist project they cannot trust.
- Movemental's royalty revenue becomes either lower than sustainable (because too many Voices priced too low) or politically toxic (because Movemental is taking percentages of revenue it had no role in setting).
- The Pricing Council emerges anyway, but emerges reactively — as crisis management after one or two pricing decisions have already damaged the network's coherence.

If, on the other hand, Movemental publishes recommended bands, sets cross-Voice product pricing transparently, and establishes the annual Pricing Council from the beginning, the most likely outcome is that the network develops a recognizable pricing identity in the first year: *moderately priced, transparently structured, accessibly designed, with a visible scholarship mechanism.* That identity becomes part of the network's strategic moat.

#### What needs to be decided when

A working sequence:

**Before the next ten Voices sign** — Movemental drafts the recommended bands document, publishes it as a v0.1 for internal review, circulates to the existing Voices (Alan, Brad, and the founding cohort) for feedback. Bands are presented to new Voices during onboarding as part of the participation framework.

**At the first formal Voices convening** — recommended bands are ratified by senior Voices as the network's starting position. The Pricing Council is constituted with initial members.

**Within the first six months of operation** — Movemental sets prices for the first cross-Voice products (initial book bundles, the first institutional license, the network-level subscription if launched). Royalty splits are documented and shared with affected Voices before any product launches.

**At twelve months** — first annual review by the Pricing Council. Real data, real conversation, real adjustments.

#### A closing note on what this is for

The pricing model is not just commerce. It is the network's posture toward the people it serves, made visible at every checkout. Done well, it says: *we are not extracting from you; we are not exploiting your guilt; we are not selling you formation you cannot afford; we are not pretending we are a cheap content product; we are clear about what this costs and clear about how we make sure you can access it anyway.*

That posture is the same posture that runs through everything else Movemental refuses. It belongs in the pricing model not because pricing is interesting, but because the pricing model is one of the most public statements the network ever makes about who it is and who it is for.

---

*v0.1 — May 2026. Working draft, intended for review by Alan, Brad, and the founding Voices. Bands and percentages are starting points to be ratified, adjusted, or replaced by the network's own governance.*

---

## 44. Market Segmentation & EEAT — Modular Capability Edition

`market-segmentation-modular-edition.md` · 3,247 words

### Market Segmentation & EEAT — Modular Capability Edition

*Converted from the original "org-type → screens" version. This edition organizes everything around **one capability menu** — the slots a buyer already shops for — and then shows what lights up per org family and per shape. It is neither a CMS nor a CRM; those are two doors on the same menu.*

---

#### 0. How to read this document

The old version listed, for each kind of org, a long set of Public and Staff/admin **screens**. That answered "what pages exist" but not "what am I actually buying." Buyers don't shop for screens. They shop for a **capability they already have a word for** — "I need a donor database," "I need to send a newsletter," "I need the AI thing."

So this edition flips it:

1. **One master menu** of capabilities (the categories everyone recognizes), each with modules and sub-modules.
2. **Per family** (nonprofit, church, institution), we mark each capability **Core / Available / Rare / —** and say what's inside it for them.
3. **Within each family**, the old "types" become **configurations** — not separate products, just *which modules light up*.

The menu is universal. The configuration is the product.

---

#### 1. The segmentation rule (unchanged — this still governs everything)

The segmentation variable changes at every stage, and the nonprofit/church/institution label is the right variable at only **one** of the four. Keep the method universal; segment by the thing actually doing the work:

- **Safety** → segments by **data sensitivity, population served, regulation** — not the org-type label. (High-sensitivity data and vulnerable populations are the one place generic is genuinely dangerous.)
- **Sandbox** → segments only by **example tasks**. Same posture for a pastor, a development director, a dean. A small library of starting tasks, nothing structural.
- **Training** → segments by **role** (comms, development, programs, admin, senior leader). The three labels are nearly noise here.
- **Tech** → segments **structurally**, by **functional axes + module selection**, with a **vocabulary skin** on top. This is the only stage where the three labels even approximate the right cut — and even here the real driver is the axes underneath (single-org vs. network, do they form people, publish vs. report, revenue model).

**The rule on the wall:** segmentation lives in the content and configuration, never in the methodology. The three labels are a **front door**, not a product architecture. Underneath, the product is *one path + one spine + a configured module library.*

A note on the two layers at Tech, because they cost very differently:

- **The vocabulary skin** (cheap) — donors vs. members vs. students; giving vs. tithing vs. tuition. Makes the platform *feel* tailored.
- **The module selection** (expensive) — which capabilities are actually on. Makes the platform *be* tailored.

You want both. Don't confuse them.

---

#### 2. The master capability menu (the universal SSOT)

Ten categories. The first four are **doorways** — the buyer already has the word, so that's where they self-locate and where the sale happens. The next four are the **foundation** — the buyer can't name them yet, but they're what make this one connected platform instead of a pile of disconnected point tools. Then a practical shelf, and one structural add-on.

##### Doorways (the buyer walks in asking for these)

**Publication — your publishing engine** *(the WordPress + Mailchimp slot; fine to call it the CMS)*
- **Website & pages** — your public site, editable by you.
- **Articles** — long-form writing. *Sub: pillar pieces · cluster pieces · essays / commentary.*
- **Stories** — impact and program stories that show what you actually did.
- **Newsletter / email** — what you send to your list. *Sub: broadcasts · automated sequences (welcome, re-engage) · segments · public archive.*
- **Media library** — audio/video with transcripts (sermons, talks, podcasts). *Sub: upload · auto-transcribe · publish · related content.*
- **Research / publications** — for orgs whose product is ideas: papers with citations.

**Formation — your teaching engine** *(the Teachable / Thinkific / Circle slot; the LMS)*
- **Pathways** — guided journeys, lighter than a full course.
- **Courses & lessons** — the actual course player.
- **Cohorts** — running a group through together. *Sub: scheduling · rosters · facilitator tools · completion.*
- **Community** — discussion spaces for participants.
- **Assessments & reflection** — checks and prompts inside the learning.
- **Certificates** — proof of completion.
- **Enroll / apply** — how people get in.

**Relationships — your CRM** *(the Neon / Bloomerang slot; the "customer engine")*
- **Contact records** — one page per person, full history.
- **Segments & lists** — group people by what they've done or who they are.
- **Stewardship pipelines** — move someone from first touch to committed. *Sub: donor journeys · visitor→member→leader (church) · lapsed re-engagement.*
- **Communications log** — every touch in one place.
- *(Church skin of the same engine: members, households, attendance — what they'd otherwise buy as a ChMS.)*

**Giving — your fundraising engine** *(the Givebutter / Donorbox / Classy slot)*
- **Donations** — one-time and recurring.
- **Campaigns** — time-bound pushes with a goal and a progress bar.
- **Pledges** — commitments over time.
- **Receipts & statements** — what donors and your bookkeeper need.
- **Store / e-commerce** — sell books, merch, resources.
- **Paid membership / subscriptions** — recurring access or dues.

##### Foundation (comes attached to the doorway; the buyer feels it but can't name it)

**AI Assistant — your agent platform** *(the new slot: ChatGPT, but it knows your org)*
- **Public assistant** — answers visitors: "what do you do, what's your impact?"
- **Staff assistants** — draft the grant report, turn one event into a newsletter and three posts, answer the repeat question, find the 2019 document.
- **Smart search** — ask your whole library a question and get a cited answer back.

**Library — everything you've ever made, gathered and searchable** *(the slot most orgs don't know they're missing)*
- **Bring it in** — import documents, reports, archives; transcribe audio and video.
- **Search** — one box across all of it.
- **Public index** — the browsable front of it.
- *(This is what we used to call "corpus." A buyer doesn't shop for "corpus ingestion" — they feel it as "finally, one place where all our stuff lives and can be found." It's also what makes the AI Assistant and the Publication engine actually work, so it's foundation, not a side feature.)*

**Visibility & Trust — being found and believed by Google and AI** *(the SEO slot, extended)*
- **Search & AI visibility** — structured so Google *and* AI answer engines get you right (SEO plus the newer "GEO").
- **Sources & citations** — every claim backed by a source.
- **Real profiles** — your people and your org as entities machines recognize.
- **Network & endorsements** — who cites you and vouches for you.

**Governance — your AI rulebook, live** *(a slot nobody really sells yet)*
- **AI Handbook** — your policy (what you'll do, what you refuse), live and searchable, not a PDF in a drawer.
- **Roles & permissions** — who can do what.
- **Analytics** — what's working.
- **Readiness check** — where your team actually is.

##### The practical shelf

**Operations**
- **Events & registration.**
- **Volunteers** — opportunities, shifts, hours.
- **Forms & intake** — applications, requests, sign-ups.
- **Grants** — pipeline, deliverables, deadlines, and report drafting (leans on the AI Assistant).

##### The structural add-on

**Network — HQ plus chapters** *(the association-management slot; only for parent orgs and denominations)*
- **Member sub-sites** — each affiliate gets its own mini-platform.
- **Provisioning & templates** — stand up a new member from a default.
- **Roll-up analytics & governance** — see and steward across all of them.

> **The four foundation categories (AI Assistant, Library, Visibility & Trust, Governance) are always on.** They are the spine. Every build includes them no matter the family. The doorways and the shelf are what get configured.

**Legend for the tables below:** **Core** = on by default for this family · **Available** = turn on if it fits · **Rare** = occasional · **—** = not typical.

---

#### 3. Nonprofit — *"be understood and funded"*

**Vocabulary skin:** donors · giving · grants · impact · programs · volunteers.
**What they walk in asking for:** a donor database (Relationships), a way to take donations (Giving), a newsletter and a website (Publication), and increasingly "an AI thing" (AI Assistant). Those are the doorways. Everything else comes attached.

| Capability | Nonprofit baseline | What lights up |
|---|---|---|
| **Publication** | Core | Website & pages, **Stories** (impact), Newsletter/email. Articles available. |
| **Relationships (CRM)** | Core | Donor/stakeholder records, segments, **stewardship pipelines** (donor journeys, lapsed re-engagement), comms log. |
| **Giving** | Core | Donations (recurring + one-time), campaigns, pledges, receipts. |
| **AI Assistant** | Core (foundation) | Public "what do you do / what's your impact" agent; staff assistants (draft the grant report, event → posts, find the document). |
| **Library** | Core (foundation) | Impact history, program records, reports, board minutes — gathered, searchable, cited. |
| **Visibility & Trust** | Core (foundation) | Verifiable provenance on outcomes and claims; people and org as real entities; optional network place. |
| **Governance** | Core (foundation) | The AI Handbook live, with donor-data and beneficiary-data lines drawn; roles; analytics; readiness. |
| **Operations** | Core | **Grants** (pipeline + agent-drafted reports), events & registration, volunteers, forms/intake. |
| **Formation (LMS)** | Available | Only if they deliver programs or training (→ becomes Core in the formation shape). |
| **Network** | Rare | Only for the network/intermediary shape. |
| *Giving → Store / subscriptions* | Rare | Occasional resource sales. |

**The four nonprofit shapes — same menu, different modules lit:**

- **Direct-service / program** *(shelter, food bank, clinic — the default)*. The baseline exactly as above: Relationships + Giving + Publication(stories) + Operations(grants), foundation underneath. Formation light or off; Network off.
- **Formation / program-delivering** *(Youthfront-type)*. **Formation flips to Core** — pathways, courses, cohorts, certificates, enroll/apply become the center of gravity. Relationships shifts toward a **learner CRM**; Giving gets lighter; grants usually stay. This is the one nonprofit shape that leans toward the church/institution build.
- **Think-tank / thought-leadership** *(research org, policy shop, author-built ministry)*. **Publication → research/publications** and **Library + Visibility & Trust** become the center — papers, citations, the credibility graph. Giving often shifts to **membership/subscriptions**. Relationships stays light; Formation off. This is *institution-lite* — it barely behaves like a service nonprofit.
- **Network / intermediary** *(grantmaker, association, parent org)*. **Network flips to Core** — member sub-sites, provisioning, roll-up analytics and governance. Operations' grants becomes a full **grantmaking pipeline**. Multi-tenant; shares its build with denominations, not with shelters.

---

#### 4. Church — *"reach, disciple, shepherd"*

**Vocabulary skin:** members · households · tithing/giving · groups · next steps · attendance.
**What they walk in asking for:** church management (Relationships, ChMS-grade), giving, the sermon archive (Publication → media library), and discipleship (Formation). Four doorways, and unusually for this family, **two of them — Formation and the media Library — are non-negotiable**, because discipleship and the sermon corpus *are* the church's core product.

| Capability | Church baseline | What lights up |
|---|---|---|
| **Publication** | Core | **Media library** (sermons: audio/video + transcript) is central — this is the church's corpus surface. Plus website, ministries pages, newsletter. |
| **Formation (LMS)** | Core | Discipleship pathways, classes, next-steps journeys. Rarely optional — discipleship *is* the product. |
| **Relationships (CRM)** | Core | **ChMS-grade**: members, households, attendance, groups, **assimilation pipeline** (visitor→member→leader), care/follow-up (with data-sensitivity guardrails). |
| **Giving** | Core | Recurring, pledges, campaigns. |
| **AI Assistant** | Core (foundation) | Sermon → weekly study/devotional/posts, generate the bulletin, answer repeat questions, public agent grounded in actual teaching. |
| **Library** | Core (foundation) | Every sermon and teaching transcribed, searchable, cited. |
| **Visibility & Trust** | Core (foundation) | Teaching verifiably theirs; people as entities; faithful representation (never words in a pastor's mouth). |
| **Governance** | Core (foundation) | The Handbook live with the **pastoral and member-data lines** drawn (AI + counseling, AI + the sermon, disclosure to the congregation). |
| **Operations** | Available | Events & registration, groups admin, prayer/care requests (forms), app/notifications. |
| **Network** | Available | Core in the multi-site shape. |
| *Voice modules* | Available | If the pastor is also an author — see the teaching-church shape. |
| *Giving → Store / paid courses* | Rare | Merch, resources, paid classes. |

**The three church shapes:**

- **Single congregation.** The baseline above — and the most "fused" product on the whole menu (church management + publishing + formation + agents in one). The default church shape.
- **Multi-site / network church.** Single-congregation modules **plus Network → Core**: per-campus sub-sites, a shared teaching publisher, a multi-campus dashboard, network governance. Same multi-tenant requirement as a denomination, smaller scale.
- **Teaching church / pastor-as-author.** The whole single-congregation build **plus a second Voice stack** scoped to the pastor as a public author: Publication (their articles, books, corpus), Formation (their pathways and courses), an AI Lab in their voice, an author newsletter, and a Visibility & Trust author-entity (credentials, sameAs, place in the network). Two products in one.

---

#### 5. Institution — *"credibility and coherence"*

**Vocabulary skin:** students · faculty · alumni · tuition/advancement · programs · credentials · departments.
**What they walk in asking for:** an LMS and credentialing (Formation), admissions (Operations), and — uniquely to this family — **verifiability and governance at scale**, which they often *can* name because it's their whole reason to be here. This is the heaviest version of the foundation: the spine isn't background, it's the point.

| Capability | Institution baseline | What lights up |
|---|---|---|
| **Visibility & Trust** | Core — *the crux* | Verifiable provenance **at scale** (distinguishable from a well-made fake); the credential and canon made coherent; the credibility graph. This is the institution's entire reason to be here. |
| **Governance** | Core — *central, not background* | The Handbook across departments, AI policy and ratification, multi-department roles. |
| **Library** | Core — *the heaviest* | Decades of scholarship, archives, faculty work, committee records — gathered, deduplicated, searchable, cited into one source. |
| **AI Assistant** | Core (foundation) | Scholarship-bounded agents, governance/policy assistants, a public agent that represents the institution accurately. |
| **Publication** | Core | Scholarship/publications index, cited paper pages with provenance. |
| **Formation (LMS)** | Core *if teaching* | LMS + **credentialing**: courses, programs, continuing ed, certificates, transcripts. |
| **Operations** | Core *if teaching* | **Admissions / application management**; events/lectures. |
| **Relationships (CRM)** | Available | Alumni/advancement CRM; student records (with academic-records guardrails). |
| **Giving** | Available | Advancement / giving. |
| *Giving → Membership / subscriptions* | Available → Core for associations | Journals, denominational membership, paywall. |
| **Network** | Available → central for denominations | Multi-tenant: propagate a platform to every church/school/department underneath. |

**The three institution shapes:**

- **Seminary / school (teaching institution).** Corpus + verifiability + governance Core, **plus Formation/credentialing and Admissions → Core**. Faculty as entities; student records under academic guardrails; alumni/advancement available. The teaching-institution shape.
- **Denomination / network body.** **Network → Core**, and the most demanding case: governance-at-scale plus propagating a platform to every member church (each member church gets the **single-congregation church build** as its sub-site). Add credentialing/ordination where applicable. This is the "two timelines" turned into product. Shares its spine with multi-site churches and network nonprofits.
- **Association / accreditor / publisher / journal.** **Giving → membership/subscriptions becomes Core** (often with a paywall); Publication runs an **editorial / peer-review workflow** (submission → review → publish); verifiability Core; accreditation admin lives in Operations/forms. Light on Formation. The credibility-and-membership shape.

---

#### 6. Individual Voice — the reference implementation *(the Alan platform)*

Kept because it's the build everything else was reverse-engineered from, and the teaching-church shape reuses it wholesale.

**Identity:** *"be coherent, found, and connected."* **Doorways:** Publication + Formation, on the foundation.

- **Publication** — Core: pillar/cluster articles, essays, newsletter.
- **Formation** — Core: pathways + courses + cohorts (the formation engine).
- **Library** — Core (foundation): the full corpus (books, talks, articles) indexed, cited, unique-intent-per-URL.
- **AI Assistant** — Core (foundation): the AI Lab agent, corpus-bounded and voice-configured; a public agent in the author's voice.
- **Visibility & Trust** — Core (foundation): the voice constitution, the author as a real entity, the scenius cross-citation graph (you're a node).
- **Giving** — Available: paid subscriptions/membership, paid courses, store (books/resources).
- **Relationships** — Rare: beyond a subscriber list. **Operations** — Rare: occasional events.

---

#### 7. EEAT — the Visibility & Trust + Library + AI Assistant categories, in action

The EEAT work isn't a separate product; it's what the foundation categories *produce*. Both flows below run the same spine: **person/org entity → gathered corpus → cited claims → endorsements → network position.** Experience and Expertise come from the body of work being real and gathered (Library). Authoritativeness comes from entities and who-cites-whom (Visibility & Trust). Trust comes from provenance, refusals, and how-we-use-AI (Governance + Visibility & Trust).

##### A. About Movemental & the founders

**Public-facing**
1. About Movemental (org overview) — Authoritativeness
2. Why we exist / the thesis (fragmentation + AI) — Expertise
3. How we use AI on ourselves — Trust *(we eat our own cooking)*
4. What we refuse to do (the refusals) — Trust
5. Founders index (Alan, Brad, Josh) — Authoritativeness
6. Founder profile ×3 — Experience + Expertise
7. The story / origin (the two-year conversation, 2026) — Experience
8. Our research / writing index — Expertise
9. Research / paper page (cited, provenance) — Expertise + Trust
10. Endorsements / who trusts us — Authoritativeness
11. The network / scenius overview — Authoritativeness
12. Security & data trust — Trust
13. Contact / talk to us — Trust

**Entity / machine layer** — 14. Org entity + schema (Organization, sameAs) — Authoritativeness · 15. Founder person-entities + sameAs — Authoritativeness · 16. Citations layer (every claim sourced) — Trust

*The founder flow leans on the refusals and "we use it on ourselves."*

##### B. About a Movement Leader / Voice

**Public-facing**
1. Voice profile / home — Experience + Authoritativeness
2. Their corpus index (books, talks, articles gathered) — Expertise
3. Corpus item page — Experience
4. Article / essay index — Expertise
5. Article page (cited, unique-intent-per-URL) — Expertise + Trust
6. Pathways index — Experience
7. Pathway page — Experience
8. Courses index + course page — Expertise
9. The AI Lab (their corpus-bounded agent) — Experience *(the "talk to the work" proof)*
10. Citations / sources — Trust
11. Who cites them / endorsements — Authoritativeness
12. Their place in the network (cross-citation) — Authoritativeness
13. Newsletter / subscribe — Trust *(direct relationship)*

**Entity / machine layer** — 14. Person entity + credentials + sameAs (ORCID, VIAF, etc.) — Authoritativeness · 15. Author-to-work links — Expertise + Trust · 16. Cross-citation graph (the scenius edges) — Authoritativeness

*The Voice flow leans on the corpus and the AI Lab.*
