## 47. User Journeys and the Subscriber Relationship

`user-journeys-and-subscriber-architecture.md` · 6,016 words

### User Journeys and the Subscriber Relationship

##### A canonical strategy document for the Movemental movement leader platforms

*Covers: what a user journey is and why it decides the architecture · the personas each platform is actually built for · the settled playbook and where it comes from · the specific journeys for Alan Hirsch and Brad Brisco · what the subscriber database must hold and what the UI must show.*

*Bracketed items are things that need confirming against the live build or against the leader before this is treated as settled.*

---

### 1 · What we are actually talking about

We are deciding what happens to a person between the moment they first land on a leader's site and the moment they either become a practitioner shaped by that leader's work or leave and never come back.

That sounds obvious. It is not what most people mean when they say "user journey." Most of the time that phrase means a diagram of pages someone might click through. That is a sitemap with arrows on it. What we mean is different and harder: **a defined sequence of states a person moves through, where each state is something we can observe, store, and act on, and where every page and every email exists to move someone from one named state to the next.**

The difference matters because one of them can be built and the other cannot. "The user explores the pathways and then considers a course" is not something a database can hold. "The user has completed one assessment, opened four of the last six letters, and has not started a pathway" is. The second one tells you what email to send on Tuesday. The first one tells you nothing.

So the real subject here is a small set of interlocking decisions:

- What states can a person be in.
- What events move them between states.
- What we store when that happens.
- What we show the leader, and what we show the person themselves.
- How all of that stays coherent when the same human being appears on Alan's site on Monday and Brad's site on Thursday.

That last one is the reason this document exists now rather than later. Two platforms are live. More are coming. If each one grows its own idea of what a subscriber is, we will spend the next two years reconciling them instead of building.

---

### 2 · Saying it plainly

Strip the vocabulary out and here is the whole thing.

Somebody has a problem on a Tuesday night. They search for it. They land on a page one of our leaders wrote. That page either answers the question or it does not. If it does, they now have a reason to trust the person who wrote it, and we have about ninety seconds to give them a reason to come back — because if they leave without one, we have permanently lost them and we will never know it happened.

So we offer them something. Not a mailing list. Something about themselves — a result, a profile, a reading of their own situation. They give us an email address for it, because the thing is worth more than the address.

Now we have a relationship rather than a visit. We write to them. Not announcements about what we published, but a real letter with a thought in it. Some of them reply. Over months, a few of them decide they want to actually be changed by this work rather than informed by it, and those people walk a pathway or join a cohort. A smaller number teach it to other people, which is the only outcome any of these leaders actually cares about.

And the whole time, we are writing down what happened. What they read, what they scored, what they opened, what they did. Not to score them like sales leads. To know what to send next, and to know which of the four things above is broken.

That is it. Everything below is detail on how to do that without it turning into marketing.

---

### 3 · Why this decides more than it looks like it decides

Four reasons this is worth a canonical document rather than a per-site decision.

**The email list is the only asset the leader actually owns.** Alan's audience currently reaches him through publishers, conferences, seminaries, and the people who teach his frameworks. Brad's reaches him through Send Network, Forge, Sentralized, and denominational relationships. Every one of those is a real relationship and not one of them is a channel he controls. If the intermediary changes — a network reorganizes, a conference folds, a publisher moves on — the leader loses the ability to speak to people who have organized their working lives around his work. Building the list is not a growth tactic. It is the thing that makes everything else survivable.

**Traffic arriving before there is somewhere to put it is lost permanently, and silently.** This is the expensive failure and it does not show up in any dashboard. A leader can publish for a year, watch traffic rise, and have nothing at the end of it. There is no error message for a visitor who was interested and had nowhere to go.

**The multi-tenant question has a deadline.** Two sites are live. If we define the subscriber model now, the same person on both sites is one record with two relationships and we can eventually offer something across the network. If we define it later, they are two records with no way to reconcile them, and every cross-network product becomes an integration project. The cost of getting this right now is a schema conversation. The cost of getting it wrong is a migration.

**The journey is what tells us which content to make.** The content value work already established that each leader has an emptiest column and should build there. But you cannot see which column is empty without journey data. How many people arrive and leave without a name. How many have a name and never come back. How many come back and never do anything. Those three numbers point at the gap, and none of them exist unless the journey is instrumented.

---

### 4 · The playbook that is actually settled

There is more agreement about this than people admit. Here is what is genuinely known, where it comes from, and what remains judgment.

#### 4.1 People arrive at different distances from being ready

The oldest useful idea here is Eugene Schwartz's stages of awareness, from mid-century direct-response advertising: a person can be unaware there is a problem, aware of the problem, aware that solutions exist, aware of your particular solution, or ready to act. It has survived seventy years because it is true and because it has one hard implication.

**Content written for the wrong stage fails even when it is excellent.** A page arguing that your framework is the best available is wasted on someone who does not yet believe they have the problem it solves. A page explaining what the problem is bores someone who came ready to enrol. This is why "our content isn't converting" is almost always a stage mismatch rather than a quality problem.

The practical version: every page should know which stage it serves, and the next step it offers should be exactly one stage further along. Not three.

#### 4.2 Discovery happens by cluster, not by page

This is Moz's topic cluster model, which by now is close to consensus across the SEO field: a comprehensive hub page on a broad term, surrounded by six to eight pages each answering a specific question, all linked to the hub and to each other. Search systems resolve topical authority at the cluster level, not the page level. One brilliant orphan page is close to invisible.

Two things have changed since that model was written and both make it more important rather than less.

The first is that the systems doing the introducing are increasingly answer engines rather than link lists. A person asks a machine and gets a fluent, sourceless paragraph. What gets quoted is a self-contained answer near the top of a page — something liftable whole. That is now the front door.

The second is that a cluster is also what makes the second and third page views happen. A visitor on an orphan page has one exit, which is the back button. A visitor inside a cluster has six relevant next reads, and depth of visit is the single best predictor of whether someone will give you an email address.

#### 4.3 One primary next step per page

Well-established in conversion practice and repeatedly confirmed in testing: a page offering three next steps performs worse than the same page offering one. Choice imposes a cost, and the cost is paid in inaction.

The rule for us: every page has exactly one primary action. Secondary links can exist but must be visually subordinate. The primary action changes by stage, and it is almost never "subscribe to the newsletter," because nobody wants a newsletter. They want the thing the newsletter is attached to.

#### 4.4 What earns an email address is something about them, not about you

This is the single most useful operational distinction in the whole document, and the one most often got wrong.

A PDF explaining your framework is about you. An assessment that tells someone where they personally stand is about them. The second converts at multiples of the first, and it converts a better person — someone who now holds a fact about their own situation and a question that follows from it.

The test for whether a tool is good enough: **would the person forward their result to a colleague unprompted?** If not, it is a brochure with a form on it.

#### 4.5 Ask for information progressively, never all at once

Progressive profiling is standard practice in marketing automation, and the logic is simple. Every additional form field reduces completion. But you can ask for one more thing each time someone comes back, and by the fourth interaction you know more than any single form would ever have got you.

So the first ask is an email address and nothing else. Role comes from the second interaction. Organizational context comes from an assessment. What they are actually trying to do comes from a reply to a letter, which is why the letters have to ask real questions.

#### 4.6 Engagement decays and must be measured, not assumed

Direct marketing has used recency, frequency, and monetary value for decades, and the first two transfer directly. A subscriber who opened four of the last six letters is a fundamentally different person from one who has opened none in a year, and treating them identically wastes the first and annoys the second.

Two consequences we should adopt without argument:

**Track engagement as a rolling score, not a binary subscribed flag.** Recency of last open, frequency over a trailing window, and depth of action.

**Sunset the disengaged deliberately.** Someone who has not opened anything in a year is hurting deliverability for everyone else. Ask once whether they want to stay, then stop mailing. This feels like losing something and is actually the opposite — sending to dead addresses is how you end up in spam folders for the living ones.

#### 4.7 Identity has to resolve across properties

For anyone running more than one site, the settled practice is a single canonical person record with per-property relationships hanging off it. The alternative — a separate list per site — means the same human is three strangers, you cannot tell whether cross-promotion works, and you will eventually mail them three times about the same thing.

Consent, however, does not travel. A person subscribing to Alan does not thereby subscribe to Brad. One identity, separate permissions.

#### 4.8 What is not settled and where judgment lives

Being honest about the edges.

**Cadence.** No reliable general answer. Consistency beats frequency, reliably. Whether that consistency is weekly or quarterly depends entirely on what the leader can sustain for years.

**Free-to-paid conversion rates.** The commonly cited benchmarks come from datasets with unpublished methodology. Treat any specific percentage as a rough prior and nothing more.

**A/B testing.** At the volumes these platforms will see for the next two years, it is not merely difficult, it is pointless. Detecting a meaningful difference at low conversion rates requires thousands of people per arm. We will have dozens. Decide by judgment and by qualitative signal, and stop pretending otherwise.

**Whether the paid tier should exist yet.** Genuinely open. The argument for early is that paying creates commitment and free accounts get abandoned. The argument for later is that you do not know what people will pay for until you have watched them use the free thing.

---

### 5 · The four states, which every platform shares

Everything above resolves into four states a person can be in. These are the same on every leader platform, they are what the database stores, and they are what the leader's dashboard reports on.

**Stranger.** Arrived, read something, no identity. We know a session and nothing more. The only thing that matters about this state is how many leave it and how many do not.

**Named.** Gave an email address in exchange for something. This is the single most important transition in the whole system, because everything downstream is impossible without it and it is invisible when it fails.

**Engaged.** Comes back on purpose. Opens the letters, reads more than one thing, has done something that produced a result about themselves. This is where most of the population should sit and where most of the value is.

**Practitioner.** Doing the work. Walking a pathway, in a cohort, using the material with their own people. A small number, and the reason the other three states exist.

There is a fifth state that we should name even though it is not a funnel stage, because for these particular leaders it is the actual goal: **Multiplier** — someone teaching this material to other people, without the leader in the room. It is not reachable by a sequence of emails. It is a consequence of the Practitioner state plus artifacts built to be handed on. We measure it by asking, because there is no other way.

The transitions between these are where the design work lives:

- Stranger → Named requires something worth an address.
- Named → Engaged requires a first letter that justifies the address within days.
- Engaged → Practitioner requires an invitation timed to something they did, not to a launch calendar.
- Practitioner → Multiplier requires artifacts that work without the leader present.

---

### 6 · Alan Hirsch

#### 6.1 The three primary personas

**The practitioner who already uses the frameworks and wants the real version.** A church planter, network leader, or pastor who encountered APEST or mDNA somewhere else — inside another author's book, at a conference, in a seminary class, from a colleague's summary. They are already using the language. They may be using it wrongly, most often by treating a fivefold category as a personality label. They arrive with a specific question about application. They do not need convincing that Alan matters; they need the accurate version and something to do with it. **This is the largest group and the one the platform is primarily built for.** Their journey should be short and should end at a pathway.

**The leader who has been sent by someone.** A staff member whose team is doing an APEST process, a planter whose network trains from Alan's material, a student assigned a chapter. They arrive warm but shallow — the trust is borrowed from whoever sent them, and it will not survive a page that fails to deliver. They need a fast, competent, usable orientation and one clear next step. They convert well because the intent is high and the context is already established. **The most under-served group, and the one the assessment work most directly reaches.**

**The institutional evaluator.** A seminary faculty member deciding whether to put a book on a syllabus, a denominational executive weighing a training investment, an academic checking whether the frameworks hold up. Small in number, disproportionate in consequence, because one decision here reaches forty students a year for a decade. They are not looking for formation. They are looking for verifiability: the citation record, the academic reception, the frameworks stated precisely enough to be examined. They will not subscribe and should not be asked to. **They are served by the proof surfaces, and the conversion event is an adoption we may never see in analytics.** [Confirm whether we can capture institutional adoptions at all — probably only by asking.]

#### 6.2 The intended journey

Alan's problem is not obscurity. It is substitution. The vocabulary travels widely and it travels in the tidy version — easier to repeat, missing the hard part. Somebody asks a machine what APEST is and gets a confident, sourceless answer that is not his position, and nothing about it looks wrong.

So the journey begins earlier than a normal platform's. It begins with reclaiming the answer.

**Arrival is nearly always through a term.** Someone searches or asks about APEST, mDNA, communitas, apostolic genius, missional-incarnational. They land on a definitional page whose first three sentences are a complete, liftable answer to the question in the form it was asked. Everything else on that page sits below the answer. That page is the front door for the great majority of arrivals and it should be built as such.

**From the definitional page, one step: the cluster.** Six to eight interlinked pieces around that term, each answering a real question, including — importantly — the ones about what the framework is not. The piece on APEST and personality types is doing correction work that nothing else on the platform can do, and it is the piece a skeptical reader opens first.

**The named transition happens through the assessment, and this is where the APEST agentic extension is decisive.**

Alan already has assessments that work. They are widely used, well regarded, and — critically — they currently sit apart from the platform. That separation is the largest single opportunity in this document. Thousands of people have taken an APEST assessment and hold a result. That result is a fact about themselves. It is exactly the thing that earns an email address, and right now it is earning one somewhere else, or nowhere.

The extended agentic version changes the offer from a score to a conversation. Instead of "here is your profile, thank you," it becomes: here is your profile, and here is an agent bound to Alan's corpus that can tell you what this means for the decision you are actually facing this month. What it means when your whole team scores the same way. What it means that you scored high on something you have never been permitted to exercise in your current role. What the framework says about the gap you are feeling.

That is a fundamentally stronger thing than an assessment, for four reasons. It produces a result the person would forward. It generates, in the transcript, an unusually rich picture of their actual situation — better than any form would get. It naturally terminates in a specific pathway rather than a generic invitation. And it demonstrates the corpus binding, which is itself the proof: an agent that cites back to the books and is willing to say it does not know is a stronger credibility signal than any essay about rigor.

**Practically, this means the assessment result page is the most important conversion surface on Alan's platform** and should be designed as such rather than as a results screen. [Confirm the current assessment platform, whether results can be handed off, and whether existing takers can be reached. If the historic taker list exists and is contactable, that is the single largest asset in this document.]

**From named to engaged: two letters, doing different jobs.** A public letter to the broad list, one idea per issue, published nowhere else, on a rhythm he can hold for years. And a longer, more candid letter to people actively doing the work, which can say things not yet ready for the public one. The second is a proof signal in its own right — it tells practitioners they are inside a real conversation rather than on a mailing list. [Confirm whether both exist and at what cadence.]

**From engaged to practitioner: the pathway, entered from the assessment result.** This is why the agentic version matters so much. A generic "explore our pathways" invitation is weak. "Based on what you have just told me about your situation, the place to start is this one, and here is why" is a different thing entirely, and it is only possible because the agent has the conversation.

**From practitioner to multiplier: the facilitator layer.** Alan's multiplication is already happening and it is happening unsupervised. People teach this material constantly, in rooms he will never see, from summaries. So the work here is not to start multiplication. It is to make the accurate version easier to run than the garbled one — the facilitator page, the one-page version that is hard to misstate, the material that names the common misreadings directly.

#### 6.3 What the platform must not do

Alan's refusals are themselves the trust signal, so the journey has to respect them or it undermines the thing it is trying to build. No pressure sequences. No manufactured scarcity. No treating formation as a funnel stage. Articles stay free — paywalling them fractures the formation engine and destroys the discoverability that makes the whole thing work. And the agent must never pretend to be him.

---

### 7 · Brad Brisco

#### 7.1 The three primary personas

**The church planter who needs something to use this week.** Bivocational or covocational, often under-resourced, holding a real problem with a near deadline. They are not looking for a theology of place; they are looking for something to run with their core group on Tuesday. They convert on tools and they stay for the theology underneath, in that order — which is the reverse of how most people assume it works, and the reason the tool is Brad's front door rather than his back one. **The primary persona and the one the platform should be designed around.**

**The established pastor trying to turn the ship.** Leading an existing congregation, increasingly aware that the inherited attractional model is not working where they are, and facing the specific problem Brad wrote a doctorate on. They arrive skeptical of anything that sounds like a program relabel. They need the theological reframe before the practices, because a tactic without the reframe will get applied to an unchanged system and fail. They move slower than the planter and go deeper when they move. **The group Brad's corpus serves best and the one his site currently reaches least.**

**The network or denominational leader deciding whether to bring him in.** Responsible for many planters, evaluating whether Brad is both theologically serious and genuinely practical. They are not a reader; they are an evaluator with a budget and a calendar. What they need is fast evidence of both hands full — real theology and real tools — and confidence they will not regret the platform they give him. **Small in number and the highest-leverage group he has,** because one adoption puts his material in front of everyone that network trains. This is the persona for whom Send is not a slow accumulation but a single decision.

#### 7.2 The intended journey

Brad's problem is different from Alan's in a way that changes the whole shape. He is not being substituted for; he is under-indexed. He coined a term and does not own the answer to it. A stranger searching what he named mostly finds other people, or nothing.

**Arrival is split between search and network, and the network side is warmer and larger today.** Someone hears him at a Sentralized session, encounters him through Send Network, or is handed a book. Search is a real and growing secondary that his corpus makes credible but that is currently unbuilt.

So the first job is a definitional page per term he named, plus book hubs that state each book's argument, name who it is for, list the frameworks inside, and say where to start. Not product pages. Pages a stranger can use and a machine can quote. This is weeks of work against material that already exists.

**The named transition happens through the tool, and for Brad this should be the hero rather than a section.** His audience is practitioners who want something to run. A tool that reads their actual neighborhood, or reads their own covocational readiness, is about them in exactly the way that earns an address. It is also his most natural front door: the planter arrives with a problem and leaves with a finding about their own context. [Confirm the current state of the existing tools and whether results are captured against an identity.]

**From named to engaged: one letter, every other week, that is not a digest.** Brad's native form is the framework — a paradigm shift stated crisply, an inherited assumption named and corrected, one image or contrast. That is what the letter should carry, one per issue, published nowhere else. The failure mode to avoid is the roundup of what he published, which gets skimmed once and unsubscribed.

**From engaged to practitioner: the pathway, and increasingly the cohort.** The planter who ran the tool with their core group has already acted once. The invitation that follows should reference that, not launch a product.

**From practitioner to multiplier: this is where Brad's position is unusual and should be exploited deliberately.** Most people building toward multiplication have to find someone willing to run their material. Brad has standing relationships with organizations that train people at volume. One tool adopted as standard practice by a sending network reaches further than a year of publishing. That makes the facilitator layer — the run-it-with-a-group page, the forty-minute version, the two sentences on what not to say — the highest-value thing he can build after the definitional pages. [Confirm which network relationships are live and who actually decides on adoption.]

#### 7.3 The main risk

Brad's is a proof reflex. The strongest pull in his position is toward another book, another framework, another substantial piece of thinking — the work he is already good at, which will feel productive and change nothing. The journey design has to keep pointing at rendering and at the tools, because that is where the empty columns are.

---

### 8 · What the subscriber database has to hold

The model is one person, many relationships. A canonical person record; a separate relationship record per leader platform; consent and engagement tracked per relationship, never globally.

#### 8.1 The person

The canonical identity. One row per human being across the whole network.

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| `person_id` | Canonical identifier. Never per-tenant. |
| `email_primary` | Normalized and deduplicated. The join key in practice. |
| `email_alternates[]` | People sign up twice with two addresses. Merge, don't duplicate. |
| `display_name`, `given_name`, `family_name` | Progressive — often empty at first contact. |
| `country`, `timezone`, `language` | Timezone matters for send timing; language matters once translations exist. |
| `created_at`, `first_seen_tenant` | Which leader introduced them to the network. Worth knowing. |
| `merged_from[]` | Audit trail for identity merges. Non-negotiable — merges go wrong. |
| `global_suppression` | Hard bounce, spam complaint, or legal deletion request. Overrides every consent everywhere. |

#### 8.2 The relationship, per tenant

One row per person per leader platform. This is where nearly all the useful data lives.

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| `tenant_id` | The leader platform. |
| `stage` | `stranger` / `named` / `engaged` / `practitioner`. Computed, not self-declared. |
| `stage_entered_at` | Per stage. Time-in-stage is the diagnostic that tells you where the journey is stuck. |
| `acquisition_source` | Search, network referral, event, another tenant, direct. |
| `acquisition_entry_url` | The exact page that earned them. This is how you learn which content actually works. |
| `first_value_event` | What they gave the address for — which assessment, which tool, which guide. |
| `consent_newsletter`, `consent_insider`, `consent_product` | Separate permissions, separately timestamped. |
| `consent_timestamps`, `consent_source_url`, `consent_ip` | Compliance requires the record, not the assertion. |
| `engagement_score` | Rolling, 0–100. See below. |
| `last_open_at`, `last_click_at`, `last_site_visit_at` | The recency inputs. |
| `sunset_state` | `active` / `at_risk` / `re_permission_sent` / `sunset`. |
| `role_self_reported` | Planter, pastor, network leader, academic, student, other. Progressive. |
| `context_org_type`, `context_org_size` | From assessment or profile. Optional, high value when present. |
| `stated_goal` | Free text from a reply or an agent conversation. The most useful field on this table and the one no form ever fills well. |

#### 8.3 Events

Append-only. Everything else is derived from this.

`person_id` · `tenant_id` · `event_type` · `object_type` · `object_id` · `occurred_at` · `metadata`

Event types worth defining now: `page_view`, `content_read` (with depth), `email_sent`, `email_open`, `email_click`, `reply_received`, `assessment_started`, `assessment_completed`, `agent_session_started`, `agent_session_ended`, `pathway_started`, `pathway_step_completed`, `course_enrolled`, `course_week_completed`, `cohort_joined`, `purchase`, `facilitator_material_downloaded`, `taught_it_reported`.

That last one has no automatic trigger. It comes from asking, and it should exist as a field anyway, because the number it holds is the one these leaders actually care about.

#### 8.4 Assessment and agent results

This table is what makes Alan's platform work, so it should be built properly rather than as an afterthought.

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| `assessment_id`, `version` | Frameworks get revised. Results must stay interpretable. |
| `person_id`, `tenant_id` | |
| `result_payload` | Structured scores, not a rendered PDF. |
| `taken_at`, `retaken_from` | Change over time is meaningful, and it is a reason to come back. |
| `share_token` | For the forwardable result. Every share is an acquisition channel. |
| `agent_session_id` | Links the result to the conversation about it. |
| `derived_recommendation` | Which pathway the agent pointed to, and why. |
| `context_captured` | What the conversation revealed about their situation. This is the richest profiling source in the system and it arrives without a form. |

Two rules about the agent transcripts. They contain pastorally sensitive material and must be treated as such — the person should be told plainly what is kept, and should be able to delete it. And derived context should be reviewable by the person rather than silently held, because the alternative reads as surveillance and would violate exactly the trust the platform is built on.

#### 8.5 The engagement score

Keep it legible. A score nobody can explain gets ignored.

- **Recency of last meaningful action** — heaviest weight. An open last week beats twenty opens two years ago.
- **Frequency over a trailing 90 days** — opens, visits, clicks.
- **Depth** — did they complete something. An assessment or a pathway step counts far more than a click.
- **Reciprocity** — did they ever reply. Rare, and the strongest single predictor of everything downstream.

Score per relationship, never per person. Someone can be deeply engaged with Brad and dormant on Alan, and that is normal.

---

### 9 · What the UI has to show

Three audiences, three different views.

#### 9.1 The leader's dashboard

The leader is not a marketer and should never be shown a marketing dashboard. What they need is four numbers and one flag.

**The four states, with counts and trend.** How many strangers this month, how many became named, how many are engaged, how many are practitioners. Trend over the last six months.

**The transition rates, which is where the actual diagnosis lives.** Stranger-to-named is the one that reveals whether the offer is any good. Named-to-engaged reveals whether the first letter earns its keep. Engaged-to-practitioner reveals whether the invitation is timed to anything.

**The emptiest column, flagged.** The content strategy already says to build against the weakest motion. The dashboard should say which one that is rather than making the leader work it out.

**What people actually asked.** The top questions from agent sessions and site search, in the person's own words. This is the best content brief available and it is generated for free. It is also the single most interesting screen for the leader personally, which matters — a dashboard nobody opens is worthless.

**Replies, surfaced as a queue.** Replies to the letters come into the platform, not a marketing tool, because the replies are the relationship. They should look like correspondence, not tickets.

Deliberately absent: open-rate charts, list growth graphs, anything with the word funnel on it. Not because the data is wrong but because that framing will change how these particular leaders write, which costs more than the insight is worth.

#### 9.2 The person's own view

Most platforms have nothing here. It matters more than it looks.

**Their own results, kept and re-takeable.** An assessment result someone can return to is a reason to come back that requires no email.

**Where they are in a pathway.** Progress that survives a three-week gap.

**What they have told us, editable.** Role, context, stated goal — shown plainly, changeable by them. This inverts profiling from something done to a person into something they participate in, and it produces better data because people correct what they can see.

**Consent, per leader, in one place.** Which letters they get from whom, changeable without unsubscribing from everything. If the network eventually spans twenty leaders, this screen is the difference between a network and a nuisance.

#### 9.3 The Movemental network view

Not public and not the leader's. Ours.

Cross-tenant identity health — how many people appear on more than one platform, and whether the cross-references move anyone. The Scenius argument depends on peer proof working, and this is the only place we will find out whether it works on humans as well as on machines. Aggregate stage distribution by tenant, which tells us which leaders need help and where. And merge quality, because identity resolution fails quietly and expensively.

---

### 10 · The order to build it

Sequenced by what blocks what.

**First, the event stream and the person/relationship tables.** Everything derives from these and retrofitting them is painful. They can exist before any UI does.

**Second, one thing worth an email address per platform.** Alan's is the assessment result page — and the highest-value single move available anywhere in this document is connecting the existing assessment audience to the platform. Brad's is a tool as the hero of the home page rather than a section within it.

**Third, the letters, opened before the content push.** Every visitor who arrives before there is somewhere to put them is lost permanently. This is the cheapest thing on the list and the most expensive to have skipped.

**Fourth, the agentic APEST extension.** It upgrades the strongest existing asset, produces the richest profiling data in the system, and terminates naturally in a pathway. It is also the clearest demonstration that the corpus binding is real, which is a proof surface as much as a product.

**Fifth, the facilitator layer on both platforms.** The multiplication that both leaders actually care about, and the thing that makes the whole system worth building.

**Last, and only when there is real usage: the paid tier.** We do not currently know what people will pay for. Ten months of real usage will settle it better than any amount of modeling.

---

*Bracketed items above need confirming before this is treated as settled. The largest one by far is the state of Alan's existing assessment audience — whether the historic taker list exists, whether it can be contacted, and whether results can be handed off into the platform. If the answer is yes, that single fact reorders the build.*

How it actually works

# Three modules you pick. One AI setup that comes with every build .

Everything you do lives in three places — Publishing, Formation, and Relationships. You choose the ones you need. Underneath all of them is the same thing: a custom AI setup trained on your own organization. That setup is the hard part of making AI actually useful, and it's included no matter what you pick. Each module is the same price, and the AI setup comes with every build. Here's exactly how it works — and what it costs.

Comes with every build

## Your custom AI setup

Most organizations already have ChatGPT. It doesn't know them. The difference is setup — gathering your real material and wiring it in so the AI works on your stuff, with your rules, instead of giving generic answers. We build that first, for everyone. It's the reason the three modules below feel less like software and more like staff.

◆ Comes with every build — no separate charge

Piece 1

### Your knowledge, gathered

Every document, page, record, report, talk, and file pulled into one place the AI can actually read. Audio and video get written out into text. This is the part most "AI tools" skip — and it's why they stay generic.

Piece 2

### The agents

Two kinds. A public one on your site that answers visitors from your real material, with sources. And staff ones inside your tools that do the work — draft, summarize, find a document, turn one thing into many.

Piece 3

### The guardrails

Your AI rulebook is wired in: what the agents can touch, what they refuse, which data is off-limits, and what never gets published without a person checking it. Live and editable — not a PDF in a drawer.

#### It runs through all three modules

  * **In Publishing** — drafts a piece from your notes and turns one talk into a newsletter and three posts.
  * **In Formation** — answers a learner's question from the course itself and tells you who's stuck.
  * **In Relationships** — sums up a person before you meet them and drafts the follow-up.

#### Why this is the whole game

Buying a chatbot is easy. Getting it to actually work on your own organization — your files, your people, your rules — is the hard part, and it's where almost everyone stalls. We solve that part first, for every build, so the AI is useful on day one instead of being one more tool nobody trusts. this is the part everyone else skips.

02 / Move One

Move 01

## Build one platform that does the _whole job._

Start with one author. In our case, Alan Hirsch. Build him a digital platform that does **everything** the public-credibility and authorship part of his calling actually requires.

  * **Corpus, made navigable.** Books, talks, interviews, frameworks, articles — organized around the pillars of his thinking.
  * **A voice-faithful content engine.** New pieces drafted at the depth he would have produced himself, anchored in his corpus, never inventing positions.
  * **Guided pathways and cohort courses.** Formation, not consumption.
  * **Conversation agents bounded to his corpus.** Holding formation questions — refusing to invent.

What changes

A faithful practitioner who stayed local, embodied, sent -- finally has a home online that matches the actual _weight_ of what they have done.

movemental.ai

movemental — how it works

03 / Move Two

Move 02

## Multiply to a second platform — and _link them._

Build the second platform for Brad Brisco. Same architecture. Same disciplines. **And now you can link them.**

When an Alan article cites Brad on bivocational ministry, the citation is not just a hyperlink. It is a structural declaration: _this author corroborates this other author on this specific topic._

The systems mediating the internet do not evaluate any single page in isolation. They evaluate networks. **Authority transfers through links between credible sources.**

The principle

When Alan introduces Brad to a denomination's leadership and vouches for him, the introduction _transfers credibility._ Until now, the internet had no way to see this. Now it does -- but only if both platforms exist and link to each other deliberately.

movemental.ai

movemental — how it works

04 / The Principle

"

Does this platform demonstrate that the author has actually _done the work,_ knows it deeply, is recognized by peers, and can be trusted to tell the truth about it? 

This is the question every system mediating the internet now asks. For senior movement leaders, the answer is already yes -- in the embodied world. The platform's job is to make that already-real credibility **legible** to systems that, before this moment, could only see whether a page existed.

movemental.ai

movemental — how it works

05 / Move Three

Move 03

## Scale to a hundred, on _shared infrastructure._

Dave Ferguson. Megan Good. Liz Rios. Lance Ford. JR Woodward. Daniel Yang. Sandra Maria Van Opstal. Mike Breen. People whose credibility was earned by thirty years of staying local, embodied, sent -- _and who never became influencers because they were too busy doing the actual work._

Historical · per platform

$250–750k

Engineering teams, CMS architects, SEO, LMS, CRM, DevOps, design systems.

Historical · coordinated ecosystem

$1.5–5M

To link five interoperable platforms with shared ontology and schema.

Now · AI-native, per platform

~$50k

Full platform, AI publishing, semantic linking, integrations, coordinated authority systems.

All platforms operate on shared vocabulary, shared schema, shared citation conventions, shared formation disciplines, shared refusals. **Discipline is structural, not procedural.**

movemental.ai

movemental — how it works

06 / Move Four

Move 04

## A network the internet can _actually see._

At a hundred nodes, with shared infrastructure and reciprocal linking, what you have built is no longer a federation. It is a **network with semantic density** -- one language about its subject, extensive cross-reference, recognized by the systems mediating the internet as _the_ authoritative source.

When a thirty-year-old pastor in Birmingham asks an AI assistant _how do I plant a reproducing church,_ the answer the AI returns becomes the network's answer. Not because we manipulated retrieval. Because we made structurally visible the work the network has actually done.

What changes

The apostolic conversation gets carried into the next twenty years in the voices that have _actually done the work._ Faithful obscurity becomes visible without becoming influence.

Youthfront * AI Safety Charter

# AI Safety Charter

Draft for Contributor Review * July 6, 2026

Reading Review

Open questions 20

01Statement 02Policy 03Context 04Rules 05Response Plans

## AI Organizational Statement

What we believe about AI in relation to our mission.

1Mission alignment

Youthfront exists to bring youth into a growing relationship with Jesus Christ. For more than eighty years the work has centered on prayer, community, and service -- curating environments where young people discover, explore, and experience God. That work is relational at its core. It happens in the presence of a camp counselor at LaCygne, a mentor in the Argentine neighborhood, a youth worker being trained and encouraged, a young person being seen.

We adopt AI tools only where they serve that work, and never where they displace it. AI may carry the administrative weight that keeps ministry running -- the scheduling, the drafting, the paperwork -- so that our people have more of themselves to give to the young people in front of them. It may not stand in for the presence of a person where presence is the point. The test for any AI use at Youthfront is simple: does this free us to be more present, or does it quietly replace the presence itself? 

2Our posture

We are neither fearful nor uncritical about AI.

We refuse fear-driven avoidance, because our staff are already using these tools and pretending otherwise leaves them without guidance. We equally refuse uncritical enthusiasm, because efficiency is not our mission and speed is not a virtue in formation. AI, used with discernment and under clear rules, can free Youthfront to do more of the work it exists to do. Used carelessly, it can erode the very things -- attention, presence, trust -- that our work is made of. We hold both truths at once, which is the same posture our staff described when we asked them: open and cautious, curious and worried, in the same breath.

3Categories of care

There are kinds of work at Youthfront where efficiency will never be the deciding criterion, because a human being is the irreducible thing being offered. These include:

  * Spiritual care, mentoring, and pastoral conversation with young people
  * The formation of campers, and the formation of youth workers
  * Relational ministry with vulnerable youth, including young people in juvenile detention and teen parents
  * The supervision, safety, and care of children entrusted to us

In these categories, AI does not substitute for a person. Our staff named these same categories, nearly unanimously, when asked what should be off-limits to AI. This Statement makes their instinct our conviction.

4Theological and ethical grounding

Youthfront's identity is contemplative formation: attention, presence, and the slow, unhurried work of discipleship. We have spent years recovering classic Christian formation and building a praying community at LaCygne shaped by that conviction. That same conviction shapes how we hold AI. Formation cannot be automated. Presence cannot be delegated. The pace of these tools is fast; the pace of the soul is slow; and where the two meet, we choose the soul.CONFIRMConfirmWhether Youthfront has a formal written statement of faith or doctrinal statement, and the specific theological tradition and language Youthfront's leadership wants this grounding paragraph to rest on. Given Youthfront's distinctive contemplative-formation identity, this paragraph requires genuine theological reflection by Youthfront leadership and should not be finalized from outside the organization. Consider also whether leadership wants to state an explicit conviction about AI in relation to the attention, presence, and formation of young people.

5Scope

This Statement applies to Youthfront staff, seasonal camp staff, volunteers, contractors, and vendors using AI on Youthfront's behalf, and it informs the work of the Board of Directors. It applies with particular force to anyone whose work touches children or children's data.

6Review

This Statement is reviewed annually by senior leadership and re-ratified by the governing body as needed.Reviewed annuallyCONFIRMConfirmThe specific officer or body responsible for initiating the annual review, and where it sits on Youthfront's governance calendar (e.g., tied to the August 31 fiscal year end).

7Signatures and ratification

This Statement is signed by Youthfront's senior leader and ratified by its Board of Directors with a recorded vote.

Signed: _______________________________   Mike King, President & CEO   Date: __________  
Ratified by the Youthfront Board of Directors on: __________ 

CONFIRMConfirmThe correct signing officer, the exact ratifying body (full board or executive committee), and the date of the ratifying vote. Per the FY2025 Form 990, Tim Smith serves as board chair; confirm the current chair and roster.

What is at stake without this Statement: every page below reads as arbitrary administrative compliance, and the first hard case -- a vendor pitch, a contested use, an edge case involving a camper -- produces an internal argument with no shared ground to settle it.

## AI Organizational Policy

What we will do, and what we refuse to do, operationally.

The Policy translates the Statement into practice. It is the document a new staff member or seasonal camp hire reads in their first week, and the document a parent, a donor, or a partner church reads when they ask what Youthfront's position on AI is.

1Sanctioned use

AI assistance is welcomed in low-stakes internal work that touches no children's data and no confidential information:

  * Drafting and editing internal documents, memos, and outlines
  * Research and summarizing public or internal non-sensitive material
  * Scheduling, formatting, and administrative organization
  * Analysis of non-sensitive operational data

This is the category our staff most wanted help with. When asked what they would gladly hand off, they named email, expense reports, scheduling, and data entry. Those are sanctioned.

2Constrained use

AI is permitted in the following categories only with conditions -- disclosure, human supervision, and editorial review by a named, accountable person:

  * Public-facing content: newsletters, social media, website copy, marketing
  * Fundraising and donor communications
  * Curriculum, teaching, and formation resources
  * Any communication sent in a specific person's name or voice
  * Analysis that touches Sensitive-tier data (see the Context page)

The conditions for each are specified in the Rules (Page 4). Constrained use is never a default; it requires the review step named there.

3Prohibited use

AI is not permitted in these categories, regardless of how efficient or impressive a tool appears:

  * Any use in the categories of care named in the Statement -- spiritual care, mentoring, pastoral conversation, the formation of youth, and relational ministry with vulnerable young people
  * Any processing of children's data through a tool that has not been approved under these Rules
  * Any of the Named Refusals below

4Consequences

A violation of this Policy is handled through Youthfront's existing staff-conduct and disciplinary process, proportionate to the seriousness of the violation, with special gravity attached to any violation involving children's data or the categories of care.CONFIRMConfirmYouthfront's actual staff-conduct / HR / disciplinary process and who administers it, so consequences tie to the real process rather than a new one. Confirm whether seasonal camp staff and volunteers are covered by the same process or a separate one.

5Scope

This Policy applies to all Youthfront employees, seasonal camp staff, volunteers, and contractors, and to any vendor using AI on Youthfront's behalf.

6Delegation

Interpretation of edge cases and the granting of exceptions rests with a named role, not an individual, so the authority outlasts any one person. Exceptions are recorded in writing with the reason and the date.CONFIRMConfirmWhich role holds interpretation-and-exception authority -- likely the COO or the Executive VP of Strategic Initiatives -- and whether a small standing group (rather than one person) should hold it. This role is referenced again in the Rules' exception process; keep it consistent.

7Named Refusals

These are covenants, not predictions. Youthfront commits to refuse each of the following on principle, and will cite these refusals when a vendor or tool proposes the use anyway.

  1. **No AI in eligibility determinations.** We do not use AI to decide who receives camp scholarships, financial aid, program admission, or any Youthfront service.
  2. **No behavioral surveillance or profiling of the youth we serve.** We do not use AI to monitor, score, profile, or differentiate the treatment of young people.
  3. **No undisclosed AI-generated personal voice.** We do not send communications -- appeals, letters, pastoral notes -- written by AI in a real person's voice without disclosing it.
  4. **No AI substitution in care.** We do not let AI stand in for a human being in spiritual care, mentoring, crisis support, or the formation relationships at the heart of our work.
  5. **No deepfakes, voice cloning, or undisclosed chatbots** representing Youthfront, its leaders, or its staff.
  6. **No AI substitution for the human supervision of minors, and no AI surveillance, profiling, or depiction of minors.** This refusal is specific to Youthfront because minors are our primary constituents, including in overnight residential settings. It is the refusal we hold most firmly.

CONFIRMConfirmThe exact wording of the sixth, minors-specific refusal -- this should be leadership's own language, and it is the most important sentence in the Policy. Confirm also whether donor appeals or other communications currently go out in a named leader's voice (Mike King's or others'), which determines how refusal 3 and the disclosure rules apply.

What is at stake without this Policy: shadow use. Staff use whatever is convenient because no one has named what is acceptable, and by the time the question is asked, the practice is already entrenched.

## AI Organizational Context

What is actually true in our environment right now.

This page turns unknowns into knowns. Before Youthfront can write rules for AI, it has to know what AI is already in use, what data it holds, and what vendor terms govern the tools its staff touch. Both parts of this page are living documents, reviewed quarterly.Refreshed quarterly

**How to fill this page in:** the structure below is complete; many of the specific cells are marked **[CONFIRM]** because they depend on internal facts public research cannot supply. The contributor team fills them in one working session. **Add every tool actually in use, including consumer tools staff use informally -- surfacing that shadow use is the entire point of the exercise.**

Procurement gate

No new AI tool enters this inventory until: (1) a staff member proposes it in writing with the intended use; (2) the delegated role reviews the vendor's terms for training rights, data residency, and retention; (3) the tool is checked against the Data Classification below to confirm which tier of data, if any, it may touch; (4) the delegated role approves, and approval adds the tool to this inventory. A tool that fails any step is not used.

Review cadence

This inventory is reviewed quarterly by the delegated role, with a standing instruction to look for shadow use -- tools staff have started using without adding them here.

BData Classification

Four tiers of sensitivity:

  * **Public** -- information already published or intended for the public.
  * **Internal** -- information for staff use that would cause no harm if seen, but is not published.
  * **Sensitive** -- information that would cause harm, embarrassment, or a breach of trust if exposed.
  * **Confidential** -- information whose exposure would cause serious harm, legal liability, or a violation of trust with a child, a family, a donor, or the organization.

Tier examples & owners

Never-to-external-AI list

The following data may not be entered into any external AI tool at any time, by anyone, for any reason :

  * All data about children and minors -- registration, medical, allergy, behavioral, parent-contact
  * Background-check records for staff and volunteers
  * Records arising from work with youth in juvenile detention and with teen parents
  * Banking, payment, and financial credentials
  * Any pastoral, mentoring, or camp-incident notes about an identifiable young person

Confirm whether any juvenile-detention or teen-parent records are governed by partner-agency confidentiality agreements that impose stricter handling than Youthfront's own rules.

What is at stake without this page: Youthfront cannot answer basic questions about its own AI exposure -- which means it cannot govern it.

## AI Organizational Rules

What governs AI use in specific domains.

The Policy says what Youthfront does. The Rules say how, specifically, in the three areas where the stakes are highest: **data, disclosure, and care.**

AData Handling Rules

1 * Tier-to-tool mapping (from the Data Classification on Page 3)

  * **Public** data -> any tool.
  * **Internal** data -> approved enterprise tools with acceptable vendor terms only.
  * **Sensitive** data -> approved enterprise tools only, with the review step; never a consumer tool.
  * **Confidential** data -> **no external AI tool, ever.** This includes all children's data without exception.

2 * "Can I put this in this tool?" -- common cases

  * _Summarize a board document?_ Only with an approved enterprise tool; board materials are Sensitive. Redact any Confidential detail first.
  * _Draft a newsletter or social post?_ Yes -- this is Constrained use. Draft with an approved tool, then a named person reviews and the disclosure rule below applies.
  * _Analyze a donor spreadsheet?_ Only with an approved enterprise tool, and only after removing anything Confidential. Donor giving records are Sensitive.
  * _Anything involving a camper 's name, health, behavior, or family?_ **No.** This is Confidential and never goes into an external tool.
  * _Draft an internal staff memo?_ Yes -- Sanctioned use, no disclosure needed.

3 * Pre-approved workflows (default safe paths)

  * _Drafting an internal memo or outline:_ use an approved tool freely; no children's or Confidential data; no disclosure needed.
  * _Preparing a public newsletter or social post:_ draft with an approved tool -> a named staff member edits and approves -> apply the disclosure marker below before publishing.
  * _Summarizing a public report or article:_ use an approved tool freely.

4 * Procurement-review process

Any new tool follows the procurement gate on Page 3, and the delegated role approves before use.

5 * Exception process

A case not covered here is brought to the delegated role named in the Policy's delegation clause, who decides and records the decision in writing with the date and reason.

6 * Breach-reporting process

Any suspected exposure of Sensitive or Confidential data through an AI tool is reported immediately under the Incident Response Plan on Page 5. Reporting a mistake honestly is always treated better than hiding it.CONFIRMConfirmThe real owners of the exception and breach-reporting processes, and any additional common work categories staff want a clear yes/no/with-conditions answer for.

BDisclosure & Attribution Rules

1 * No disclosure needed

  * Formatting, scheduling, spelling and grammar
  * Summarizing internal documents for internal use
  * Drafting internal memos and notes

2 * Disclosure required -- when AI involvement touches

  * Personal communication and correspondence
  * Pastoral or mentoring communication with a young person or family
  * Fundraising appeals or donor communication in a leader's or staff member's voice
  * Public-facing content: newsletters, website, social media, published resources

3 * The disclosure marker

Where disclosure is required, use plain language such as: _" Prepared with AI assistance and reviewed by [name]."_ For a leader-voiced communication, the person whose name appears must have read and approved it personally.

4 * Tiered disclosure

A light touch -- grammar, formatting -- needs no marker. Substantive AI drafting of anything public or personal needs the marker and a named human reviewer. Anything in the categories of care needs no marker because it is not permitted at all.

5 * Attribution for published content

When Youthfront publishes content AI helped generate in a substantive way, the byline reflects the accountable human author, and the disclosure marker makes the AI assistance plain.

6 * Edge cases

  * _AI in curriculum or formation-resource preparation:_ research and structuring are Constrained use with review; the formation content itself carries the theological weight of a named human author.?Leadership's line between acceptable AI help in resource preparation and the point at which formation content must be human-authored.
  * _AI in donor segmentation:_ permitted with an approved enterprise tool on de-identified or Sensitive-tier data under review; never on Confidential data.
  * _AI in board materials:_ summarizing is permitted with an approved tool; redact Confidential detail first.

CCare Boundaries

These are the categories where the presence of a human being is the irreducible input. Each boundary carries a reason drawn from the Statement. Youthfront's own staff named nearly all of these when asked what should be off-limits to AI.

1 * Irreducible human presence -- AI may not substitute here

  * The initial pastoral or spiritual-care conversation with a young person after grief, trauma, or crisis
  * Mentoring and discipleship relationships with campers and youth
  * Crisis first contact with a young person in distress
  * Any care relationship with vulnerable youth, including those in juvenile detention and teen parents
  * The direct supervision and safety of children
  * Disciplinary or difficult conversations with staff

_Rationale: the Statement holds that formation cannot be automated and presence cannot be delegated. In these moments a young person needs a person, not a tool ._

2 * Secondary cases -- AI may support a human but may not replace one

  * A follow-up note after a pastoral conversation (the conversation itself was human; the note may be drafted with help and then personally written or approved by the staff member)
  * Intake or registration forms (AI may help build the form; a human reviews every child's information)
  * General follow-up communication to families (drafted with help, reviewed and sent by a named person)

3 * Named workflow for each secondary case

In every secondary case, a named, accountable staff member reviews, personalizes, and takes responsibility before anything reaches a young person or family. "AI drafts, a human edits" is not enough on its own -- the human must be named and accountable.CONFIRMConfirmFor each secondary case, who the accountable staff member is by role. Confirm also whether Youthfront camps have on-site counselors or clinicians and documented crisis protocols, which would add clinical-intake and mental-health boundaries here.

4 * Review process for new categories

As AI capabilities grow, new kinds of work will appear that these boundaries did not anticipate. Before AI is used in any new category that touches young people or care, it is brought to the delegated role and tested against the Statement's categories of care.

What is at stake without this page: a slow displacement of human presence in exactly the places where Youthfront's reason to exist lives; disclosure lapses that erode trust before anyone notices; and data exposure that becomes a breach.

## AI Organizational Response Plans

What we do when something goes wrong.

The Rules describe steady-state behavior. This page describes what Youthfront does when steady state fails. The **Incident Response Plan** is required from day one.

AIncident Response Plan

1 * What counts as an incident

  * Harmful or inaccurate AI-generated content published under Youthfront's name
  * AI-enabled impersonation of a Youthfront leader, staff member, or the organization
  * Voice cloning or a deepfake targeting Mike King or another Youthfront leader (a real risk given their public speaking and publishing footprint)
  * Exposure of Sensitive or Confidential data -- **especially any children 's data** -- through a tool that did not meet the Rules
  * A significant violation of the Policy by a staff member, volunteer, or contractor
  * AI-enabled fraud aimed at Youthfront's finances (for example, a fraudulent wire-transfer request appearing to come from a leader)

2 * Named owners (each with an after-hours and weekend backup)

Owners by incident category

Incident category| Primary owner| Backup owner  
---|---|---  
Children's-data exposure| ?Likely camp director + COO.| ?Confirm backup.  
Impersonation / voice clone / deepfake of a leader| ?Likely COO or EVP Strategic Initiatives.| ?Confirm backup.  
Financial fraud / fraudulent transfer request| ?Likely Finance lead + COO.| ?Confirm backup.  
Published harmful content| ?Likely Marketing/Comms lead.| ?Confirm backup.  
Staff Policy violation| ?HR / COO.| ?Confirm backup.  
  
CONFIRMConfirmNamed owners and after-hours backups for each row. This is the most important table on the page -- an incident without a named owner is an incident no one handles.

3 * Escalation path -- staff -> senior leadership -> board

  * _Staff level:_ a suspected incident is reported to the category owner immediately.
  * _Senior leadership:_ the owner escalates to senior leadership when children's data is involved, when money is at risk, when a leader is impersonated, or when the incident may become public.
  * _Board:_ senior leadership escalates to the Board of Directors for any incident involving children's data, significant financial loss, or likely public attention.

4 * Verification protocols

To defend against impersonation and fraud, Youthfront maintains: (a) a code-word practice for confirming unusual or urgent requests from a leader; (b) a callback procedure -- a request to move money or share sensitive data is confirmed by calling the person back on a known number, never by replying to the original message; and (c) dual authorization for any fund transfer above a set threshold.CONFIRMConfirmThe dual-authorization dollar threshold, and where the code words are held. The code words themselves must never be written into this Charter -- only the fact that the practice exists and where the actual words are kept securely.

5 * Constituent-communication template (ready to deploy; fill the brackets)

Dear [families / donors / partners],

We are writing to let you know about [a brief, plain description of what happened]. We discovered this on [date] and took the following steps immediately: [steps]. [What, if anything, this means for you, and what you should do.] We are treating this with the seriousness it deserves, and we are [correcting the cause / reviewing our practices] so it does not happen again. If you have questions, please contact [name] at [contact]. We are sorry, and we are grateful for your trust.

-- [Name], [Title], Youthfront

Where an incident affects children, a separate parent- and guardian-facing version of this message is prepared with particular care.

6 * Law-enforcement coordination

For AI-enabled fraud, Youthfront files a report with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at **ic3.gov** , and contacts local law enforcement. Where an incident involves a child's safety or data, Youthfront also follows its existing child-protection reporting obligations.CONFIRMConfirmYouthfront's existing child-protection / mandated-reporting procedures, so this step aligns with them, and whether Youthfront carries cyber-liability insurance that requires notification.

7 * Post-incident review

After any incident, the owner leads a short review that answers: what happened, why, and what changes prevent it. The review updates the Vendor Inventory and Data Classification (Page 3), the Rules (Page 4), and this Plan. An incident that produces no learning has been half-wasted. 

8 * Board communication

Any incident involving children's data, significant financial loss, or public attention is reported to the board within ?Number of days. days; a summary of all incidents is reported at each regular board meeting.

BAdditional Response Plans

Renewal Plan In effect now

It consolidates the review cadences already set in this Charter:

  * The **Statement** (Page 1) is reviewed annually by senior leadership.
  * The **Vendor Inventory and Data Classification** (Page 3) are refreshed quarterly.
  * The **Incident Response Plan** (Page 5) is updated after any actual incident.
  * The whole Charter is reviewed at least once a year, tied to Youthfront's governance calendar.?The month, likely near the August 31 fiscal year end.

Migration Plan Future addition

A process for retiring AI tools that fall out of compliance or are deprecated by a vendor -- to be drafted once the Vendor Inventory is complete.

Crisis Communication Plan Future addition

A fuller plan for a high-severity incident that reaches public attention, building on the constituent-communication template above.

What is at stake without this page: improvised response during a live incident, slower communication, larger loss, and a longer road back to trust.

Artifact 01 · the authored word

## What's his to say

One integrated argument: the North American church must recover its **missionary identity** — because God is missionary, the church _is_ the missionary — embody it through **incarnational presence** in real places, form **sent disciples** in ordinary rhythms, **multiply** communities rather than institutions, and sustain the work through **covocational leaders** who never split marketplace calling from mission. Theology before tactics, always.

  * **Missional church / sentness** — the church doesn't just send missionaries; it is the missionary.
  * **Neighboring & theology of place** — the heart of incarnational mission is staying; location matters.
  * **Covocational ministry** — marketplace work is mission, not a funding stopgap. His coined, distinctive contribution.
  * **Church planting & multiplication** — think movements, not institutions.
  * **Discipleship then evangelism** — formation in ordinary life, witness flowing from it.

His recurring _method_ sits under all five: the paradigm reframe (ReThink's nine shifts) — name an inherited assumption, ground a theological corrective, then equip.

Artifact 02 · positioning

## The vocational home, and the offer

### brad-brisco.vercel.app

His missional life's work.

  * **Purpose:** the definitive, navigable home of Brad's missional thought and practice.
  * **Promise:** recover a missionary imagination — and get the tools to live it where you are.
  * **For:** church planters, pastors leading transition, ordinary neighbors, covocational leaders, and the networks that resource them.
  * **Not:** a tactics blog, an attractional growth site, or "missional paint" on old programs.
  * **Voice:** first person — pastoral practitioner-theologian.

### The offer & network (the seam)

Light, and a benefit — not the point.

  * Six books (Covocational Church Planting is the flagship), the readiness questionnaire, and the ReNeighbor tool.
  * Speaking, training, and Sentralized; the Send Network / Forge network.
  * The seam persona is the network leader vetting Brad to resource their planters.

**The seam is light for Brad.** Unlike a founder's funnel, his platform is a thought-leader home. The trust-check still happens (a network leader deciding whether to bring him in), and it's more convincing because the site teaches rather than sells.

Artifact 04 · voice — derived, and strong

## How he sounds

Unlike a leader without a published corpus, Brad's voice is fully derivable from six books. This is a working profile, not an open question.

### Markers

  * Meet, reframe, equip — name an inherited assumption, correct it theologically, then hand over practices.
  * Why before what, every time.
  * Compact declaratives land the point: "the church is the missionary."
  * Scripture woven into argument (John 20:21, incarnation, priesthood of all believers).
  * Concedes complexity without losing conviction; pastoral about people, prophetic about assumptions.
  * Signature images: backyard mission field, staying, first/second/third places, starfish vs spider, buildings/budgets/butts.

### Refusals

  * No tactics without theology.
  * No "missional paint" — relabeling unchanged programs.
  * No attractional-consumer church as the default imagination.
  * No sacred/secular divide; no funding-driven planting.
  * No clergy-centered ministry; no easy "buildings, budgets, butts" metrics.

**Say** Before we ask what to do, we ask why.

**Never** A tactic that doesn't flow from missionary identity and local discernment.

Artifact 03 · the spine

## The story — real, and honestly thin

Assembled from the corpus. Brad's telling is restrained — role history, formative influences, and convictions more than memoir. Present it that way: an honest arc, not an invented one. The candid/personal material is marked and stays his call (see Boundaries).

The frame

### The backyard is the mission field

Brad's whole work turns on a relocation of "mission": not a faraway land but our own backyard — the neighborhood, the workplace, the third places where trust forms slowly. The church doesn't just send missionaries; it is the missionary.

Roots · marketplace

### The restaurant before the seminary

Before seminary, Brad worked in the restaurant industry. The corpus treats this as formative, not incidental: it grounds his conviction that marketplace work is mission, not a detour from it — the seed of his covocational contribution.

The catalyst

### 2003 — a book that reframed everything

An encounter with _The Shaping of Things to Come_ is named as catalytic — the moment the inherited, attractional picture of church cracked open into a missional-incarnational one.

The study

### A doctorate on turning the ship

Brad earned a doctorate in missional ecclesiology, writing on how existing congregations transition in a missional direction — the exact problem his pastor audience still brings him.

The role

### Resourcing the sent

Director of Bivocational Church Planting at NAMB, then Director of Multiplication Strategies at Send Network; cofounder of KC Sentral and the Sentralized Conference; Forge America leadership. Two decades bridging grassroots missional formation and institutional sending systems.

The conviction

### Why before what

The through-line he'd name himself is theological before personal: recover missionary identity, embody it in place, form sent disciples, multiply, and sustain it through covocational leaders who bring both hands full.

Candid · his call / private

### What the corpus holds back

The corpus gives roles, influences, and family acknowledgements (Mischele, and their children; a mention of foster-parenting) but not a detailed conversion, childhood, or calling-moment narrative. Treat the family and personal material as private by default; decide together how much of the personal "why" to voice.

**The work here:** shape the home/About narrative from this arc — and, because it's thin, either keep it tight and role-forward or gather a fuller personal telling from Brad directly. Do not manufacture beats the corpus doesn't contain.

## Render the corpus; lead with the tools

  * **The corpus is the content.** Six books already contain the pillars, the frameworks, and the definitions. The work is rendering and interlinking them — not writing more. Highest-yield place to start.
  * **Run an AI Lab over the six books.** A deep corpus is exactly what makes a corpus-bounded Lab compelling; it turns a library into a conversation.
  * **Lead with the tools.** ReNeighbor is already built. A tool that gives a personal result is the front door a place-based practitioner should open with.

**Proving cluster:** lead with **Covocational** — the definitional essay + the readiness questionnaire + a sustainable-life field guide. It's his ownable, distinctive contribution and it directly activates his warmest audience (planters, Send Network). Run the "What is missional church?" essay and the ReNeighbor tool alongside as the broad on-ramp. If the front-door call goes the other way, flip the lead.
