Artifact 01 · the authored word

## What's yours to say

You work at the intersection of AI and the trust-dependent human worlds you actually know — movement leaders, mission organizations, the communities and families you've served. Your word is that these worlds can meet AI without losing what makes them true, and — the redemptive turn — that the very tool that threatens credibility, authorship, and formation can be turned to protect them. AI as the infrastructure around the work, never the work itself.

These become your pillars (Structure tab). Whether one is the center is still open — it may be the intersection itself rather than any single topic.

Artifact 02 · positioning

## Two properties, reframed

### joshshepherd.ai

Your vocational home.

  * **Purpose:** the person at the intersection, and the body of work that comes from it. Movemental is one expression of the calling.
  * **Promise:** _open — this is the one-line you're developing with me._
  * **For:** builders, peers, movement leaders leading with AI, the person checking who's behind Movemental, and the few who'd back or book you.
  * **Not:** the company site; a funnel wearing your name; polish that hides the person.
  * **Voice:** singular — _"I."_

### movemental.ai

The company and the method.

  * **Purpose:** explain the thesis, convert organizations onto the Path, house the proof and the network.
  * **For:** churches, nonprofits, institutions, prospective Voices.
  * **Voice:** plural — _"we,"_ fronted by Brad as the trust seat.

**The seam — now a benefit, not the point.** The trust-check still happens: someone vetting Movemental crosses over to see the human behind it. But it's _more_ believable here precisely because this site isn't built to sell them. Vocational-first delivers the instrumental payoff better than an instrumental site would.

Artifact 04 · voice — open workstream

## How you sound (to be derived, not assumed)

The markers below are a strong working draft from your record. But a full voice description is its own workstream, and yours is non-standard: you have no shelf of published books to derive it from. Your corpus is your **builds, thesis docs, field guides, and conversations like this one** — so voice gets derived from those.

### Markers (working)

  * Plain sentences. Short. No em dashes.
  * Concede the other side first.
  * Name the threat, then sell relief.
  * Lead with the gift in the hard thing.
  * Picturable noun over abstract category.
  * Bold claim, then invite scrutiny. Name who it's not for.

### Refusals

  * No manufactured urgency or scarcity.
  * No faked authorship — AI never writes the word under your name.
  * AI never touches discernment or care.
  * No unearned claim; extra care with vulnerable people.

Artifact 03 · the spine

## The story — this is the homepage, not the footnote

Assembled from your own words across past sessions. For a vocational home, this narrative is the center of gravity: it's simultaneously who you are, what you think, and proof of what you can do. It's yours to make public or hold — the candid parts are marked.

The frame

### The intersection

You work where AI meets the people and communities whose work runs on trust — and you help each meet the other without losing what's true. That's not "builder-founder." It's a bridge, and it grows in both directions at once.

Roots

### Formation you can't automate

Bilingual, frontline service to immigrant families in Kansas City. Called to ministry in 2007. Then, with your wife, a neomonastic community — extended residency alongside young adults, sharing meals, money, prayer, and life.

"That's where I learned that formation happens in relationship, in presence, over time. It can't be faked, and it can't be automated."

The pivot

### Learning to build

You learned digital marketing to tell the community's story — the craft came second to the purpose. Then, at SpecChem, you became a serious builder and proved, on real deadlines, that one person with AI can build what used to take a team and a quarter-million dollars.

The hinge

### Two things at once

Late 2025, the cost of building software collapsed almost overnight.

"Two things hit me at once: that AI was about to do real damage to the things I care most about — credibility, authorship, the slow work of formation — and that, for the first time, someone with my background could actually build the infrastructure to protect them."

The beginning

### Two people, not a product

You started building for Alan Hirsch — the voice half, letting a lifetime of thinking survive contact with AI without being faked or flattened. And for Youthfront — the formation half, training a whole organization to use these tools with discernment instead of fear.

"Two halves of the same thing. And lately those two halves have started converging into one. That's the part I couldn't have planned."

The conviction

### Redeeming the tool

The whole point: use the very technology that threatens credibility, authorship, and formation to protect them instead. AI as the infrastructure around the writing, never the writing itself — the mirror that lets a scattered movement see itself whole.

Candid · your call to make public

### What you lie awake on

The collapse of identity into vocation — the alignment between your life and this work is unusually perfect, which is exactly the condition under which a person can stop telling the calling from the self. And the diversity question: whether this gets built for the unseen, or quietly defaults to the people already within reach. _People are pastored, not processed._

**The work here:** assemble this into the site's About / home narrative and decide, with me, how much of the candid and faith material goes public (see Boundaries). The raw material is already yours and already written.

1

The person at the intersection, the thinking, the story, the builds — told truthfully and gathered in one place. Everything else flows from doing this well.

3

Byproduct · strong

The "how I built it" stories teach builders and leaders and, over time, feed GEO so the machines return you on AI, authorship, and formation.

Opportunistic

Small and high-leverage. A sharp story, checkable proof, and an obvious engage path — don't build the whole site around it.

**How you'd know** qualified inbound per quarter.

**Still your call:** the tension resolves cleanly now (depth is the engine, reach and seam are byproducts) — but one goal is unanswered: is **direct revenue** (courses, speaking fees, consulting) a goal for this site, or is it purely in service of the work and the company? ## What to make

Each type opens to a full prescription — what it is, where it lives, what it must accomplish, the elements it requires, and how it cascades out. Tap any row.

**How I built it** SAY·FIND·MOVE · flagship · all personas

+

What it is A first-person account of a real build — the two-people origin, the Alan platform, the solo seven-month build — told as narrative, not tutorial. It carries the arc, the thinking, the proof, and the résumé in one artifact. This is the form only you can make, and the reason to visit.

Where it lives The flagship hub (`/how-i-built-it`), each piece on its own canonical URL. The two or three strongest anchor the homepage.

What it must accomplish Prove what you think and can do without a pitch; teach builders as a side effect; give the checker and the leader evidence of both competence and character; seed the FIND/GEO layer so you become the answer on "one person built X with AI."

Length & format 1,200–2,200 words · 6–10 min read. One hero build-image; an optional 60–90s screen-recorded demo embedded. First person throughout.

Core components (ordered) 1 — Opening scene: the real problem, in one picturable moment. 2 — The stakes: why it mattered (the conviction under it). 3 — The build: what you did, told chronologically, the key choices, and the one hard part that broke. 4 — The proof: one checkable result — a number, a link, a before/after, a capture. 5 — The turn: the thesis it demonstrates. 6 — The close: a question that invites thinking-alongside, not a CTA. 7 — Provenance: how AI was used, plainly.

Rubric of execution Lead with the scene, not the setup. One build = one story — never cram two. The wrinkle is the credibility, so keep the hard part honest. Proof must be verifiable, not asserted ("grew a lot" fails). Keep the teaching implicit: a builder should be able to follow it and a leader should feel the conviction without either being lectured. Plain voice, short sentences, no em dashes. You run the company that argues for verifiability — every build claim here is true and checkable. _Failure modes:_ tutorial-dry, brag-without-wrinkle, vague proof, the human buried under the tech.

Creative choices Foreground the human story (Alan / Youthfront) _or_ the technical feat (seven-month solo) by audience: leaders and checkers → human; builders and backers → feat. Include a code/architecture snippet only in builder-heavy pieces. Let the demo clip lead or merely support. Recommended default: human-forward, one technical detail, demo supporting.

Cascade LinkedIn narrative excerpt + link (your warm network lives here) → a short build-in-public thread → a 60–90s screen-recorded demo clip to YouTube + LinkedIn native → featured in the next newsletter → the demo embedded in the AI Lab or a case page.

**Essay (thinking)** SAY · peer · leader · checker

+

What it is Your authored argument on one pillar idea — fragmentation, authorship, formation, legibility. The SAY layer at depth: the thinking the "how I built it" pieces demonstrate.

Where it lives The thinking hub; each essay is a pillar or cluster page, interlinked hub-and-spoke so a reader can move through the body of work.

What it must accomplish State a point of view sharp enough to be cited and argued with; anchor the thesis; over time, become the machine-returned answer on these topics.

Length & format Three tiers. **Pillar** (the definitional anchor of a theme) 3,500–5,000 words · ~20 min. **Cluster** (a deepening) 2,000–3,000 words · ~12 min. **Note** (a single sharp provocation) 1,000–1,800 words · ~6 min. Show reading time.

Core components (from the nine-section spine) 1 — Hook / reframing question. 2 — Definition anchor: the key term in plain language (the FIND surface; must stand alone as a quotable answer). 3 — Why it matters now. 4 — The core argument, strongest counter-case conceded first. 5 — What this is _not_ (common misunderstandings). 6 — At least one picturable example or case. 7 — The formation invitation: something to do or reconsider. 8 — How this connects (links to sibling pieces / the pillar). Optional FAQ block for search-shaped questions.

Rubric of execution Say the true thing first — never open from search demand. The definition anchor must be liftable verbatim by an answer engine. Concede before you counter. One picturable noun beats three abstractions. End by moving the reader (at minimum: dissonance + one next action), not just informing. Sources named at the foot; no invented quotes. Hold vocabulary steady across essays — same term, same meaning — because that consistency is what makes the whole body of work legible to people and machines. _Failure modes:_ throat-clearing intros, abstraction stacking, confirming what the reader already thinks, unsourced assertions.

Creative choices Pick the tier by role: pillar to anchor a theme, cluster to deepen, note for a single take. How personal to run it — measured argument vs first-person conviction; your vocational home tilts personal. Include the FAQ block when the topic carries real search-shaped questions. One signature "reframe" move per essay, where the structure calls for it — not more.

Cascade Newsletter feature → LinkedIn post carrying the core claim + link → 2–3 quotable lines pulled for social → a strong essay seeds a podcast talking point.

**Newsletter** MOVE · all · the owned relationship

+

What it is The owned, algorithm-proof relationship — a regular, plain letter to the people who chose to hear from you. The one channel no platform can take away.

Where it lives Your list (a simple ESP or Substack-style tool — platform TBD), with every issue archived on the site at a public URL.

What it must accomplish Keep a warm relationship independent of any platform; carry each new piece to the people most likely to act; be the destination everything else points to.

Length & format 400–900 words · 2–4 min. Plain-text feel over heavy design. One primary link, one primary image at most.

Core components (ordered) 1 — A short authored opening: a real thought, what's on your mind (2–4 sentences — this is what earns the open). 2 — The feature: the new piece framed in one paragraph (why it matters, not a summary). 3 — One or two secondary links (older work, or a peer's — the scenius move). 4 — One clear next step: read, reply, or share. 5 — A human sign-off.

Rubric of execution The opening earns the click — make it a thought, never "here's my new post." Frame, don't summarize (leave a curiosity gap). One primary CTA only. Write to one person, not a list. Cadence over polish: a plain letter sent reliably beats a designed one sent rarely. Archive every issue at a public URL so it also feeds FIND. _Failure modes:_ newsletter-as-changelog, competing CTAs, over-design, irregularity.

Creative choices Cadence — every two weeks is the recommended floor; weekly only if volume supports it without strain. Occasionally write original short-form _in_ the letter (a "thinking out loud" issue) rather than always featuring a site piece — the mix keeps it alive. Reply-driven (end on a real question) vs broadcast; reply-driven builds the relationship faster.

Cascade It _is_ the owned destination. Every page and every social bio carries a signup. Each issue's public archive URL feeds FIND. LinkedIn posts periodically invite subscribes.

**Build-in-public note** SAY·MOVE · builder · peer

+

What it is Short, in-the-moment posts as you ship — the smaller, faster sibling of "how I built it." Presence between the big pieces, and the raw material they're later assembled from.

Where it lives Primarily LinkedIn and X (rented), collected on the site as a notes stream.

What it must accomplish Show the work as it happens; keep a steady heartbeat; feed the eventual flagship narratives.

Length & format 80–250 words, social-native. One image, screenshot, or snippet. A thread (3–5 beats) only when the thing genuinely has 3–5 beats — never manufactured.

Core components (ordered) 1 — The one concrete thing you did or learned (specificity is the hook). 2 — A visual: screenshot, snippet, before/after. 3 — The honest wrinkle (what was hard or surprising). 4 — A light link home, only when it truly adds.

Rubric of execution Specific beats clever — "I cut retrieval latency by moving X" outlaps "thoughts on AI." Show, don't announce. One idea per note. The wrinkle is the value — people follow builders for the real parts. Don't force a CTA; presence is the point. _Failure modes:_ vague musings, humblebrags, over-linking, threads spun from a single thought.

Creative choices Platform emphasis — LinkedIn for the warm ministry/founder network now; add X only if you deliberately build a dev audience later. How raw to go is a Boundaries decision (client / Movemental-internal exposure). Cadence is as-you-ship, not scheduled.

Cascade Native social first → batch a month of notes into a newsletter roundup or fold them into a longer "how I built it" piece.

**Podcast / guest** FIND·MOVE · peer · leader

+

What it is Appearances on others' shows (guest first; hosting only if ever), borrowing trusted hosts' networks — starting inside Brad's and Alan's orbit, which is where your audience already is.

Where it lives Their platforms; the episode embedded and transcribed on your site.

What it must accomplish Reach warm-adjacent audiences through people who already vouch for you; discovery plus intimacy; and every appearance becomes an article.

Length & format The appearance is the host's — typically 30–60 min. Your asset is a one-page talking map. The derived article runs 1,500–2,500 words; clips are 30–90s, 2–4 per episode.

Core components (your prep + follow-through) 1 — Your 2–3 core stories, tight (the two-people origin, one how-I-built-it, one conviction). 2 — The thesis in three spoken sentences. 3 — 3–5 "bridge" lines to get from any question back to your point. 4 — One clear "where to find me" — the newsletter. 5 — Post-show: transcript → article, clips, a newsletter mention, within the week.

Rubric of execution Tell stories, don't recite arguments — audio rewards narrative. Leave one takeaway the host can restate in their own words. Name the newsletter once, naturally. Be generous to the host's audience: teach, don't pitch. Repurpose while it's warm. _Failure modes:_ rambling, jargon, no clear "find me," letting the episode die un-repurposed.

Creative choices Which stories to lead with, per the show's audience. Pre-write the derived article vs transcribe-then-edit — transcribe-then-edit keeps your spoken voice and is recommended. Guest-only now vs hosting later: stay guest-first — borrow networks before building one.

Cascade Transcript → article on your site → clips to YouTube + LinkedIn → featured in the newsletter → the host's audience routed to your list.

**Selected work / proof** SAY (proof) · backer · checker

+

What it is The résumé layer — the builds and their results, gathered and checkable. Not narrative like "how I built it"; fast, scannable evidence.

Where it lives A `/work` page, with individual case pages for the biggest builds.

What it must accomplish Give the backer and the checker fast, verifiable proof; anchor the credibility that quietly backs Movemental.

Length & format The index is scannable — a grid, ~40–60 words per entry. Full case pages for the biggest 3–5 builds run 600–1,200 words with one visual each.

Core components Per index entry: 1 — what it was (one line). 2 — your role, precisely (built / led / advised). 3 — the result: a number, a link, a checkable artifact. 4 — a one-line "why it mattered." Case pages add: the context, the key decision, the outcome, a visual.

Rubric of execution Honest over impressive — inflation is the one thing that kills this page for the checker. Numbers carry sources. Name your actual role exactly; the whole site argues for verifiable authorship, so practice it hardest here. Link to live proof wherever it exists. _Failure modes:_ vague superlatives, unclear role, unlinked claims, too many entries diluting the strong ones.

Creative choices How many entries — curate hard; 6–10 strong beats 20 mixed. Which get full case pages — the 3–5 that best serve the backer and checker. Whether to show client logos/names — a Boundaries + permission decision.

Cascade Mostly a destination, not a broadcast. Linked from the About/story, from every "how I built it" piece, and from your LinkedIn "Featured" section.

**AI Lab (talk to my work)** FIND·MOVE · all

+

What it is A corpus-bounded agent over your own writing and builds — the product running on you. The single strongest demonstration of the thesis, because you eat your own cooking.

Where it lives `/ai-lab`, plus a floating "talk to my work" affordance across the site.

What it must accomplish Let a visitor interrogate your thinking directly; prove the product on the most credible possible subject (you); serve both FIND and MOVE.

Length & format Not a word count — a product surface. Corpus target: ideally your whole published body of work; minimum to launch is the essays + how-I-built-it pieces. Plus a short "about the Lab" page (~300–500 words) and 3–6 starter questions.

Core components (ordered) 1 — The bounded corpus (essays, how-I-built-it, thesis docs). 2 — A clear grounding + boundaries statement (what it draws on, what it won't do, that it won't invent). 3 — 3–6 starter questions that show range. 4 — A visible provenance/disclosure posture. 5 — Citations back to the source pieces.

Rubric of execution Bind it to the corpus and say so — the entire point is that it won't fabricate, which is the live demo of your thesis. Disclose plainly. Cite back to real pieces. Starter questions should span a thinking question, a how-did-you-build question, and a "what do you believe about X." Never let it speak in a way you wouldn't ratify. _Failure modes (one is fatal):_ unbounded / hallucinating — it would disprove your thesis; no disclosure; no citations back; gimmick starter questions.

Creative choices How conversational vs archival the persona reads. Whether to gate anything — recommend fully open, it's a demo. Whether to surface the provenance/authorship log publicly — on-brand to do so.

Cascade A launch "how I built the AI Lab" piece → a demo clip → featured in the newsletter → embedded inside relevant essays.

The reimagine move — for you

## The build is the content — literally

  * **The build is the story.** One build becomes the "how I built it" piece, the AI-Lab demo, and the clips. For you this is the deepest form of "the build is the content," because your builds _are_ your arc.
  * **Run your own Evergreen Engine and AI Lab.** You built these for others. joshshepherd.ai should be the first place they run on your own corpus.
  * **GEO-first authorship** — be the answer the machine returns. You do GEO for a living; be the case study. (A later bet — see Distribution.)

**Proving cluster:** lead with the **How I built it** cluster — the two-people origin, the Alan build, the solo build. It's the one place that satisfies goal 1 (the vocation) and the byproduct goals at the same time, and it's where your truth and your volume are highest. Authorship and formation essays run alongside.

The prioritized build queue

## What to make first — in order

The concrete pieces, sequenced. Do them top to bottom. The order follows the vocation: the story first, then the proving cluster ("how I built it"), with the owned channel opened early so every later piece has somewhere to land. Each item opens to the full prescription and its publish-and-share cascade.

**Two rules that hold across the whole queue.** Owned first: everything you make lives on joshshepherd.ai and routes to the newsletter — social is a spoke, never the home. And warm before cold: your first distribution is a direct note to your network and the Brad/Alan orbit, not a search play. Search and GEO compound later.

## Network-warm first, search later

Your audience arrives warm through Movemental and Brad's and Alan's network. So the early engine is relationship and referral; search and GEO are a real bet, but a later one.

A build → how-I-built-it piece → newsletter → clips → a talk

An essay → newsletter → social posts

A guest podcast → transcript → article

Channels

  * **Earned (your real engine):** Brad & Alan intros, guest podcasts, peer citations, network referral.

FIND / GEO — the later bet

The seam + the scenius

Founder profile on movemental.ai ⇄ this platform; "the company I built to solve this." And your site links to Alan's and Brad's — you're a node in the scenius, cross-citing honestly. A benefit of the vocational home, not its purpose.

Artifact 05 · boundaries & rules — internal workstream

## What's public, what's private, what's the line

Developed with you, not asserted. Some already decided; the rest are open. This is the rulebook the whole site is governed by.

### Private by default

  * The personal anchors — age, INFP, Enneagram 4w5, the faith-journey language, the lost-role-over-a-capital-campaign story. decided
  * The ownership split (80/10/10). decided

### Public — the commitments

  * The refusals, stated as commitments: no manufactured urgency; no faked authorship; AI never touches discernment or care; no unearned claim; extra care with vulnerable people.

Open — to decide with you

  * **Faith.** It's the ground of the whole thing. How much goes public, and in what register, is your call — we'll set it together.
  * **The candid material** (the collapse of identity into vocation; the diversity conviction). Powerful, and yours to publish or hold.
  * **Client & Movemental internals.** How transparent build-in-public goes — what you'll name, what stays behind the curtain.
  * **The diversity rule as a public standard.** "Build for the unseen, not the already-reached" — internal conviction, or stated commitment?

Movement Leader Platform · Reference

# Copy and About variations.

Every approach a home page and an About page can take, section by section: what the hero leads with, how each headline is written, the supporting lines, and the structural variants for both pages. Tenant slugs mark copy that is live today.

Hero

Lead types Priority ladder Headline approaches Patterns to retire Supporting lines Hero media Hero variants

Home bands

Peer proof Welcome Identity Signature quote Themes portal Library Featured book Volumes & open draft Framework AI Lab Formation Signature tool Content sampler Assessment Partner & strip Work with me Donate About band Newsletter Interest router

About page

About hero Vocation line Narrative bio Credentials & stats Timeline Frameworks Organizations Endorsements Recognition & expertise About CTA

Limits

Length budgets

## What the hero leads with

Seven lead types. One per page. The lead decides the headline approach, the action and the media.

Lead| First viewport says| Primary action| Lead media  
---|---|---|---  
tool| Here is something you can do now, with its cost and time.| The tool's first input| Walkthrough or real output  
movement| The network or movement this person leads.| Find your theme| Place or gathering  
thesis| The defining idea, citable to a book.| Find your theme| Portrait over an art plate  
work| A flagship book, or the body of work.| Open the library, or read the first chapter| Cover beside the portrait  
presence| The person, as someone people come to be taught by.| Join the next cohort| Full-bleed landscape portrait  
question| An open question the research answers.| Start with the first theme| Archival or place image  
name| The name, with the thesis moved to the subheading.| Find your theme| Portrait, or a paired portrait  
  
### Priority ladder

Take the first rung that is true.

1| **A live tool.** The contract gives the tool the primary action whenever one exists.  
---|---  
2| **A known movement,** when its name is better known than the person's.  
3| **One defining idea** you can state in a sentence and cite to a book.  
4| **A flagship book** that carries the reputation.  
5| **Teaching presence,** only with a landscape portrait that passes eligibility.  
6| **A research question** readers already hold.  
7| **Default:** name lead with a thesis subheading. Safe on thin data.  
  
Dated invitations never take the headline. They go in the announcement line and come down when the date passes.

## Headline approaches

Fourteen. Slugs mark live headlines. Italic examples are patterns only and are never published as written.

Approach| Example| Use when| Lead  
---|---|---|---  
H1 Thesis| “The church was made for movement” alan-hirsch| The idea is the reputation.| thesis  
H2 Assignment| “Your address is your assignment.” brad-brisco| The work asks the reader to act where they are.| tool, thesis  
H3 Conviction| “God looks like Jesus” meghan-good| A theological claim anchors everything else.| thesis  
H4 Paradox pair| “Gathered and scattered” hugh-halter| The framework holds two things together, both affirmed.| thesis  
H5 Named work| “Organic Church” neil-cole| A book title is better known than the author.| work  
H6 Named movement| “The Underground” brian-sanders| The network is the public face.| movement  
H7 Name| “Dr. Liz Rios” liz-rios| The name is the brand, or the site belongs to a pair.| name  
H8 Story| “How a first-century city became a movement.” michael-cooper| The research has a narrative spine.| question  
H9 Question| What would it take for a church to multiply?| Readers already ask it and the corpus answers it.| question  
H10 Posture| “Formation takes the time it takes.” kate-coleman| The approach itself is the difference.| presence  
H11 Audience promise| “Formation for Leaders Who Teach” roy-moran| The reader is one clearly named role.| work, presence  
H12 Mission line| “Joining Jesus outside the walls of the church” rowland-smith| The organization already states it this way.| movement  
H13 Cited line| One sentence from a book, with the title beneath.| One published sentence is widely quoted.| thesis, work  
H14 Scripture anchor| A short verse with its reference, thesis as subheading.| One text organizes the whole body of work.| thesis  
  
### Two patterns to retire

**Topic labels** (“Discipleship in place”) name a subject and make no claim. Five tenants use one. **Antithesis headlines** (“Hero makers, not heroes”) break the voice rules. A published book title used verbatim is the one exception: keep the title, drop the negating half.

From| To| The move  
---|---|---  
Topic label| H1 Thesis| Find the claim the main book makes about the topic and state it as a sentence.  
Topic label| H4 Paradox| Name the two things the framework holds together.  
Topic label| H7 Name| Name in the headline, claim in the subheading. Safest on thin data.  
Antithesis| H5 Named work| Keep the title. Move the contrast into the welcome band, stated positively.  
Antithesis| H2 Assignment| Turn the rejected half into what the reader is asked to do instead.  
  
## Supporting lines

Eyebrow, subheading, actions, announcement and caption.

Slot| Approach| Pattern and rule  
---|---|---  
Eyebrow| Role line| “Author · Speaker · Peacemaker” danielle-strickland. Three roles at most.  
Tool introduction| “Brad Brisco introduces the Neighborhood Intelligence Report”. Tool lead only.  
Affiliation| Current organization and title. Verifiable and current.  
Welcome label| “A word of welcome” belongs to the welcome band. Keep it out of the hero.  
Subheading| Proof line| “Four decades of books, teaching, and movement thinking” alan-hirsch. Every count checkable.  
Mechanism line| Says what the tool produces: “A complete picture of any neighborhood”.  
Thesis line| Carries the idea when the headline is a name.  
Audience line| Names who the work is for, in one role.  
Title list| A string of job titles. Move titles to the about band; the hero needs a claim.  
Primary action| Tool input| “Read my neighborhood”, on the input itself. Mandatory when a tool exists.  
Door verb| “Find your theme”, “Open the library”. Nav vocabulary only.  
First chapter| “Read the first chapter”, for a work lead.  
Cohort| “Join the next cohort”, when one is open.  
Assessment| “Take the assessment”, when nothing outranks it.  
Secondary link| One text link| “See a sample report”, “Read the story”. Never a second button. “About” never leads.  
Announcement| Dated line| A cohort, launch or new book, with a date. Removed when the date passes.  
Portrait caption| Place and year| Where and when the photograph was taken. Adds provenance.  
  
### Hero media

Media| Spec| Rule| Serves  
---|---|---|---  
M1 Studio portrait| 4:5, 1200px tall or more| Real photograph. The default.| all  
M2 Environmental portrait| 16:9, 1920px wide or more| Room for a scrim and headline.| presence  
M3 Portrait over art| 4:5 on a 16:9 plate| Art behind a real portrait. alan-hirsch today.| thesis  
M4 Paired portrait| Two 4:5, matched light| Both people at equal size.| name  
M5 Teaching still| 16:9| Leader teaching or leading a room.| presence  
M6 Tool walkthrough| Video with poster| Screen recording. brad-brisco today.| tool  
M7 Tool output| 16:9 still| A real sample result.| tool  
M8 Cover object| 2:3| The flagship book beside the portrait.| work  
M9 Place photograph| 16:9| No identifiable people. Licensed or owned.| movement  
M10 Archival image| Public domain| Credited in a caption.| question  
M11 Ambient video| Muted loop with poster| Still under `prefers-reduced-motion`.| presence, movement  
M12 Typographic| No lead image| Type carries the hero, portrait sits small.| index, question  
  
**Always:** the leader's own photograph appears in the first viewport. Real before generated; art sits behind or beside the person, never as the person. One moving element at most.

### Hero structural variants

Variant| Structure| Serves  
---|---|---  
portrait| Headline block beside the portrait. Lead media may sit behind as a plate. Teaching card optional.| thesis, name, question, work  
media_led| Lead media is primary; headline sits over or after it. Portrait required as an inset unless the media is the leader's own photograph.| presence, movement  
tool_entry| Headline block with the tool's first input as the primary action and a sample link beside it. Portrait small.| tool  
  
## Home band copy

Copy approaches and structural variants for every band below the hero. Required bands first.

### Peer-proof band required no variants

#### Copy approaches

  * **Single introduction.** One named peer, quote, date, link.
  * **Fellowship line.** “Writes and teaches alongside…” brad-brisco, with faces.
  * **Book endorsement,** cited to the book it appeared in.
  * **Co-author credit** for shared work.
  * **Institutional fallback:** organizations founded, led or served.

**Rule:** named, dated and linkable, never generated. Mode is data, not presentation, so the band has no variants. Spread introducers across the network so every site does not route back to one person.

### Word of welcome

#### Copy approaches

  * **Host's welcome.** “Welcome to…” alan-hirsch
  * **Origin in three sentences.**
  * **The question I keep asking.**
  * **What you will find here,** in voice.
  * **A letter to one reader:** the planter, the pastor.

#### Variants

letter| Paragraphs, then a signature line. No image, no doors.  
---|---  
with_image| Paragraphs and signature beside the image.  
with_doors| Paragraphs, then the three doors as a short “where to start” list.  
  
**Rule:** two or three short paragraphs, first person, the only first-person prose on the page, no buttons.

### Identity band no variants

One statement of who the leader is and what they are for, with an optional action. Single sentence; the action's presence is data, not a variant.

### Signature quote no variants

#### Copy approaches

  * **A book line** with its citation.
  * **A framework definition.**
  * **The scripture** the work keeps returning to.
  * **A published phrase** the leader is known for.

**Rule:** verbatim from the corpus, with source, linked to its book or theme.

### Themes portal required

#### Heading approaches

  * **Count and noun.** “Five threads that run through Brad's work”; “Six doorways into the work” alan-hirsch
  * **A starting question.** “Where do you want to start?”
  * **The framework's name.**
  * **Reader-state line.** “Start where you are.”

#### Card line approaches

  * **Reframe,** **stakes,** or **promise,** in one sentence of 18 words or fewer.

#### Variants

grid| All themes as equal cards with image, title, framework and one line.  
---|---  
lead_plus_list| First theme as a full card with image; the rest as a text list.  
numbered_index| All themes as a numbered text list, no images.  
  
### Library band required

#### Heading approaches

  * **Audience.** “Written for the sent church” brad-brisco
  * **Span of years** in print.
  * **Start-here trio.**
  * **Newest first.**
  * **Flagship feature.**

#### Variants

shelf| Three to eight covers in reading order, then view-all.  
---|---  
start_here| Exactly three titles, each with a one-line reason.  
chronology| Titles in publication order with year labels.  
  
**Rule:** real covers, co-authors credited, one forthcoming title at most.

### Featured book

blurb| Cover, title, blurb, actions.  
---|---  
excerpt| Cover, title, a verbatim excerpt with its page, “read the first chapter” as the primary action.  
endorsed| Cover, title, blurb, one approved endorsement of that book.  
  
### Volumes and open draft no variants

**Volumes:** a forthcoming series with numbered items, status and a notify form. **Open draft:** a manuscript open for peer commentary, with chapter count, status and a real participation count. Both have one structure each, tied to the live book format.

### Framework band

list| Elements in order, each with its line.  
---|---  
cycle| Elements as a closed sequence where the last leads back to the first.  
pairs| Elements grouped into held-together pairs.  
  
### AI Lab band required

#### Framing approaches

  * **Ask the books** (access).
  * **Bring your situation** (application).
  * **Test an idea** against the work (argument).
  * **A study partner** for a course (formation).

#### Starter question approaches

  * Situational, definitional, contrast between two frameworks, local application.

#### Variants

ask| Input with starters beneath, plus the source statement.  
---|---  
starters_only| Starters as links into the AI Lab. No inline input.  
worked_example| One stored question and answer excerpt, then the input.  
  
**Rule:** three or four starters the corpus can answer, and a plain statement that answers come from the published work through AI.

### Formation spotlight required

#### Copy approaches

  * **The four necessities** named plainly: dissonance, reflection, practice, community.
  * **Problem first,** opening with the dissonance.
  * **Outcome first.**
  * **Cohort date first.**

#### Variants

single_course| One course with both format actions.  
---|---  
course_list| Two or three courses, each with format tags.  
cohort_led| Next cohort date and seats first, course second.  
  
**Rule:** hold the band if nothing has shipped.

### Signature tool

inline_input| Name, output line, price and time, the first input, sample link.  
---|---  
sample_first| Sample output leads, then name, price and time, then the input.  
steps| Name and output, three steps, then the input.  
  
**Rule:** the entry control is the tool's real first input. “$10 · 10 minutes” brad-brisco is the output-price-time pattern.

### Content sampler

recent| Latest items across enabled types.  
---|---  
by_type| One latest item per type.  
featured_plus_recent| A featured item, then the latest.  
  
**Rule:** recency only, kept distinct from the library band.

### Assessment CTA

individual| Name, result line, time and cost, one action.  
---|---  
individual_and_team| Two paths side by side.  
result_preview| A real sample result first, then the action.  
  
**Rule:** the copy promises a commission and a local practice, never a profile.

### Partner invitation and partners strip no variants

**Partner invitation:** heading, body and two or three columns, each a way to partner. **Partners strip:** a label and three to ten organizations with logos. Both have a single structure; column count is data.

### Work with me

tracks| Two to four consulting or coaching tracks, closing line, action.  
---|---  
speaking_only| Speaking note and topics, then the action.  
single_offer| One offer as a paragraph, then the action.  
  
### Donate no variants

Headline, subline, appeal, one action.

### About band required

#### Copy approaches

  * **Third-person short bio.**
  * **Vocation line.** “Missiologist, author, and practitioner” brad-brisco
  * **Present tense:** what I do now.
  * **Credential first.**

#### Variants

bio| Heading, bio, action.  
---|---  
bio_stats| Heading, bio, two to four stats, action.  
bio_people| Heading, bio, co-leaders, action. For shared sites.  
  
**Rule:** exact, sourced numbers. Stats like “20+” and “1k+” cannot be published.

### Newsletter required

#### Copy approaches

  * **Named publication with cadence.** “Field Notes · A note every week” brad-brisco
  * **Field-guide offer.**
  * **What arrives and how often.**
  * **The latest issue's first line.**

#### Variants

form| Headline, subline and cadence, email field, action.  
---|---  
offer| Field-guide offer first, then the form.  
external| Headline and cadence, action linking to the external publication.  
  
### Interest router

two_selects| A role choice and an intent choice, then one action.  
---|---  
role_cards| One card per role, each listing its routes.  
single_question| One question with two to four answers.  
  
**Rule:** every route ends on one of the four doors.

## About page

Twelve sections. Only the hero is required; the rest vary by leader.

### About hero required

portrait| Heading and lead sentence beside the portrait.  
---|---  
name_first| Heading and lead sentence lead; the portrait is small.  
media_led| A landscape portrait leads; the heading follows or sits over it.  
  
### Vocation line no variants

One line naming the work. Live on most tenants as `about.vocationLine`.

### Narrative bio

continuous| The bio as continuous paragraphs.  
---|---  
chaptered| The bio split under chapter headings.  
with_facts| The bio beside a short facts list: based in, education, church, family.  
  
**Rule:** the bio comes from the author identity record. An override has to be ratified.

### Credentials and stats no variants

**Credentials:** one line of degrees and positions, live on 19 tenants. **Stats:** two to four labelled numbers, each with a source. Both have a single structure.

### Timeline

full| All entries in order.  
---|---  
milestones| Four to six selected entries.  
by_decade| All entries grouped under their decade.  
  
### Frameworks

list| Each framework with its definition and links.  
---|---  
lead_framework| One framework explained through its elements, the rest as a list.  
by_book| Frameworks grouped under the book that introduced them.  
  
### Organizations

list| Name, role, years and link.  
---|---  
founded_and_served| Two groups, split by relation.  
logos| Logos with names only.  
  
### Endorsements

quotes| Each endorsement with quote, name, role, date and link.  
---|---  
single_featured| One endorsement in full, then names and roles.  
names_only| Names, roles, dates and links. No quotes.  
  
**Rule:** verified endorsements only, each with a date and a source.

### Recognition and expertise no variants

**Recognition:** awards with issuer, year and link. **Expertise:** experience, expertise, authority and trust statements, which mostly feed structured data and can be hidden from the page.

### About CTA no variants

An optional heading and one to three links onward.

## Length budgets

Starting values, to confirm at 390px before they go in the registry. A copy option over budget for a layout shows as locked with its word count.

Arrangement| Headline words| Subheading words| Eyebrow characters  
---|---|---|---  
Canonical| 10| 24| 48  
Editorial| 12| 28| 48  
Portrait-led, over a photograph| 7| 18| 40  
Tool-forward, subheading names the output| 8| 20| 48  
Split| 9| 22| 40  
Gallery| 8| 20| 40  
Index| 6| 16| 32  
Movemental · Copy and About variations · Companion to the page-sections structure spec and the home picker guide.
